reports.headline: Deer Island's night tide is where the real fish are living right now
reports.subhead: Daytime bass have gone quiet on the harbor and North Shore both — the program's shifted to dark water and moving current.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday to skip the daytime harbor run and give Deer Island a look on the last two hours of the outgoing, starting around 9 PM. That decision came from watching three straight days of flat, disappointing daytime trips — the kind where you mark bait on the machine, drop down, and get nothing but a shrug. Surface temps in the harbor are pushing toward 70, maybe a hair over in the shallow coves off Winthrop, and that's enough to shut the daytime bite down almost everywhere except right at the margins of first light and last light.

So nights it is. The rip that forms off the northern tip of Deer Island on the back half of the ebb has been the most consistent thing I've fished all month. Current stacks up against the flushing tunnel outflow and the edge of the drop where it goes from eight feet to better than thirty in a hurry, and that's holding bass through the dark hours. I've been drifting live mackerel — snagged fresh right there off the same rip on a small hook and treble jig — back into the seam, freespooled on a fishfinder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in the current. Fish have been in the 28 to 34 inch class mostly, one push toward midnight last Thursday that had three of us into fish over 36 inches on live mac before it shut off as fast as it started. That's the pattern right now — short, violent windows, then dead water. You have to be there when it happens, and you have to be patient through the lulls.

Spectacle Island's north drop-off has been giving up smaller stripers on the same tide stage, but bluefish have actually been the more reliable player out there the last week, chopping bait on top right at dusk before the bass show. If you want visible, aggressive action, that's your window — Deceivers and 1-ounce Kastmasters worked fast across the surface will draw strikes from blues in that 3 to 6 pound class, and it's a nice warm-up before you settle in for the real bass program after dark.

Nahant's been quieter than I'd like it to be this week. The rocks off East Point are still holding fish, but they've gone deep and nocturnal just like everywhere else in the harbor complex — daytime casters working topwater in that classic July light are mostly getting skunked unless they're there at gray light. I fished the boulder field off Bass Point on a dropping tide last Sunday morning, 5 AM, and picked up two decent bass on a swimming plug worked slow along the current seam, but by 6:30 with the sun up it was over. That's the window now — tight, early, and gone fast.

Gloucester and Cape Ann are holding to the same script, though the water up there runs a touch cooler thanks to the Gulf of Maine influence, which has kept some daytime activity alive longer than in the harbor proper. Guys working the ledges off Eastern Point and out around Thacher Island have still been picking at bass on umbrella rigs and diamond jigs worked deep, 40 to 60 feet, on the last of the incoming. Mackerel schools are thick up there right now too — if you need bait, that's the run, and it doesn't take long to load a bucket working small jigs off the rocks at Gloucester Harbor's outer breakwater.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect stable, unspectacular conditions with no major thermal shift, and that's exactly what's played out. Nothing's blown up, nothing's collapsed. The water's just settled into that mid-summer holding pattern where the fish know the rules better than we do.

Plymouth and Duxbury Bay have been the wildcard. Cooler water moving through the bay off the back side of the Cape has kept some daytime striper activity alive in spots — the flats off Duxbury Beach on the early incoming have produced schoolies to 26 inches on soft plastics, 5-inch white paddle tails on light jig heads, worked slow over the sand. Nothing to write home about, but it's daylight fishing that's actually working, which right now feels like a luxury.

Flounder have been steady but unspectacular in the harbor's mud bottoms — Deer Island Flats and the channel edges off Long Island have given up fish to guys soaking clam bellies on the bottom, standard spreader rigs, small hooks. It's not a program that's going to make anyone's week, but it's honest, catchable action if you want something to do while waiting for dark.

Looking ahead, I don't see this pattern breaking soon. The moon's past full and heading toward the next quarter, tides are moderating, and without a real cold push or a stiff northeast blow to mix the water column, the bass are going to keep living deep and dark through the coming week. If I had one night to fish, I'd be back at Deer Island on the outgoing, live mackerel in the water, waiting for that rip to load up. Daytime anglers, your best shot is still that narrow window right at gray light — get there early, because it closes fast once the sun's up.

reports.headline: Bay bait's balled up and nervous — first albies can't be far
reports.subhead: Rain bait showering off Cuttyhunk and silversides thick in Quick's Hole have every rip in the corridor primed for the season's first false albacore and bonito.
reports.body_markdown:
The bait's telling me something's close. I ran the west end of Quick's Hole Tuesday morning on the last of the ebb and the silversides were balled so tight against the rocks they looked like a school of anchovies from a Gulf Stream trip, not a Buzzards Bay rip in late July. Terns were working them from above, and every few minutes you'd see that nervous flash-and-scatter that means something's under them pushing up. I never got a hookup, but I didn't fish it long — I was there to look, and what I saw was enough to keep me up at night thinking about Friday.

We flagged this corridor last week as one of the better bets in southern New England for the season's first albies and bonito, and standing on that rip Tuesday, nothing about that call feels like a stretch. Water's sitting in that upper-60s-to-low-70s window that's historically the trigger down here, and the bait behavior — tight, nervous, showery — is exactly what precedes the first scout schools at Robinson's Hole and off the backside of Cuttyhunk. No confirmed albie or bonito yet in my zone as of this week. I want to be straight about that. But every year it starts with bait acting exactly like this one is acting right now.

While we wait on the main event, the bluefish have picked up the slack and then some. Menemsha Bight has had bunker schools getting worked over hard on the last two hours of the incoming, blues in the 3-to-6-pound class blowing up on the surface close enough to shore that guys are casting from the jetty rocks. Poppers are the move — a white Super Spook or a Yo-Zuri Sashimi popper worked with an aggressive walk-the-dog retrieve draws vicious strikes when the blues are actively feeding, and when they get finicky, switching down to a 1-ounce diamond jig with a tube teaser above it will still connect. This bluefish push matches what's happening the length of the coast right now — bunker schools pinned by warm surface water, blues working them without letup — and there's no reason to expect it to slow here as long as those bunker pods keep holding tight against the Vineyard shoreline.

Striped bass have gone quiet in the way they always do this time of year. Daytime effort in Buzzards Bay proper has been mostly a formality — a few fish picked off deep structure around the Weepecket Islands and the drop-offs south of Naushon on bucktails bounced slow along bottom, but nothing consistent. The better program has been working the rips at Robinson's Hole and Woods Hole itself right at first light and again after dark, when stripers slide up onto the current edges to feed before the sun pushes them back down. A 1-ounce bucktail tipped with a strip of squid, drifted through the seam where the fast water meets the slower eddy, has been the most dependable presentation — slow, natural, right on the bottom. Live eels after dark around Tarpaulin Cove have also produced, though you need to commit to the late shift; nothing's happening on that program before 9 or 10 PM.

Fluke have been steady but unspectacular — the kind of bite where you catch a lot of shorts and have to grind for keepers. The best water has been the deeper edges off Cuttyhunk, 25 to 35 feet, and the channel drop inside Quick's Hole on the tail end of the ebb when the current is still moving enough to keep bait pinned but not so hard you can't hold bottom. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a squid strip, dragged just fast enough to feel the tail kick — that combo has out-produced bare bucktails two-to-one in my boat this week. Scup fishing remains the reliable fallback around the Woods Hole pilings and the rocks off Nonamesset — small hooks, squid strips, bottom rigs, and you'll fill a cooler in an hour if you want dinner guaranteed.

Tide-wise, we're coming off a moon that's kept the current honest — good push through the holes, not the dead slack water that makes albie scouting a waste of gas. That current strength matters enormously for the next week: albies and bonito, when they show, want moving water and bait getting funneled through the rips, not sitting in a calm bay. Robinson's Hole and the west end of Quick's Hole on a hard-running tide are where I'll be spending my mornings through the end of the month, small metal in hand — a Deadly Dick or a half-ounce Albie Snax — ready the moment that first tail slice shows up.

If I had one day this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb at Robinson's Hole, right where the current squeezes between the islands and the bait gets pinched into a narrow lane. That's the classic setup for the first arrivals, and with the bait already acting spooked and balled up the way it is, I don't think we're more than a few days out. Bring the light spinning gear, bring patience, and don't be surprised if the first fish you see busting bait this season isn't a bluefish at all.

reports.headline: Great Point still empty of albies — but the bass under the birds say patience
reports.subhead: No bonito, no albies yet off Nantucket, but the bluefish and stripers working the rips are keeping rods bent while we wait on the real show.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood on the point at Great Point Wednesday morning with the light just coming up pink over the rip, glassing for that first nervous flash of bait getting pushed to the surface — the kind of thing that means albies or bonito showed. Didn't see it. Saw gannets working way out past the bar, saw terns dipping over a bluefish blitz closer in, but the specific, frantic, small-bait-getting-shredded-from-underneath pattern that means tuna-family fish arrived — not yet. Two weeks now I've been watching for it, same as every July, and the water's finally sitting in that window where it should happen any day.

Here's the thing though — the rip itself has been plenty alive without them. Fishing the ebb off the Point Tuesday, we had bluefish stacked from the surface down to maybe fifteen feet, blitzing on sand eels getting swept off the bar. Poppers got bit instantly — Doc's and Gibbs pencils, white and chartreuse, worked with a stumbling retrieve right through the froth. Fish running four to eight pounds, mean as always, cutting leaders if you're not running at least 40-pound fluoro bite tippet. That blitz has been the most reliable thing on this end of the Sound for going on ten days, and it fits exactly what we've been seeing spread up the coast — bunker and sand eel schools pinned tight against beaches with blues working them relentlessly. We said last week that pattern would keep spreading as long as the bait stayed concentrated, and out here it's held true — the Point blitz hasn't broken up once.

Under that blitz, though, is where it's gotten interesting. Guys jigging deeper through the bluefish with 2-ounce Kastmasters and Ava jigs have been picking off striped bass in the 28 to 34-inch range, mostly on the last two hours of the ebb when the rip is really cranking and that current seam forms hard off the northeast corner of the bar. Stripers are doing the typical mid-summer thing here too — daytime bites have softened with the water sitting warm, so first light and last light are your windows, same as everywhere south of the Cape right now. Fish are holding tighter to structure and the thermocline break, then sliding up onto the rip edges to feed when the light's low and the current's pushing hard.

Sankaty's been quieter than Great Point but not dead — a scattering of keeper bass off the bluff on bucktails worked slow along bottom during the last hour of the outgoing, water depth there running maybe 20 to 30 feet close to the rip line. Nothing to write home about, but if you want to avoid the bluefish circus at the Point and just soak a bucktail for bass, that's where I'd point the boat.

Down at Monomoy, the southwest wind we've had on and off has been setting up the rips the way it usually does — pushing bait and current together off the south end near the Powder Hole and out toward the elbow. Fluke fishing there has been decent but not great, which tracks with what's happening everywhere south of us this month — the shallow water's warm enough that the better fish have slid into deeper channel edges and humps, leaving mostly shorts up top. Working 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp swimming mullet along the drop-offs in 15 to 25 feet on the stronger stages of the tide has produced fluke to 4 pounds, but you're culling through a lot of dinks to get there. Bring patience, not just tackle.

Horseshoe Shoal has stayed a bluefish and scup program mostly, steady but unspectacular, which is about what you'd expect with the Sound sitting in this stable mid-summer holding pattern — warm, settled, no real disruption from wind or a big tide swing since we're coming off the neap. That should start to change some as the tide rebuilds strength over the next few days, which typically sharpens up structure fishing around the shoals and rips generally.

As for the bonito and albies — every signal says they're close. Water temps pushing up through the corridor from Buzzards Bay through the Vineyard and out toward us have crossed into that range where scout schools historically show, and there's chatter of squid showing thick inshore, which is exactly the kind of forage that pulls albies onto the Great Point rip once they arrive. I don't have a confirmed fish yet to report, and I won't pretend I do. But if I had one morning to burn this week, I'd be back on that point at first light with an epoxy jig tied on and a popper rod rigged and ready, glassing hard for that first nervous bait push. When it happens here, it happens fast — one morning there's nothing, and two days later the whole rip's snapping with three-pound footballs ripping drag on 10-pound tippet.

For now: fish the blues while they're thick, work the bass on the low-light tides, and keep one eye on the horizon. The real show at Great Point is close. It's just not here yet.

reports.headline: Race Point at first light: bass to 34 pounds on live mackerel before the sun climbs high
reports.subhead: The Bay's holding cooler water than the Sound and the Cape's south side, and that's buying us a longer window before the fish slide deep.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, 4:45, I had the boat idling off Race Point waiting for enough light to see the rip form up. There's a spot out there where the tide runs hard against the bar and you can watch it happen — the water goes from flat to nervous, then you get that seam, that dark line where the current stacks against itself. A guy I've fished with twenty years, Gary, was working the livewell, and he said what he always says this time of year: "They're either here or they're not." That morning they were here. First mackerel we dropped back into the seam got hit before it swam ten feet, and the rod bent over into the rail. Thirty-four pounds, fat, full of herring, came up thrashing in that gray early light. We had three more like that before eight o'clock, then it just stopped, like someone closed a door.

That's been the story on the Race all week — good, sometimes very good, but it's a window, not an all-day proposition anymore. We're deep into summer now, water's warmed enough that the big fish are doing what big fish do this time of year: feeding hard at first light and again toward dusk, then dropping down onto structure through the heat of the day. The difference for us up here is the Bay's still running cooler than the Sound or the south side of the Cape, so that window's staying open longer than it is for the boys fishing Buzzards Bay or the Vineyard side. We flagged this pattern last week and said it'd hold steady — it has. Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars are still giving up quality bass in the early hours, and that's not something everybody south of us can say right now.

Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, 20 to 30 feet of leader, just enough weight to keep it down in the current without killing the swim — that's still the ticket on the rip. We're anchoring up-current of the seam and letting the mac drift back naturally into the disturbed water. If you're not catching your own bait, there are still pogies and mackerel schools showing on the sounder off the back side of Race Point, easy enough to jig up with a small diamond jig or Sabiki rig before you set up on the drift.

Peaked Hill Bars has been the secondary program — same tide-driven bite, same early morning window, but the fish there have run a little smaller, mostly schoolies up through low twenties, mixed in with a few bigger fish pushing thirty. That's typical for this stretch; the bars hold a lot of resident fish that don't move as much as the Race Point migrants. Bucktails, white and chartreuse, three-quarter to one ounce, worked slow along the bottom on the last of the ebb, have been picking at those fish when the mackerel bite goes quiet.

Cod fishing has been a grind, which is honest to say. Billingsgate and the deeper water off Wellfleet are holding fish, but you've got to work for them — jigging diamond jigs and teasers tight to bottom in 60 to 90 feet, and you might get two or three keepers in a morning if you're putting in the time and marking bait on the sounder first. The deeper structure out toward the middle of the Bay, where the whales have been working, is worth a look too — where there's whale activity there's usually sand eels and mackerel balled up underneath, and cod will sit under that bait column. It's not a fast bite. It's a patient man's game right now, and I'd rather tell you that straight than have you burn a tank of gas expecting a limit.

Bluefish have been scattered but present, mostly showing on the same rips as the bass, chopping up whatever bait gets pushed to the surface. Metal — Deadly Dicks, Hopkins — worked fast on the surface during that same dawn window has been drawing strikes, and a few of the blues have been decent, six and seven pounds, enough to make you check your leader.

Fluke's been a side dish, not the main course. Sandy Neck and the flats off Barnstable have some keepers mixed with a lot of shorts, and the better fish are sitting in that 20 to 30 foot depth where the water stays a touch cooler. Gulp on light bucktails, drifted slow, still the standard approach, but you're sorting through a lot of fish to find a keeper.

Tide's been the deciding factor everywhere out here — the rips only really turn on when there's enough current moving, so the two hours around the peak of the ebb or flood at Race Point and Peaked Hill are worth more than the rest of the day combined. Moon's past full now, tides easing back a bit heading into this weekend, which usually softens the rip bite slightly until we build back toward the next good push.

Looking ahead, if the weather holds calm like it has, I'd keep working that same dawn program at Race Point — anchor up on the rip before first light, live mackerel in the seam, and don't be afraid to leave once the sun gets up and the bite shuts off. Afternoons I'd rather be looking for cod on structure or working the Peaked Hill Bars bucktail program than sitting on a dead rip waiting for something to happen. The fish are here. You just have to fish the hours they're willing to work.

reports.headline: 120 feet on the Stellwagen gravel: cod stacking, haddock still on the mud edges
reports.subhead: Bluefin are pinning mackerel on top of the Bank while the bottom bite grinds along steady in July heat.
reports.body_markdown:
120 feet of water on the southwest corner of the Bank, gravel bottom, and my sounder looked like static for a solid ten minutes this past Tuesday. That's cod marks, stacked tight to the structure, not spread out chasing bait like they do in the fall. This time of year they're holding right on the hard edges where the gravel gives way to broken bottom, and that's exactly where we found them — jigging diamond jigs and teasing them up with clam bellies on a standard cod rig, 6 ounces of lead to hold bottom in the current.

We said last week to expect stable conditions to hold through the stretch, and that's exactly what's played out. No fronts pushing through, no big blow to stir up the water column, just steady southwest breeze in the 10-15 knot range and a bank that's fishing the way it should in late July. The whales are thick out there right now too — humpbacks working bait balls on the surface most mornings, which tells you everything about how much forage is stacked up on this piece of real estate.

Haddock are still on the mud, like they've been all summer, sitting in that 130-140 foot range on the eastern side toward Tillies. Softer bottom, less current push, and the haddock like it that way — they're not fighting the tide like the cod are on the harder gravel. We've been finding them on standard haddock rigs, two hooks, squid strips or sandeel imitations, and the average fish has been a solid 3 to 5 pounds, with enough keepers mixed in to make it worth the run. It's not a bent-rod-every-drop fishery right now — you've got to work for it, moving the boat if the marks thin out, but a half day on the mud has been putting fish in the cooler consistently.

The real story this week has been the bluefin showing up on top of the Bank chasing mackerel schools. We've had fish busting bait in 90 to 100 feet of water right on the edge, and it's been a mixed bag — some days the slot fish are eating everything we throw at them, other days they show, blow up on the bait for twenty minutes, and vanish. Trolling small spreader bars and green machines around the bait schools has worked when the fish are up and moving, but when they go down, we've switched to jigging — Shimano butterfly jigs worked vertically through where the marks are holding, 80-150 feet, has drawn some strikes. This is post trophy-closure fishing now, so everything we're seeing is slot-class fish, and the recreational fishery around here is grinding along at a decent pace given that restriction. Nobody's filling the boat every trip, but there's enough action to keep you paying attention every time a bird starts working.

The mackerel themselves have been thick on the Bank, which is exactly why the bluefin and the whales are both camped out here. When you see the birds diving and the whales rolling through bait, that's your cue to slow down and watch the water — sometimes the tuna show right underneath that same bait ball fifteen minutes later. We've marked mackerel schools in 60 to 80 feet all along the western edge of Stellwagen, and jigging a few up for fresh bait has been worthwhile even if you're not planning to troll — a livelined mackerel drifted back near a bait ball has drawn a couple of solid takes from fish that wouldn't touch the trolled gear.

Pollock have been mixed in with the cod on the gravel edges, and a few nice ones in the 8-12 pound class have come over the rail as bycatch on the diamond jigs. Hake have been scattered in the deeper basin water, 180 feet plus, but we haven't spent much time targeting them specifically with the groundfish and tuna both producing shallower.

Looking at the week ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. The wind's supposed to stay manageable, no major system pushing through the Gulf of Maine, and that means the Bank should keep fishing the way it has — cod holding tight to the gravel in that 110-130 foot range, haddock working the softer mud toward Tillies, and bluefin opportunistic on the mackerel schools whenever the bait stacks up tight enough to trigger a feed. If you're planning a trip, I'd get out early before the wind builds in the afternoon, and I'd have both a jigging rod and a trolling spread rigged before you leave the dock — you want to be ready for whatever shows up on top when you're running out to the bottom spots. The one thing that could change things is if that mackerel bait starts thinning out or pushing off the Bank; when that happens the tuna go with it, and we'll need to start scouting Tillies and the northern edge to relocate them. For now, though, the Bank's holding everything it should for late July, and that's worth the run from either Plymouth or Gloucester.

reports.headline: Appledore's ledges still holding cod while the flats give up stripers after dark
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coast, one boat, and the shoals are still paying off if you're willing to run before sunrise.
reports.body_markdown:
People from away look at a map of this state's coastline and figure there's nothing here worth trailering a boat for. Thirteen miles, they say, like it's a punchline. I've fished from the Merrimack line to the Piscataqua for going on twenty years now and I can tell you those thirteen miles stretch about as far as you let them. The Isles of Shoals alone are six miles offshore and hold more structure than most fleets see in a season — ledges, humps, boulder fields, current lines that split around Appledore and White Island like something's down there deciding where the fish go. I run my 20-foot Lund out of Rye Harbor most mornings before the sun's up, and I fish it like the run to the Shoals is nothing, because out here it isn't.

This week the pattern held about like I expected — I said last time it'd hold 72 hours and it's basically still doing that, groundfish steady, stripers pushed into a nighttime program same as everywhere south of us, just a little later to the party because our water hasn't gone through the mid-70s the way the Sound and the Jersey beaches have. That's the whole story of the Gulf of Maine in July — everybody else is dealing with warm, stratified water pushing bass deep and nocturnal, and we're sitting here in the low-to-mid 60s still getting some daytime action, just softer than June.

Cod fishing off the Shoals has been the most dependable thing I've touched all week. I've been working the ledges south and east of Appledore, 60 to 90 feet, right on the slack before the tide turns — that's the window, twenty minutes either side of dead slack, because once that current starts ripping around those boulders you can't hold bottom with anything less than a pound of lead and you spend more time re-rigging than fishing. Jigging diamond jigs, the 6- to 8-ounce depending on drift speed, tipped with a chunk of clam or mackerel belly if I've got it. Cod have been running 3 to 8 pounds, with a couple of better ones — one push past 10 on Tuesday morning that about pulled the rod out of my hands over the rail. Haddock mixed in on the same drifts, smaller average size right now, mostly a pound and a half to three pounds, but steady enough that a few boats have been limiting out before 9 a.m. Whiting show up on the same bottom and I don't mind them — good eating, and they keep the rod bent between the better bites.

Mackerel have been thick around the Shoals moorings and along the edges of White Island — small ones, schoolies really, but there's enough bait there that it's worth jigging up a dozen before you set the drift for cod. Fresh mackerel belly outfishes anything from the bait shop on those ledges, no question.

Stripers are the trickier read right now. Daytime bites along Great Boars Head and the beach south of Hampton have gone soft the last week and a half — not dead, just inconsistent, a fish here and there on umbrella rigs and bunker chunks fished off the bottom on the outgoing. The better program has shifted to first light and last light, which tracks with what's happening everywhere from here to Jersey — warm surface water, fish sliding onto structure and feeding in low light instead of grinding it out at noon. I've had my best luck working the mouth of Hampton Harbor on the last two hours of the incoming tide, right around dusk, throwing swimming plugs and soft plastic paddletails on 3/4-ounce jigheads along the edge of the channel where it meets the flats. Fish have been 24 to 32 inches mostly, with a few slot fish mixed in, holding tight to the deeper cut where the tide funnels bait past the jetty rocks.

The Piscataqua has actually been a bright spot for stripers willing to work current. Below the Memorial Bridge and down past the Coast Guard station, the tide rips hard enough to hold fish on structure all day, not just dawn and dusk — the moving water and depth keep it cooler and more oxygenated than the open beaches, so the bite's held up better through the heat. Bucktails, half-ounce to an ounce depending on the stage of tide, bounced along the bottom near the pilings and rock piles, have been picking up stripers to 30 inches on both the ebb and flood, best window being the last two hours of ebb when bait gets flushed down through the narrows.

Odiorne Point has been quiet for bass but decent for flounder — small boat guys anchoring up over the mud-sand mix off the point, squid strips and clam on a simple two-hook bottom rig, picking away at winter flounder and a few blackback in that 12- to 14-inch range. Nothing to write home about, but a nice change of pace and good eating.

No bluefish to speak of in close yet, which surprises me given what's happening south of us — the blitz tearing up bunker from Jersey through the Sound hasn't pushed this far north in any real numbers, though I'd keep an eye on the outer beaches over the next couple weeks if bunker schools keep working up the coast the way they have been.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. Water's stable, no big blow in the forecast, tides are building back toward the next moon. If you want groundfish, get to the Shoals ledges on the slack — that window's short and it's the whole game. If you want stripers, fish the Piscataqua current or work the Hampton Harbor mouth on that evening incoming. I'll be doing both, probably before most of you finish your coffee.

reports.headline: SW Ledge slack at 10:40: bass still there, but the albies aren't yet
reports.subhead: The bite's gone nocturnal on the Ledge, sea bass are bailing out the daylight charters, and the water's inching toward that first bonito flash off the Block.
reports.body_markdown:
Slack tide at SW Ledge hit 10:40 this morning and I had two rods bent inside four minutes — both fish came off before the leader, which tells you everything about the size class we're dealing with right now. Big stripers, working the last of the ebb before the turn, using that current break the way they always do this time of year: staged deep, waiting for the moment the water goes still and the bait gets confused. That window — call it fifteen minutes either side of slack — has been the whole program at the Ledge for the last ten days. Outside that window, you're just soaking bait in open water.

Here's the thing nobody wants to hear in the third week of July: the daytime bass bite off Galilee has gone quiet, and it's not coming back until the water cools or the sun goes down. Surface temps pushing into the mid-70s have shoved the better fish onto the thermocline, and at SW Ledge that means working the deeper edge of the rip — 35 to 55 feet — with big paddletails or a fresh chunk of bunker on a fish-finder rig, bounced right on the bottom where the current stacks bait against the ledge structure. I had a 34-pound fish come up on a live eel two nights ago, fished on the outgoing around 9:30 PM, about a half mile off the Ledge in that deep slot where the current really rips. That's been the pattern — dusk into full dark, not midday. If you're only fishing this spot from 10 to 2, you're leaving fish on the table.

Fluke has been the honest bite. Not a spectacular one, but an honest one. We've been picking through a lot of shorts drifting the deeper humps south of the Ledge and around the mouth of the Harbor of Refuge, but the keepers — fish to 5 and 6 pounds — are coming from the channel edges in 40 to 60 feet, on the stronger half of the tide. White Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, 3/4 to 1 ounce depending on drift speed, tipped with a fresh squid strip. Slow-dragged, not ripped. The warm shallow water has fluke doing exactly what Hooper's crew flagged coastwide — pushing quality fish deeper and making you work for them instead of just anchoring up anywhere and waiting.

Black sea bass has quietly been the best deal going for anybody who wants steady rod-bending without overthinking it. The reef structure off Block Island — the humps north and east of North Light, and the rockpiles working out toward Southwest Ledge itself — have been stacked. Squid and clam belly on a two-hook bottom rig, 60 to 80 feet, and you're not waiting long between bites. Not the biggest fish of the year but plenty of 16- to 18-inchers mixed in, and it's been a reliable fallback on days when the bass program requires patience you don't have.

Now — the story everybody's actually asking me about at the dock. Bonito and albies. Nothing confirmed yet off the Block, but I'll tell you straight: we flagged this exact scenario a few days back, watching the same warm-water breaks that are now showing up on the surface temp readings creeping toward that trigger range. I was out past Sandy Point yesterday afternoon watching for nervous water and diving terns, and saw bait balling up tight off Clay Head — small silversides, maybe some rain bait mixed in — but no speed demons crashing through it yet. That's usually the tell 48 to 72 hours out. If the pattern holds and this stretch of stable weather doesn't get knocked sideways by wind, I expect the first scout schools to show around the Block — probably off the rips at Southeast Light or out past North Rip — sometime in the next few days. When they do show, small Deadly Dick or a 7/8-ounce Kastmaster, fished on the fastest retrieve you can manage on light spinning gear, is exactly what you want rigged and ready.

Bluefish have been the reliable chaos machine everywhere else on the coast, and while we haven't had the same beach-blitz scenario Galilee sometimes sees, there's been solid blue activity mixed in around the bunker schools working the mouth of the Harbor of Refuge and along the breachway. If you're marking bunker on the sounder, there are blues under them, and a wire leader will save you a lot of bucktails.

Tide-wise, we're working with a moon that's keeping the current honest — good push through the Ledge, good drift speed for the fluke game, and that slack window at SW Ledge staying predictable enough to plan around. My read for the coming week: keep the daytime hours for fluke and sea bass, shift the bass program to first light and last light at the Ledge, and keep your eyes on the water off Sandy Point and Clay Head for that first real albie flash. If the wind stays out of the south-southwest and this warm stretch holds, I wouldn't be surprised if we're writing about confirmed bonito by next week's column. Until then, work the tides you know and don't burn daylight hours chasing a bite that's moved to the dark.

reports.headline: Bunker pinned tight on the south beaches, blues working them from Second to Weekapaug
reports.subhead: Bass have gone to bed until dark, tog are still a scattered pre-season story, but the bluefish blitz is the realest thing happening on the rocks right now.
reports.body_markdown:
Bunker are stacked so thick against the sand at Second Beach this week you can see the school turn dark, then silver, then dark again as it rolls with the swell. That's the tell. When the bait balls up tight like that and won't leave the wash, something's pushing it, and this week it's blues — not albies, not yet — but a real, sustained bluefish blitz working the south-facing beaches from Second all the way down through Charlestown Breachway and out toward Weekapaug. We flagged this exact pattern building last week, said it'd keep spreading as long as the bunker stayed pinned and the weather stayed calm, and that's exactly what's playing out. Calm mornings, light southwest air in the afternoons, water sitting warm on the surface — the bait has nowhere to go and the blues know it.

I've been working these blitzes with a simple approach: park the truck where I can see the bait nervous, walk down, and throw a Hopkins or a Kastmaster in silver/blue right into the froth. No finesse needed. Blues this size — mostly 3 to 6 pounds with the occasional bigger fish mixed in — will hit anything that moves fast through the melee. Tin lures, poppers, even a bare bucktail dragged through it. The trick out here on the rocky stretches is footing, not presentation. Charlestown Breachway's rock jetty has been a good stage for this — bait gets funneled through the cut on the outgoing and the blues pile up right where the current speeds up against the rocks. Fish the last two hours of the ebb there and you'll find them.

Striped bass are the quieter half of this story right now, and if you're expecting daytime bass action on the south shore, you're going to be disappointed. Surface temps have pushed well into the 70s along here, same story as the rest of southern New England, and the bass have done what they do this time of year — they've gone deep and nocturnal. I'm not seeing much daytime bass activity on the ledges at all, even around usually reliable structure like the rocks off Sakonnet Point or the drop-offs at Napatree. If you want stripers this week, you're fishing dusk into full dark. Eels and bunker chunks fished on the bottom around the deeper ledges off Brenton Point or the rock piles at the mouth of the Sakonnet River have been the play after 9pm. Don't waste daylight hours on bass right now — put that time into the bluefish or scout for albies instead.

Speaking of albies — nothing confirmed yet in our waters, but I'd be watching close over the next week to ten days. Water's climbing into the range where the first push usually shows, and Block Island sits close enough that fish moving into that corridor tend to filter into Sakonnet Point and eventually Napatree not long after. I haven't heard a single confirmed hookup yet on this stretch, so don't let anyone tell you different — but the conditions are lining up the way they usually do right before the first fish show. I'll be walking the rocks at Sakonnet Point with a bag of small Deadly Dicks and Albie Snax just in case, because when they do show, it's usually with zero warning.

Tog fishing right now is early and patchy — this isn't peak season yet, but a few guys have been picking at fish on green crabs around the deeper humps off Jamestown and the rockpiles outside Newport Harbor on the slack tide. Nothing worth planning a trip around specifically, but if you're already out there working blues and want to drop a bait, it's not a bad time to start scouting which cracks are holding fish for when the real bite kicks in come September and October. I like fishing green crab on a simple high-low rig, small hooks, right on the edge where the rock face drops into deeper water — 15 to 25 feet on the outside ledges. Patience pays more than volume at this point in the season.

Fluke have been a mixed bag off the south shore — plenty of shorts working the sandy stretches inside Charlestown Pond and around the Harbor of Refuge, but keeper-class fish are harder to come by unless you're working deeper water. The channel edges outside Point Judith and the deeper humps off Watch Hill Reef have given up some better fish — 20 to 22 inches — on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished slow on the drift in 25 to 35 feet. Stronger tide stages have produced better than the slack, which tracks — moving water keeps the bigger fish active instead of buried in the mud.

Looking ahead, I'd keep my time split between the bluefish blitz during daylight and bass after dark, because right now those are the two honest programs on this stretch. If the bunker schools hold along the beachfront through the week — and there's no sign yet of them breaking up — expect the blue bite to keep spreading further along the coast, same as it has been. The bigger story to watch is the albies. Conditions are lining up. I wouldn't book a charter around it yet, but I'd have the light tackle rigged and ready, because when that first fish shows at Sakonnet or Napatree, it won't give you much notice.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool at first light: bass rolling on mackerel, and my knuckles still remember it
reports.subhead: The incoming tide at the Pool turned on like a switch this week, and Pine Point's blues are chewing anything silver.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday, five-forty in the morning, still gray enough that I needed the headlamp to thread a hook, and a striper close to twenty-eight inches nearly took the rod out of my hand off the rocks at the mouth of the Pool. Second cast. That's the kind of morning that makes you forgive this stretch of coast for every skunking it's handed you in June. The fish was sitting right where the current pinches around the ledge on the incoming, holding in maybe six feet of water, and it hit a Danny plug like it meant it. Landed three more before the tide finished filling, biggest one twenty-nine inches, all of them fat and chrome and clearly fresh off a mackerel diet.

That's been the story all week down here — mackerel pushing into the river mouths and the bass following them in tight to the beach on the push. Biddeford Pool remains the best hour of striper fishing in this state when the water's coming in around the sandbar and pinning bait against the rocks. I've had my best luck starting an hour before the bottom of the low, working a big swimming plug — the Danny, a Bomber Long A in mackerel pattern, anything that throws a wide wobble — right along that rock line where the channel necks down. Slow retrieve, let it dig, don't rush it. The fish are eating with real purpose right now, not just pecking.

Pine Point's been a different animal entirely — that's where the bluefish have shown up and started tearing through peanut bunker pods right off the jetty and along the beach toward the Scarborough River mouth. Choppers in the three-to-six-pound class, occasional bigger ones mixed in, blitzing hard enough on some mornings that you can see the water churn white from fifty yards off. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader if you don't want to donate every lure in your bag — these blues don't care what you throw as long as it's got some flash. Kastmasters, Hopkins spoons, and a bucktail with a white tube on it have all been getting hit. This lines up with what we've been tracking coastwide — the bluefish push that's been running the beaches from New Jersey up through the Sound has finally found its way into our water, and with bunker and mackerel schools still holding tight along the beachfront here, I don't expect that bite to slow down until the bait scatters or we get a real wind shift.

Higgins Beach has had flashes of the same thing but it's spottier — you'll walk into a blitz one morning and find dead water the next. The birds are the tell. If you're not seeing gulls diving, don't waste your morning standing there. Prouts Neck has been fishing well on a southwest wind, which we've had a few days of this week — that wind pushes bait against the rocks on the ocean side and the bass tuck in tight to the ledges off the point. Bucktails tipped with a strip of mackerel belly, worked slow along bottom in fifteen to twenty feet, have been the ticket there for a mixed bag of school bass and the occasional keeper.

Water temps are still running cooler than most of the coast to our south — we're sitting in the low sixties nearshore, which is exactly why this zone keeps fishing better in daylight than places from Boston south where the stripers have gone nocturnal on account of warm surface water. That cold Gulf of Maine water is a gift right now. While guys from Cape Cod down are grinding out dawn-and-dusk-only bites because the fish are pushed deep and sour on the heat, our stripers are still willing to eat mid-morning in six to fifteen feet of water. Don't sleep late this time of year — it's not required the way it is farther south.

Groundfish program has been steady but unspectacular. Flounder are still coming out of Wells Harbor and the flats around the Kennebunk River mouth on sandworms and clam bellies fished on the bottom during slower tide stages, mostly dinner-plate size with the occasional bigger one mixed in. Cod fishing offshore of Cape Elizabeth has been a grind — you need to find the right piece of structure and jig it patiently, nothing's stacked up thick, but a few decent fish in the eight-to-twelve-pound range have come over the rail on diamond jigs worked right off bottom.

Moon's waning toward the new phase this week, which means tides are building again after sitting on the smaller side — that should tighten up the current at the Pool and improve the push of bait into the estuary mouths through the weekend. If the wind stays out of the southwest like it has been, I'd fish Prouts Neck early and then slide over to the Pool for the last two hours of the incoming — that's been the most consistent one-two punch all week. If it swings onshore and kicks up surf, I'd rather be at Pine Point working the bluefish blitz than getting hammered by whitewater trying to swing a plug through the wash at the Pool. Watch the bait. Where the mackerel show, the bass aren't far behind, and right now that's most of this coastline.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock holds the pattern: mackerel thick, bass working the ledges on the push
reports.subhead: The Gulf of Maine's cooler water is buying us daytime bass while the rest of the coast fishes the dark — take advantage while it lasts.
reports.body_markdown:
I took the outer route past Peaks and out toward Halfway Rock on Tuesday morning, and what struck me wasn't the fish so much as the water itself — that dark green-blue color holding steady, none of the murky freshwater push you sometimes get after a heavy rain week. Casco Bay is running clean and cool for late July, and that single fact is doing more work for us right now than any tide table.

Here's the thing worth understanding, and I say this having watched the coast from a professor's remove for thirty summers now: south of us, from Jersey up through Long Island Sound, the striper fishery has gone nocturnal. Surface temps down there are pushing into the mid-70s, forcing bass onto thermoclines and deep structure, feeding only at the edges of daylight or in full dark. We don't have that problem here. The Gulf of Maine keeps its foot on the brake, and Casco Bay's water — even inshore around the coves — hasn't hit that threshold. So our bass are still willing to work shallow ledges and estuary mouths in daylight, particularly on the push of the tide. That's a real advantage this time of year, and it's worth planning around rather than assuming it'll last forever.

Mackerel are the backbone of the week. Schools have been thick off Halfway Rock and along the drop north of Jewell Island, showing up as nervous water and diving terns any time from mid-morning through early afternoon. Small chrome Swedish Pimples and mackerel jigs strung three or four to a line, dropped to 20-30 feet and worked with a short snap, are filling coolers fast. If you're marking bait but not connecting, drop deeper — I've had mornings where the mackerel sat tight to bottom in 40 feet even with birds working the surface, chasing something smaller we couldn't see.

Those mackerel schools are exactly why the striper bite has held up on the ledges around Bailey Island and out toward Cape Small. Bass are shadowing the bait, and I've taken fish to 30 inches working live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, fished right on the last two hours of the incoming near the ledges off Ragged Island. The take is subtle — a slow pull-down rather than a hit — so keep your drag light and let the fish load up before you set. Bucktails in white and chartreuse, 1 to 1.5 ounce, worked slow along bottom on the slack before the ebb, have also been productive around the mouth of the New Meadows River and the ledges off Cundy's Harbor. Nothing explosive, but steady — three or four keeper-class fish on a good tide, which for mid-summer bay fishing is a fair result.

Groundfish remain a Halfway Rock story, as they generally are this time of year. Cod and a scattering of haddock are holding on the structure in 60 to 90 feet, and the pattern hasn't changed much from what I described last week — the slack water either side of the tide change is when you want your bait down. Clam and herring chunks on a standard cod rig, fished tight to the rock's northern face where the bottom breaks up into boulder and gravel, have produced fish in the 6 to 10 pound range. It's not fast fishing. You're putting in time for quality over quantity, and that's been true of this rock for as long as I've fished it. Two Lights hasn't been as productive for groundfish this month — too much boat traffic and not enough structure relief close in — but it remains a reliable spot for mackerel and the occasional bluefish push when the bait runs thick along that stretch of coast.

Bluefish have made a modest appearance in the bay's outer reaches, nothing like the blitz conditions unfolding to our south where blues are tearing through bunker schools from Jersey to western Long Island Sound. Here we're seeing occasional cutoffs on mackerel rigs and the odd blue mixed in with striper catches off Jewell and Cliff Island, nothing organized enough to target specifically yet. Worth keeping a wire leader in the tackle box regardless.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect steady action on the tide changes through this stable weather stretch — and that's held true. The bay hasn't given us anything dramatic, but it's given us dependable fishing, which this time of year is worth more than a hot week that burns out fast.

Looking ahead, the moon is working toward the next quarter, which means tidal swings will be moderate rather than extreme — good news for anyone fishing the ledges, since you won't be fighting the kind of hard current that makes bottom fishing at Halfway Rock miserable. If the weather holds calm through the weekend, I'd focus effort on the first two hours of the incoming at the Cape Small ledges for bass, and shift to Halfway Rock's slack water windows for cod and haddock. If a front comes through and stirs up the surface, expect the mackerel to push deeper and the bass bite to compress into narrower windows around first light. Either way, this cooler water is a gift right now — the rest of the coast would trade for it. Fish it while you've got it.

reports.headline: Monhegan pollock on top, mackerel holding the bay together
reports.subhead: Groundfish still down in the channels, bass working the river mouths at first light, and the mackerel schools are doing more work than they get credit for.
reports.body_markdown:
Back in the late 80s I had a sternman, Dale, who used to say the bay didn't care what the calendar said — it fished the way it fished, and your job was to figure out which day you'd gotten. Forty years later that's still the only forecasting system I trust. This week the bay gave us a pretty fair hand, provided you were willing to run early and fish the tide instead of the clock.

Starting with what's easy: mackerel are thick from Ram Island out past The Cuckolds, and they've been thick for two weeks now, which is exactly what's kept the striper program alive in the tidal rivers. You don't hear much fuss made over mackerel, but they're the reason there's bait to hold bass in the Sheepscot and up around Wiscasset on the last of the ebb. I had a customer Tuesday morning jigging a small chrome Diamond jig off the Sheepscot bridge pilings at first light, and inside forty minutes he'd boated eight mackerel and had two decent stripers — one a hair under 30 inches — follow a school right up into the current seam and swat at his jig on the retrieve. Switched him to a 6-inch olive Slug-Go, weightless, and let it swing dead-drift through that seam, and that's when the bass started eating for real. Nothing huge, mostly 24 to 28 inches, but a solid dozen fish over two hours on the dropping tide before the sun got up over the trees and shut it down.

That's the pattern right now, and it's the same one we called last week — conditions here have stayed stable, water's held in that comfortable mid-to-high 50s range close to shore, cooler out in the bay proper, and that's kept our stripers shallower and more willing to feed in daylight than what you're seeing from the Cape Cod Canal on south, where the heat's pushed everything down to a dawn-dusk program. We're the lucky zone this time of year. I don't say that often.

Offshore and down around Monhegan, the story's been groundfish, and it's been a genuinely good week for it. Pollock are up on the surface around the ledges off the eastern side of the island — Norton Ledge and out toward Smutty Nose — chasing pogies and sand eels in that nervous, boiling way pollock do when they're really into bait. I had a report from a captain I trust who ran out there Saturday on the last two hours of the incoming and found pollock busting the surface for a good twenty minutes straight, took fish to 8 pounds on white bucktails and swimming plugs cast right into the melee. That's a fun fish to catch on top, and it doesn't last — usually blows out once the tide turns and the bait scatters, so you've got a window, not an all-day bite.

Down deeper, in that 90 to 130 foot water off Monhegan's western side and out toward the deeper channels between the island and Matinicus, cod are still holding where they always hold this time of year — hard bottom, ledge edges, structure that breaks up the current. Jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, working them slow off bottom, has been the most consistent producer. Sizes have been modest — most fish 3 to 6 pounds, a few pushing 10 — but for late July that's about what you'd expect and about what we've been getting for years now out there. Haddock have been scarcer, a few mixed in on the same drifts but nothing to build a trip around specifically.

Eastern Egg Rock continues to hold its bass in that scrappy, opportunistic way it does all summer — stripers working the edges where the current runs past the rock, feeding on whatever the tide pushes past, sand eels mostly. Light tackle, small soft plastics, nothing fancy. Not a numbers fishery but a reliable one if you're passing by on the way out to Monhegan and want to make a stop.

Penobscot Bay itself has been quieter than I'd like to report. The deeper channels off Vinalhaven and down toward Isle au Haut still hold some groundfish — pollock mostly, a scattering of cod on the drop-offs — but it's spotty work, and I heard from two different boats this week that put in three, four hours and had to work hard for a handful of keepers. If you're going to fish the bay proper right now, fish the tide change hard, right at the top or bottom, and don't waste time on slack water. That's when what fish are there tend to feed.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. Water temps in close have stayed steady, mackerel show no sign of thinning out, and as long as that bait stays put the striper bite in the rivers and around the bay mouths should keep holding through the week. Monhegan's groundfish should stay put too — that's deep, cool water and it doesn't turn on a dime. If I had one day to fish this week I'd run out to Monhegan on a rising tide, hit the ledges for pollock on top first light, then work down to cod once the surface bite dies, and finish the day back in close chasing bass off the river mouths on the evening ebb. Long day, but that's about as complete a Midcoast trip as you're going to string together right now.

reports.headline: 180 feet on Jeffrey's: haddock thick on the mud, cod holding tight to the gravel edge
reports.subhead: The bottom's doing exactly what it should this time of July — you just have to fish the right five feet of it.
reports.body_markdown:
Two hundred and ten feet of water on the west side of Jeffrey's, mud bottom, and the sounder with that fuzzy grey haze eight feet off the bottom that means haddock are stacked and feeding. That's been the story most of this week — you find the soft stuff, the mud basins between the humps, and you find fish. Move fifty yards onto the gravel and hard rubble on the ledge's spine, up around 130 to 160 feet, and the picture changes completely. Marks get sparser, tighter to bottom, less spread — that's your cod water, and you've got to fish it different.

I've had my best mornings this week working that exact transition zone, where the mud gives way to broken gravel on the northeast corner of the ledge, inside of Cape Ann but still well out past Thatcher. Anchoring up on the gravel edge with clam and squid combo rigs, cod have been running a solid mixed bag — plenty in the 24 to 30 inch class, a few pushing better than that, though nothing that's going to make the scale groan this week. Jigging with 8 to 12 ounce diamond jigs, teaser dropper above, has worked when the current's moving right — slack tide kills it, so I've been timing my drifts around the two hours either side of max flow.

Haddock have been the more consistent producer, and honestly the better eating too. Working the mud basins in 180 to 220 feet with standard haddock rigs — two hooks, bait up with squid strips or clam belly, small bit of green or chartreuse tube for attraction — and letting it sit just off bottom rather than dragging it. These fish want it presented clean, not bounced around. Limits haven't been automatic but a well-fished drift has been putting a dozen keepers in the box most trips, mixed in with a few pollock that come through in that mid-water column when the tide's really humming.

Platts Bank has been fishing similar to Jeffrey's — same mud-versus-gravel read applies, and I had a trip out there Tuesday that mirrored what we've seen closer to home, haddock thick on the softer bottom west side, cod scattered but present on the eastern rubble. Tillies has been quieter for me this week, water's a touch warmer out that way and the bite's been softer, more of a pick than a program. I'd put my time closer to home right now if you're choosing between the two.

The bluefin piece of this puzzle is starting to develop the way it does every summer before it really turns on in the fall. We're seeing whale activity pushing bait up onto Stellwagen's approaches and along the edge of Jeffrey's itself — sand eel and herring balls getting worked hard by humpbacks and fin whales, and where the whales are, the tuna show up to clean up behind them. I had one client hook and lose a fish trolling a spreader bar over a bait ball on the southern end of the ledge last week, decent fish, probably 200-plus, gone after a short fight on light drag. That's the pattern right now — scattered giants working bait balls opportunistically, not the concentrated push we'll see once the mackerel and herring really stack up in September and October. If you're rigging for bluefin now, I'd keep gear ready but not build a whole trip around it yet. Better odds are still a month or two out.

Regionally the recreational slot fishery down toward Block Island and the canyons has been grinding steady since the trophy closure came through July 3rd, and that pattern holding stable is a decent sign for what's coming our way once the giants really commit to the ledge later this season. Worth watching.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect steady, if unspectacular, structure fishing through the next few days — and that's exactly what's played out. Nothing explosive, but reliable numbers if you fish the right bottom type for the right species and don't waste time working gravel for haddock or mud for cod.

Wind's been cooperative, nothing over 15 knots most days, and that's let us hold position properly on both the gravel and the mud without a lot of drift-and-reset headaches. If that holds through the weekend I'd expect the same read to continue — haddock steady on the mud in that 180 to 220 range, cod a more disciplined pick on the gravel edges where you need patience and a well-placed bait rather than covering water.

Looking ahead, I'd keep an eye on any building southwest wind later in the week — that can push a chop onto the ledge that makes precision anchoring tougher, especially working that gravel-mud transition where five feet of position matters. If it stays clean, my plan is the same one that's worked all week: hit the mud early for haddock while the bite's fresh, shift onto the gravel edge as the tide builds, and keep a rod rigged for anything that shows on the bait balls if we cross paths with the whales again on the way home.

reports.headline: 4:52 AM max ebb: the only window that mattered this week
reports.subhead: Daytime current in the Canal is producing bait movement without bass commitment — the real bite is happening before the sun's up and after it's down.
reports.body_markdown:
4:52 AM. That's when max ebb hit the east end Tuesday morning, and that's when I put two fish over thirty inches in the net off the Herring Run rocks before the sky even started to gray up. Both came on an olive Savage Gear sand eel, swimming it with the current instead of against it, letting the rip do the work. By 6:15, with the sun up and the current still running strong but the light flooding the water, it was over. Dead over. That's the story of the Canal right now and it's been the story for about two weeks — the tide's doing exactly what it should, the current's got plenty of push, but the bass have gone nocturnal on us the same way they have from the Jersey shore up through the Sound.

I've fished this ditch thirty years and I can tell you the current itself hasn't changed a bit. East end still turns on hard around the top of the ebb, that rip line stacking up off the Route 6 bridge piling and running out toward the tower, same as it's done every July of my life. West end's still setting up its current seam off the Mashnee flats on the flood, pushing bait into that eddy on the inside of the bend. The mechanics are all there. What's changed is the water's warmed up enough — surface temps pushing into the low 70s the way they have coastwide — that the stripers don't want to commit to those seams under a bright July sun. They're doing what bass do everywhere right now: sliding down, going quiet in the heat, and turning it back on when the light drops out.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the bite would stay tide-dependent with the best windows on max ebb and max flood as bait gets funneled through — and that's exactly what's playing out, just compressed into a smaller clock than usual. The difference this week is timing. It's not enough anymore to just hit max current during daylight. You need max current AND low light, and right now in late July those two things only overlap for about ninety minutes at each end of the day, plus the night tides in between.

Night fishing has been the better program, honestly. I had a report from a guy working the Sagamore side around midnight Sunday who did well on eels — bridled, drifted through the seam under the Sagamore Bridge on the last two hours of the ebb, three fish in the mid-30s, one that pushed 20 pounds released after a quick photo. That's the kind of quality that's still in this system. It hasn't left. It's just gone underground, or under-dark, however you want to put it.

Scusset Beach side has been decent for the bluefish crowd, and that's tracking with what's happening everywhere else on this coast right now — bunker have been getting pushed into the east end approach by the same bait movement that's got blues blitzing from the Cape Cod Bay side down through Buzzards. Guys throwing Deadly Dicks and Hopkins spoons off the rocks at Scusset during the last hour of the flood have been into blues steady, 3 to 6 pounds, occasional bigger fish mixed in. That bite's been more reliable during daylight than the bass have, which tells you something about how sun-shy the stripers have gotten.

Fluke have been a west end story, mostly around Mashnee Island and down toward Phinneys Harbor, working the deeper cuts on the tail of the ebb when the water's clean and moving but not screaming. Nothing huge — most fish 16 to 19 inches, a few keepers mixed in on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom where the current softens against the channel edge. It's a pick, not a program, but it's there if you want a change of pace between bass tides.

No albies or bonito through the Canal yet, and I don't expect them to show here first — this isn't their water, not really, though Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard corridor are exactly the kind of leading-edge zones where I'd expect the season's first scout fish to show given how the water's trending. If that happens down there in the next few days, don't be surprised if a stray albie shows up chasing bait through the east end on a hot flood tide later in the season. It's happened before. Not this week though.

Moon's swinging toward the new moon early next week, which means the currents are going to build back up after sitting on this softer neap stretch — I called that softening last week and it's held, current speeds down maybe 10-15% off a full spring tide. When the new moon current kicks back in, that funnel effect through both ends gets stronger, which should concentrate bait harder and give the bass a more defined reason to commit even during marginal light. If I had one window to fish this weekend, I'd take the pre-dawn max ebb Saturday at the east end — should be running around 5:10 AM — and I'd have an eel rigged and ready before the current even reaches full strength. Get there early, because once that rip lays down, the window's closed and you're just watching water go by.

reports.headline: Bunker Pods Off Holgate Turned the Beachfront Into a Feeding Line
reports.subhead: The blitz we said was coming from Belmar finally showed up at the jetties, but stripers went nocturnal while bluefish took over the daylight.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran the drone over the Holgate stretch Tuesday morning and the water told me everything before I even rigged a rod. Big dark ovals — bunker, thousands of them — pushed tight against the beach from the old Coast Guard station down toward the tip, and under them, that nervous, flashing chop that means blues are already in the school. By the time I got down there with a rod, the birds had found it too. Terns diving, a few gulls working the edges, and every third or fourth minute the whole pod would explode white for a second and go quiet again.

We flagged this last week — said the bunker pods pushing south from the Belmar blitz zone would funnel past Barnegat and Beach Haven on the tide changes, and that's exactly what's playing out. The bait's been thick enough that you don't need to guess where the fish are, you just need to get there before the pod moves. That's been the trick all week — this isn't a park-and-wait bite, it's a drive-the-beach-and-watch bite.

The blues have been the most honest fish out there right now. Cocktails to mid-teens crashing bunker from Barnegat Light down through Ship Bottom, and when a pod pins up against the jetty rocks at the inlet on the last of the incoming, it gets stupid for ten or fifteen minutes. Bucktails with a strip of bunker belly draped off the hook have worked, but honestly a naked white Ava 27 ripped through the school on a fast retrieve is just as deadly and you don't lose a lure to a cutoff every other cast. Guys throwing poppers into the boils off the north end of Holgate have had some of the most violent surface strikes I've seen all summer — topwater explosions that'll put a hitch in your heart rate.

Stripers are a different animal right now, and this is where I have to be straight with you — the daytime bass bite has gone quiet. Water's pushing into the mid-70s along the beachfront and that's shoved the bass off the surface layer entirely. They're down deep during daylight, probably holding on the thermocline break off the outer bars, and they've gone almost fully nocturnal. If you want stripers this week, you're fishing dawn, dusk, or full dark — no way around it. I worked the trough off Brant Beach at first light Wednesday with a black/purple Danny plug, slow swim through the inside slough, and picked up two schoolies in the 24-26 inch range before the sun got high enough to shut it down. Nothing to write home about, but it confirms they're still there, just working a tighter window.

Little Egg Inlet and the cut at Holgate are worth your time on the night tide — that structure holds current even when the moon's not doing much for you, and bass will slide up onto the edge of the bar to ambush bait moving through on the ebb. Bucktails in the 1 to 1.5 ounce range, white or chartreuse, bounced along the bottom of the cut on the outgoing has been the most consistent producer after dark. Don't overwork it — let the current do the work and just keep contact.

Fluke has cooled off exactly like it does every year once the shallow water heats up like this. The inshore humps in Barnegat Bay that were holding fish in June have gone quiet during the day, but the channel edges near the causeway bridge and the deeper humps off Ship Bottom are still giving up keepers on the stronger stages of the tide — moving water is doing all the work for you right now. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel drop where it meets the flat, has been the pattern. Morning incoming has outproduced the afternoon for us — cooler water, more willing fish. Shorts are everywhere if you want numbers, but you've got to work the deeper edges for anything over 18 inches.

Weakfish have been a rumor more than a pattern up here — nothing consistent to report on the LBI side, though I'd keep an ear out if that Delaware Bay resurgence starts pushing fish up the coast. Kingfish have shown in small numbers on bloodworm rigs off the surf at Beach Haven on the calmer mornings, nothing to build a trip around but a nice bonus if you're already out there for blues.

Tide-wise, work the last two hours of the incoming at the inlets for the bluefish blitz — that's when bait gets pushed tight against structure and the blues pin them. For bass, you want the first hour of the outgoing after dark at Little Egg and Holgate, when moving water pulls bait off the flats into the cut. Wind's been light out of the southwest most mornings, which is keeping the surf manageable, but it's building a little haze and warming the shallows even more — expect the bass pattern to stay nocturnal as long as this holds.

Looking ahead, if the bunker keep working north past Holgate like they have been, this blitz should stay hot through the weekend — I'd bet on it holding at least another 72 hours unless a wind shift scatters the bait. Best case, the pods stack up right on the Beach Haven side and give the pier and jetty guys a shot without even needing a boat. Worst case, a stiff onshore blow pushes everything out past the bar and we're back to searching. Either way, I'd rather be on the beach at first light with a topwater in hand than sitting home wondering.

reports.headline: Sea Bright at 5 AM: bluefish choppin' bunker while the bass hide till dark
reports.subhead: The rocks are loud with blues and gulls, but the real striper bite is happening after everyone else goes home.
reports.body_markdown:
Quarter to five, Sea Bright rocks, and there's already a guy out on the third jetty north of the Rumson bridge who beat me there. Again. Older fella, doesn't talk much, throws a white bucktail like it owes him money. We nodded at each other the way you do when you both know the other guy isn't going anywhere. Then the water in front of us just erupted — bunker skying, blues underneath them cutting the school to ribbons, birds dropping out of a still-dark sky like they'd been shot. That's been the show all week from Sea Bright down through Monmouth Beach. Loud, violent, and honestly kind of a relief after how quiet the striper bite's gotten.

We called this one — said last week the bluefish blitz would keep spreading north toward Sandy Hook as long as the bunker stayed pinned along the beach, and that's exactly the picture right now. Every jetty from the Hook down to Monmouth Beach has had at least one morning this week where the water just went white. Poppers are almost unfair right now — a black-and-white Yo-Zuri Hydro Popper or anything that throws spray gets bit on the first cast if you land it inside the bait ball. Metal works too if you want distance — Ava 27s or a 3-ounce Kastmaster, worked fast enough to stay above the blues' teeth. These aren't cocktail blues either. Plenty of 8- to 12-pound choppers mixed in, the kind that'll cut you off if you're running straight mono leader. Sixty-pound fluoro, minimum, or you're re-tying every third fish.

Here's the part that's been humbling: the bass have essentially disappeared during daylight. Water's sitting warm — mid-70s off the beach, and even the deeper holes around the Sea Bright groins aren't holding much heat relief. That pushes stripers onto the thermocline and into nocturnal mode, which is exactly what we flagged happening zone-wide. I fished the Manasquan Inlet rocks three mornings this week at first light and managed one bass — a 26-incher on a 5-inch white Slug-Go, weightless, worked slow along the north jetty face on the last of the outgoing. That fish came at 5:20, right at the edge of usable light. After that, nothing but blues.

The real bass program right now is a night program, and if you're not willing to fish dark water you're going to be frustrated. Shark River Inlet after 10 PM has been the most consistent thing I've heard about or seen myself — the jetty rocks on the north side, working a black Bomber Long A or a bone-colored Gibbs Danny plug on the last two hours of the incoming into the top of high. Slot fish, mostly, 26 to 32 inches, holding tight to the rocks where the current breaks. Nothing epic — two or three fish a tide if you put the time in — but it's real, and it's about the only place bass are eating with any consistency close to shore. Belmar's fishing similarly after dark, same tide window, same idea: current break, dark plug, patience.

Fluke's been the background hum it always is in late July — steady, unspectacular, and exactly what we expected with all this bait keeping things close to the beach. Shark River Inlet channel, drifting bucktails tipped with Gulp in white or chartreuse, 3/4-ounce jigheads working 15 to 20 feet on the deeper edges near the Route 35 bridge, has produced keeper counts in the 2-to-1 short ratio — meaning you're culling through a lot of dinks to find a 19- or 20-incher, but they're there. Same story off Manasquan Inlet's outer edges on the bigger tide swings — fish the last two hours of the ebb when the current's still got some push, because dead slack water in this heat just shuts everything down.

Porgies have been a nice consolation prize for anyone who wants meat in the cooler without babysitting a plug rod all night. The rock piles off Belmar and the pier areas around Spring Lake are loaded with them — squid strips or bloodworms on a high-low rig, small hooks, and you can fill a bucket in an hour on the right tide.

Blackfish are still weeks off — that's an autumn program, not a July one, so don't waste tide time on the wrecks yet.

Looking ahead: I don't see any reason for the bluefish blitz to slow down unless we get a wind shift that scatters the bunker, and there's nothing in the pattern suggesting that happens in the next few days. If you want blitz action, mornings on the Sea Bright-to-Monmouth Beach stretch are the play, and I'd get there before first light because once the sun's up and the joggers show up on the seawall, the bite tends to slide north out of casting range. For bass, I'd commit to a night tide at Shark River or Manasquan — pick the incoming into high, fish it dark, and don't expect volume. Expect quality, and expect to earn it. If the offshore water stays this warm through the week — and there's nothing forecast to cool it down — this nocturnal pattern holds. Plan your trips around dark water, not daylight, and you'll do alright.

reports.headline: Conimicut ledge holds after dark, bluefish tear up Greenwich Bay bunker
reports.subhead: Bass have gone nocturnal on the bay's warm water, but the blues won't let you feel bad about it.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into Dominic down at the Sabin Point launch Tuesday morning, hauling his kayak up the ramp looking like he hadn't slept — because he hadn't. Told me he anchored up off Nyatt Point at eleven the night before and didn't touch bottom with the plug until almost 1 a.m. when the bass finally showed. That's where we're at now on the bay. It's July, the water's sitting in the mid-70s off Conimicut and Rocky Point, and the stripers have punched out on the daytime program almost entirely. If you want them, you're fishing the dark.

We flagged this last week — said the pattern would hold with no big thermal shift coming, and that's exactly what happened. The bay didn't cool, didn't get a flush of fresh water, nothing changed the equation. Bass are stacked deep off the drop at Conimicut Point, sitting on that hard bottom in 25 to 35 feet, and they're not coming up to feed until the sun's been down an hour or two. Guys working the outgoing tide after 10 p.m. with eels — live or the SP Minnow in black — are getting into fish in the mid-20s to low 30-inch class right off the light. Same story working the west side of Prudence, along that deep edge that runs off Sandy Point down toward the south end. Slow-trolled bunker chunks on a three-way rig, fished right on the bottom during the last two hours of the ebb, has been the more consistent producer than anything thrown on the surface.

Daytime, if you insist on fishing sunlight, your better play is bouncing bucktails — half-ounce to an ounce, white or chartreuse — along the rocky ledges off Rocky Point and out toward the Hope Island reef structure.
