No wahoo either, though a smoker-class fish did cut off a green machine clean at the leader around 8am, which is as close as we got to confirming they're moving through. That's the kind of loss that sticks with you longer than it should.

The run home was the long part. Wind came around out of the southwest in the afternoon, nothing dangerous, but enough to slow us to fifteen knots and add ninety minutes to the trip. We tied up at Montauk with about 140 gallons left in the tanks, which is cutting it about as close as I like to cut it. That's the honest math on this run — Veatch and Atlantis both take a full tank and a full night's commitment, and if you're not comfortable running six-plus hours each way in the dark, you're better off working the closer pieces off Block Island canyon or waiting for a flatter window.

Looking at the week ahead, the high pressure shows no sign of breaking, which means I'd expect the yellowfin bite to hold steady at Veatch and push similarly at Atlantis and Hydrographer where the same warm water's sitting on the edge. If you're planning a trip out of Montauk, Block, or one of the Rhode Island ports, I'd watch the wind forecast closer than anything else — a calm run out buys you fuel margin for working the grounds longer, and that margin is what turns a mediocre trip into a two-bigeye morning. Squid signs building around Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound suggest the bait situation inshore is improving too, which down the line should help pull more bluefin up onto the shallower structure. For now, my money's on another solid week at the east wall if the weather cooperates — but I'll believe it when the fuel gauge says I can afford to find out.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Slow start at Spencer, then Norfolk turned it on: yellowfin steady through the week
reports.subhead: A shaky Monday at Spencer gave way to a Norfolk chunk bite that never quit, with mahi riding shotgun the whole way.
reports.body_markdown:
Monday I ran the numbers to Spencer expecting the same warm push we'd been riding, and it just wasn't there. Marks were soft, water looked right on the temp gauge but the fish weren't stacked on it the way they'd been the week before. Pulled the spread for four hours along the 100-fathom curve, one flat-fall knockdown, no hookup. That's canyon fishing — you go where the intel says and sometimes it's stale by the time your spread hits the water. I picked up and ran south.

By Wednesday I had Norfolk dialed and it was a different world. Clean blue water, a hard edge sitting right along the 300-fathom line on the north wall, and yellowfin stacked under it from 60 to 90 feet down. We anchored up on the edge with the chunk — butterflied bunker, a slow bag going out, and it turned into as steady a bite as I've had all month. Fish from 25 to low 40s, a couple pushing 50, all on 6/0 circle hooks buried in the butterfly, 40-pound fluoro leader, no wire. The current was moving nice, maybe a knot and a half, which kept the chunks sliding at the right pace instead of piling up under the boat. That's the difference between a good chunk bite and a dead one — current speed dictates everything.

We flagged this last week — said the canyon bite would hold as long as the offshore water stayed put, and it did exactly that. High pressure never budged, the shelf break stayed loaded with warm, clean blue water pushing into the high 70s at the surface, and Norfolk cashed in on it while Spencer took a breather.

Thursday we ran Poor Man's on a tip about a temp break showing warm water wrapping the western edge, and found mahi before we found tuna. Weed line stretched almost two miles, holding gaffer-sized mahi in the 8 to 15 pound range, plus a pile of schoolies that kept the rods bent on spinning gear with skirted ballyhoo. Green machines and pink Ilanders on the troll picked off a few yellowfin working the same structure, 30 to 35 pounds, but the real show was under that weed. If you've got light spinning tackle rigged with a small popper or a chunk on a jig head, that's money on floating structure like that — don't just run past it on the way to the drop.



Lindenkohl was the one I skipped this week. Had two separate calls saying the water there had gone soft and green along the edge, temp break not holding shape, and I've learned not to burn fuel chasing a broken edge when three other canyons are producing. That's the whole game running four canyons out of Cape May and Ocean City — you're not married to one piece of water, you're reading which one's holding structure day to day and moving the boat accordingly.

Bluefin showed up mixed in at Norfolk too, slot-class fish in the 50 to 70 inch range crashing the chunk slick a few times, quick fights, quick releases since we're still working inside the post-July 3 slot rules. Nothing trophy-sized showed, which tracks with what's been happening fleet-wide since that closure — steady grinding on the smaller class fish rather than the giants.

No billfish action to report this week out of any of the four. Had one bill swipe at a naked ballyhoo trolling the temp break at Poor Man's Thursday morning but no eat, no hookup. Water's right for white marlin, temp's holding in that window, but the reports just aren't backing it up yet. Wahoo were quiet too — one solitary fish, mid-40s, caught on a high-speed diving plug trolled at 14 knots along the Norfolk edge Wednesday afternoon, but that was the only wahoo intel I've got worth passing along.

Looking at the week ahead, I like Norfolk to keep producing if that north wall edge holds its shape — the chunk bite there has the kind of rhythm you want, steady current, steady marks, fish committing to the slick instead of just flashing under it. I'd run there first if I only had one day. Second choice is Poor Man's for the weed line mahi if it's still floating out there — those lines move with the current so it might not be exactly where we found it, but the pattern of warm water holding structure along that western edge should persist as long as high pressure doesn't break down. Spencer I'd give another look by midweek — sometimes these edges just need a few days to reload after they go quiet, and the same thermal pattern that's fueling Norfolk and Poor Man's should eventually wrap back around. Lindenkohl I'm leaving alone until somebody calls me with a better report than 'soft and green.'

Bring extra leader material regardless of which canyon you pick — the fish have been leader-shy on the troll, biting better on fluoro than mono, and losing a couple rigs to bluefin teeth is just part of the cost of doing business out there right now.

reports.headline: 71.2°F at the Bight buoy, but the canyon edge is running 6-8 degrees warmer — that's your yellowfin water
reports.subhead: A stable high has held the Hudson's warm-core structure in place for a full week, and the tuna numbers reflect it.
reports.body_markdown:
71.2 degrees. That's what 44025 was reading out in the Bight earlier this week, which tells you almost nothing about what's happening on the canyon edge — and everything about why I run 100-plus miles instead of fishing the inshore lumps. The Hudson wall itself has been holding surface temps in the upper 70s to right around 80 along the break, which means we're carrying a 7-to-9 degree gradient from the Bight buoy out to the 100-fathom line. That's the number that matters this week. When you see a spread that wide with settled high pressure sitting on top of it, you get warm-core water pinned against the canyon structure instead of getting pushed around by wind-driven mixing, and that's exactly the setup that's been parked over the Hudson for going on ten days now.

We called this direction last week — said the stable pattern was quietly building one of the better yellowfin and bigeye setups of the season, and that's precisely what showed up. I ran out of Manasquan Tuesday, put the spread in the water at the 90-fathom curve on the northeast side of the canyon, around 39°32' N, 72°38' W, and had color change and a hard temp break within the first half mile of trolling — you could see it in the water itself, that blue-to-green transition with a visible slick line of foam and debris riding the edge. Yellowfin were stacked on the warm side of that break, 68 to 76 degrees on the surface reading, and we boated six inside of three hours on a standard spread: Green Machines and small Islanders in the shotgun and long rigger, ballyhoo naked and rigged behind a bird on the short corner. Fish ran 20 to 35 pounds, nothing giant, but steady enough that we never had more than a 20-minute lull between strikes.

The better fish came off the chunk once the sun got high and the troll bite went quiet, which is the pattern I've seen play out at the Hudson for fifteen years now — troll early and late, chunk through the heat of the day. We anchored up on the edge of the Dip in 700 feet, butterflied fresh bunker on 60-pound fluoro leader, circle hooks, and let it soak with the chunks drifting on a slow current. That's where we picked up a 45-pound bigeye around 1:30 in the afternoon, deep bite, rod bent double on 50-pound stand-up gear. Mahi showed up opportunistically around a scattered weed line south of the Claw — nothing major, a half dozen schoolies in the 5-to-10 pound class, but they'll eat a small skirted lure or a chunk bait if you're marking floating structure and want to burn twenty minutes on the way out or back.

White marlin have been the wildcard. We raised two on Tuesday's run, neither one committed, both came up on the long rigger ballyhoo and just looked at it before sliding off. That's typical for this stage of the season — the fish are around, the water's right, but they're not eating with any consistency yet. If you want a shot at one, I'd downsize the leader to 20-pound fluoro and pull naked ballyhoo rather than rigged, and have a pitch bait ready the moment you see one show color behind the spread.

Wahoo have been scarcer than I'd like given the water temps, but one of the other boats working the 100-fathom line south of us picked off a decent one, mid-30s, on a high-speed lure pulled at 12 knots through a temp seam near the Texas Tower drop-off. That's a program I'd try again if I had a dedicated wahoo day — those fish like a hard break and a fast presentation, and the Tower area has been holding the kind of structure and current edge that sets that up.

Bluefin have been more of a Block Island and Massachusetts story than a Hudson story this week — the slot fishery up there is grinding steady post-closure, but down here they've been incidental, a couple jumped off the troll spread and one 60-pounder gaffed on the chunk Tuesday afternoon. Not the primary target, but worth having a heavier stand-up rod rigged in case one shows.

Here's my honest read: this is a good bite, not a great one. Six yellowfin and a bigeye in a full day is solid work for late July, but it's not the kind of numbers day where you're boxing fish every fifteen minutes. The fish are there because the water's set up right — that wide temp gradient between the coast and the canyon is doing exactly what it should, holding bait and tuna against structure instead of letting it scatter. But you still have to find the exact edge, and it's moved a few miles east since last week as the eddy shifts with the Gulf Stream's meander.

Looking ahead, if this high pressure holds through the weekend — and right now there's no reason to think it won't — I'd expect the yellowfin bite to hold or even improve slightly as more bait gets pushed up against that warm-core structure. I'd run straight to the northeast side of the canyon first, check your surface temp against that 76-78 degree window, and if you're not seeing bait or birds within the first hour, slide south toward the Claw where the bottom contour tends to funnel current and hold structure tighter. Bring gear for both troll and chunk — you'll want both before the day's out.

reports.headline: The bass went quiet at night — and that's exactly where you'll find them now
reports.subhead: Block Island's stripers have slid deep and nocturnal, but the first bonito scouts may be closer than anyone thinks.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a smell to the air out here in late July, a kind of stillness that settles over the island around 8 PM when the wind drops and the day-trippers head for the ferry. I noticed it three nights running this week — the kind of calm that makes you look twice at the water off the bluffs, because you know something's about to change. And it has. The bass have gone underground on us, the way they do every summer once the surface water settles into that warm, glassy mid-70s feel. If you want stripers right now, you fish the dark.

I worked the North Rip Tuesday night on the tail of the flood, anchored up in eighteen feet with the current pushing hard against the ledge, and it was a different fishery than the one we had in June. No surface commotion, no birds, just that steady mechanical thump of a fish taking a bait off bottom. Eels did the work — plain and simple, an 8-inch live eel on a fish-finder rig, enough weight to hold bottom in that rip current, and a long enough leader to let it swim natural. We put four bass in the boat between 10 PM and 1 AM, biggest one 34 pounds, and every single one came on that slow incoming push when the water stacks up against the ledge and the current really starts to sing.

Southwest Ledge has been more of a dawn program lately. I like being anchored up there by 4:45, right as the sky starts to gray out, working bucktails — the 2-ounce white ones with a chunk of mackerel belly hooked through the skirt — bounced right along that rocky bottom in 30 to 40 feet. The fish are down deep chasing bait that's stacked up on the thermocline, and you need to get down to them fast and stay there. We're not seeing the daytime blitzes we had a month ago. That's just where we are in the calendar. The water up top is too warm and too bright, so the fish do their feeding in the low-light windows and then drop back down and go quiet through the heat of the day.

The bluefish, on the other hand, haven't gotten the memo about subtlety. We flagged this pattern building last week, and it's still the most reliable action going — aggressive blues chewing through bunker schools anywhere there's bait pinned against structure. Off Sandy Point and down toward Charlestown Breachway, we've had fish blitzing bunker in broad daylight, and it hasn't slowed a step. Metal — a 1-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins — thrown right into the surface chaos will get bit on almost every cast right now. Bluefish to 10 pounds, sometimes bigger, and they're not picky about presentation. If you want fast action and don't mind retying leaders all afternoon, that's your play.

Fluke have been a grind, honestly. The shorts are everywhere — inside the Great Salt Pond, along the sand edges off Old Harbor — but keeper-sized fish want depth and current right now. I've had better luck working the drift along the deeper edges off Charlestown, 35 to 45 feet, dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, tipped with squid strip, moving slow on the last two hours of the outgoing. You have to cover water and pick through a lot of dinks to find a 20-incher, but they're there if you're patient.

Porgies have been steady and mostly ignored, which is a shame because they're good eating and easy fishing right now — bottom rigs with squid or clam off the Coast Guard station in 20 to 30 feet will keep a rod bent most of an afternoon. Blackfish season's closed, so that's a non-issue till fall, but I mention it because guys keep asking.

Now here's the piece everyone on the dock wants to talk about — bonito and albies. Water temps around the island and up through the Buzzards Bay corridor have crossed into that zone where the first scout schools typically show, and I've got a gut feeling we're closer than people think. No confirmed catch yet as of this week, but the bait's right, the water's right, and every August for the last several years the first fish have shown up right around this stretch of the calendar. If I had one afternoon to burn looking for them, I'd be running light spinning gear with small Deadly Dicks or Albie Snax off the Southeast Light rips, working the moving water where bait gets funneled and squeezed. It's a scouting mission more than a sure thing, but that's the fun of it this time of year.

Tide-wise, we're coming off a moon that's kept the current honest — good push through the rips, which the bass have been using to their advantage at night. Wind's been cooperative, mostly light out of the southwest, which keeps the water clean around the Ledge and the North Rip. If that holds through the weekend, I'd keep the program the same: eels and bucktails after dark for bass, metal on the blues whenever you see working birds, and a scouting run out toward the lighthouse rips if you've got the itch for something new on the line. The water's telling us summer's fully set in — deep bass, hungry blues, and a bonito arrival that feels like it's just days away, not weeks.

reports.headline: Ran to the Wilmington Tuesday instead of the Baltimore Canyon — here's why that paid off
reports.subhead: Six hours trolling the northeast edge put three yellowfin and a mahi in the box, and confirmed the warm-water setup we've been watching build all month.
reports.body_markdown:
Had three boats calling me Monday night asking whether to run to the Baltimore or stick with the Wilmington, and I made the call to stay home water — northeast corner of the Wilmington, up around 38°28' N, 72°40' W, working the push where the warm eddy has been sitting against the shelf break. That decision came down to fuel math and what I'd seen the week before: the temperature break out there has been holding tighter and cleaner than anything to the south, and I didn't want to burn an extra hour and a half of diesel chasing a report from a boat that fished it two days prior.

Good call this time. We ran the troll spread — naked ballyhoo and a mix of Green Machines and small Ilanders in the pattern, six lines out — along the edge where the water goes from a milky green inshore chop to that dark, almost black-blue offshore color. That line was sitting in about 300 to 900 feet of water, right where the bottom starts to fall off the shelf into the canyon proper. Water temp on the break was pushing into the upper 70s, close to 79 in spots, which is exactly the kind of warm-core structure we flagged building last week. We said the yellowfin bite would hold on that temperature break through the canyons, and out on the Wilmington's edge, that's precisely what we found.

Three yellowfin in the 25 to 40-pound class came off the spread between 8 and 11 in the morning, all on the troll — two on a green-and-yellow machine run short on the shotgun, one on a naked hoo pulled long off the left flat line. We picked up a bull mahi around 15 pounds trolling past a small weed line drifting on the surface just inside the break — nothing dramatic, no real grass mat, just a scattered patch of sargassum that had a few small mahi stacked under it. Worth a look every time you see anything floating out there right now; even a five-gallon bucket's worth of weed can hold fish this time of year.

What we didn't find was bigeye, and I want to be straight about that. We marked some deep bait on the machine around 600 feet but never got a jump from anything heavier than the yellowfin class, and I talked to two other captains that night who had similar days — decent yellowfin counts, no bigeye to show. If bigeye's your target, I'd be thinking about a night chunk on anchor over structure rather than running the troll pattern during daylight. That's a different program and a different day, and right now I'm not seeing enough bigeye sign to justify switching off the troll during daylight hours.

White marlin showed once — a single fish that came up on the right flat line, took a look at a naked ballyhoo, and never committed. No hookup, no second look. That's been the pattern most of July out here — marlin are around, but they're not eating aggressively, and I think that's tied to the amount of bait suspended in that upper 60 feet of water column. When there's that much natural forage stacked up, your trolled spread is competing with a full pantry, and the marlin just aren't hungry enough to chase plastic and rigged bait when there's real food everywhere.

No wahoo this trip, which surprised me a little given the water temp. Usually when you're seeing upper 70s on the break this time of year, you start marking a few wahoo runs, especially if you're pulling a high-speed spread with cedar plugs or small Yo-Zuris off a planer. We didn't run that gear Tuesday — stuck with the standard ballyhoo/skirt spread for the tuna program — so it's possible we just didn't present the right bait. Next trip out I'm planning to run one wahoo bait high-speed off the corner just to test it, since the water's right even if we didn't connect.

Bluefin have been more of a Block Island and canyon-corridor story than a Wilmington story lately — the slot fishery up north is grinding along steady since the July 3 trophy closure, but down here we're just not seeing the bluefin numbers we'd expect. If you're set on bluefin, that's a longer run and a different trip plan, not a Wilmington day.

Looking at the week ahead, the high-pressure pattern that's been parking over the mid-Atlantic shows no sign of breaking, which means the warm-core water sitting on the Wilmington's edge should hold its position and its temperature. If that eddy stays put through the weekend, I'd expect the yellowfin bite to remain the most dependable program out there — troll in the morning while the light's low and the fish are still up chewing, then switch to a chunk with butterflied bunker if the bite goes quiet by midday. That's the pattern I'll be running Thursday with a full boat, and it's the same play I'd suggest to anyone weighing a Wilmington trip this week: go early, work the break, and don't be afraid to sit on the chunk if the troll goes cold by noon.

reports.headline: Late July at Washington: this is why we don't wait for the other canyons
reports.subhead: Yellowfin have been on the troll wall since the Fourth, and the calendar says we've still got a month of this before the wahoo show up to complicate things.
reports.body_markdown:
By the third week of July I've stopped being surprised by anything Washington does — I've fished this piece of bottom long enough to know it runs its own calendar, usually two to three weeks ahead of Hudson and Wilmington, and this season is no exception. We were seeing quality yellowfin activity here before most boats had even splashed for their first canyon run, and now that we're deep into the settled summer pattern, the fish have simply stayed put. That's not luck. That's the shelf break doing what it does at Washington every year once the Gulf Stream noses in close and the warm water sets up shop along the edge instead of sliding past it.

Right now the money water is stacking along the northeast wall, out toward the 200-fathom curve, with the temp break holding steady in that upper 70s to near-80-degree range. That's the number that matters more than any single buoy reading — when you find that break sitting tight against structure instead of smeared out over open water, you've found where the bait's going to hold, and where the bait holds, the yellowfin hold. I've been marking the strongest concentrations where the color goes from that dirty green Gulf Stream edge to clean cobalt blue, usually somewhere in the 100 to 150 fathom transition before you even hit the true canyon depths. Troll that seam with a spread of cedar plugs and small Ilanders — green/yellow and pink/white have both been drawing strikes — and you're going to find fish in the 40 to 60 pound class without needing to run all the way to the eastern wall.

The chunk bite has been the more consistent producer for the boats willing to commit to an overnight. Set up on the edge where the current is pushing bait against structure, deploy a slow butterflied bunker chunk on a long leader — 6 to 8 feet of 50 or 60-pound fluoro, small hook, no swivel showing — and let it drift down naturally in the chum slick. That's been putting bigger fish in the box, yellowfin pushing 70 pounds, along with the occasional bigeye showing up in the middle of the night bite when the moon's dark enough to keep the deep-water feeders comfortable coming up. We're past full moon now and heading toward the new phase, which historically has been good to us here — less moonlight up top usually means a better late-night chunk bite as the bigeye push shallower to feed.

Mahi have been the bonus fish all month, and they haven't slowed down. Any bit of floating structure — a lobster pot buoy, a mat of sargassum, even a stray piece of dock debris — is worth a look and a few pitched baits. Small feathers or a strip of squid on a light spinning rod will get you a quick mixed bag while the bigger baits keep soaking for tuna. I wouldn't plan a whole trip around them, but they've saved more than a few slow mornings out here.

White marlin have been scattered through the same water as the yellowfin, mostly showing on the troll spread rather than committing hard, which is typical for this stage of the season. A couple of teams have had multiple bites in a day without converting all of them — that's just white marlin being white marlin in late July. Drop back a natural bait quickly if you see one crash the pattern and give it time before you set the hook.

Wahoo have been quiet so far, which tracks with where we are in the season. Washington usually doesn't turn on wahoo-heavy until we get into that August water — once the break sharpens up further and the current really starts ripping across the edge. I wouldn't be running dedicated wahoo bombs yet, but keep a couple of high-speed lures in the middle of the spread just in case; they show up early some years and this canyon has surprised me before.

We flagged this pattern building last week — said the yellowfin bite would hold given the settled high pressure, and that's exactly what's happened. No storms to break up the structure, no cold water intrusions to scatter the bait, just steady clean water sitting on the edge and fish stacking up on it day after day. That kind of stability is rare enough in late July that you don't question it, you just fish it.

Looking ahead, I don't see a reason for this to fall apart in the next week unless the weather pattern shifts. The high pressure's been parked over the mid-Atlantic long enough that the thermal structure out here is mature and settled rather than fresh and jumpy, which usually means the fish stay committed to the same stretches of the wall instead of wandering. If I had a boat and a weather window this week, I'd run straight to that northeast wall temp break first, work it with the troll spread for two or three hours to locate the pod, then switch over to the chunk and sit on it through the evening bite into the night. That's been the winning one-two punch all month, and there's no read on the water right now telling me to change it. Keep an eye on the moon phase heading into early August — as it darkens up further, I'd expect the overnight bigeye bite to get another notch stronger before wahoo season properly kicks off behind it.

reports.headline: The Point Is Turning: Bunker Boils, Night Bass, and the First Whisper of Albies
reports.subhead: Late July at Montauk means the striper bite goes underground and something faster starts moving in off the back side — here's what's holding and what's coming.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a week every summer when Montauk stops being one fishery and starts being three or four stacked on top of each other, and this is that week. I've fished this Point since I was tall enough to lean into the rail at the Lighthouse, and I know the rhythm by feel now — the bass go quiet in the daylight, the blues turn the surface white, and somewhere out past the Elbow the first albie of the year is already circling, even if nobody's boated one yet.

Water at the Point is sitting around 69 degrees, which sounds modest until you remember what that number does out here. It's the number that starts waking up the false albacore and bonito schools working their way up from the Rhode Island and Block Island side. We haven't had a confirmed albie yet — I want to be straight with you on that, nobody I trust has boated one off the Point as of this morning — but the water's right, the bait's right, and the pattern is exactly what I flagged last week when I said the headboats out of the Viking dock should start seeing early sign within seven to ten days if this warmth held. It's held. I'd be shocked if we don't have a real report by the weekend, somewhere between the Point and Shagwong Reef, maybe out toward the Elbow where the current really rips.

For right now, the loudest story on the water is bunker and blues, and it is a story worth chasing. Pogy schools have been pinned tight against the beach from the Lighthouse down through Turtle Cove, and the bluefish have been relentless on them — proper blitz conditions, birds working low and diving, bunker exploding on the surface like popcorn. This is the pattern I called last week too: bunker-driven blitz action holding as the dominant visible story until the bait disperses or a wind shift breaks it up. Neither's happened yet. If you want blues, don't overthink it — a Hopkins or a 2-ounce Kastmaster fired into the boil, or if you want to keep tackle intact, a wire-leader popper worked fast across the top. They're not picky right now, they're just violent.

The bass, though — that's where it gets serious, and where you need to change your whole approach. Stripers have gone nocturnal on us hard, exactly the pattern you'd expect once surface temps push into this range. Daytime, the boulder fields off the North Bar and the rip lines off the Point have been mostly quiet, maybe a fish or two picked off deep on bucktails worked slow along bottom structure, but nothing to build a trip around. Night is a different animal entirely. Guys working the incoming tide after dark around the Point and down toward Shagwong have been connecting on real fish — eels swum slow and deep along the boulder edges, bucktails with a curl-tail trailer dropped right into the white water where the rip meets the calm. I had a report of a 38-pound fish taken off the south side structure on a black eel, fished on the building tide around 11 p.m., worked tight to the rocks where the current stacks bait against structure. That's the program right now — full dark, slack water avoided, current moving, eels or bucktails, patience.

Fluke have slid into that midsummer pattern everybody who's fished this water long enough recognizes — shorts everywhere in the shallows, but the keeper-class fish have pushed out to the deeper structure and channel edges where the water stays cooler. I'd be working the drift outside Frisbie's or along the deeper edges toward Fort Pond Bay on the stronger tide stages, white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, 30 to 45 feet, dragged slow along bottom contours. You'll cull through a lot of shorts to find the keepers, but they're there if you're willing to grind for them.

Porgies have been steady and reliable off Shagwong Reef and around the harbor structure — bloodworms or clam on standard bottom rigs, nothing fancy, just consistent action if you want to fill a cooler without overthinking it. Blackfish season's still a ways off but I mention it because guys are already scouting structure for the fall, and that tells you something about where heads are turning.

Offshore, the canyon boats running out of Montauk have kept finding yellowfin and some bigeye in consistent numbers, and that program should hold as long as this high-pressure stretch stays put. It's a long run but the payoff's been worth it for boats willing to make the trip.

Looking ahead, I think this coming week is the pivot point of the whole summer out here. If the warm water holds and the bait stays thick, I expect confirmed albie and maybe bonito sign within the next few days — that's where I'd put my attention if speed and light tackle are your thing, working the rips off the Point and out toward the Elbow with small metal and epoxy jigs once they show. If you're chasing bass, stay committed to the night program — full dark, moving current, eels and bucktails tight to structure at the North Bar and down through Shagwong. And if the wind stays cooperative, don't sleep on the bunker blitz along the beach — it's been the most dependable show on the Point all week, and there's no sign yet it's ready to break up.

reports.headline: Bluefish blitz owns the shoreline, bass go dark till dark from Execution to the Throgs Neck
reports.subhead: Bunker schools have blues chewing along the beach in broad daylight, but the bass have punched out until the sun does too.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop in City Island asked me Tuesday if the stripers "packed up and left the Sound." I told him no, they didn't leave — they just got smart. Thirty years watching this water and every mid-July it's the same story: the bass go nocturnal on us, and the guys who don't adjust go home skunked wondering where all the fish went.

Here's what's actually happening. Kings Point is reading just under 71 degrees on the surface, and that's plenty warm enough to push mature stripers off the flats and down onto structure they can sit tight to during daylight — the deep water off Execution Rocks, the basin edges around Hart Island, the channel drop-off inside the Stepping Stones. During the day those fish are hunkered low, barely feeding, waiting for the sun to lose its grip. Come dusk, through the night, and into that gray hour before dawn, they climb back up onto the rockpiles and rip lines and they feed hard. If you're fishing this water at 10am wondering why your bucktail isn't getting bit, that's why.

I had a guy out Sunday night — we anchored up-current of Execution on the last two hours of the outgoing, right where that rock pile breaks up the tide, and we picked at bass to 28 inches on live eels drifted back with just enough weight to keep them down near bottom. Nothing crazy, but steady enough to keep the rods bent every twenty minutes or so from about 9pm until the tide went dead around midnight. That outgoing push off Execution has been money for as long as I've fished it, and it doesn't stop being money just because it's July — it just means you fish it after the tiki torches go out on the beach houses instead of during the day.

Now the real story on the Western Sound this week, and I mean the story everybody's talking about at every dock from Throgs Neck to Oyster Bay, is the bluefish. We flagged this pattern building last week and said it would keep spreading as long as the bunker held tight to the beach — and that's exactly what's happened. Big pods of bunker are stacked shoulder to shoulder off Matinecock Point, off the Whitestone side of the Throgs Neck, and scattered right along the Hempstead Harbor mouth, and the blues are absolutely tearing through them in broad daylight. This isn't a subtle bite — you'll see the surface erupt, bunker skying out of the water, gulls diving, and you idle over and start firing poppers or metal into the chaos.

Best producer this week has been a 2-ounce Kastmaster or a bunker-colored Hopkins worked with a fast, erratic retrieve right through the edge of the melee — don't throw into the thickest part, work the perimeter where the bigger blues are hanging back picking off cripples. Guys are also doing well snagging a bunker off the school with a weighted treble and drifting it back on a stinger rig; that's producing the bigger cocktail blues, some pushing 8 to 10 pounds, right off the rocks at Matinecock and along the Sands Point shoreline. The blitzes have been showing mid-morning and again in that late afternoon window when the sun angle pushes the bait tight against the beach — keep your eyes on the birds, because when they go from circling to diving, you've got maybe five minutes before the school sounds and moves.

Fluke fishing is doing what it always does this time of year — background noise, dependable but unspectacular. The reef structure off Hart Island and the drop-offs around the Stepping Stones are holding fish, but you're picking through a lot of shorts to find keepers. Best move has been dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, 3/4-ounce, tipped with a strip of squid, working the deeper edges — 25 to 35 feet — on the tail end of the incoming when there's still enough current to keep your bait moving without getting swept sideways. Porgies remain steady on the same structure; a simple high-low rig with sandworms or clams over any of the rockpiles from Execution down through Manhasset Bay will keep you busy, even when nothing else wants to cooperate.

We're coming off the first-quarter neap now, which means current everywhere in the Sound has been on the soft side this week — that's part of why the structure bite has actually held up better than the open-water trolling program. Weaker current means fish sit tighter to rockpiles and channel edges instead of spreading out, which is exactly why Execution and the Stepping Stones have kept producing even with the tide moving at half speed. Expect that current to start rebuilding over the next several days as we move away from the neap, and when it does, I'd look for the bass bite at Execution and off Hart Island to sharpen up, especially on the night tides.

Looking ahead — if the bunker stay pinned along the beach and the warm surface water holds, I don't see any reason the bluefish blitz backs off through the weekend. That's the play right now: chase the birds, work the edges of the bait schools, and don't be shy about running from Matinecock to Whitestone if one spot goes quiet. For bass, I'd be planning trips around the two hours before and after the tide change, after dark, at Execution or the Stepping Stones — bring eels if you can get them, or a big paddletail swum slow along bottom. Daytime bass fishing is going to stay tough until we get a real cool-down, and with this weather pattern, I wouldn't hold my breath for that anytime soon.

reports.headline: The West Cut Is Loading Bunker and Blues Are Cashing In
reports.subhead: Moriches Inlet's main channel is running deeper and tighter to the west jetty than it was in June — and the bait knows it.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the west jetty at Cupsogue on the last of the outgoing Tuesday morning and the current line told me everything I needed to know. The main scour channel has tightened up against the rocks — I'd guess it's pushed another ten, fifteen yards west since the spring blow reshaped things back in April. That's not unusual for this inlet. Moriches doesn't sit still. Every big northeast blow moves sand around inside that throat, and this year the deeper water is hugging the jetty tighter than it has in a couple seasons. What that means practically: the current is running harder and faster through a narrower slot, and anything moving bait through that cut is getting squeezed into a smaller, more concentrated lane. Bass, blues, whatever's out there — they don't have to work as hard to find the conveyor belt. They just sit on the edge of it.

And there's plenty riding that conveyor belt right now. We flagged this last week — said the bluefish blitz was coming as bunker pushed along the south shore beaches — and it's here. Cupsogue and the ocean beach stretch east toward Pikes Beach have had bunker schools pinned tight to the bar most mornings, and the blues have been working them hard enough to see it from the dune line. Birds diving, bunker getting nervous and bunching, then that telltale slick of oil and scale on the surface. If you're fishing the beach, get there at first light before the wind builds — poppers and metal, Ava 27s and 40s in bare or teaser-dressed, cast into the edge of the bait ball, not the middle of it. Blues in the 4 to 8 pound class, some bigger mixed in, and they're not fussy right now. The bite's been reliable enough that I'd call it the most dependable action in the zone this week, but it's also short-lived most mornings — an hour, hour and a half before the sun gets up and the bunker scatter into deeper water.

Striped bass is a different story, and it's the same story we're seeing up and down the coast this time of year. Surface water in the bay and along the beach has settled into that mid-70s range that pushes stripers off the daytime program entirely. I fished the inlet on an evening high this week and didn't touch a bass until the light was mostly gone — then had three fish in about forty minutes, all in that 26 to 30 inch window, working bucktails tipped with white Gulp along the deeper edge of that west channel scour, right where the current drops off into 12, 14 feet. That's the pattern to lean on right now: dusk into full dark, working the deeper cuts inside the inlet or the channel edges off Tuthill Point on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, when bait gets flushed out of the bay and funnels through that narrower western slot. Don't waste daylight hours on bass here unless you're fishing deep bay structure — the flats are too warm, fish have pulled off them.

Fluke are around but it's a grind, not a program. The bay-side humps off Smith Point and the deeper holes inside the inlet proper are holding fish, but you're sorting through a lot of shorts to find keepers. I had a decent day drifting the channel edge near the Coast Guard station with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, and the better fish — one going close to 5 pounds — came off the deeper side of the drift where the bottom drops from 8 feet to about 14 on the edge of the old scour hole. That deeper, cooler water is where the quality fish are sitting this time of year, same pattern you're seeing everywhere from here to the Great South Bay. Weakfish have been scarce for me this week — a few reports of fish coming out of the deeper bay channels near Pattersquash, but nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet.

Porgies are steady if unspectacular around the bridge structure and the bay side of the inlet rocks — bloodworms and squid strips on a hi-lo rig will keep you busy on the bottom stages of the tide, decent eating-size fish mixed with the usual shorts.

Looking ahead: as long as this bait stays pinned to the beach and the weather holds stable, I expect the bluefish blitz to keep running the ocean side through the week — that's the surest bet going right now. If we get a wind shift out of the southwest that pushes hard for a couple days, watch for that bunker to scatter and push into the bay itself, which could actually improve things for bass and weakfish on the inside if the bait relocates rather than disperses entirely. For bass, I'd keep working the dusk-to-dark window at the inlet's deeper cuts — that's where the fish are stacking with the water this warm, and until we get a real cooldown or a stretch of onshore wind that mixes the water column, that nighttime program is going to be the reliable one. Cupsogue at first light for blues, the inlet after dark for bass — that's my week, and it's a decent split if you've got the stamina for both ends of the day.

reports.headline: Bunker Pods Pinned in the Narrows — Blues Chewing, Bass Gone Nocturnal
reports.subhead: The bait tells the story this week: bunker balled up tight from the Norwalk Islands to Stratford Shoal, and everything with teeth is underneath them.
reports.body_markdown:
First thing I do every morning is stand on the bulkhead and watch what the bait's doing before I even look at a rod. This week the bunker told me everything. From the Norwalk Islands across to Charles Island, and pushing east toward Stratford Shoal, I'm seeing bunker schools balled up so tight they look like oil slicks from a distance — that nervous, flickering shimmer on the surface that means something's underneath pushing them. Terns are working them hard, diving and screaming, and every so often the whole pod erupts as blues come up through the middle of it.

That's the visible story on the Central Sound right now, and it's a good one. Bluefish have taken this bait and made it their own from the Norwalk Islands down through Stamford, Greenwich, and across to the Oyster Bay side. We flagged this pattern building over a week ago, said it would keep spreading as long as the bunker stayed pinned and the weather held calm — and here it is, right on schedule, still expanding. I had a report from a buddy running out of Norwalk who hit a blitz Tuesday morning off Sheffield Island that lasted a solid forty minutes, cocktail blues to 4 pounds crashing bunker on the surface, poppers and metal — Ava 27s, white bucktails with a strip of pork rind — getting bit on nearly every cast. That's the kind of action you drop everything for when you see the birds working.

The bunker themselves are the key variable here. Surface water in the mid-70s (Kings Point reading 70.9°F, and it's likely a touch warmer than that in the shallow coves by afternoon) has these bait schools pinned tight to structure, not roaming open water. That's exactly the kind of setup that concentrates predators instead of scattering them thin across the Sound. As long as we don't get a hard blow out of the southwest to break the bait apart, I'd expect the blitz activity to keep rolling along the Connecticut shoreline and spreading toward New Haven.

Striped bass are a different conversation entirely right now, and I want to be straight with you about it — daytime bass fishing in the Central Sound has gone quiet. Water's warm enough that the fish have pushed down onto the thermocline and gone nocturnal, which is the textbook mid-summer move. If you're bass hunting between 10 AM and 6 PM over Stratford Shoal or Middle Ground Light, you're better off vertical jigging deep — I'm marking fish in 45 to 60 feet on the shoal itself, working diamond jigs and 4-ounce bucktails tipped with a chunk of fresh bunker down to them. It's slow, deliberate fishing, not exactly exciting, but it's producing keeper-class fish in the mid-20s to low 30s for guys willing to work the sonar and drop right on the marks.

The better bass program right now is after dark, and that's not a secret to anyone who's fished this water a few summers. Norwalk Islands rock piles, the back side of Charles Island, the drop-offs around Middle Ground — all holding fish that come up shallow to feed once the sun's off the water. Live eels drifted on the current edges, or bucktails cast tight to the rocks and swum slow, have been the ticket. The neap tide we're coming off has softened the current through the deeper channels, which hasn't helped — less push means less concentrated feeding, and the bite's been more scattered than aggressive. That should change as we build back toward the next stronger tide cycle over the coming week, and when the current picks back up around the Norwalk Islands and Stratford Shoal, I expect the night bite to sharpen up considerably.

Fluke are in that classic summer pattern where quantity and quality have split apart. Shorts are everywhere — drift the flats off Oyster Bay or Port Jefferson Harbor and you'll bend a rod every few minutes, but most of them go back. The keepers are sitting deeper and cooler, and the better fish this week came from 35 to 50 feet along the channel edges off Port Jefferson and the deeper humps north of the Norwalk Islands, on the stronger half of the tide. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom, with a squid strip added for scent, has been the winning combo. Don't waste time on the shallow flats past mid-morning once the sun's cooking that water — push out to depth.

Porgies remain the most dependable meal-ticket fish on this beat right now. The reef structure off Eaton's Neck, around Middle Ground, and the rock piles near Charles Island are stacked with them, and a bag of clams with small hooks on a high-low rig will fill a cooler without much drama. Blackfish season's closed this stretch, so that's off the table until fall, but I'm already hearing chatter about early scouting trips once the season reopens.

Looking ahead, I'm watching two things closely. First, whether that bunker-bluefish blitz keeps its grip on the Connecticut shoreline or starts thinning out as bait disperses — if the calm weather holds, I'd bet on it spreading further toward New Haven before it breaks. Second, and more interesting to me, is the calendar. Bonito and albies typically start showing in the Sound's narrower stretches — right around Stratford Shoal and the Race — in the first half of August, and with this warm water pattern established early, I wouldn't be shocked to see the first scout report a little ahead of schedule this year. I'll be watching the bait for it, same as always.

reports.headline: Midnight on the Outgoing: Bass in the Cut, Bunker Getting Hammered on Both Tides
reports.subhead: With the moon waning and the bunker still stacked, the smart money is fishing dark and fishing the ebb — here's where and why.
reports.body_markdown:
Eleven-thirty last night I'm parked on the rocks at the east jetty, rod tip twitching in the dark, and I make the call I make most nights this time of year: I'm not fishing the incoming. I'm waiting for the outgoing to get some current under it, and I'm not casting until the tide's got teeth. That's the whole game right now at Shinnecock Inlet — patience, darkness, and current that means business.

Here's why. Surface water's pushed into the mid-70s across the bay and the inside of the inlet, and that's shoved the bass onto the nocturnal program same as everywhere else on the South Shore. Daytime, you might mark them deep on the drop-off by the Coast Guard station, but they're not eating much until the sun's off the water. So I've been showing up around 10 PM, rigging up on the jetty rocks or working the boat along the rip on the ocean side, and waiting for that outgoing current to really start ripping through the cut — usually a good hour to hour and a half after the tide turns at the bridge.

The pattern's been consistent: bass stacking in the deep hole just inside the inlet, the one that drops to 18-20 feet off the north side, using the current edge as a conveyor belt for whatever bait's getting flushed out of the bay. I've been throwing 2-ounce bucktails with a white or chartreuse curl-tail trailer, casting up-current and letting it swing down through the hole on a tight line, bouncing bottom the whole way. Eels have worked too — a 10-inch live eel drifted through that same seam on an outgoing tide after midnight has been my most consistent producer for fish in the 28-34 inch range, with a few better ones mixed in that I couldn't get a tape on before they let go.

Don't sleep on the jetty rocks themselves on a hard outgoing — bass will sit right in the wash where the current pushes around the rock pile, and a big paddle-tail swimbait worked slow through that foam has fooled some quality fish close enough to see them.

Now, the loud story in this zone right now is bluefish, and I flagged this one myself last week — said the bunker blitz would stay the dominant surf and inlet story until the bait dispersed or the wind broke it up, and that's exactly what's happening. Bunker schools are getting worked over hard right at the inlet mouth and along Tiana Beach, and the blues are chopping through them on both tide stages, not just the outgoing. If you want fast, aggressive action, that's daytime fishing — bring a metal, a Deadly Dick or an Ava jig, and cast into the nervous water where the bunker are getting pushed to the surface. It's not subtle. Blues to 8-10 pounds, sometimes bigger, and they'll cut a bucktail trailer to ribbons if you're not using wire.

Fluke has been the steady, unglamorous program it always is in late July. The flats out toward the middle of the bay, off Cormorant Point and along the edges of the channel toward the canal, are holding shorts in good numbers but the keepers want depth and current. I've had better luck working the deeper edges of the main channel on a stronger tide stage — incoming has been slightly better than outgoing for fluke specifically, which is the opposite of my bass program, so I'll sometimes split a session: fluke on the last of the incoming in daylight, then switch gears and wait for dark for the bass turn. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom in 15-20 feet, have been the ticket, with a squid strip added for scent when the bite's been finicky.

Weakfish at Ponquogue Bridge have been spotty — a few nice ones in the 4-6 pound class coming off the pilings on the outgoing at night, fished with a bucktail-and-bait combo or a bounced bunker chunk, but it's not the every-night thing it can be some Julys. I'd call it a bonus fish right now, not a target species you build a whole trip around. Worth a stop on your way out to the inlet if the tide's right, but don't expect fireworks.

Looking ahead, I don't see much changing in the next few days — the warm water's parked, the bunker aren't going anywhere fast, and that means bluefish stay the headline act while the bass keep working the dark hours. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it's been, I'd keep doing exactly what I'm doing: fishing the outgoing after 10 PM at the inlet, working the deep hole and the jetty wash with eels and bucktails, and using daylight hours for fluke on the bay flats when the tide's pushing hard. If a front comes through and breaks up that bunker concentration, watch for the blues to scatter and possibly push the bass into more predictable feeding windows at dawn — that's when I'd adjust and start fishing first light instead of last light. For now, though, the night owns this inlet, and I'm not changing my clock for anybody.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: bunker got the blues going wild, bass gone to bed
reports.subhead: Fluke are steady if you find the deep humps, but the real show at Fire Island right now is happening on the surface.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy pulls up to the fuel dock Tuesday morning, still shaking, telling me he ran out of the inlet at six and thought he'd hit a school of bass busting bait off Democrat Point. Wasn't bass. Wasn't even close. Blues, and I mean stacked — bunker getting shredded on the surface so hard the water looked like it was boiling from underneath. He said he threw a Deadly Dick into the mess and had three fish in the boat before he even got his motor properly shut off. That's been the story all week out here, and I told him straight: we called this one. Said last week the bunker-bluefish thing would keep spreading as long as the bait held and the weather stayed calm, and here we are — it's still going, maybe even better.

Let's talk about that first because it's the loudest thing happening on this beach right now. Bunker schools are pinned tight along the barrier beach from Democrat Point stretching east past Robert Moses, and the blues are working them like they've got something to prove. You don't need finesse for this — a bucktail with no trailer, a Hopkins, even a bare umbrella rig pulled through the edge of a blitz will get bit. The birds tell you where to look before your eyes do — wheeling, diving, sometimes just sitting on the water waiting for scraps. If you see gulls stacked up and working low over a patch of nervous water off the beach, point the bow there and don't overthink it. Blues in the 4 to 8 pound range, some bigger, and they're not shy about it in the morning or the evening. Midday sun seems to push the action tighter to the beach or drives it deeper for a stretch, but it comes right back with the tide change.

Striped bass, though — that's a different conversation, and I've had it about ten times this week at the dock. Ocean water's pushed into the mid-70s along the beach, and the bass have done what they do this time of year: gone deep, gone nocturnal, and stopped playing during daylight unless you're fishing structure that holds cooler water. If you want bass right now, you're getting up stupid early or staying out stupid late. Inside the inlet, working the seam off Democrat Point on the last of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, guys are still picking off fish on bunker chunks fished on the bottom, or bucktails with a swim shad trailer worked slow along the drop where the channel meets the flat. Best window has been that gray hour before real light, when the water's still holding the night's cooler temp. Once the sun gets up and starts baking the flats, the bite shuts like someone flipped a switch.

Fluke are the honest, unglamorous producer right now, and I'll take honest over flashy most weeks. The bay's warmed up enough that the shallow stuff is mostly short fish and bait-stealers — if you want keepers you've got to go find the deeper humps and channel edges where it stays a few degrees cooler. I've had good drifts in 25 to 35 feet off the Robert Moses bridges, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid for insurance. Slow drift, bounce it right off bottom, let the current do some of the work for you. The bite's better on the stronger stages of the tide — dead slack kills it fast out there this time of year. Same story working the deeper edges toward the inlet itself, where the current runs harder and keeps things stirred up and cool. Nothing crazy, but a solid keeper or two mixed into a pile of shorts is a fair day right now.

Weakfish and porgies have been quieter than I'd like to admit — porgies still around the reef structure and rubble patches inside the bay, biting on bloodworms and clam if you drop right on them, but it's not the kind of numbers game it can be in a good year. Blackfish, obviously, way off — that's an autumn conversation, not a July one.

Here's what I'd do if I had one shot this week. I'd be at Democrat Point before first light, throwing metal into whatever's busting on the surface — that bite's been reliable enough that it's worth building your whole morning around it. If the blitz hasn't started or has moved off, I'd shift into the inlet channel and work bunker chunks on the bottom through the last of the outgoing, hoping to connect with a bass working that current seam before the sun climbs too high. Afternoon, I'd go find fluke on the deeper humps off the bridges and grind out a limit the honest way.

Wind's been mild, seas offshore have had a little bump to them but nothing that's kept the inside water dirty, and as long as that bunker stays pinned along the beach I don't see any reason for the blues to slow down. If a front comes through and scatters that bait, this whole picture changes fast — so if you've got a window this week, I wouldn't wait on it.

reports.headline: Slack Water at Plum Gut — Time to Wait It Out
reports.subhead: The neap has gutted the current everywhere I fish, and the bass know it — here's where I'm putting my time until the tide rebuilds.
reports.body_markdown:
Two a.m. Wednesday, chest-deep on the Fishers Island side of the Gut, and I'm throwing a 2.5-ounce black Darter into what should be five knots of ripping current. Instead I get a lazy swirl, barely enough push to load the plug. That's the neap talking. We flagged this last week — said the first-quarter neap on the 21st would soften the Gut's current and change the presentation window, and that's exactly what's happened. The problem is it's softened it more than I wanted. This isn't the controlled, easier-to-work current we like — it's borderline dead water during the mid-stages of the tide, and the bass have noticed.

Here's the read: with Kings Point pushing 70.9 and even New London sitting at 69.4, the whole Sound's warm enough that stripers have gone full nocturnal, and they want current to ambush from. Take the current away and they scatter off the structure instead of holding tight to it. I worked The Race Tuesday night on the last of the max ebb — still got a push there, it holds current longer than the Gut on a neap — and connected on two bass in the mid-20s on a 3-ounce bucktail with a white pork rind trailer, bounced right along the eastern edge where the rocks drop into 40 feet. But the bite window was tight. Fifteen, twenty minutes around the peak, then it went dead calm and the fish just quit.

Plum Gut itself has been a grind. I fished it four nights this week and only two produced anything worth keeping — a 28-incher and a fish just under 30 that came off a swimming plug worked slow along the north side rip line, right where the sandy bottom meets the rock pile off Orient Point. Both fish came in that narrow window right before max current when the flow was building but not yet howling. That's the pattern right now — you're not fishing the peak, you're fishing the approach to the peak. Show up too early, nothing's moving. Show up right at max on a neap tide, there's not enough push to matter anyway. The sweet spot has shrunk to almost nothing, and if you're not standing in the right spot at the right ten minutes, you're just casting into flat water.

Fluke have actually been the more dependable program this week, which tells you something about how tough the bass bite's been. I've been picking up keeper-class fish to 21 inches on the drift off Plum Island in 35 to 45 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, working the deeper humps where the current still moves enough to keep bait stacked. Mixed in with a lot of shorts, but the quality fish are there if you're willing to grind through them. Same story as everywhere else in the Sound right now — warm shallow water has pushed the good ones deeper, and you've got to fish the humps and channel edges instead of the flats.

Blues have been sporadic out here compared to what's happening to the west. I haven't seen the kind of bunker-driven blitz that's tearing up the South Shore and pushing into western Long Island Sound, but I've had pockets of jumbo blues — eight, nine pounds — show up unannounced off Orient Point breaking on peanut bunker schools mid-morning. When that happens, it's fifteen minutes of chaos on top water poppers, then they're gone. Worth having a rod rigged and ready if you're out there, but I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet. If that bunker migration keeps pushing east like it has been west of here, that changes fast — and given how aggressively it's been spreading, I wouldn't be shocked to see a real blitz develop off Orient or Fishers Island within the week.

Porgies and blackfish have been the honest, blue-collar program right now — steady, not exciting, but they're feeding. I've been anchoring up on structure off Fishers Island in 25 to 30 feet, clam and green crab on standard porgy rigs, and putting decent numbers in the cooler even on the slower tide stages. That's your fallback when the current-dependent spots go quiet, and this week it's been a legitimate fallback, not a last resort.

Looking ahead: the moon's working toward full in early August, which means the current in the Race and the Gut should start rebuilding fast over the next several days as we move off this neap cycle. That's when I expect the bass bite to snap back into shape — the current edges will sharpen, the ambush points will reload, and the nocturnal feeding windows should get a lot more productive because the fish will actually have moving water to work with. If I had one night to fish this weekend, I'd wait for the current to build back toward the third or fourth day past the neap and hit the Race on the last two hours of the ebb, eel or a big swimming plug, right along that eastern rock edge in 35 to 45 feet. Until then, I'm splitting time between fluke on the humps and blackfish on structure, and I'm not wasting energy fighting dead water in the Gut waiting for a current that isn't there yet.

reports.headline: Marine Parkway at midnight: the bass are there, you just gotta wait for dark
reports.subhead: Daytime's dead in the bay, but the bridge and the inlet blues are keeping this a two-tide, two-species week worth working around.
reports.body_markdown:
I took the kayak out of the launch at Sunset Cove Tuesday morning because I figured I'd beat the heat and the boat traffic both. Wrong on the heat, right on the traffic — I had the flats mostly to myself by 6 a.m., which tells you something about where everybody else's head is at right now. Nobody wants to paddle in July soup unless they know something's biting, and honestly, that's fair. It's been a quiet week on the daytime program.

Here's the honest version: the bay has slid into that classic late-July pattern where the stripers just don't want to play during daylight. Water's sitting warm and stable, no wind to speak of, and that combination pushes bass off the flats and onto the thermocline or tight against deep structure where it's cooler. I marked fish on the sounder over by the Cross Bay Bridge pilings in about 14 feet and couldn't get so much as a look during the mid-morning hours. That's not bad luck, that's just where we are in the calendar.

So I've shifted my whole week to the night program, and if you want fish right now, you should too. Marine Parkway Bridge on the last two hours of the outgoing has been the most consistent thing I've fished all month. I've been running there by boat right at dusk, anchoring up-current of the pilings on the Rockaway side and drifting bucktails — half-ounce white with a strip of fresh bunker on the hook for scent — right down into the shadow line. The bass are stacking on that current edge waiting for whatever gets swept through, and they'll hold there most of the night once the tide gets moving good. Had three keepers in the 26 to 29-inch range last Thursday night working that exact drift, all right in that first hour of hard outgoing water. After the tide goes slack, it shuts off fast, so don't waste your whole night there — get in position, fish the push, then move.

For shore guys who can't get out at midnight, Breezy Point after dark is your play. Swimmers — I like a 6-inch Redfin in bone or bunker pattern — worked slow along the surf line where the beach drops into that first trough. You're fishing the edge where the bay water meeting the ocean creates just enough temperature break to hold bait, and the bass know it. It's not a numbers game out there right now, more like two or three solid fish a night if you put in the time and fish the two hours around the tide change.

Now the blues — this is the one story in the whole zone that doesn't require patience or darkness. We flagged this pattern building last week, said the bunker-driven blitz would keep spreading as long as the bait stayed put and the weather held calm, and that's exactly what's happening. Rockaway Inlet has had bluefish on bunker schools nearly every morning this week, visible from the beach at Beach 9th and Beach 90th, birds working right over the bait balls. If you can get out in a boat or even paddle the kayak out toward the inlet mouth, casting into those boils with a metal — I've been throwing a 2-ounce Hopkins in chrome — is about as close to guaranteed as this bay gets right now. Just watch your leader, these blues are chopping through 20-pound fluoro like it's nothing. I've gone to 40-pound mono leader just to stop losing lures every third cast.

Fluke fishing is the disappointment of the week, if I'm being straight with you. The flats between Ruffle Bar and Big Egg Marsh are still holding fish, but it's short after short after short. If you want a keeper, you need to get onto the deeper channel edges — I'm talking 18 to 22 feet along the edges of the Cross Bay Bridge channel — and slow-drift white Gulp Swimming Mullets on a 3/4-ounce bucktail right on bottom. That's where the bigger fish are hiding out from the heat. Don't waste your morning on the shallow grass flats unless you're fine with a bucket of shorts and no dinner.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. No real wind in the forecast, water's stable and warm, so I'd keep planning around the tides rather than the clock — fish the last two hours of any outgoing after sundown for bass, and hit the inlet at first light for blues while the bunker are still balled up tight. If a front comes through and stirs things up, that could actually help the daytime bass bite by mixing some cooler water back into the upper bay, but until that happens, I'm sticking with my night rod and my early alarm for the blues. Canarsie Pier folks, don't sleep on the blues either — they've been showing up along that stretch too when the tide's right, so it's worth a look even without a boat.

reports.headline: Skip the boat ramp line — the blues are stacked right off the beach at Jones
reports.subhead: Everybody's booking fluke charters for the bay while bunker schools get shredded to pieces thirty yards off the sand.
reports.body_markdown:
I had a guy at the bait shop this morning tell me he was heading out to drift Sloop Channel for fluke and I just about spit my coffee. Not because fluke's bad right now — it's fine, we'll get to it — but because he was driving right past the best fishing on this whole stretch of coast to go sit in a boat in the heat. The bluefish blitz is happening right now, right off the beach, and half the guys around here are still treating it like a footnote.

I said it last week and I'll say it again — this bunker-bluefish thing isn't slowing down, it's spreading. We flagged this pattern building and here it is in full swing: bunker schools are getting pinned against the jetty rocks at Jones Inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, and the blues are just wrecking them. I watched it happen three mornings this week from the rocks at the west end near the Coast Guard station — bait skying out of the water, birds diving, blues cutting through pods so hard you can hear it from fifty yards off. That's not subtle fishing. That's just showing up and not messing it up.

Tactics are dead simple right now and that's the beauty of it. I'm throwing a 2-ounce Hopkins Shorty or a bunker-colored Ava jig, no wire needed if you're not afraid of losing a few bucktails to bluefish teeth — but if you want to keep your gear, tie on 30 pounds of fluorocarbon leader minimum, because these fish are 4 to 10 pounds and they're not shy about biting through mono. Bombers and topwater poppers are also getting hit hard when the blitz comes up shallow, which it's been doing right around the last hour of the outgoing when bait gets squeezed against the rocks with nowhere to go. That's your window. Don't sleep past 6:30 AM out there — once the sun gets up and the tide slacks, the whole thing goes quiet until the next push.

Now for the bass — and I'll be straight with you, daytime striper fishing off the surf right now is basically dead. Water's pushed into the mid-70s along the beachfront and these fish know better than to sit in that soup during daylight. They've gone nocturnal on us, which means if you want stripers you're fishing dawn, dusk, or full dark. I've been working the Short Beach jetties right at first light, drifting live bunker on a fish-finder rig in maybe 12 to 15 feet right off the rocks, and picking up a few schoolies and the occasional slot fish in that 28 to 32 inch range. Nothing to write home about volume-wise, but it's honest work and it beats fishing empty water at noon. If you want a real shot at a bigger bass, fish the two hours around the bottom of the tide change at night with a bunker chunk sitting on the bottom in the deeper cuts off the inlet — that's where the bigger fish have been holding, out of the warm surface layer.

Fluke's steady, not spectacular. The drift through Sloop Channel and out toward the deeper water off Jones Inlet is still producing, but you've got to work for keepers. Shorts are everywhere — I mean everywhere, you'll go through two dozen before you find one that measures. The better fish, the 20-inch-plus stuff, are sitting in that deeper channel water, 25 to 35 feet, and they want the stronger tide stages. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along the bottom on the meat of the incoming or outgoing — that's been my producer. Don't bother drifting the shallow flats in the middle of the day right now, the water's too warm and the good fish have moved off it.

Weakfish are a genuine bright spot if you know where to look. I've been picking a few up in the deeper holes around the Wantagh Bridge pilings on the last of the outgoing, fishing bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, working it slow near bottom. Nothing like the old days but there's real life there this summer, more than I've seen in a few years, and if that pattern keeps building the way it has, this could turn into something worth chasing seriously by August.

Blackfish and porgies are basically off the table until the water cools — not worth your gas right now.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for the bluefish blitz to quit. Bunker are still thick along this beach and the weather's calm and stable, which is exactly the recipe that keeps bait pinned tight and blues fed. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it has been, I'd fish that same outgoing window at Jones Inlet again this weekend — same spot, same tide, same jigs. If a stiff northeast blow comes through and scatters the bunker, that could shut it down fast, so get out there while it's good instead of waiting for someone to tell you it's still going. For bass, keep it dark and keep it patient — that's the program until this heat breaks.

reports.headline: Robinson's Hole is loaded with silversides — no albie yet, but the table's set
reports.subhead: Bait is stacking in every rip from Woods Hole to Menemsha; fluke and scup are paying the bills while we wait on the first bonito flash.
reports.body_markdown:
Stand on the Robinson's Hole bridge an hour before the tide turns and you'll see it — silversides balled up so thick the water looks like it's got a pulse, terns working the edges, and every so often that little nervous ripple that makes your heart jump because for a half second you think it's a bonito push. It isn't. Not yet. But the bait is exactly where it needs to be, and that's the story of this week: the table is set, and we're just waiting on the guest of honor.

I've been running the rips — Robinson's, Quick's Hole, the backside of Nashawena — every day this week on the last two hours of the ebb, and the bait pattern is textbook late July. Peanut bunker are working down from Buzzards Bay proper, silversides are thick in the current seams, and there are enough sand eels showing on the sonar around the Sow and Pigs reef off Cuttyhunk to keep the stripers interested after dark. Water in the bay is sitting in the low 70s, which is warm enough that the bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal — I'm not seeing much daytime interest anywhere inside Buzzards Bay unless there's a hard tide and low light to go with it.

We flagged this pattern last week — said this stretch of water, Buzzards Bay through the Vineyard, is one of the first zones to watch for the albie and bonito push, typically showing in early-to-mid August as temps peak. Nothing confirmed yet on my end, no flashes, no reports off Menemsha or the Middle Ground, but Block Island's now sitting in that 68-degree comfort range that usually means bonito are close behind. I'd put money on the first scout fish showing at Robinson's or off Squibnocket within the next two to three weeks. Keep a bag of Deadly Dick or a small epoxy jig rigged and ready — when they show, they show fast, and you don't want to be re-spooling when the blitz starts.

In the meantime, fluke are doing the heavy lifting. The channel edges around Woods Hole and the sandy stretch off Quick's Hole have been holding fish all week, and the bite's been genuinely good — not spectacular, but consistent, which this time of year I'll take over a one-day miracle. Best drift has been over 20 to 35 feet of water on the last of the incoming into the first hour of the outgoing, when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping your bucktail sideways. White Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, tipped with a squid strip, dragged slow along bottom — that combo has out-produced everything else I've thrown. Had a mixed bag Tuesday with three fluke over 20 inches and a pile of scup mixed in around the same structure, fishing small strips of squid on light jigs right on bottom. Scup have been thick around any rock pile or mussel bed from Tarpaulin Cove down to Cuttyhunk — easy action if you want to fill a cooler while you wait on bigger things.

Striped bass are around, but you have to work for them right now. The bay water's warm enough that daytime fishing inside is mostly a waste of gas — I tried the flats off Naushon midday Wednesday and didn't get a sniff. Dawn and dusk at the Cuttyhunk rip, and especially after dark working eels or a swimming plug over the Sow and Pigs, that's where the keeper-class fish are showing. Nothing huge — mostly 26 to 32 inches — but a legit bite if you're willing to fish the hours nobody wants to fish. Menemsha basin at first light has also been worth a look, bass working the edge of the current where the bite starts to slack.

Bluefish have been the wildcard, showing up in the middle of the day when you least expect them, usually right on top of the same bait balls the terns are working. Had a solid 20 minutes off Tarpaulin Cove where blues in the 3-to-5-pound range tore through a school of peanut bunker like they were angry about something — poppers and small metal got bit fast and often before they moved off. Worth having a rod rigged for that specifically, because it comes and goes in a hurry.

We're heading into the July 21 neap, which is going to soften the current through these rips for the next several days — Robinson's and Quick's won't rip as hard, which actually widens the window for working bucktails and eels without getting swept off structure. If I had one day this week, I'd fish the Cuttyhunk rip at first light for bass, then slide into Robinson's Hole midday to watch bait and be ready if that first bonito flash finally shows. It's close. The water says so. We just need it to commit.

reports.headline: Stellwagen Edge in 120 feet: cod stacked on the gravel, haddock chewing the mud
reports.subhead: A soft neap tide has settled the bank down, and that's put steady groundfish in the box while the bluefin play hard to find.
reports.body_markdown:
120 feet on the Stellwagen Edge, gravel bottom, and the rod tip is doing that short, stuttering bounce that means cod. That's where I've had my best mornings this week — the northern edge where the gravel patches run up against the sand, water column reading clean down to about 60 feet before it goes gray and cold. Bottom temp's still holding in the low 50s even with the surface pushing toward 68. That split is exactly what you want in the third week of July — warm water up top holding the bait, cold water down deep holding the fish that matter.
