The cod have been on the smaller side but consistent — 3 to 8 pounds, a few better fish mixed in, taking clam bellies on a bucktail teaser rig fished tight to bottom. I'm not jigging hard out there right now, just lifting and dropping, letting the sinker find the gravel and feeling for that tick. The bigger fish have been coming off the steeper drops on the northeast corner of the Edge, where the gravel gives way fast into deeper water. If you're marking bait balls tight to bottom on the sounder, that's your spot — drop right through them.

Haddock have been the more reliable box-filler, and Middle Bank in 100 to 110 feet of mud has been the address. Diamond jigs with a green tube and a squid strip trailer have been doing the damage, worked with short, sharp lifts a foot or two off bottom. The neap tide we're sliding into off this first-quarter moon has actually helped here — less current means better bottom contact, less scope on the line, and the haddock have been stacking up thick enough that a good drift can put a dozen keepers in the cooler before you drift off the school. Tillies Bank has been giving up a similar mixed bag — haddock with some pollock mixed through the water column, especially up higher, 40 to 60 feet down, where the pollock like to hang off the structure edges chasing bait.

The bluefin have been the trickier story. We're seeing them — mackerel schools have been thick over the Basin and along the southern flank of the bank, and the whale activity out there has been about as good as I've seen it all year, humpbacks working sand eel pods right up on the surface in 90 to 120 feet of water off Tillies. Tuna are following that same bait, but they've been scattered and moving, not parked. Some days you run out and find them busting mackerel right on top and it's an easy troll pass with green machines and a spreader bar; other days you burn three hours covering the Basin and Carter Canyon approaches and never see a fin. That's the pattern coastwide right now with the trophy fishery closed since the start of the month — the slot fish, 27 inches up to just under 47, are around in decent numbers, but they're not holding still for anybody. Best luck has come to boats willing to run and gun off visible bird work and busting bait rather than anchoring on yesterday's numbers.

What's driving all of it is that soft current. First-quarter neap tides don't push bait the way a new or full moon does, so instead of getting concentrated pushes of sand eels and mackerel funneling through specific rips, we're getting looser, more spread-out bait fields — good for groundfish sitting tight to structure, tougher for tuna that want that bait pinned up against a hard edge. I'd expect that to change some as we build back toward the full moon at the end of the month, when the current picks back up and starts squeezing that bait tighter against the edges and canyons.

For this coming week, if I've only got one day, I'm starting on the Stellwagen Edge gravel early, working the cod bite before the sun gets high, then sliding over to Middle Bank for haddock on the back half of the tide once the current's really laid down. If the mackerel show thick and tight on the sounder anywhere along the southern flank, I'll pull the groundfish gear and put the troll spread out for an hour — those windows have been short but real. Carter Canyon's edge is worth a look too if you're running a bigger boat and want a shot at larger tuna passing through on the deeper contours, but I wouldn't build a whole day around it right now. Best case, the bait tightens up as we move off this neap and the bluefin start pinning against the edges again. If it stays loose and scattered like it has been, I'd rather bank a solid trip of cod and haddock than chase ghosts on the surface.

reports.headline: Great Point Boils on the Ebb — Bass and Blues Show, Bonito Still a Rumor
reports.subhead: The rip at Great Point is loaded with bass and blues on the low-light tides, but two weeks of watching for the first bonito has come up empty — for now.
reports.body_markdown:
I was standing on the beach at Great Point Thursday morning, coffee going cold in my hand, watching a knot of terns work a rip line about 200 yards off the lighthouse. My first thought — every year around this date it's my first thought — was bonito. That tight, nervous diving pattern, the way the birds hover and drop instead of wheeling wide. I grabbed the binoculars and it wasn't bonito at all. It was bluefish, chopping through a pod of sand eels hard enough to turn the surface white, with a few bigger swirls underneath that I'd bet money were bass working the leftovers. Still a good sight. Just not the sight I've been waiting on.

That's where we sit in Nantucket Sound right now — a genuinely productive bass-and-blues bite riding on top of a bonito watch that's stretching into its third week without a confirmed fish. The water's warmed into a range that should be comfortable for them — Montauk's been reading right around 69°F, and the Sound tends to track close behind that number this time of year — so the ingredients are there. I just haven't put my hands on one, and I haven't heard from anybody on this island who has either. When it happens it usually happens fast, so keep a rod rigged with something small and shiny — a half-ounce Deadly Dick or a Yo-Zuri epoxy jig — every time you're anywhere near a rip.

While we wait, the striper fishing has settled into the pattern you'd expect with the water this warm — low light or nothing. Dawn and dusk at Great Point are producing the most consistent action, with fish stacked on the north side of the rip where the ebb dumps bait around the point. Bunker chunks fished on the bottom in 15 to 20 feet have been drawing keeper-class bass after dark, and at first light the same water gives up fish to a Danny swimmer or a Gibbs pencil worked slow across the seam where the clean water meets the churn. Monomoy's doing the same trick on its own schedule — the rips off the north end and down toward the Powder Hole are holding bass that feed hard on the last two hours of the ebb and go quiet fast once the sun climbs. If you're fishing Monomoy or Chatham inlet in daylight, you're mostly fishing for bluefish, and there are plenty of them — solid choppers in the 3 to 6 pound class hammering topwater plugs and bucktails wherever bait gets pushed against structure.

The real bright spot this week, if I'm honest, is fluke. Nantucket Shoals and Horseshoe Shoal have both been throwing quality fish, and it's been steady enough that a few boats out of the island have made it their whole day rather than a stop on the way to somewhere else. Structure and channel edges in 25 to 35 feet are the play — drifting white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid when the current's really moving. The bite's been best on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, right when the water's got some push but hasn't gone slack. We're coming off today's first-quarter neap, so the current through the Shoals and around Horseshoe won't be screaming this week — that's actually good news for the fluke game because it widens the window where the drift speed stays in that sweet, manageable zone instead of blowing you through the good bottom in ten minutes.

That softer neap current is worth factoring into your bass and blue plans too. Monomoy and Chatham's rips depend on a hard-running tide to really turn on, and with the moon in its quieter phase this week, expect the bite windows to stretch out rather than concentrate into one short, violent hour. That can mean less frantic top-water blitzing but more time on the water when fish are willing — a fair trade if you're working around a day job and can only get out for a few hours.

Looking ahead, I'd keep doing what I've been doing — working the low-light hours at Great Point and Monomoy for bass, running metal through any bluefish activity you find, and hitting the Shoals or Horseshoe on the better half of the tide for fluke. On the bonito front, I'd start checking the temperature breaks off Sankaty and the outer edge of the Shoals every time you're out there, because if the regional warming trend holds, this is exactly the kind of week they show up without much warning. When that first one gets caught, you'll hear about it inside a day — this island doesn't keep that kind of secret for long.

reports.headline: Race Point on the neap: bass to 30 on live mackerel while the rip goes quiet
reports.subhead: The tide slowed down this week and so did we — but the bass and the mackerel didn't mind one bit.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, half past five, I had the engine cut off Race Point and we were just drifting — no push from the current, no chop, just the boat easing along like it was on rails. My sternman Pauly leaned over the rail and said, "Donny, this don't feel like the Race." And he was right. We're coming off a first-quarter neap, and out here that means the rip that usually snaps your line taut and makes you brace against the gunwale was barely moving. Some guys hate neap water. I don't mind it. It spreads the bite out instead of cramming it into twenty minutes of slack, and this week that's exactly what it did.

We marked a thick pod of mackerel stacked about eighteen feet down on the sounder, right where the bar drops off into deeper water north of the Point, and we started jigging a few for the well. Didn't take long — small hooks, no weight, and they came over the rail two and three at a time. Once we had eight or ten flopping in the bucket, we rigged them live on 5/0 circle hooks, balloon set about twelve feet under a slip float, and drifted them back over that same edge. First fish came within ten minutes — low twenties, nothing to write home about, but a keeper is a keeper. Then around 6:15 the drag started peeling and Pauly's rod bent into something with real shoulders. Twenty minutes later we had a thirty-one pounder in the net, fat, chrome, full of herring. That's been the pattern all week off Race Point and down along Peaked Hill Bars — not a blitz, but a steady, honest bite on live mackerel and menhaden chunks, best in that first hour of light and again as the sun's dropping, though I'll say the Bay's cooler water has kept a few fish willing to eat through the middle of the day too, which is more than I can say for the beaches south of the Cape right now where the bass have gone strictly nocturnal in that warm water.

Billingsgate has been the story for anybody wanting bottom fish. We've been running out there in 35 to 55 feet, working the edges of the shoal where the bottom breaks up into rubble and mussel bed, and the haddock have cooperated better than I expected for late July — fish from 17 inches up to a nice 6-pounder on diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, worked with a slow lift-drop right off bottom. Cod have been mixed in but scattered, mostly smaller fish, and you have to hunt for them a bit more than the haddock. If you're drifting Billingsgate, keep an eye on your speed — anything over half a knot and you're dragging your jig sideways instead of working it. Neap tide again works in your favor here; slower drift means more time in the strike zone.

Down toward Sandy Neck and into the Barnstable flats, fluke fishing has held up about as well as anywhere on the whole coast this summer. We've been drifting the channel edges off the Neck in 15 to 25 feet, dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, tipped with a sliver of squid for insurance, and picking through a lot of shorts to find keepers in the 18 to 22 inch range. Best water has been the last two hours of the incoming, when clean water pushes across the flats and pulls bait with it. Nothing dramatic, but steady — the kind of fishing where if you put in three or four hours you'll have fish for dinner.

Bluefish have shown up behind the bunker schools that have been working their way along the beach from Barnstable up toward the Neck — we flagged this pattern a couple weeks back, said the blues would follow the bunker up the coast, and sure enough they're here now, chopping through pods in the wash close to shore, visible some mornings right off the beach in Sandy Neck's surf line. Nothing like the blitzes they're seeing further south, but enough that if you see the bunker balled up and nervous, it's worth a few casts with a metal lip swimmer or a topwater popper before you move on.

Looking ahead, the neap tide's going to keep softening through the weekend before the current starts building back toward the next full moon push. That's going to keep widening the bite windows at Race Point and Peaked Hill — good news if you're working live bait and don't want to be a slave to a thirty-minute slack. I'd focus mornings on the Race with mackerel, midday on Billingsgate for haddock if the wind stays manageable out of the southwest, and save the last light for a pass along Sandy Neck watching for bunker and blues working the surf. If the wind swings northeast and kicks up any real sea, Billingsgate gets ugly fast in that shallower water, so keep an eye on the forecast before you commit to a long run out there. Otherwise, it's been an honest week on the Bay — nothing explosive, but steady enough that anybody willing to put in the drift time is coming home with fish.

reports.headline: President Roads on the Ebb: Bass on Live Mackerel, Blues Push Into Broad Sound
reports.subhead: Cooler Gulf of Maine water is keeping the harbor's bass feeding through daylight while bluefish finally show off Nahant.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Monday morning standing at the wheel with coffee going cold — harbor this week, not the North Shore rocks. The forecast is stable, the neap tide off the first-quarter moon is softening the current through President Roads, and when the water's not ripping through there I can work the edges slow with live mackerel instead of fighting a four-knot drift. That's the kind of week to fish structure patiently instead of covering ground, and it paid off.

Deer Island Light has been the honest producer. I've been anchoring just off the north face on the last two hours of the outgoing, live mackerel on a three-way rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in eighteen to twenty-two feet, and it's been steady — not blazing, but steady. Bass from 26 to a fat 34 inches, with a handful of shorts mixed in that tell you there's a real class of fish working that drop. The mackerel schools stacked around the light are doing the heavy lifting here. Snag one on a small diamond jig, drop it right back down on a wide-gap hook, and let it swim naturally into the current seam off the ledge. That's the whole program. No need to overthink it.

Spectacle Island's north side has been giving up similar fish on the same tide stage, though it's more of a drift-and-cast deal — soft plastics, 4-inch white paddletails on 3/8-ounce jigheads, worked along the rocky face where the current wraps around the point. That spot fishes better right at the top of the tide through the first hour of the ebb, before the neap current really gets moving.

Flounder are still around on the flats inside Deer Island, though the bite there has cooled from where it was a couple weeks back — sandworms and squid strips on a spreader rig, fished dead slow on the slack around low water, still worth thirty minutes if you're already in the neighborhood. I wouldn't make a special trip for it right now.

The real story this week is bluefish showing up in numbers off Nahant and pushing into Broad Sound behind the mackerel schools. We flagged this pattern building along the coast a few weeks back — blues following bait wherever it holds — and here it is, right on our doorstep. Boils have been visible off the Nahant causeway in the mornings, blues slashing through mackerel pods in open water, and a chrome popper or a 2-ounce Deadly Dick worked fast through the melee will get bit hard. Bring wire leader or expect to lose a few. These aren't giants — mostly two to four pounds — but they're aggressive and they've turned a slow morning of casting into something worth getting out of bed for.

Gloucester and Cape Ann have been quieter than I'd like to report. The rocky structure around Brace Cove and out toward Halibut Point is still holding bass, but it's a low-light game right now — first light and last light, eels or a soft-plastic jerkbait worked slow along the boulder fields. Daytime has been tougher out there than in the harbor, which tells me the bass on the open coast are getting more particular as the sun climbs, even with Gulf of Maine water keeping things cooler than anywhere south of the Cape. That daylight window we usually count on up here hasn't completely closed, but it's narrower than a normal July.

Haven't run south to Plymouth or Duxbury Bay yet this week — that's next on the list if the neap holds and the wind stays light out of the southwest like it's been. Kingston Bay flats should be warming nicely for flounder and there's usually a decent striper push working the edges of Duxbury Bay on the last of the incoming, but I want a full tide cycle down there before I put my name on it.

Looking ahead, I'd stick with the harbor through the weekend. The neap tide means longer, more workable bite windows instead of a tight thirty-minute current slam, and that favors the live-mackerel program at Deer Island and the popper bite off Nahant. If the wind stays out of the southwest and holds under 10 knots, I'd also make the run to Gloucester for an early-morning shot at the rocks before the boat traffic and the sun push those bass deep. Cod and haddock reports remain thin close to shore this time of year — that's a fall conversation, not a July one. For now, it's mackerel, structure, and reading the tide right, which is exactly how this harbor likes to be fished in the middle of summer.

reports.headline: East End's 5:42 Ebb: Stripers Hold the Rip, Blues Crash the Mackerel
reports.subhead: A softening neap current is stretching the bite window at both ends of the Canal, and the night shift is carrying the load.
reports.body_markdown:
5:42 AM, East End, current running maybe 3.8 knots on the ebb — down a full knot and a half from what I clocked on the last new moon two weeks back. That's your first-quarter neap talking, and if you've fished this ditch as long as I have you know exactly what that number means: softer push, longer window, fish spread out a little more instead of getting pinned against the rip in a tight 90-minute burst. That's the story of this week on the Canal, and it's a decent one if you're willing to work around it instead of fighting it.

The East End rip off the Herring Run and down toward the Cribbon revetment has been the most consistent thing going, but only on the two bookend tides — the last hour of the dawn ebb and the first hour of the dusk flood. Stripers are stacked on the current seam where the outflow meets the bay water, and they're eating mackerel-pattern swimmers hard. I've had guys doing well on 7-inch Bomber Long A's in mackerel and on the Gibbs Danny-style poppers worked with a slow subsurface wobble right through the seam. Bluefish are mixed right in on the same water — some real cocktail-to-3-pound blues busting bait on top mid-tide, which tells you there's still mackerel and silversides getting pushed through the ditch on that current. If you see the birds working tight over the rip instead of scattered, that's your green light — get a bucktail or a Deadly Dick down through it on the drop before the blues shred it, then work topwater once the sun's fully up.

West End's been the sneaky better bite for guys willing to fish it after dark, and this is exactly what we flagged last week — that night fishing was going to carry the Canal through the heat of summer, and that's precisely what's happening. Water temp in the ditch is holding cooler than the bay flats on either side, and the bass know it. They're sliding up onto the current seams off the Herring Run jetty and down toward the Days Beach side on the tail of the flood, laying in the eddies where the current curls behind the rocks. Eels — 10 to 12 inch, fished on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom without killing the swim — have been the most consistent producer from about an hour before to an hour after the top of the tide. Guys throwing bucktails, the white-and-chartreuse ¾-ounce with a curl-tail trailer, worked slow along bottom on the last two hours of the ebb, have been picking off keeper-class fish too, mostly in that 28 to 34 inch range with the occasional better one mixed in.

Fluke have been the honest bite for anyone who wants a daytime option while the stripers sulk through the bright hours. Mashnee flats and the channel edge off Hog Island have both been giving up decent numbers on the last two hours of the incoming, drifting Gulp Swimming Mullets in white on ½-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid when the current's really moving. Nothing giant — most fish 16 to 19 inches with a few pushing 20 — but it's steady enough to fill an afternoon when the sun's got the stripers locked up tight to structure and unwilling to eat.

Phinneys Harbor and the water off Wings Neck are still a bonito watch more than a bonito bite — nobody's iced one yet that I've heard of — but Buzzards Bay water is creeping into that range where they typically show, and I wouldn't be shocked to hear of the first scout fish in the next two to three weeks if this settled weather holds. Worth running a few casts of a small Deadly Dick or an epoxy jig through any nervous water or diving terns you see out there, just in case one shows early. No albies confirmed yet either, but that's the same clock — mid-to-late summer temperature break, and we're getting close.

Here's what I'd do this week: fish the bookend tides at the East End for the mackerel-and-blues combo, and save your best effort for a night session at the West End on the flood if you can manage the hours — that's where the better-class stripers have been living while the current's soft. The neap is going to keep easing through the next few days before the tide starts building back toward the full moon, which means the aggressive, short-window bite at both ends will stretch out a bit longer than usual — good news if your schedule doesn't line up perfectly with peak current, bad news if you're used to a hard 45-minute window and nothing else. Keep an eye on the surface for nervous bait and diving birds, because with mackerel still running through the ditch, that's where the next blitz is going to show. And don't sleep on fluke as your daytime fallback — with stripers mostly a low-light game right now, that channel edge bite off Hog Island is the difference between a slow trip and a good one.

reports.headline: Monhegan pollock on top, Penobscot haddock deep, and a lobsterman's bycatch tells the real story
reports.subhead: Cool Gulf of Maine water is keeping stripers feeding through the day from Boothbay to Eastern Egg Rock while groundfish hold tight to Penobscot Bay's channels.
reports.body_markdown:
Had a call Tuesday morning from a fellow I've hauled traps near off Two Bush Island for going on twenty years. Said he pulled a trawl up through a school of stripers thick enough he had to shoo them off his buoy line, right there in forty feet of water at ten in the morning. Now, that's not something you'd have seen much of ten years back — bass working open water in broad daylight, midweek, no birds working, no bait busting the surface. But that's exactly what this Gulf of Maine water is doing to the pattern this July. While the water south of the Cape has pushed the bass into feeding at night and around the edges of light, our water up here hasn't warmed enough to shove them off that daytime bite. It's one of the few advantages we get for running colder than everybody south of us, and right now it's paying off.

The Damariscotta River mouth and the ledges off Ocean Point have both been holding stripers this week, schoolies mostly, up to maybe 28 inches, with a scattering of better fish mixed in on the bigger tides. Soft plastics — 5-inch white or bone Slug-Go rigged weightless, worked slow over the eelgrass edges on the last two hours of the incoming — have outfished bucktails most mornings. If you want to put a bigger fish in the boat, live mackerel under a slip float off Fisherman Island has been the ticket at first light, though you'll need to catch your own bait, which this week hasn't been hard.

Eastern Egg Rock is fishing the way it does every July — puffins overhead, bass underneath. The bass there have been holding tight to the ledge on the northeast corner, feeding on the pollock fry and sand eels that pile up when the tide runs hard. Best window is the last hour of the ebb into the first hour of slack, working eels or a 3/4-ounce bucktail with a white curl-tail trailer down along the rockweed line. It's not a five-fish-a-drift bite, but it's steady, and the fish have run a decent average size — mid-20s to low-30-inch class.

Monhegan is where I'd send anybody looking for a mixed bag worth the run. The pollock have been thick on top around the Washington Ledges and off the back side toward White Head, chasing bait right at the surface on calm mornings — you can see them roll before you even rig up. Diamond jigs, the 4-ounce chrome ones, worked with a fast retrieat and a pause, will connect on pollock to eight or nine pounds. Underneath them, in 90 to 120 feet on the drop-offs south of the island, cod and haddock have been coming up on herring-tipped jigs, though I'll be honest — the haddock bite has been spotty this week, better on the last two hours of the ebb than anywhere else in the tide. You've got to be willing to work the drift and not just anchor and hope.

Penobscot Bay itself has settled into its summer groundfish pattern — cod and a few haddock holding in the deeper channels off Vinalhaven and North Haven, 130 to 170 feet, where the water stays cool enough to keep them comfortable through the warm stretch. Jigging bait-imitation soft plastics or a straight diamond jig tipped with clam has worked better than trolling down there this week. The current in that part of the bay runs hard enough that you want the tide working with you, not against — plan your drift for the last of the ebb or the first hour of the flood and you'll cover the fish without dragging bottom the whole way.

We called this one last week when we said the bunker-driven bluefish pattern would keep spreading up the coast as long as the weather held calm — and sure enough, we're finally seeing a few scattered blues mixing into the mackerel schools off Stonington and around Isle au Haut, though nothing close to a real run yet. Worth keeping a metal jig tied on if you're mackerel fishing off the Deer Isle bridge or the Stonington breakwater, because when those blues show, they show fast and clear out just as quick.

The moon goes first quarter this week, which means we're sliding into a neap tide — softer current, less water moving, and that tends to widen the bite windows rather than shrink them, especially through tighter spots like Eggemoggin Reach and the Deer Isle Thorofare. If you've had trouble timing the rip at those spots on the big tides, this is your week to fish them without fighting three knots of current the whole time. I'd expect the striper pattern to hold steady through the weekend as long as we don't get a stretch of southerly wind pushing warm water up the bay — that's the one thing that could push these fish back into a low-light pattern like everywhere south of us. Barring that, fish the tide, watch for the pollock rolling on top at Monhegan, and don't be surprised if a lobsterman tells you where the bass are before any chart does.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock steady on the neap: mackerel thick, bass working the tide seams
reports.subhead: Cooler Gulf of Maine water is keeping Casco Bay's striper bite going through daylight while the rest of the coast goes nocturnal.
reports.body_markdown:
I was out past Peaks Island Tuesday morning, engine idling, watching a raft of gulls work a patch of water no bigger than my old lecture hall, when the surface just erupted with mackerel. Hundreds of them, maybe more, driven up by something underneath — I never did see what, though I'd wager bluefish given how the school scattered and regrouped twice before I got a line in. That's the tell for this bay right now: the bait is here, it's dense, and it's drawing everything up through the water column instead of pinning fish to the bottom after dark, which is the story everywhere south of us.

The mackerel run has been the backbone of the week. Diamond jigs — the small ones, half-ounce to an ounce, in chrome or that green-and-yellow combination — are still filling coolers off Peaks, off the eastern side of Cushing, and out toward Halfway Rock itself. Mackerel trees work too if you want volume for bait, and that's really the point: everyone I've talked to at the co-op is jigging mackerel first thing not to eat them but to have fresh bait rigged for bass and cod by mid-morning. A lively mackerel on a stinger rig, drifted along the current seam off Halfway Rock in 40 to 60 feet, has been the most consistent producer for stripers this week — better than plugs, better than soft plastics, at least when the sun's up.

And that's the piece worth understanding. The Gulf of Maine's cooler water is doing us a favor. While the Sound and the water south of the Cape have pushed their keeper bass into a dawn-dusk-and-dark pattern because the shallows are too warm to hold fish comfortably in daylight, our water hasn't hit that threshold yet. Stripers are still willing to feed at ten in the morning on the ledges off Bailey Island and around Cape Small, provided there's current moving. That's the catch this week — provided there's current moving. We're coming off the first-quarter neap, so the swings are soft, and I found the bite noticeably slower through the dead stretch of slack water than it was on the push of the flood. If you're fishing the Bailey Island ledges or the drop-off south of Jewell, plan around the tide, not the clock. An hour either side of max flow has been outfishing anything at slack by a wide margin.

Bluefish have shown up in real numbers along the same lines as the mackerel — no surprise there, since they're feeding on the same bait. I had two respectable blitzes reported to me from the Peaks Island backside and one off Two Lights, blues in the three-to-five-pound class chopping through pogies on the surface. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, Hopkins in the one-ounce range — have been the ticket when they're up top. We flagged this pattern building last week, that bluefish would keep following bunker and staying active as long as the weather held calm and the bait didn't scatter, and that's exactly what's played out here. The stable high pressure we've had has kept the bait pods tight instead of pushing them off the structure.

Groundfish have been steadier than showy, which is about right for this time of year. Cod and haddock are still coming off the deeper structure around Halfway Rock — 70 to 90 feet on the down-current side — on clam bait and diamond jigs worked slow off bottom. Nothing to write home about in terms of size; most of what's coming over the rail is in the 18 to 24-inch range, with the occasional better haddock mixed in. I'd call it a keep-two-for-dinner fishery right now rather than a fill-the-cooler one, and anyone telling you different this week probably isn't being straight with you. The soft neap current has actually helped the bottom bite some — easier to hold position and keep bait in the strike zone without a heavy sinker dragging you off the ledge.

What surprised me a little was how quiet Harpswell Sound itself has been compared to the open ledges. I made two passes through there hoping to find bass working the mussel beds on the last of the outgoing and came up with nothing but a single schoolie. The fish seem to want the harder structure and the current lines right now — Halfway Rock, the Bailey Island ledges, the mouth of Cape Small — rather than the softer bottom inside the sound. Worth remembering if you're planning a trip based on last month's pattern.

Looking ahead, if the mackerel schools hold through this week — and there's no reason yet to think they won't, the water's clean and the bait's thick — I'd expect the bass bite off Halfway Rock and Bailey Island to stay a daylight game a while longer. The moon moves toward full over the next week, which will build the tide swings back up and likely sharpen those current-seam bites considerably. If I had one morning to fish, I'd be jigging mackerel at first light off Peaks, then running that bait straight out to the Rock to fish the last two hours of the incoming. That's where I'll be.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's holds 200 on the mud: haddock stacked thick, cod tucked tight to the gravel edge
reports.subhead: A stable July high kept the ledge fishable all week, and the first scattered bluefin showed on sand eel patches north of Platts.
reports.body_markdown:
Two hundred and five feet on the north end of Jeffrey's Ledge, soft mud bottom, and the sounder painted haddock stacked eight to ten feet off the bottom in a wall that ran the length of two drifts. That's the number I want to see in late July — haddock don't hold tight to structure the way cod do, they sit up over the mud in loose schools and you catch them on the drift with a standard hi-lo rig, size 6/0 hooks, clam or squid strip, jigged slow off the bottom. We had a mixed bag of keeper haddock in the 22 to 26 inch class out there Tuesday, with the biggest fish coming right at the top of a slow drift as the tide started to turn.

Cod is a different game entirely, and this is where the bottom type matters more than anything else I can tell you. You want the gravel — the hard, broken bottom on the transitions where mud gives way to rock, particularly along the western edge of Jeffrey's where it drops from 180 into the deeper basin toward Scantum. That's where we found cod this week, not big numbers but quality fish, several in the 8 to 12 pound range, caught on diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, worked right on bottom with short hops. Cod don't like to be pulled far off structure this time of year — keep the jig within a few feet of bottom and let the boat's drift do the work. Platts Bank produced similarly on its gravel patches, though it took more running around to find them concentrated versus just scattered singles.

Pollock were mixed in wherever there was current moving bait — we picked up a few nice pollock in the 8 to 15 pound class suspended mid-water over Jeffrey's, and those fish will eat a diamond jig worked faster and higher off bottom than you'd fish for cod. Hake showed up mostly at first light and last light, typical pattern, soft bites down deep in the basin areas where the mud runs 220 feet plus. Nothing to build a trip around but a welcome bonus in the box.

Mackerel have been thick enough this week that we didn't need to buy bait — small schools showing on the sounder in 40 to 60 feet as we ran out past Cape Ann, and a few passes with Sabiki rigs filled the tuna tubes before we ever got to the ledge. That mackerel, along with a good showing of sand eels working the surface north of Platts, is exactly what's pulling the first bluefin through. We had two fish come up on a spread trolled with green machines and a naked ballyhoo north of Platts Bank on Thursday, neither one stuck, but the sign was real — birds working, bait balled up tight, occasional boils. This is early for giants on the ledge; the real showing typically doesn't stack up here until September and into October when the big fish push through chasing herring and mackerel in earnest. What we're seeing now is scattered fish moving through on the sand eel bite, opportunistic, not settled in yet. If you want to put time into tuna right now, I'd stay mobile — work the edges where birds are diving rather than anchoring your hopes on one spot, and have both trolling gear and a couple of stand-up rods rigged with live mackerel ready if you find a workable pod.

We're coming off a new moon push into a first-quarter neap this week, and on the ledge that matters — less current means the drift over the mud slows down, which is actually a plus for haddock fishing because your bait stays in the strike zone longer instead of getting swept through too fast. Cod fishing on the gravel gets a little tougher with less current moving bait around, so I found myself working smaller pieces of structure more methodically rather than covering as much ground. Weather's been the real story behind the consistency — stable high pressure held through most of the week, seas running one to two feet on the ledge most days, which let us fish the outer grounds like Tillies Bank and the Stellwagen approaches without losing a day to weather. That's not something to take for granted in the Gulf of Maine in July.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the mud on Jeffrey's for haddock while that pattern holds — it's been the most dependable fishery of the week by a good margin. For cod, stick to the gravel transitions and don't expect big numbers, just quality if you're patient and willing to move when a spot goes quiet. The tuna picture is still forming. If the sand eel patches hold through the weekend and mackerel stay thick along Cape Ann, I'd expect more scattered bluefin sign on the ledge, but it's too early to call it a pattern worth building a dedicated trip around just yet. Best case, that bait stays put through the neap and we start seeing fish stick on the troll rather than just showing and disappearing. If it scatters east toward Stellwagen like it sometimes does this time of year, I'll shift the search out that way and report back.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool Incoming Hour Still Owns July — Bass to 28, Blues Crash Higgins on Bunker
reports.subhead: A neap tide softened the rips but the bass never got the memo — and the bluefish finally found the beach in daylight.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday evening, incoming tide at the Pool, a guy I've fished next to for maybe fifteen years hooks a bass on a black-and-purple Danny plug that damn near pulled him off the rock. Twenty-eight inches, fat as a football, came up through that channel current like it owned the place. That's the Pool doing what the Pool does on the last two hours of the flood — bait gets squeezed through the gut between the beach and the ledges, and the bass sit right on that seam waiting for the buffet line to start. Best hour of the striper day in this state, and it hasn't slowed down one bit.

We're coming off the first-quarter neap now, which means the big swings are behind us for the moment and the current through spots like the Pool channel and the Saco River mouth isn't ripping the way it was two weeks back. That's not a bad thing. Softer current widens the window — instead of a tight forty-five minutes where the plug bite turns on, I'm getting closer to ninety minutes of good water on both sides of peak flood. If you've been showing up right at the tide change and leaving disappointed, push your window out. The fish are more forgiving right now, not less.

Cooler Gulf of Maine water is still the story north of Boston, and it's the reason this whole stretch is fishing better in daylight than anything south of the Cape right now. Down in the warmer water they're pushing bass into night-only patterns. Up here the fish are still willing to eat at ten in the morning if the bait's moving. I had a solid daytime session off Prouts Neck this week on a southwest wind — that wind pushes a little chop onto the outside rocks and gets the bass feeding up on top, chasing pogies right in the wash. Threw a Gibbs Pencil Popper, walked it through the froth off the eastern side near the point, and connected on three fish in the 24 to 26-inch range before the wind swung and killed it. Southwest breeze under 15 knots is the number to watch for that spot — any harder and it gets unfishable off those rocks.

The blues showed up at Higgins Beach this week, and this is exactly the pattern we said was coming — bunker schools working up the coast, blues riding right behind them, and once that bait pushes into range of a beach the blitz follows. Wednesday morning, bunch of guys standing in the wash at Higgins watching pogies get shredded thirty yards off the sand. Blues in the 3 to 6-pound class, gorging hard enough that you could throw damn near anything and get bit. I did best on a 1-ounce Deadly Dick worked fast just under the surface — the erratic wobble matches a wounded pogy better than most swimmers. If you're chasing that blitz, watch the water off Higgins and Pine Point in the early morning — bunker pods show as dark nervous patches, and the birds working over them will tell you before your eyes do.

Mackerel are still thick off Wells Harbor and Ogunquit, schooling tight around the harbor mouths and out past the breakwaters. That bait is doing double duty — it's keeping the striper feed going even where bunker haven't pushed in yet, and it's good enough eating that a lot of guys are jigging strictly for macks with small diamond jigs or Sabiki rigs off the rocks. If you want a bass instead, tip a bucktail with a mackerel strip and work it along the current edges outside Wells Harbor on the last of the outgoing — that combination has been quietly productive while everybody's chasing the blitz noise.

Down on the flats, Pine Point mud has been giving up decent flounder on sandworms and clam bellies fished on a simple two-hook flounder rig, best on the slower water either side of dead low. Nothing spectacular in size, but steady enough for a bucket if you're patient and willing to move around the flat looking for the softer mud pockets where they hold.

Cod fishing stays a boat game right now — the ledges off Cape Elizabeth are producing for guys jigging deep with diamond jigs or dropping bait rigs down 80 to 120 feet, but it's not a beach story and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Looking ahead, if this southwest wind pattern holds through the weekend, I'd be at Prouts Neck early with topwater plugs before the breeze builds past that 15-knot mark. And I'd still make the Pool incoming my anchor session — with the neap softening the current, that window's forgiving enough to fish twice a day if you've got the legs for it. The bunker are still pushing north, so don't be surprised if Pine Point and the stretch toward Kennebunk start showing the same blitz behavior Higgins had this week. Bring the Danny plugs, bring the Pencil Poppers, and watch the birds.

reports.headline: Bunker in the Breachways, Bass Gone Nocturnal, Fluke Chewing the Neap
reports.subhead: The bait's stacking up in every breachway from Sakonnet to Napatree, and the bass have figured out the dark is safer than the daylight.
reports.body_markdown:
Stood on the rocks at Napatree before first light Tuesday and watched a pod of peanut bunker come pouring out of the mouth of the breachway like someone pulled a plug. Thousands of them, balled up tight, nervous, with something underneath pushing them around. That something turned out to be a pack of schoolie-to-mid-thirties bass working the edge of the current seam where the outgoing water meets the open Sound. Same story at Watch Hill Point, same story down at the Weekapaug cut. The bait's here. The question this week has been figuring out when the fish are willing to eat it in daylight, because mostly, they aren't.

Water's been sitting warm along this whole stretch, low-to-mid 70s depending on where you check it, and that's pushed the keeper-class stripers into a strict low-light program. I'm not seeing much worth chasing between 9am and 6pm unless you're fishing deep structure, but dusk through dawn has been good and steady. My best window this week was the last hour of the outgoing into the start of the flood at Sakonnet Point — fished a black/purple 1.5-ounce bucktail with a white pork rind trailer off the rocks below the lighthouse, and picked off four bass in the 26-32 inch range in about ninety minutes, all on a slow bottom bump through the rip. Second Beach in Middletown has been giving up similar fish to guys soaking bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs off the sand right at the mouth of the Sakonnet River, fishing the last two hours of dark.

The moon just went first-quarter, so we're sliding into neap tides through the weekend — less current push, softer rips, which is actually working in our favor right now. Anything that depends on a hard-running rip to hold bait tight, like Beavertail or the Jamestown side of the East Passage, has widened out. The current's not screaming through there like it does on the new and full, so the bite window at those spots is longer and more forgiving. If you're throwing eels or swimbaits at night off Beavertail, you've got more time to work the water instead of one tight slack-into-flood window.

Fluke have been the one bite you can set your watch to, and daylight-friendly to boot. We said a week or two back that summer fluke fishing would keep building through August as the back-bay fish push out toward the inlets and ocean structure, and that's exactly what's playing out. The mid-bay drifts off Jamestown — the flats south of the Newport Bridge in 18 to 25 feet — have been holding solid numbers on the last of the outgoing and first hour of the incoming. White and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom, drifting with the current instead of fighting it. Mixed bag of shorts but enough keepers in the 18-20 inch range to make it worth staying with. Charlestown Breachway is doing the same thing on a smaller scale — work the deeper channel edge right where it dumps into the salt pond side, moving water only, dead water is dead water there.

Bluefish have shown up in patches, not everywhere, but where the bunker schools are thick — Second Beach, the stretch off Sachuest Point, and the beach in front of Weekapaug — you'll get slashing surface action for twenty, thirty minutes at a time before they push off. That matches what we've been seeing up and down the coast this month, bunker pods dragging blues along with them, and I expect that pattern to keep showing up here as long as the bait stays put and we don't get a blow that scatters it. Topwater poppers or a simple diamond jig with no tube, worked fast through the froth, is all you need when it happens. Just be ready — it's not a sit-and-wait bite, it's a run-and-gun one.

Tog are off the table right now — season's closed here till the first of August — but I've been out checking a few of my ledges anyway, just scouting. The rock piles off Newport's Ocean Drive and the drop just outside Watch Hill Cove are still holding bait and structure exactly like they should be, so when the season flips back on I've got a short list ready.

Too early yet for albies — that first push into the breachways is a September story around here, and I'm not seeing any scout fish or bait signs that say otherwise. But the water's warming the way it needs to, and by mid-to-late August I'll start checking the mouth of the Sakonnet and the rips off Napatree for the first signs. For now, if I've only got one trip this week, I'm fishing the last two hours of dark at Sakonnet Point on the outgoing, bucktail and rind, and I'm covering the Jamestown flats midday on the moving water for fluke. Both are producing consistent enough numbers to be worth the drive, as long as you respect the tide and don't waste time fishing it slack.

reports.headline: Nine-Pound Cod off Appledore, Stripers Riding the Piscataqua Neap
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline doesn't sound like much until you've spent a July morning working the slack at the Shoals and still made it back before the tourists find parking.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and figure there's nothing to talk about up here. I've fished New Jersey with guys who cover more water in one tide than I do in a season, and I still put a better box of fish on the dock most weeks. You don't need more coastline. You need to know what's under the water you've got. My Lund's twenty feet, open console, no frills — but I fish it like it's rigged for the canyons, because six miles offshore of Rye the bottom does things most guys never see because they never bother running out there.

This week that meant the Isles of Shoals, and the Shoals have been good to the guys who respect the slack. We're coming off the first-quarter neap, which knocked the current down around White Island and the ledges off Appledore, and that's exactly when you want to be sitting over structure with a jig in your hand instead of fighting to hold bottom. I had a morning on the Appledore ledges in about 75 feet where the haddock showed first — schoolies mixed with a few keepers on diamond jigs tipped with a strip of mackerel belly — and then the cod came through on the change, biggest one going nine pounds on a plain white/red jig worked slow off bottom. Nothing dramatic, but steady enough that four rods kept bending through the last hour of the ebb. Halibut Rocks and the Sisters have been holding similar fish in that 60-90 foot range. If you're marking bait balls on the sounder before you drop, that's your green light — cooler Gulf of Maine water is keeping mackerel schools thick and tight to structure out there, and where the mackerel sit, the groundfish sit under them.

Speaking of mackerel, they've been stacked from the Shoals in tight to Odiorne Point, and jigging a string of six for an hour will fill a bait bucket and half your dinner plate in the same trip. That cooler water column is the whole story right now — while the water south of Boston pushes stripers into a strictly dawn-and-dark pattern, we're still getting daytime bites up here because the Gulf of Maine hasn't let this stretch get soupy-warm the way the Sound has. We called this exact pattern last week — said summer striper fishing would carry through August up here — and that's holding up so far, no surprise given how stable this water column has stayed.

Inshore, the Piscataqua has been the more consistent bass producer than the open beaches. Current seams below the Memorial Bridge and down along Pierce Island have been holding fish on the last two hours of the incoming, with schoolies to mid-20-inch class eating swimming plugs and soft-plastic paddletails worked with the current instead of against it. A few better fish, high-20s to low-30s, have come off the deeper water near the Route 1 bridge on live mackerel drifted on a fish-finder rig — makes sense given how much bait we're seeing stacked in that river right now.

Hampton Harbor has been the tide-dependent play it always is in July. The inlet mouth on the last of the outgoing, when the water's pouring out past the jetty and pushing bait with it, has been giving up decent numbers of schoolie bass to guys throwing white bucktails and Sluggos in the 5-inch range. Wait for that stage of the tide specifically — fish it too early on the ebb and you're just casting into slack water with nothing moving. Rye Harbor's channel has had similar action on the same tide stage, plus a few bluefish mixed in chasing the same bait pods, snapping off soft plastics if you're not running wire or at least a heavier leader.

Bluefish overall have been more of a presence than a headline up here — nothing like the blitzes you're hearing about further south where bunker schools are stacking blues right on the beach. Ours have been scattered fish working the harbor mouths and Great Boars Head on incoming water, chopping bait on the surface for twenty-minute windows before disappearing. If you catch that window, small metal — quarter-ounce Deadly Dicks or similar — worked fast will get bit. If you miss it, you're just casting at empty water.

Flounder have been a quieter story, but Hampton Harbor's channel edges and the flats inside Rye Harbor have produced decent numbers on standard flounder rigs with sandworms, best on the slower stages of the tide when the current isn't ripping bait rigs sideways.

Looking ahead, I don't see a reason for this to change much through the coming week. The neap tide should keep softening current at the Shoals through the weekend, which means more slack-water windows to work the ledges without fighting the drift, and the cooler water column isn't going anywhere fast enough to push our stripers into a strictly nocturnal pattern like they're dealing with south of us. If I had one morning to spend, I'd run to Appledore early, work the slack for cod and haddock, then swing back into the Piscataqua on the tail of the incoming for bass before the wind picks up in the afternoon. That's the trip that's been working. No reason to overthink it while it still does.

reports.headline: SW Ledge Slack at 6:52: Bass on Eels, Bonito Closing the Gap
reports.subhead: A softening neap tide is stretching the bite window at the Ledge, and the water off Block Island is finally warm enough to start watching for the first bonito.
reports.body_markdown:
6:52 AM. That's when SW Ledge goes dead slack this Tuesday, and if you've fished this rip as long as I have you already know the trick — you don't fish the slack, you fish the twenty minutes on either side of it. That's the window this week, tighter than usual because we're sliding into a first-quarter neap, and the current off the Ledge just doesn't have the shoulders it had ten days ago. Less push means the bait sits lower in the water column longer, which is exactly why the bass have been hanging on the down-current edge in 40 to 55 feet instead of blasting through the top third of the rip like they do on a big moon tide.

We've been running eels on that edge — 12 to 14-inch live eels on a fish-finder rig, 3 ounces of egg weight, letting them swim naturally into the seam where the sandy bottom drops off toward the deeper water east of the Ledge. Fish to 35 pounds have come off that program in the last week, though I want to be honest — it's not every drift. We're averaging one to two quality fish per tide change, sometimes a double, sometimes nothing until the last five minutes before the current builds back. The softer neap current is a double-edged sword: it widens your workable window, but it also means the bait isn't getting pushed as hard into the ambush zone, so the bass have to be actively hunting rather than reacting. Patience matters more than usual right now.

Bunker chunks on the bottom in that same stretch have also produced, especially in the last hour of the outgoing when the tide is still moving enough to carry scent but not so hard you're constantly re-baiting. If you're marking bunker on the meter anywhere between the Ledge and Sandy Point, that's worth a slow pass with cut bait before you commit to the eel program — some days the bigger fish want the oil in the water more than a swimming profile.

South of the Judith, the reef grounds are still the most dependable thing going, and I said as much last week — fluke and sea bass down there have been the backbone of this port all summer, and nothing's changed. We're working 40 to 60 feet on the humps south of the breachway, dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails on the drift, tipped with a squid strip for the sea bass that come up on the same drops. Fluke to 6 pounds have shown up on that combo this week, with a good number of shorts mixed in — keep moving until you find the size class you want, because it's patchy from hump to hump. Sea bass have been thick and cooperative, 14 to 17 inches on average, sometimes stacked so tight you're picking through doubles just to find the keepers. That bite doesn't care much about tide stage — it's more about getting your bait down clean, so fish it on the slower push if you can, less scope, better bottom contact.

Now here's the one I've been watching closely, because we flagged it last week — said bonito and albies should show within a week or two, and the water's finally getting there. Off the Southeast Light and out toward North Rip, the surface temps are edging into the same range that's had Montauk holding around 69 degrees and the open ocean off the Bight pushing past 71. That's the number that matters. Bonito don't show on a calendar, they show on a thermometer, and we're right at the doorstep. I haven't had a confirmed hookup yet — nobody I've talked to at the dock has either — but the bait's right, small silversides and rain bait are stacking up off Clay Head and around the North Light rip, and that's the setup. If you want to be the first guy with a bonito story this year, keep a light spinning rod rigged with a half-ounce Deadly Dick or a green machine epoxy jig ready on the rail when you're running out to the Ledge. You'll know it when you see it — the terns will tip you off before the fish do.

Bluefish have been mixed in with the bass on the Ledge drifts, mostly 3 to 5 pounds, happy to jump on the same eels and chunks, which is fine by most of my charters but can shred a bag of eels fast if they show up in numbers. No giant blitzes locally yet, though the bunker pods pushing along the mainland beaches to our west have kept that bite alive elsewhere on the coast, and if that bait keeps drifting our way, expect the blues to thicken up around Galilee and the breachway in the next week or two.

Looking ahead, the neap tide keeps softening through midweek, which should keep stretching that bass window at SW Ledge — more patience required, but a longer runway if you're willing to sit on the drift. The reef bite south of the Judith should stay steady regardless of tide phase; that's been the safe bet all summer and I don't see it slowing. And if this water keeps creeping warmer around North Light and Clay Head, I wouldn't be shocked to hear about the first bonito of the season inside the next seven to ten days. I'll be watching the rips closely — if they show, you'll hear about it here first.

reports.headline: Klondike Wreck 8-19, 210 Feet: Bluefin Slots Stacked, Sea Bass to 4 Pounds Inshore
reports.subhead: The tuna are holding tighter to the beach than they should this deep into July, and the reef sites are still paying the bills while boats wait for a weather window to the canyons.
reports.body_markdown:
Two-hundred-ten feet. That's what the sounder read Tuesday morning sitting over Klondike wreck 8-19, and the bait column stacked from 140 down to the deck was thick enough that I made three passes before I even dropped a jig. Twenty years of running this piece of water and I've learned that when the bait's holding that deep in July, it's because the thermocline's doing something interesting — and sure enough, we found a clean break at 68 feet, cooler water underneath pushing that bait tight and giving the bluefin a reason to sit on the structure instead of running the open lumps.

We flagged this last week — said the warm-water filaments pushing toward the Hudson and Wilmington canyon approaches would put yellowfin and mahi within range of the Jersey fleet, and that's exactly the window that's cracking open right now. Buoy 44025 out in the Bight is reading 71.2 degrees on the surface, which doesn't sound like much until you factor in the blue water pushing inshore on those eddies. That's canyon color showing up closer to the beach than it has any business being in mid-July, and it's why guys running out of Manasquan and Belmar are covering the Wilmington approach in a day trip instead of an overnighter.

The bluefin bite itself has been steady rather than spectacular, which is fine by me — steady is what pays for fuel. We're inside the slot window now, 27 inches to just under 47, two-fish limit, and the fish cooperating on that class have been sitting on the Mud Hole lumps in 120 to 160 feet, particularly the hump just east of the Chicken Canyon drop where the bottom breaks sharp. Green machines and small cedar plugs behind the spreader bars have been drawing strikes on the troll around daybreak, and once the sun gets up we've had better luck slowing the spread down and working ballyhoo naked baits through the same water. Nobody's boating giants right now — the trophy category's been closed since July 3rd — but a 34-inch bluefin on 30-pound tackle still makes for a good morning, and we've had multiple-fish mornings three trips out of the last five. That's a solid number for this time of year, though it's not automatic — you need to be on the temperature break at first light, not chasing it at nine.

Mahi are starting to mix in around anything floating out past the Mud Hole edge — lobster pot warps, weed clumps, the odd pallet. Nothing dramatic yet, a fish or two per stop, but that's how the August pattern usually starts. If you're running past a pot with any color of weed hanging off the buoy line, it's worth a pitch bait or a small feather before you keep moving. I expect that pattern to build through the next two to three weeks as the water keeps warming.

Inshore, the reef and wreck network is carrying the week for anyone who doesn't want to burn the fuel to run offshore in that leftover swell — 44025 was showing close to four feet at five seconds Tuesday, short and choppy, uncomfortable enough that I kept my six-pack trip tucked in tighter to the beach than planned. Sea Girt Reef in 60 to 70 feet has been holding good numbers of black sea bass, fish running 14 to 17 inches with a scattering of 4-pounders mixed in on the deeper pieces. Same story at Axel Carlson Reef, a little shallower at 55 feet, and Shrewsbury Rocks has been quietly productive too if you can find the right piece of structure among the boulders — that's not a spot you fish blind, you need a number in the book or a very patient sounder pass. Green crab and squid strips on a double-hook bottom rig, 3/0 hooks, 4 to 6 ounces of lead depending on drift speed, has been the standard producer. Jigging bucktails tipped with Gulp works too when the current's moving hard enough to keep them off bottom, and it thins out the throwbacks faster than bait soak.

Barnegat Ridge has been a mixed bag — some boats scoring well on sea bass in the 80-foot depths off the northern end, others reporting a slower pick. My read is the fish are there but scattered across a wider stretch of structure than usual, which means covering ground on the drift rather than anchoring up on one number pays off right now.

Tog season's closed this time of year so I'm not chasing blackfish, and cod are strictly a cold-water target we won't see again until late fall. Bonito haven't shown in our water yet — the temperature signature isn't quite there — but with water pushing into the high 60s and low 70s up toward Montauk and the Vineyard, I'd start watching the temperature breaks off Sea Girt and Shrewsbury by early August.

Looking ahead, if the high pressure holds like it's been holding, I'd put my next trip on the Mud Hole lumps at first light for bluefin, then work back inshore to Sea Girt or Axel Carlson for a sea bass bag once the sun's up and the tuna bite typically slows. That's the play as long as the wind stays cooperative — if it swings onshore and builds that swell back up, I'd scrap the offshore leg entirely and just fish structure close to the inlet.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point after dark: bass on bunker while scup and fluke carry the daylight shift
reports.subhead: The bay's gone warm and lazy in the sun, so the stripers punched out for the night crew — everything else is picking up the slack.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into Sal down at the Fields Point pier Tuesday morning, coffee in one hand, a rod he hadn't even rigged yet in the other, just standing there watching the water move. He said it plain: "Bay's warm, Vinny. Warm and slow." And he wasn't wrong. You can feel it in the air off the river now — that thick, still July heat that sits on the water and doesn't leave with the tide. Buckeye Brook's herring run is long done, the alewives pushed through back in April and May, and the bass that rode that bait into the upper bay have scattered out and gone quiet during the day. What's left is a nighttime program, and if you're not willing to fish dark or first light, you're leaving fish on the table.

I've been working the bridge structure — Mount Hope, the Jamestown side, pilings down by Conimicut — after 9 PM with success that daylight just isn't giving up right now. Eels are still the call, six to nine inches, drifted or slow-swum right along the current break where the light from the bridge deck cuts the shadow line. Bass are sitting right on that edge waiting for bait to get confused by the light, and they'll eat an eel fished slow better than anything with a hook in it right now. Bunker pods have been showing in the upper bay too, rolling off Nyatt Point and down toward Conimicut Light on the last of the ebb, and where you find bunker stacked tight, there are bass underneath them even in this heat — they just won't touch it till the sun's off the water. Snag-and-drop with a circle hook has worked for guys willing to sit on those pods till dusk.

Daytime, it's fluke and scup carrying the report, and honestly they're carrying it well. Fluke have been steady in the west passage off Rocky Point and down around the Hope Island flats, four to twelve feet of water, drifting the moving tide with a white or pink Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, three-quarter ounce when the current's got some push, half ounce when it slacks off. Nothing giant — most going 16 to 19 inches — but there's enough of them stacked on that softer bottom to make an afternoon worth it, especially with the neap tide we just rolled into softening the current everywhere in the bay. Weaker moving water means longer, more comfortable drift windows instead of getting blown through the zone in ten minutes flat.

Scup are doing exactly what scup do in late July — piled up on every rocky ledge and rubble pile from Prudence Island down to the Colt State Park side, and around the rocks off Rocky Point itself. Small hooks, sandworms or squid strips, right on bottom, and you can load a bucket in an hour if you find the right piece of structure on the last two hours of the incoming. It's not glamorous fishing but it's about as close to a sure thing as this bay's got right now, and it's good eating besides.

Greenwich Bay's been the other bright spot — weakfish have started showing again on the calm, warm evenings, right where we figured they'd come back once the water settled. We called that one last week, said the weakfish bite would rebuild on quiet nights, and that's exactly what's happened along the edges of the eelgrass flats there, small soft plastics on light jigheads worked slow just after dark. Nothing to brag about in numbers yet, but the pattern is real and it's building.

There's also been squid pushing into the bay, which is a good sign even if nobody's specifically targeting them — it means there's forage stacking up, and that's usually the thing that gets predators moving with more confidence once the heat breaks a little. I don't expect a big thermal shift in the next several days, so I'm not calling for anything to change dramatically. What I am saying is this warm-water pattern isn't going anywhere soon, so plan around it instead of fighting it.

If I've got one night this week, I'm fishing the last two hours of dusk into full dark off the Mount Hope Bridge rocks with eels, betting the bass show up once the light goes flat. If that doesn't produce, Plan B is first light at Rocky Point ledges for scup and a fluke drift on the way back in. Keep an eye on the bunker — if those pods hold in the upper bay through the week, the night bite off Conimicut and Nyatt should only get better as more bass slide up under them. Watch the neap tide too — slower water this week means longer bites, not shorter ones, so there's no reason to rush your drift.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips: B-minus by day, A after dark — fluke steady, drum's long gone
reports.subhead: Daylight rips fishing is a grind with warm water pushing stripers nocturnal, but the fluke bite and a rebuilding weakfish pattern in the bay are keeping rods bent.
reports.body_markdown:
If you're grading the Rips this week, I'd call it a B-minus in daylight and an A-minus after the sun goes down. That's not a knock — that's just where we are in late July with water this warm. My father used to say the Rips never lie, they just tell you what time to show up, and right now that clock says dusk to dawn if you want keeper stripers.

Here's the why. Water off Cape May Point and through the Rips has been sitting warm — mid-to-upper 70s inshore, and that kind of heat pushes mature bass into a low-light pattern almost every summer. I saw it with my dad running this water in the '90s, I see it now. Fish that would happily crush a bucktail at noon in May are laid up on structure through the heat of the day and only coming up to feed at first light, last light, or full dark. So we've adjusted — I've had better luck the last two trips running the outer edge of the Rips at 5 AM on the tail of the outgoing, drifting live eels and bunker chunks over the humps in 30 to 45 feet, than I have grinding it at noon on bucktails. The bass are there. They're just not stupid about when they eat.

Fluke, on the other hand, don't care what time it is — they care about moving water, and that's been the more dependable game this week. Best action's been on the last two hours of the incoming into the first hour of the outgoing, working the inlet structure at Hereford and the deeper edges off the Cape May Canyon approach. White and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom in 25 to 35 feet, have been putting keeper fluke in the box — nothing giant, mostly 18 to 20 inches with the occasional 4-pounder mixed in, but steady enough that a half-day trip is worth your gas. If the current's really ripping, I'll switch to a heavier head and slow my drift with the motor rather than fight it — that's the difference between five keepers and one.

Now, the drum. I know some of you are still asking, and I've got to be straight with you — the black drum run in Delaware Bay is done. That fishery is a May event around Miah Maull, the Fishing Reef, and up toward the mouth of the Cohansey, and by the time we hit late July those big drum have pushed back offshore and out of the bay entirely. If somebody tells you they're marking drum in the bay right now, they're marking something else. Don't waste a tide looking for them.

What is building nicely, and what I flagged last week as a bite worth watching, is weakfish. We said the warm, calm evenings would rebuild that pattern in the back-bay channels and marsh creeks, and that's exactly what's showing up around Fortescue and the marsh cuts off the main bay channel. Nothing blitz-like yet — this is a numbers-building situation, not a blow-up — but working the channel edges on the dropping tide with bucktail-and-squid-strip combos or 4-inch pearl white soft plastics on a light jighead has been producing solid weaks in the 16 to 20-inch range for guys willing to fish it quiet and slow. Evening bite's been the strongest window, an hour before sunset through dusk, which tracks with how weakfish have always behaved in this bay — they don't like bright sun on slick water.

Bluefish are stacking up hard north of us right now, blitzing on bunker from Belmar into Raritan Bay, and I expect that pattern to keep sliding south along the beach as those bunker pods keep moving. We haven't seen that show up at full strength inside Hereford or along the Cape May beachfront yet, but with bait already staging off Wildwood, I wouldn't be surprised if we get a taste of it by early August. Keep an eye on the birds working close to the beach — that'll tell you before I can.

Offshore, if you've got the boat and the fuel, Washington Canyon has been worth the run. Stable high pressure's held warm blue water tight to the edge and boats are finding improving yellowfin and some bigeye activity out there, which makes Cape May one of the better canyon jump-off points on the whole coast right now. Not my usual beat, but I hear the radio chatter at the dock and it's been good enough that a few of the local boys are running out weekly instead of waiting for a weekend window.

Looking ahead, we're sliding into the first-quarter neap, which is going to soften current through the Rips over the next few days. That's not bad news — it actually widens your fishing window past the peak of the tide for eel and swimbait presentations, since the water won't be ripping through so hard that you're fighting drift the whole time. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the last hour of dark into first light at the outer Rips on eels, then swing into Hereford on the tail of the incoming for fluke before the sun gets too high. Two bites, one tide cycle — that's the two-bay game working the way it's supposed to.

reports.headline: Where Did the Bass Go? A Lesson in Warm-Water Behavior
reports.subhead: Daytime stripers have gone to school after dark, but fluke, bluefish, and weakfish are keeping the classroom open on the back bays this week.
reports.body_markdown:
I get the same question every July, usually from a guy leaning on the rail at the Ninth Street bridge with a rod he hasn't bent since June: "Professor, where'd all the bass go?" It's a fair question, and it's got a fair answer. Water temp off the beach is sitting around 71 to 72 degrees, and in the shallow back bay guts around Brigantine and the Rainbow Channel behind Ocean City, it's running warmer than that by midday. Striped bass don't like working hard in warm, low-oxygen water under a July sun. They go nocturnal. That's not a mystery, that's biology — same lesson every summer, different year.

So if you want stripers this week, you fish the edges of the day. Dusk into dark around the Route 30 bridge pilings in Absecon Inlet, working a white paddletail on a 3/4-ounce jighead tight to the structure on the last two hours of the outgoing. Same story at the Great Egg Inlet railroad bridge — that current funnel holds fish after sundown, and a bunker chunk fished on the bottom with just enough weight to hold in the tide has been the more consistent producer than artificials there. Daytime stripers are there, but they're stacked deep and sluggish, and you're better off not wasting your best hours chasing them.

Which brings me to what daytime hours are actually for right now — fluke. This remains the most dependable program on this whole stretch of coast, and it hasn't slowed a bit with the heat. The sod banks off Absecon Inlet, in that 12 to 18 foot stretch along the edges of the marsh channels, are holding fish through the last of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, when the current is strong enough to keep a 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail moving naturally along bottom without you having to add weight. Great Egg's channel edges, particularly the drop from the ICW into the inlet proper, have been giving up keeper fluke to 4 and 5 pounds on the same rig, sometimes better on a chartreuse/white combo when the water's got a little color to it after a tide change. Nothing extraordinary in numbers — you're working for your five fish, not filling a cooler in an hour — but it's steady enough that I'll take clients there with confidence most days this month.

Now, the bluefish. We flagged this last week — said the blitz pattern working the bunker schools up around LBI and Belmar would keep pushing south, and it has. Birds have been diving on bait pods off Ocean City and down toward Sea Isle City the last several mornings, and the blues chasing those bunker schools have been chopping bait right at the surf line in daylight, which is unusual enough to notice. If you see the gulls working tight to the beach at first light, get a metal lip swimmer or a Hopkins spoon out there fast — that window can close in twenty minutes once the bunker push through. It's not a guarantee every morning, but three mornings out of the last five have produced fish, and that's a good number for late July blues on the beach.

Weakfish are the quiet story right now, and I mean that literally — the bite's been a nighttime affair in the back channels around Stone Harbor and Townsends Inlet, calm evenings with little wind producing the best results. We noted last week that warm, settled evenings would rebuild that weakfish bite, and the calm stretch we've had has done exactly that. A 3-inch chartreuse Gulp shrimp on a light jighead, fished slow along the drop-offs where Townsends Inlet channel meets the marsh flats, has been picking up weakfish in the 16 to 19 inch range on the last two hours of the outgoing after dark. Not a blitz, but a real, repeatable pattern if you're willing to fish it at 9 or 10 at night.

Kingfish have been steady in the surf at Stone Harbor and the south end of Ocean City on bloodworm and Fishbites combos fished on a simple high-low rig in the second and third sandbar troughs — small fish, good eating, easy on a summer evening when the ocean swell (we've had a bumpy stretch, 3 to 4 feet at short period off the coast) makes bigger surf targets tough. Triggerfish continue to show around the Great Egg reef structure and the rock piles at the Absecon Inlet jetties, taking small pieces of clam fished tight to the rocks — a bonus fish more than a target, but worth knowing they're there if the fluke bite goes quiet on you.

Looking ahead, we're sliding into the first-quarter neap, which means softer current for the next several days. That's going to widen the productive fishing window at the inlets — less brutal peak-tide current means you can fish fluke and stripers comfortably through more of the tide cycle instead of just the last hard hour. If the bunker keep pushing south and the calm weather holds, I'd expect the bluefish blitz pattern to keep showing at Ocean City and work its way toward Great Egg by the weekend. Worth having a rod rigged and ready before the coffee's done.

reports.headline: Holgate's New Cut Is Holding Bass at Night — Bluefish Chew Through the Bunker at Beach Haven Inlet
reports.subhead: A fresh cut reshaped the south end after last week's swell, and it's funneling both the bait and the bite right where I said it would.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate refuge line Sunday morning at low water and the beach looked different than it did two weeks ago. That swell we picked up off the back of the offshore fetch — buoy readings out at the Bight were pushing close to four feet at five seconds — did some real work down there. There's a new cut forming about three hundred yards north of the old one, a deeper trough cutting in at an angle instead of straight, with a sandbar building up on the inside edge that's holding water even on the bottom of the tide. That's the kind of structure change that gets me excited, because a new cut means new current, and new current means bait gets pushed and pinned in places it wasn't a month ago.

And sure enough, that's exactly where the bunker pods have been stacking up on the last two hours of the incoming.
