We flagged this last week — said the bait would keep funneling south with the tide and the blitz activity would spread down toward LBI, and that's precisely what's happening. Beach Haven Inlet and the jetty rocks at Barnegat Light have both had bluefish working through bunker schools on the tide changes, mostly the last hour of the ebb and first hour of the flood when the current squeezes bait through the throat of the inlet. These aren't the giant coastwide blitzes you're seeing up in Belmar and Sandy Hook, but they're real — cocktail blues to six pounds, occasional bigger ones mixed in, busting bait on the surface for ten, fifteen minute windows before they slide off. Poppers and metal — Ava jigs, Deadly Dicks — thrown right into the froth on the BL jetty rocks has been the play. Don't waste time false-casting. When you see the wash go white, get the lure in the water.

Stripers are the trickier story right now. Water's warm enough along this whole stretch that the bass have gone nocturnal on us, same pattern you're seeing from here up through the Sound. Daytime jigging in the inlet has been mostly a bust — I had two charters last week that worked bucktails through the Little Egg Inlet channel for three hours combined and came up with one short fish. But after dark, working bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig off the tip of Holgate, or live-lining a bunker back in the wash off Beach Haven Ridge, that's been putting bigger fish in the box. One angler I know well boated a 34-inch fish off the Ridge Tuesday night on a livelined bunker, bite came right at the top of the tide around 10:30 with almost no current running — that neap tide we're sliding into off today's first-quarter moon is softening the push through the inlet, which is actually opening up a wider bite window instead of one hard-and-fast peak. If you're going after bass right now, plan your trip around dusk through midnight rather than midday, and fish the slower water on the inside of structure where bunker schools tend to bunch up when the tide goes quiet.

Fluke are the one thing on this beat you can set your watch to right now, and that hasn't changed. Little Egg Inlet channel edges, the deeper cuts off Graveling Point, and the flats running out toward the Mullica mouth have all been holding fish on the moving water — both stages of the tide, though the last two hours of the ebb has been the more consistent producer as bait gets pulled out of Great Bay through the inlet. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on quarter to half-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom in eight to fourteen feet, is still the go-to combination. A few guys working the deeper holes off Beach Haven have had fluke to five pounds on chartreuse bucktails tipped with squid strips, fished right on the channel drop where the sand gives way to mud.

Weakfish have been a quiet bright spot in the upper Mullica and around the mouth of Great Bay on calm, warm evenings — small numbers, but real fish, mostly in the 16 to 19 inch range, working soft plastics like three-inch Gulp shrimp on light jigheads right at last light when the water goes glassy. That rebuild we expected on stable, warm nights looks like it's happening, slowly. Not a bite you plan a whole trip around yet, but worth a stop if you're already out there working the tide near Graveling Point.

Kingfish are scattered but present in the surf from Ship Bottom down through Surf City, mostly on bloodworm strips fished on a high-low rig in the second and third bar troughs during the morning incoming.

Looking ahead, I'd keep an eye on that new Holgate cut — cuts like that tend to hold their shape for two to three weeks before another swell reworks them, so there's a window here. With the neap tide softening current through the end of the week, I'd focus striper efforts on the after-dark bunker bite around Beach Haven Ridge and Holgate, work the fluke on the stronger ebb tides through Little Egg Inlet, and keep bucktails and poppers rigged and ready at the jetties in case the bluefish push further south the way the bait's been moving. If the bunker keep funneling this direction through the weekend, Barnegat Light could see the blitz intensify rather than fade.

reports.headline: Niantic Fleet Whispers: Fluke Sliding Off the Grass and Onto the Reefs Now
reports.subhead: A neap tide is softening the current through Twotree and the Race, and the drift boats are cashing in on fluke, sea bass, and a stripers-after-dark pattern.
reports.body_markdown:
I was leaning on the rail at the bait shop Tuesday morning when one of the Waterford boat mates came in for a second load of squid strips and said something that stuck with me: "They ain't in the grass no more, they're all on the humps." He meant the fluke, and he wasn't wrong. We flagged this a week or so back — said the back-bay fluke would start pushing out to inlet mouths and ocean-adjacent reef structure as the water warmed through July, and that's exactly what's happening from Niantic Bay out through Twotree Island Channel right now.

The drift boats working out of Niantic and Waterford have been putting together solid fluke counts in 35 to 45 feet off the reef edges around Twotree and out toward Hatchett Point, with the better fish coming on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the drop. Pink and white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a squid strip, has been the go-to combo — nothing fancy, just a slow drag right along bottom where the structure breaks up the current. New London's reading around 69 degrees, which is a touch cool compared to the western Sound, but that's actually helping keep these fluke locked onto structure instead of scattering into open water. Sizes have been a mixed bag — plenty of 16 to 18 inchers getting tossed back, but every drift is putting at least one or two keepers in the 20 to 22 inch range over the rail. It's not a banner week, but it's a dependable one, and dependable counts for a lot in late July.

Sea bass have been the more consistent story on the same structure. Guys working ledge and rockpile around Hole-in-the-Wall and the Twotree drop-offs are finding steady numbers of sea bass in the 14 to 17 inch class, with the occasional heavier fish mixed in — nothing quite like that 28-inch, five-pound brute that got weighed in over toward Plum Gut, but that tells you the size class is out there on this eastern end of the Sound if you find the right piece of bottom. Green crab and squid combo on a two-hook bottom rig, fished tight on structure with just enough weight to hold in the current, has been the standard. Porgies are riding shotgun on the same drops — smaller stuff mostly, but a good bend-your-rod distraction between fluke drifts, and they'll eat the same squid strips you're already carrying.

Striped bass are the tougher conversation this week. The shallow water from here down through the western Sound has stayed warm enough that the keeper-class fish have gone almost entirely nocturnal — dawn, dusk, and after dark around the rips and structure is where the action's concentrated, and daytime trips have been mostly quiet unless you're working deep current breaks. Black Point and McCook Point have both given up fish after sundown to guys drifting live eels or working large soft-plastic swimbaits through the current seams, but you need to be out there in that low-light window, not mid-morning. A few schoolies are still showing on top around the Niantic River mouth on the early outgoing, chasing peanut bunker, but the bigger fish want the dark and the moving water together.

Bluefish haven't really made their presence felt out here yet the way they have further west — the bunker-driven blitzes tearing up the beaches from Belmar into Raritan Bay haven't pushed this far east in any real numbers. I wouldn't be shocked if that changes as bunker schools keep working the coast, but for now blues in this zone are more incidental — a few slammers mixed into the fluke drift here and there, nothing you'd plan a trip around.

The bigger structural story this week is the neap tide. We're coming off the first-quarter moon, and that means softer current through the rip-dependent stretches — Twotree Channel, the approach toward the Race — over the next several days. That's actually good news if you're working bucktails or bottom rigs, because the window of fishable current widens out instead of being crammed into that one violent hour of max tide. It also means slower, more finesse presentations are going to outfish the heavier gear for the time being — lighter jigs, slower retrieves, less horsepower needed to hold bottom.

Looking ahead, if the current stays soft through the week like it should on this neap cycle, I'd keep working the fluke and sea bass pattern on structure with lighter tackle — that's the higher-percentage play right now. For stripers, I'd plan around the tide and the clock together: fish the last two hours of light into full dark on the outgoing around Black Point or the river mouth, and have eels or a bulky swimbait ready. If the wind stays out of the south and holds calm like it's been, I don't expect much to change fast — just keep showing up on the structure and let the tide do the rest of the work.

reports.headline: Bunker Push Into Raritan Bay: Blues on the Pods, Fluke Holding the Channel Edges
reports.subhead: With bait pouring in from Belmar and a soft neap tide easing the rips, I'm staying inside the Hook this week — here's where I'd put the boat.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Sunday morning standing on the dock watching the swell roll in off the Bight — ocean side is a washing machine right now, pushing close to four feet at five seconds out past the buoy line, and that's not fishable water unless you're on a party boat hull. So the decision was easy: stay inside the Hook this week. Work the bay, work the rivers, let the ocean sort itself out on its own time.

Good thing, because the bay's got something building. Bunker schools that have been getting hammered by blues from Belmar on north are finally pushing into our end of the water. I've watched the pods thicken up off the beach between the Highlands and Sandy Hook for two days straight, and if that keeps up — and there's no reason it shouldn't with this calm, stable stretch of weather sitting on top of us — bluefish should follow those pods around the Hook and into the bay within a day or two. We flagged this exact thing last week, said the bay would settle into its summer rhythm of bait and blues and fluke on the tide, and here we are watching it happen in real time.

The first place that pattern always shows up locally is the ferry channel and the Rip at the Hook on the tide change. That's where I'd have eyes Tuesday and Wednesday morning — first light, incoming water pushing bait against the channel edge, gulls starting to work overhead. When the blues do show, don't overthink it. A 1-ounce diamond jig with a green tube tail, or a bucktail with no trailer at all, gets eaten the second it hits the wash when they're on bunker. Match the size of whatever peanut or adult bunker they're chopping and you're in business.

While we wait on that to fully develop, the fluke bite has carried the water the way it always does in late July. Sandy Hook Bay and the Reach remain the most dependable thing going right now — a daytime program on moving water, nothing fancy required. My best drifts the last two weeks have come working the channel edges off Flynn's Knoll on the last two hours of the incoming, four- to five-ounce bucktails tipped with a five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along the bottom where the sand drops into the channel. Keyport Flats has been giving up shorts by the bucket with the occasional keeper mixed in over that soft mussel bottom in 15 to 18 feet — adding a strip of squid on top of the Gulp has been the difference-maker for me when the current goes light.

Speaking of light current — today's first-quarter neap has taken some of the snap out of the rips, and that's actually working in our favor on the fluke grounds. Instead of one tight window right at max tide, the drift stays fishable through a longer stretch on either side of the swing. You don't have to be married to the exact moment the tide turns. At Flynn's Knoll and out toward Romer Shoal, that means more usable hours on the water for the same trip out.

Striped bass are the trickier piece of the puzzle right now, and I'll be straight with you — daytime bass fishing in the bay this time of year is mostly a low-percentage play. The water's carrying that heavy summer warmth, and with it the keeper-class fish have slid into a low-light and after-dark pattern, same as pretty much everywhere south of the Cape right now. If you want a real shot at a slot fish, you're fishing dawn, dusk, or full dark, working bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig around Romer Shoal and the deeper edges off the Hook, or drifting a live bunker if you can snag one out of the pods moving through. The Navesink mouth and the deeper bend by the Highlands bridge have both given up fish after dark to guys soaking eels — old-school, but it still works when the moon's this quiet.

Snapper blues are thick in the Navesink and Shrewsbury right now, which is a good problem to have if you've got a kid in the boat — small silver spoons or a sliver of bunker on a number 6 hook off any dock will keep them busy for hours. Porgies are holding steady over the reef structure off Romer Shoal and along the Highlands side, bloodworms or clam on a hi-lo rig in 20 to 25 feet — nothing spectacular, but a reliable box-filler on a slow bay day. Weakfish are scattered at best — a fish here and there over the Keyport Flats on soft plastics at dusk, but I wouldn't build a trip around them the way we could a decade back.

Look ahead: if the bunker keep pushing the way they have the last couple days, I expect the ferry channel and the water off Flynn's Knoll to turn into the bite everybody's chasing by the weekend. Watch the birds before anything else — they'll tell you it's happening before you see a single swirl. If the bait scatters or a wind shift breaks the pattern, don't force it; fall back on the fluke program in the Reach, because that bite isn't going anywhere with the water this stable. Either way, I'm keeping the boat inside the Hook this week and letting the ocean chop settle down before I run anything out past Romer.

reports.headline: Double Creek fluke stack the drop-offs while the sedges finally give up weakfish again
reports.subhead: Warm bay water has fluke tight to the channel edges and put the weakfish bite back on schedule — bluefish are riding bunker right through the inlet on the flood.
reports.body_markdown:
Back when I was mating on the Point Pleasant boats — I couldn't have been more than sixteen — there was an old captain named Sal who used to say the bay teaches you twice: once when the water's cold and once when it's warm, and if you only learn one lesson you're only half a fisherman. I think about that every July when Barnegat Bay goes soft and green and everybody assumes the good fishing packed up with the mayflies. It didn't. It just moved to the edges.

That's exactly where I found the fluke this week — tight to the drop-offs along Double Creek Channel, right where the mud flats fall off into eight, ten, twelve feet of water. The flats themselves are running warm, mid-70s by feel, and that pushes the fluke off the open bottom and down onto the lip of the channel where there's a little more oxygen and a little less current chop. I worked the outgoing tide Tuesday and again Thursday morning, drifting from the Route 9 bridge down toward the Forked River mouth with a half-ounce white bucktail tipped with a four-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet, bounced slow along bottom. Kept three keepers to four and a half pounds each day, threw back better than a dozen shorts. Nothing to write home about, but steady — and on a summer bay bite, steady is what you take.

The better news, honestly, is the weakfish. We said a couple weeks back that the evening bite would rebuild once the water settled into a calm, warm pattern, and that's exactly what's happened. The sedge banks south of Waretown and up around the mouth of Oyster Creek have started giving up weakfish again on the last hour of daylight into dark — one-to-three pound fish, mostly, with the occasional four hanging around the deeper pockets. Live grass shrimp under a popping cork is still the deadliest thing you can throw at them, but a three-inch pink Gulp shrimp on a light jighead worked just as well for me Wednesday evening, twitched slow along the edge where the sedge grass gives way to open water. Weakfish don't like a hard tide push, so target the slack around the tide change or the first hour of the new flood — that's when they come up off bottom and commit.

Bluefish are the loudest thing happening on the bay right now, and it's all bunker-driven. Big pods have been pushing through Barnegat Inlet on the higher stages of the tide, and the blues are riding right in behind them into the back bay. I've been anchoring just inside the inlet mouth, off the rock jetty on the Barnegat Light side, working the last two hours of the incoming with diamond jigs and metal — half-ounce Kastmasters, chrome or gold, worked fast through the bait. When the bunker get pinned against the rocks the blues go into a slashing frenzy you can see from fifty yards off, and for ten or fifteen minutes it's about as good as bay bluefishing gets. It doesn't last, though — once the tide turns the bait scatters and the blues follow it back out. Time it right or you'll miss the whole show.

Striped bass are around, but this warm shallow water has them doing what warm shallow water always makes them do — feeding low-light and after dark, then sulking on deeper structure through the heat of the day. I've had my best luck working bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig right at the inlet mouth in that first gray hour before sunup, and again for a short window right at dusk. During the day, if you want a shot at a bass, you're better off working the deeper holes off Barnegat Light with a bucktail dragged slow than casting the flats — the fish just aren't up there feeding when the sun's high and the water's this warm.

Don't overlook the smaller stuff either. Kingfish are showing on the ocean side along Island Beach State Park in the surf troughs, small but steady on bloodworm-tipped high-low rigs fished right in the wash. And Tices Shoal has turned on for blowfish the way it does every summer once the bay water settles — clam strips on a small hook, patience required, but a fun way to spend a slack tide with the kids if the fluke and weakfish aren't cooperating.

We're coming off the first-quarter neap now, which is softening the current through Double Creek and around the inlet — good news for anybody working slower presentations, because the bite windows widen out when the water isn't ripping. Expect that to hold for the next several days before the tides build back toward the full moon. My read for the coming week: the fluke pattern along the channel edges should hold steady as long as the bay stays warm and clear, the weakfish should keep improving into early August if these calm evenings continue, and the bluefish will keep riding the bunker in and out of the inlet as long as those pods keep pushing south. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be at the inlet mouth at first light with bunker chunks out for bass, then switch over to bucktails on the last of the outgoing to chase fluke down into Double Creek before the sun gets too high.

reports.headline: Manasquan Rocks at First Light: Blues Busting Bunker, Bass Gone to Bed
reports.subhead: The bunker showed up thick this week and the bluefish found them in broad daylight — the bass, meanwhile, want nothing to do with sunlight.
reports.body_markdown:
Five-fifteen Tuesday morning, north jetty at the inlet, and there's already three guys spread out on the rocks like it's a religious service. One of them — didn't get his name, wasn't going to interrupt a hookset — is doubled over on a metal-lip swimmer working the incoming current seam off the tip. He lands a bluefish that would've been respectable in October, mid-July be damned. Behind him a kid maybe nineteen years old is chunking bunker on a fish-finder rig into the same seam and getting bounced around by cocktail blues before his bait even settles. That's been the story all week from Manasquan north to Sea Bright, and it's not subtle.

The bunker showed up thick off the beach — pods stacked so tight off Belmar and Spring Lake you could see them nervous-watering from the boardwalk before the sun cleared the horizon. Where there's bunker like that in July, there's blues, and this week they came up shallow and stayed up shallow, blitzing in full daylight instead of waiting for the low-light windows they usually respect this time of year. We flagged this pattern holding last week — said as long as the high pressure stayed put and nothing scattered the bait, the blitz would keep rolling and start spreading up toward Sandy Hook. That's exactly what's happened. I had reports of bunker pods getting worked over as far north as the Sea Bright rocks by Wednesday, and the Reservation stretch was seeing gulls stacking up mid-morning, which if you've fished that beach long enough you know means something's happening under them.

The blues have been running mixed — plenty of cocktail-size fish in the 2 to 4 pound range, but enough slammers pushing 8 to 10 pounds mixed in that it's worth carrying a wire leader even if you hate the way it kills your action on a popper. Poppers and darters have been the move when you can see fish working the surface — a white Super Strike darter or a Gibbs pencil popper thrown past the edge of the blitz and worked back through it will get bit fast. When the surface action cools between waves of bait, Ava 27s and 47s jigged straight down off the jetty rocks into 15 to 20 feet of water have been picking off blues that dropped under the bunker schools.

Now here's the part that's been frustrating the guys who came out expecting stripers with the blues — the bass have gone quiet in daylight, and it's not a mystery why. Water's sitting in the low 70s along this stretch, warm enough that the bass want no part of feeding hard under a bright July sun. They're still around — I know guys who worked the Manasquan jetties an hour before first light and after last light this week and connected on schoolies to 28 inches on bunker chunks and darker Bomber swimmers worked slow through the current break at the tip. But if you're fishing 9 to noon expecting a bass blitz next to the blues, you're going to be disappointed. This is a low-light and after-dark fish right now, full stop, and that's going to hold as long as this warm, calm stretch of weather sits on top of us.

Fluke have been the quiet workhorse all week while everyone's chasing bunker noise. Shark River Inlet has been steady on the last two hours of the incoming, drifting white and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails along the channel edges in 15 to 22 feet — nothing enormous, mostly 16 to 19 inches with the occasional keeper pushing 20, but a consistent pick if you can find moving water. We noted a couple weeks back that back-bay fluke would start pushing toward inlet mouths and ocean structure as the water kept warming, and that's basically what's happened at Shark River and off the Manasquan jetties — the ocean-side structure bite has gotten steadily better while the shallow back-bay stuff has slowed down some.

We're rolling toward the first-quarter neap now, which is going to soften the current push through these inlets over the next few days. That's actually good news for the bass — a slacker tide means those low-light windows at the jetty tips stretch a little longer and the bait doesn't get ripped through as fast, giving stripers a better shot at working a current seam without burning energy fighting it. If I'm picking a window this weekend, I'm on the Manasquan north jetty an hour before first light on the tail of the incoming, throwing a darker swimmer or a bunker chunk soaked tight to the rocks. Blackfish and porgies are still around the deeper structure off Belmar and Asbury for anyone who wants a change of pace, though nobody's rushing that bite while the bunker show is running. Watch the bait — if the pods stay put and this high pressure holds, the blitz should keep sliding north toward the Hook and the bass will keep doing their business after dark. If the wind swings and scatters that bunker, all bets are off and we're back to soaking bait and hoping.

reports.headline: The Neap Takes the Edge Off Fort Trumbull, and the Bass Follow It Down
reports.subhead: Softer current at the river mouth pushed stripers into deeper holding water while bunker-chasing blues took over the surface show.
reports.body_markdown:
The first thing I noticed this week wasn't a fish — it was the water itself. Fort Trumbull on the ebb usually has that hard, defined seam where the river current meets the harbor swing, a visible crease you can read from forty yards off. This week, with the moon sitting on first quarter and the tides going neap, that seam went soft. Still there, still pushing bait, but with none of the teeth it has on a big spring tide. That tells you everything about where the fish have gone and why.

When the rip loses its punch, stripers stop holding right on the current edge and slide down into the deeper holding water — 20 to 25 feet off the Fort Trumbull point, tight to the riprap, and out along the deeper channel edge toward the Gold Star Bridge pilings in 30 to 35 feet. That's where I found them this week, and it's a pattern I've watched repeat every neap cycle for two decades on this river. The bite isn't gone, it's just relocated and it's compressed into shorter windows — first hour of light and the last hour before dark, with the best of it coming after the sun's fully down. Bunker schools have been thick in the upper harbor and pushing into the river mouth on the last of the incoming, and that's pulling bass up out of the channel to feed. Eels fished on a light three-way rig, and 6-inch paddletail swimbaits in bunker colors worked slow along bottom, have been the ticket after dark. Nothing gaudy — slow, deliberate presentations right on the bottom where the current still has some shape to it even on a soft tide.

The bluefish have been the more visible story, and we flagged this coming — bunker moving the coast, blues following, and that's exactly what's happening at our end of the Sound. Ocean Beach and Pleasure Beach have both had morning surface chop from blues working bunker pods right off the sand, close enough to see from the boardwalk on a calm morning. These aren't monster blues, mostly 3 to 5 pounds, but there are numbers of them and they're aggressive. Metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks — fished on wire leader has been more than enough. If you see the bunker balled up and nervous, don't overthink it, just get a lure in the water before the school moves. They don't sit still long, especially with harbor traffic pushing through this time of year.

Porgies have been the dependable, unglamorous bread-and-butter option, and with the neap tide slowing everything else down, that steadiness matters. Gold Star Bridge pilings in 25 to 35 feet, and the humps up around the state pier, have been holding good numbers of scup in the 10 to 12 inch range, with the occasional 14-incher mixed in. Sandworms and clam on a simple high-low rig, fished right on bottom on the slower stages of the tide, has been steady work — not exciting, but it fills a cooler when the bigger stuff is playing hard to get. Water temp readings for the Sound put New London around 69 degrees, a touch cooler than the western Sound pushing 71, and that gradient matters more than people think — it's part of why our porgy and bass action stays a notch behind Western Sound reports you might be hearing about. Cooler water, later peak.

Hickory shad, worth mentioning only because people ask — that spring run through the upper Thames wound down weeks ago. If you're still working the shad darts up by the old dam pools expecting river action, you're behind the calendar. That fishery's done until next April. Blackfish are a similar story right now — most guys aren't targeting tog seriously yet this time of year, and the smart money is waiting for that fall push when water starts cooling again and they group up tight on structure. Not worth burning bait on them in July.

Looking ahead, this neap cycle runs a few more days before the tides start building back toward the next spring cycle. That means Fort Trumbull and the bridge pilings should keep fishing on this same soft-current, low-light pattern through midweek — work dawn, dusk, and after dark, target the deeper holding water rather than the rip line itself, and be patient with your retrieve. Once the tides build back up, I expect that current seam at Fort Trumbull to sharpen back up and pull bass back onto the edge where they'll feed more aggressively and through a longer window, including some daylight opportunity again. If the bunker stay thick in the harbor through that transition, and there's no reason right now to think they won't, the bluefish should keep pace right along the beach. I'd plan around the tide change first, the bunker second, and worry about everything else after that.

reports.headline: Wamphassuc rocks go quiet at noon, loud at midnight: eel bite on and fluke picking up the slack
reports.subhead: A soft neap tide is stretching the striper window into the dark hours while fluke and sea bass carry the boulder fields through the day.
reports.body_markdown:
First light off Ram Island and the bait tells you everything before you make a cast. Peanut bunker pinned tight against the rocks, silversides skittering along the boulder faces where the current still has some shape to it, terns working low and quick. By nine o'clock the wind lays down, the sun gets on the water, and it all goes still. That's the tell this time of year — the bait isn't gone, it's just gone quiet, and so are the fish that were pushing it.

Water's running warm through here. New London's reading 69.4, and up toward the western Sound Kings Point is pushing 70.9. That's enough heat in the shallows to shove the bass into a nighttime pattern, and I'm seeing it in my own water — the boulder fields off Wamphassuc Point and the rock piles tight to Fishers Island are dead calm and empty at midday, then come alive after the sun drops. If you want a daytime striper in Fishers Island Sound right now, you're mostly fishing for a mistake. If you want a real bite, you're fishing dusk through first light.

Eels are doing the work. I've been putting 8- to 10-inch rigged eels on spinning gear and working them slow along the base of the rocks in 8 to 15 feet, right where the boulders drop into the channel edges between Ram Island and the Fishers Island side. No burn on the retrieve — just enough to keep contact and let the current work it. Fish are holding tight to structure, not roaming, so you need to put the eel right on the rock, not near it. Bass to 34 inches came off that pattern this week on the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the slack, right around 10 p.m.

Here's the piece that's actually helping the eel guys — we just came off the first-quarter neap, and the rip through the Race and down into Fishers Island Sound has gone soft. That current usually rips hard enough to sweep an eel off the structure before it gets down. Right now it's not doing that. The flow is gentle enough that you can hold a presentation right on the rock for longer, work it slower, and cover a piece of structure properly instead of getting one drift and moving on. That window should hold for a few more days before the tides build back toward the full moon, so if you've been frustrated fishing eels through the Race in past weeks because the water moves too fast to control, this is the stretch to try it again.

Daytime, fluke and sea bass are carrying the program, and honestly carrying it well. Fluke fishing on the sand-to-rock transitions inside the Sound has been one of the more dependable things going — drifting white 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails over the channel edges in 20 to 35 feet, working the last of the incoming into the top of the tide. Nothing giant, but a lot of keepers in the 18- to 20-inch range, and enough short fish mixed in that you're never bored on the drift. Little Narragansett Bay has been quietly good for this too, especially along the edges where the channel deepens off the flats.

Sea bass on the structure have been the best-kept secret of the week. The rock piles off Watch Hill Reef and the boulder fields on the Fishers Island side are holding good numbers, and the quality's been real — fish in the 3- to 4-pound class on green crab and on 3-inch Gulp on ½-ounce jigs, worked slow and vertical right down into the cracks. That matches what's been coming out of the structure over toward Plum Gut, where a 28-inch, five-pound fish turned heads this past week. Our rock piles are holding the same class of fish. If you're picking bottom, don't be shy about bouncing right on top of the boulders — that's where they're sitting, not off to the side in the sand.

No bonito yet, and I want to be straight about that. We flagged two weeks back that the water was lining up for an early push into the Sound, and it still is — Block Island's holding in the upper 60s, which is right in the window these fish like when they start scouting west. I haven't had a confirmed sighting in Fishers Island Sound yet, and neither has anyone I trust at the dock. But the water's right, the bait's right, and I'd be surprised if we don't start seeing scattered fish working the rips off Watch Hill and around the east end of Fishers Island within the next week or two. Worth having a bag of small epoxy jigs and a 6-weight rigged and ready in the boat just in case you run into a nervous patch of water.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the eel bite hard through the soft current the next few nights while the neap holds, then expect the rip to tighten back up as we build toward the full moon — that'll mean shorter windows but harder pulls once the tide gets moving again. Daytime, keep drifting the fluke grounds and don't ignore the sea bass on the rock — that's the most consistent meat in the boat right now. And keep one eye on the horizon past Watch Hill. When the bonito show, they won't announce themselves quietly.

reports.headline: The Race at 3.8 Knots: Neap Tide Softens the Rips, Sea Bass Fill the Gap
reports.subhead: A first-quarter neap has taken the bite out of the strongest water on the coast, but Plum Gut structure and dawn bass are still paying off for those who adjust the clock.
reports.body_markdown:
3.8 knots max ebb through the Race yesterday afternoon — soft by our standards. On a big spring tide this time of year I'm seeing 5, sometimes 5.5 knots ripping past Valiant Rock, current so hard it'll strip drag off a reel just holding bottom. This week's first-quarter neap has taken the teeth out of it, and that changes everything about how you fish this water.

Here's the practical version: slack at Valiant Rock has been running about 20 minutes longer than it does on a full moon spring tide, which means the window to get wire line down and bucktails ticking bottom without getting swept into the boulder field is wider than usual — good for guys who don't want to fight the current to get a bait in the zone, bad for anyone counting on the rip to concentrate bait and fish the way it does when the water's really moving. New London buoy readings are holding at 69.4°F, and that's mild enough that stripers in this stretch of the Sound have settled into the same low-light pattern we're seeing coastwide — they want dawn, dusk, or full dark, and they want it around structure where bait gets pinned.

Bass fishing has been a night-and-dawn game at Race Rock and along the Valiant Rock ledge, 40 to 60 feet, wire line with bunker spoons or a big Danny-style swimmer worked slow, or bucktails with a chunk of pork rind bounced right on the rock pile at the top of the tide change. Daytime has been mostly quiet unless you're marking a bait ball on the meter and can get a bucktail down into it fast — I had one solid fish, mid-30s, come off a jig dropped through a bunker school stacked over the eastern edge of Race Rock on the last of an incoming tide, but that was one fish in three hours of otherwise dead water. That's the honest read right now: the bass are here, they're just not eating on your schedule during daylight.

Sea bass have been the more dependable story. Structure around Plum Gut and out toward the Sluiceway is holding good numbers, and there's a 28-inch, right around 5-pound fish that came off the Gut structure recently that tells you the quality is there if you're willing to work bottom rigs with squid strips or Gulp on 3/4-ounce jigheads in 40 to 55 feet. The current through the Gut has been manageable enough on this neap to actually hold bottom without a ton of extra weight, which is a nice change from the spring tide slugfest where you're dragging 8 ounces just to stay down.

Fluke remain the most consistent thing going in this entire zone. Drifting the edges of the Sluiceway and the flats off Great Gull Island with white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on bucktails, 25 to 35 feet, moving water — outgoing has been better than incoming this week — keeps putting keepers in the box. It's not a blitz, but it's steady, and steady is worth something when everything else is working on a delay.

Albies and bonito haven't shown yet in the Gut or around Little Gull Island, but the water's getting into the range where I start paying attention — Montauk's reading 69.1°F and that end of the Island typically sees the first scouting fish before we do out here. I've got epoxy jigs rigged and ready on two rods, because when they show up around the Gut it's usually with almost no notice — one morning there's nothing, the next there's a rip full of nervous water and green backs slashing bait on the surface. If I had to guess, we're two to three weeks out, but that's a guess built on temperature trend, not a promise.

We flagged the offshore piece last week — said warm filament water pushing toward the CT grounds would put tuna within range of boats running south out of Sound ports, and that's exactly what's playing out. It's a longer run than most of what I cover in the Race and the Gut, but a few boats out of New London and Groton have made the run and found fish, which tells you the same warm water pattern that's kept our bass nocturnal is also stacking bait and predators further offshore.

Looking ahead: this neap holds through the weekend, and I'd use the wider slack windows at Valiant Rock and Race Rock to fish structure you normally can't hold bottom on — deeper boulder fields, the base of the Gut's eastern edge — with bucktails and wire line during the dawn push. Once we roll back toward a stronger tide midweek, expect the rips to tighten up again and the bass bite to concentrate hard into those short slack windows, which is when this water does what it's famous for. Keep the epoxy jigs rigged. Watch Little Gull Island for the first nervous water. That's usually how it starts out here.

reports.headline: Cockenoe on the Neap: Fluke and Porgies Deep, Bass Punching In After Dark
reports.subhead: A softening tide and thinning weekend traffic put the reef bite back in reach — but the stripers want you out there when the moorings go quiet.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday to skip Penfield and run Cockenoe Reef on the back half of the ebb, and it was the right chess move. Here's the thinking: we're sliding into the first-quarter neap, current speed easing off across the whole western basin, and on a soft tide Cockenoe's structure holds bait tighter than Penfield's broader bar. Less current means less scatter — the porgies and fluke stack right on the rockpile instead of getting strung out across open sand. Add in a Tuesday morning with no regatta traffic out of Norwalk Cove, and I had that reef mostly to myself for three hours. That's the kind of window you plan a week around.

The fluke bite has been the most honest thing going in this zone. Cockenoe in 14 to 18 feet, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, produced four keepers and better than a dozen shorts on that ebb. The channel edge between Sheffield Island and the mainland is doing the same thing — moving water pushing bait off the flats into that deeper cut, and the fluke are sitting right on the seam waiting for it. Best window is the last two hours of either tide, when there's still enough push to make the bucktail work but not so much you're bouncing bottom every other cast. Slack water on Cockenoe is dead — I've proven that to myself twice this month, no sense doing it a third time.

Porgies are thick on the Cows off Stamford, and I mean genuinely thick — top-and-bottom rigs with sandworm or clam in 20 to 25 feet putting anglers into steady action, fish running 10 to 12 inches with enough jumbos mixed in to make it worth the trip. That bite doesn't care much about tide stage, which makes the Cows my go-to when I want a sure thing instead of a tactical gamble. Same water is starting to produce black sea bass in better numbers — 20 to 30 feet of structure holding fish now, and that's exactly the pattern I flagged last week: sea bass fishing improving as we move deeper into summer, and it's playing out right on schedule. Squid strips or clam on a high-low rig, bounced tight to the rockpile, is all it takes. Expect that bite to keep building through August as water stays warm and those fish settle deeper into the structure.

Blackfish are off the table right now — Connecticut's summer closure has tautog shut down until September, so if you're marking fish on the Cows or Greenwich Point structure, note the spot and come back for the fall reopener. Plenty of guys are doing exactly that, dropping waypoints now for when the season flips back on.

Striped bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal, and that's not a surprise this deep into July with Kings Point reading 70.9 and the shallow basin holding heat all day. Daytime bass fishing in this zone right now is mostly a lost cause — I've made peace with that. The move is Greenwich Point and the rockpiles off Great Captain Island from last light through the first couple hours of dark, fishing bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig or swimming a live eel along the current edge. The bass are pushing up on bunker pockets working through the Sound after dark, and there've been enough marks and a few solid fish taken on those chunk baits to say the pattern's real, even if it's not a blitz. If you want blues instead, daylight bunker schools moving past the Norwalk Islands have triggered a couple of surface flurries this week — nothing sustained, but enough slashing bait to make it worth keeping a bucktail rigged and ready if you see birds working tight over bait off Sprite Island or Copps Island.

Weekend traffic is still the other variable you have to fish around out here. Saturday and Sunday, the mooring fields off Norwalk and the anchor fleet on Cockenoe get stacked by 9 AM, and that pressure pushes fish off the shallower structure. My move stays the same — first light or last two hours of daylight, before or after the recreational fleet shows up, especially on the reefs closest to the harbors.

Looking ahead, the neap should keep softening current through midweek, which widens the productive window on Cockenoe and the Sheffield channel beyond just peak tide — good news if you can only get out midday. I'd keep leaning on fluke and porgies as the bankable bite, treat sea bass on the Cows as the building story worth checking weekly, and save your best effort for the bass after dark. If the bunker schools hold their current push through the islands, I wouldn't be shocked to see a real daylight blitz develop off Norwalk before the week's out — but until birds are working and bait's exploding on the surface, I'm not betting the trip on it.

reports.headline: Wild Rice Greening the Coves — Bass Hug the Current, Fluke Show at the River Mouth
reports.subhead: With the river running warm and slack water gone soft, Lower Connecticut stripers and a fresh wave of summer flounder are both keying on moving water this week.
reports.body_markdown:
The wild rice is standing tall and green in the coves off Great Island now, thick enough that the marsh hens are working it, and the osprey chicks up on the Nott Island poles are down to their last few weeks before they're flying full circuits over the flats. That's where my calendar sits every July — shad long gone, the spring run just a memory by Memorial Day, and the river settled into its deep-summer rhythm. I've watched this happen fifty times now, and it never fails to surprise new guys how much the fishing changes once the water goes from cool-and-pushy in May to warm-and-lazy in late July.

The river itself is running warm in the coves and flats — the kind of warm that makes a striper sluggish and looking for a reason to move. But the main stem, especially from the Baldwin Bridge down through the Essex Elbow to Saybrook Point, is still getting a flush of cooler, oxygenated water off the Sound on every tide change. Kings Point over on the west end of the Sound is reading close to 71 degrees, New London out east closer to 69 — and Saybrook sits right in that gradient, catching the cooler edge of it on the incoming. That's exactly why the bass in this stretch haven't scattered into total lockjaw the way some of the western Sound backwaters do in a heat spell. They've just gotten smarter about when they'll eat.

Striped bass are holding tight to structure and current — the rock pile off Saybrook Point, the pilings under the Baldwin Bridge, the deep bend by Calves Island, and the channel edge off Nott Island where the current really rips on the ebb. Daytime, with the sun high and the flats baking, those fish are down in the deeper bends where the moving water keeps things livable. Dawn and dusk is when they'll slide up onto the edges to feed — I had two customers working live eels off the Point breakwater last Tuesday at first light, and they took a 28-inch fish and a schoolie inside twenty minutes before the bite went quiet as the sun came up. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, tight to the current seam below the bridge, have also been producing after dark — that's been the more consistent pattern than daylight casting right now. If you're set on daytime fish, work the deepest part of the channel bends slow, with a bucktail or a soft plastic swimbait bounced right along bottom where the current's still moving something.

White perch have pushed up out of the warmest shallow flats and into the deeper holes — Selden Creek, the mouth of Whalebone Creek, the deeper bends up toward Essex. A simple grass shrimp rig or a small piece of bloodworm on a perch spreader, fished slow along bottom in eight to fifteen feet, has been steady, not spectacular. It's a good afternoon fishery when the bass have gone quiet in the heat — not the kind of thing that fills a cooler fast, but reliable if you're patient and willing to move a little to find where they've stacked up.

Bluefish have been showing at the outer edge of the river mouth, out around the Griswold Point bar and the sandbar off the outer breakwater, chasing peanut bunker on the falling tide. It's not a blitz — more a scattered pattern of blues cutting through bait pods for twenty or thirty minutes at a time before moving off — but if you're out there on the last two hours of the ebb with a metal jig or a bunker spoon, you can find them.

We flagged it last week and it's holding up — summer flounder are pushing into the lower river now, right on schedule. I've had reports of keeper-class fluke coming off the sand flats inside the breakwater at Saybrook Point, drifted with three-inch white Gulp swim mullets on quarter-ounce jigheads, fished right on the bottom where that sand gives way to the channel edge. It's not a heavy showing yet, more a scout wave than a full push, but it's exactly the pattern I'd expect as water keeps warming through late July.

We're coming off the first-quarter moon into a neap tide cycle, which means less current overall through the next several days. That's going to soften up some of these current-dependent spots — the bridge pilings and the Point breakwater won't be ripping as hard on peak tide, which actually widens your window to fish them well past the top of the flood or ebb rather than just the hour around max current. I'd use that to my advantage this week — fish longer stretches of the tide instead of racing to catch the peak.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a dramatic change through the end of July. The river will stay warm in the coves, the bass will keep holding to the moving water and the low-light windows, and I'd expect that fluke push to build a little more as the week goes on. If I had one morning to fish, I'd be at the Point at first light on the last of the incoming, eel in hand, betting on that cooler water doing what it's done for fifty years running — pulling the bass up to feed before the sun gets high enough to send them back down.

reports.headline: Neap Tide, Fat Porgies: New Haven Breakwalls Turn On While Bass Go Nocturnal
reports.subhead: Slack current on the first-quarter neap put sea bass and porgies stacked tight to the rock, but the stripers want the dark now.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday, half-tide out, I dropped a two-hook rig baited with fresh skimmer clam into eighteen feet of water off the outer New Haven breakwall and felt that unmistakable thump-thump-thump before the rod even loaded up. Came tight to a porgy that pinned the scale past two pounds — the kind of fish that makes the net operator on the party boats do a double take. That's been the story all week on the rockpiles: when the current goes soft, the porgies and sea bass stack up tight to structure and forget to be careful.

We're riding into the first-quarter neap right now, and if you fish this beat the way I do — vertical presentations over broken bottom — this is exactly the water you want. Less current means less scope on your line, which means you're actually fishing the rocks instead of dragging bait across sand trying to find them. I worked the inside corner of the New Haven outer wall on the last two hours of the outgoing and never had to go heavier than a 2-ounce bank sinker. Porgies to two and a half pounds, a mixed bag of sea bass mostly in the 14 to 16 inch range with a couple that pushed past 17, all on clam and green crab fished right on bottom. Falkner Island's south side rockpile did the same thing on the incoming Wednesday morning — same depth range, same story, slightly bigger average sea bass. One of my regular dock buddies iced a sea bass out there that had real shoulders on it, not far off the class fish coming out of the eastern Sound structure lately.

Stratford Shoal is fishing well too, though you have to time it right. That current rips through there on anything but the neap, so this window is a gift — anchor up-current of the high spots on the shoal at low light, drop clam or squid strips, and let it sit. I had a triple-header there Thursday with two anglers aboard, porgies both times, nothing huge but steady enough that we never had an empty hook for more than two minutes.

Now for the bad news, or at least the complicated news: the stripers have gone quiet in the daylight. Water's sitting in the low 70s across the western basin — Kings Point read almost 71 the other day — and that's enough to push keeper bass into a strict low-light and after-dark pattern. Charles Island's sandbar, which has been money on the flood all June, is basically dead by 9 a.m. now. I fished it twice this week at first light with a white bucktail and Storm swim shad, and both mornings the bite was over in about forty-five minutes flat once the sun climbed. Got two schoolies and a fish that just cleared 28 inches on the second morning, working the drop-off on the south side of the bar right as the flood started pushing bait over it. If you want bass off that bar right now, you need to be there before the sun, or come back after dark and fish the same structure with a bunker chunk soaking on the bottom. That's the play until the water cools a notch.

Fluke have been the pleasant surprise. They're doing exactly what you'd expect this time of year — sliding off the softer back-bay mud and setting up on hard structure and channel edges where the current keeps things moving. Milford Gulf has been solid on the last of the outgoing, drifting 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails right along that channel drop. Nothing giant, mostly fish in the 16 to 19 inch range, but a steady pick, and I heard of a couple pushing 20 inches coming off the harbor mouth structure near the breakwalls on the same tide stage. We flagged a couple weeks back that back-bay fluke would push toward inlet mouths and structure as the water warmed, and that's precisely what's happening now — if you're still working the mud flats expecting summer numbers, you're behind the fish.

Bluefish have been a non-event in my zone so far, which surprises me a little given how loud the bunker-driven blitzes have been to our west. I haven't seen any real bait pods pushing into New Haven Harbor or along Hammonasset yet, though the warm water and the bunker moving up the coast make me think it's a matter of time, not a matter of if. Keep a wire leader and a Hopkins jig in the boat just in case — if a bunker school wanders into the Sound proper, that bite can turn on fast and ugly.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the neap window on the rockpiles through the weekend — Falkner Island and the Stratford Shoal high spots especially, since that current relief won't last once we build back toward the full moon tides. For bass, plan your trip around dawn and dusk, not midday, and don't be afraid to fish Charles Island bar well after dark with a chunk bait if you want a crack at something better than a schoolie. Fluke guys should keep grinding the channel edges at Milford Gulf on the moving water rather than anchoring up hoping fish come to you. It's not an easy week, but it's a honest one — the fish are exactly where the water temperature and the tide say they should be, you just have to fish the right window for each species.

reports.headline: Neap's Coming to Plum Gut — Slow Your Jig Down and Fish the Dark
reports.subhead: Porgy and fluke keep the boat busy by day, but the bass want the Gut after the sun's gone.
reports.body_markdown:
My father used to say a rip has a temper, same as a man, and you learn to fish it by knowing when it's calm and when it's looking for a fight. He fished Plum Gut for forty years with nothing but a compass, a chart he'd drawn himself, and a healthy respect for the fact that the water there doesn't care how long you've been doing this. I think about that every time I idle out past Orient Point and watch the current start to build against the light. This week it's been building slower than usual, and that's telling.

We're sliding into a first-quarter neap, and anybody who's fished the Gut long enough knows what that means — the current through there and through the Race backs off, the standing waves flatten out some, and the fish that were pinned tight to the roughest water start spreading a little wider across the flow. It's not a bad thing. It just means you've got to adjust. I've gone from a three-ounce diamond jig down to a two, sometimes a ounce-and-a-half bucktail with a white pork rind trailer, because the water isn't ripping the way it does on the big tides, and a heavy jig just plows through without working right. Slower presentation, more time in the strike zone. That's the whole trick this week.

Striped bass have been in the Gut on the tide changes, same as always this time of year, but I won't stand here and tell you it's been a daylight bite, because it hasn't. The water's warm enough now — mid-to-upper 60s pushing 70 depending where you check it, warmer out toward the Race than it was a few weeks back — that the better fish have gone nocturnal on us. Dawn and dusk are your windows, and after dark if you've got the stomach for running that water at night, which I'd only recommend to somebody who already knows where the rocks are. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig, drifted through the Gut on the last two hours of the ebb, have taken slot fish and a few overslot up toward 38, 40 inches. Bunker chunks have worked too when there's been current to move the scent, fished right on bottom where the rip meets the flat water off the Plum Island side.

During the day, though, it's fluke, porgy, and blackfish keeping the rods bent, and that bite has been honest and steady, which is more than I can say for the bass. Fluke are coming off the drop-offs and channel edges from Horton Point on east — Gulp swimming mullet in pink shine or white, three to four-inch, on a half-ounce bucktail, drifted with the tide over sand-to-rock transitions. Nothing enormous, mostly 16 to 19 inches with a keeper mixed in here and there, but a full box isn't hard if you keep the boat moving and stay on structure instead of drifting open sand. Porgy have been thick on the reef stretches off Rocky Point and around the mussel beds — small hooks, squid strips, bottom rigs, and you don't need much finesse, they'll find the bait. That bite has held up all summer without a hiccup and I don't see a reason it changes soon. Blackfish, same story on structure, though they're a touch quieter with the water this warm — green crab on a jig head, fished tight to the rock piles, still worth the trip if you're patient with it.

Weakfish have been scarce, and I won't pretend otherwise. A few showed early in the season around the inlet edges but they've thinned out with the warmth. If the evenings stay calm and settled the way they have been, I'd expect a rebuild on some of the mud-bottom stretches toward dusk — that's a pattern I've seen plenty of times, weakfish liking a quiet, warm evening more than a bright hot afternoon. Worth a cast or two with a bucktail and twister tail if you're passing through, but I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet.

Bluefish have been around in patches, not the kind of blitz you'd see farther down the coast where the bunker schools are thick, but enough that if you find bait pushed up along the beach near Mattituck Inlet or off Horton Point, you'll get slammed on a diamond jig or a topwater plug fast enough to lose some tackle. They come and go with the bait, no real pattern to it beyond that.

Looking ahead, the neap should keep softening through the weekend, which widens your workable window at the Gut beyond just the peak of the tide — good news if you've been getting shut out trying to time it perfect. I'd fish the last of the outgoing at first light for bass, switch over to fluke and porgy through the meat of the day on structure, and if the wind stays out of the south and lays down like it has been, I'd try one evening drift for weakfish just to see. No promises there, but the conditions are lining up the way they usually do before that bite rebuilds.

reports.headline: Nine Hours to Atlantis, Two Slot Bluefin, and a Wahoo We Never Saw Coming
reports.subhead: The run's still long and the fuel math still matters, but the canyon edges east of Montauk are finally paying for the trip.
reports.body_markdown:
We left the dock at Montauk at 0300 Tuesday, and by the time the loran numbers matched the chart plotter's guess at the Atlantis edge, we'd burned through a third of a tank and most of the coffee. That's the math out here — call it four hours running at twenty-two knots to cover the ninety-some miles, and that's if the swell cooperates. It didn't complain much this week. Three-to-four foot period swell out of the south, nothing that put anybody on the rail wishing they'd stayed home, but enough to remind you why you fuel heavy and never trust the gauge on the way back.

We found the temperature break we wanted about a mile inside where the chart said it should be — cooler shelf water running 69 degrees butting up against warmer canyon water pushing into the mid-70s. That's the kind of seam that holds bait, and where there's bait on the Atlantis wall this time of July, there's tuna working it. We set up a chunk line on the down-current side, butterfish and a handful of menhaden, 6/0 circle hooks on 60-pound fluoro, and let it soak with the current instead of against it. Took about forty minutes before the first rod bent — a bluefin right in that 27-to-under-47-inch slot everybody's fishing for since the trophy category closed on the third. Second fish came an hour later, same size class, same story. Two-fish limit filled by 0800, which on a long run like this is about as good a morning as you can ask the ocean for.

What we didn't boat was the wahoo that hit a high-speed lure on the way to the chunk spot — ran the drag down hard for maybe ten seconds and then came unbuttoned on a jump we only half saw. That's wahoo fishing for you out here; you get a look and a story, not always a fish in the box. If you want a better crack at them, the morning bite window right at first light on the edge, trolling deep-diving plugs or wahoo bombs at 10 to 12 knots along the drop where the bottom falls from 600 to 1,200 fathoms, is when they show. We'll try again next trip.

The bigger picture this week backs up what the boats running to Veatch and Hydrographer have been reporting — stable high pressure has held for the better part of ten days now, and that kind of weather window is rare enough out here that you fish it hard while it lasts. Warm eddy water has pushed in tight to the canyon edges, and it's dragging yellowfin and a scattering of bigeye up onto the troll. Standard spread — Ilanders and naked ballyhoo, cedar plugs off the shortest rigger, green machines out the back — worked at 6 to 7 knots along the 68-to-72-degree break has been putting fish in the boat at Hydrographer, with reports of similar action pushing east toward Oceanographer. Mahi have been mixed in wherever the boats find floating structure or a stray lobster buoy — nothing to build a trip around by itself, but a welcome bonus when the tuna bite slows midday.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the East Canyons were sitting within range of a strong charter push out of Montauk and the Rhode Island ports, and that's exactly what's playing out. Boats out of Galilee and Block Island running to Veatch are covering the same warm-water push we found at Atlantis, just from a different angle and a slightly shorter number on the plotter depending on which slice of the canyon they're working.

White marlin sign is starting to show along these same edges — a few boats working the temp breaks near Veatch have reported tailing fish and free-jumpers around the weed lines, which tracks with what we've been watching build through the month. Nothing to plan a dedicated billfish trip around just yet, but if you're already trolling the edge for tuna, it's worth dropping a spreader bar or two into the spread rather than running a straight cedar-plug program.

The honest part of this report: it's still a long day or a longer overnight, and the fish don't owe you anything for making the run. We had two good bluefin and a wahoo bite we didn't close out — that's a solid trip for late July, not a banner one. Bring enough fuel to fish the whole window and get home with a real reserve, not a guess.

Looking ahead, the first-quarter neap settling in over the next couple days should soften the current across these shelf breaks a bit, which typically widens the productive trolling window rather than concentrating it into a short tide-driven burst. If the high pressure holds through the weekend — and right now there's no reason to think it won't — I'd run to the same warm-water seam we found at Atlantis and expect the yellowfin and bigeye numbers at Veatch and Hydrographer to keep building rather than fade. Watch the eddy charts before you commit a full tank to one canyon; the warm water's been stable, but it still moves.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Rough Monday Run, Strong Finish: Spencer Yellowfin Take Over the Troll by Thursday
reports.subhead: A sloppy start off Cape May gave way to a building bigeye and yellowfin bite once the swell laid down and the warm water held its ground on the edge.
reports.body_markdown:
If I had to grade this week, I'd call it a C-minus Monday and an A-minus Thursday through Sunday. That's the canyon game for you — you run four different pieces of bottom out of Cape May and Ocean City, and the one that's dead on Tuesday is stacked by Friday. Early in the week we were fighting a leftover groundswell, 3 to 4 feet at a short, chunky 5-second period out past the Bight — the kind of sea state that makes a 60-mile run to Norfolk feel like a chore and turns the ride to Spencer into a rodeo. I had two boats bail on Poor Man's Tuesday morning because the ride out was uglier than the fishing was going to be worth. But the water underneath that chop never went anywhere, and once the wind backed off midweek, the bite caught up fast.

We flagged this last week — said the bite would hold as long as the offshore water stayed put — and that's exactly what happened. The warm push riding up out of the Stream never backed off, and once the sea state settled, boats running out to the 50 and 60 fathom curve off Spencer found bait stacked and fish willing. That's the canyon that carried the week. Daytime trolling around the edge — I'm talking the drop from about 38°32'N, 73°50'W down along the break — produced yellowfin in the 35 to 55 pound class on a mixed spread: naked green machines and cedar plugs up front, a couple of small Islander/ballyhoo combos in the shotgun, running 6 to 8 knots right on the color change where the green Jersey water meets that cleaner blue. When you see birds working bait balls on top and the water temp needle jump a degree and a half in a mile, that's your green light to put the spread in.

Night chunking stayed the bigeye play, same as it always is down here. Anchoring or drifting on the northeast side of the canyon with butterfish chunks and a couple of whole squid mixed in, running long fluorocarbon leaders — 100 to 130 pound — down to a 6/0 circle hook, glow stick clipped a rod length up. The bite windows were tight, mostly that first hour after dark and again right before first light, but the fish that came aboard were quality, several pushing well past 150 pounds. Patience wins that game — you can burn through a slow four hours before the current line sets up right and the fish start feeding under the boat.

Bluefin mixed in right on top of the yellowfin grounds at Spencer and pushed a little into Lindenkohl too, mostly slot-class fish in that 27 to 47 inch window everybody's still working with since the trophy fish closed out July 3rd. Nothing wrong with that — a two-fish limit on 40-pound bluefin eating the same trolled ballyhoo as the yellowfin is a good problem to have, and several boats filled out mixed bags without ever switching gear.

Mahi were the wildcard, same as they always are in late July. Found some solid chicken dolphin and a handful of slammers pushing 15 pounds around any bit of floating structure — lobster pot buoys, weed lines, a broken-up patch of sargassum drifting off the edge at Poor Man's. Small chartreuse feathers and a naked ballyhoo worked when we slowed the spread down to check structure, and it's worth having a rod rigged and ready any time you spot color change or floating junk, because those fish show up fast and disappear just as quick.

Wahoo came mostly on the run — high-speed trolling with black and purple Ilanders and cedar plugs while transiting between grounds, especially crossing structure edges at Lindenkohl and the deeper contour lines south toward Norfolk. Nobody's targeting them exclusively down here yet, but enough came over the rail on the troll-through that it's worth a couple of extra rods rigged heavy while you're running.

White marlin are the story building underneath all of it. We called this one too — said the billfish migration was building through July, and Poor Man's threw a few flags this week, along with some raised fish at Norfolk that never committed. Switch-bait tactics with dink ballyhoo and a naked circle hook teaser worked better than straight dead-bait spreads; these early-run fish are still a little green and want to be teased before they eat.

Looking ahead, if the high pressure holds through the coming week like it has, I'd keep leaning on Spencer for the bulk of the day-trip yellowfin and bigeye work, with Poor Man's as the marlin play if you've got the extra fuel and daylight. Norfolk's worth the long run if Spencer gets crowded or the fish slide south with the bait — that's happened before in late July. Watch the wind forecast closer than the tide chart this week; we're sliding into a neap cycle that'll soften current on the inside stuff, but out here it's the sea state, not the moon, that decides whether you're fishing or just riding.

reports.headline: July 21 and Washington's Already Three Weeks Into Its Prime Window
reports.subhead: The eddy that pushed warm water onto the canyon in early July hasn't budged, and the yellowfin bite is proof Washington doesn't wait for August like the other boys.
reports.body_markdown:
Every year around this time I get the same question at the fuel dock — "Wash, is it too early for Washington?" And every year I give the same answer: it's never too early for Washington. This canyon has a habit of running two to three weeks ahead of Wilmington and the Hudson, and 2026 is no exception. We're not waiting on August water temps to get a real bite going out here. We're already in it.

Here's why. That warm Gulf Stream eddy that set up against the shelf break in late June never pulled off. It's still sitting right where it was, pushing blue water up onto the canyon edge and holding bait tight against the underwater terrain instead of letting it scatter into the Slope Sea like it usually does this time of year. That's the whole ballgame for Washington in July — when the eddy holds, the fish hold, and day-boat range becomes real range. Boats running out of Ocean City and Indian River have had one of the shortest steams to blue water I've seen at this point in the season in years.

We flagged this back on the 13th — said the new moon spring tide would push hard current across the shelf break and stack bait against the structure. That's exactly what happened, and the residual effect is still paying dividends even now that we've rolled into the first-quarter neap. The current's softer this week, no question, but the eddy's doing the heavy lifting now, not the tide. That's an important distinction if you're planning your week — don't expect the ripping current of ten days ago, but don't expect the bite to fall off either.

The western wall — I'm talking the stretch running along the 50-fathom curve down through the elbow — has been the most consistent piece of structure all week. Yellowfin in the 30 to 55-pound class have been eating a mixed spread of green machines, cedar plugs, and small chugger heads pulled at 6 to 7 knots right along that break where the green water meets the blue. Water temp on the edge itself has been holding in the mid-to-upper 70s, and that thermal line is razor sharp right now — you can see it in the color change without even looking at the graph. Work the seam, not the middle of either color.

Bigeye have been showing at night on the chunk, mostly butterflied sardines and small chunks of bluefin belly fished on 50 to 80-pound fluoro leaders, drifted off the stern in that same western wall zone. It's not a wide-open bite — guys are picking off one or two fish a night, sometimes going hours between bites — but the quality has been excellent, fish pushing 150 to 200 pounds on the ones that have come tight. If you're grinding it out after dark, keep your spread thinned down and your scent trail heavy. These fish are eating out of an eddy that's concentrated but not endless.

Mahi have been scattered around any floating structure holding current — lobster pot buoys, weed lines, the occasional current seam breaking off the hook at the canyon's north end. Nothing giant, mostly schoolie-class fish in the 3 to 8-pound range, but they'll eat almost anything you throw at them — small spoons, ballyhoo, even bucktails if you're already fishing bottom structure for something else. Good fun for the crew while the bigger stuff is being patient.

White marlin have been around the temp break too, which tracks with what we've been seeing building up the coast all month — this billfish migration has been gaining steam since early July and Washington's getting its share. Most of the marlin action has come on natural bait — ballyhoo behind Sea Witches, worked slow through the color change on the troll. It's not a stacked bite, more like two or three shots a day if you're covering the right water, but the fish are there and they're eating.

Wahoo have been the wildcard. A few boats running high-speed spreads — bonito strips and dark-skirted lures at 12 to 15 knots along the deeper edges of the western wall — have picked off a wahoo or two in that 40 to 60-pound range, usually right at first light before the yellowfin bite turns on. Not a target-worthy pattern yet, more of a bonus fish if you're already out there early.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for this to slow down unless the weather turns on us. The eddy's stable, the high pressure's been steady, and every report I'm hearing out of the neighboring canyons says the same thing — this bite is building, not fading. The neap tide will keep current lighter through the week, which might soften the bite window slightly on the structure-dependent spots, but Washington's not really a tide-driven canyon in July — it's an eddy-driven canyon, and that eddy isn't going anywhere I can see. If I had one day this week, I'd run the western wall at first light, work the temp break hard on the troll until the sun gets up, then switch to the chunk if the current stays manageable into the evening. Bring extra ballyhoo — you'll want options.

reports.headline: Ran to Wilmington instead of Hudson — burned less fuel, found more bigeye
reports.subhead: A chunk-all-night, troll-at-dawn trip on the east wall paid off with bigeye, a stacked yellowfin bite, and our first white marlin shot of the season.
reports.body_markdown:
I had a decision to make Tuesday afternoon — Hudson or Wilmington. Both canyons were showing decent reports, but Hudson meant another 20 miles of running each way, and with fuel where it is, that's not nothing on a 30-hour trip. I looked at the eddy positioning, saw the warm water pushing in tighter to Wilmington's east wall than it had been the week before, and made the call to save the diesel and fish closer to home. Good call this time — it usually pays to fish what's in front of you instead of chasing a rumor 40 miles up the shelf.

We ran out to the 600-fathom curve on the east side, around the corner where the canyon starts widening out past the Baby Wilmington, and found a hard color change — hard blue water butting up against a greener, cooler push off the shelf. That's the kind of edge that holds bait, and it held bait. Flying fish were nervous on the surface most of the afternoon, always a good sign, and we marked bait balls stacked from 120 feet down to almost 300 on the sounder right on the break.

We committed to the chunk that night instead of trolling into dark, and it was the right move. Set up on the edge with the current pushing us slowly along the wall, butterfish chunks in a slow drip, and by 10 pm we had our first bigeye — a fish right around 140 pounds that took a long time to get up from depth on 80-pound fluoro leader and a plain hook buried in a butterfish chunk. We picked at two more through the night, lost a couple to green mono and sharp turns near the boat, but ended up boating three bigeye by first light. That's a solid night's work for one boat — not a stacked-up, every-bait-getting-bit kind of bite, but steady enough that nobody was standing around.

Daylight, we pulled the chunk gear and put the spread back out — naked ballyhoo behind Sea Witches, a couple of small Ilanders in blue/white and green/yellow, and a spreader bar down the middle. Yellowfin showed up almost immediately working the same temperature seam, mostly in the 35- to 55-pound class, and we picked away at them trolling the break in both directions for about four hours before it went quiet around 10 am. Six yellowfin in the box, plus a wahoo that smashed a high-speed planer rig with a green Yo-Zuri bomber we had out wide — that fish nearly emptied a reel before we turned it.

We also had a legitimate white marlin shot — a fish came up on a dredge teaser mid-morning, wouldn't commit to a hookbait, but it's the first real billfish sign we've had out there this year. We flagged a couple weeks back that the marlin migration would build through July, and this is exactly the kind of thing you'd expect to start seeing right about now. Doesn't mean they're stacked up yet, but the pieces — warm water, bait, the right depth — are lining up.

Mahi were a bonus, not a target. We picked up four dolphin, biggest around 12 pounds, off a scattered weed line we crossed running between the chunk grounds and the troll spread the next morning. If you've got time between tuna stops, it's always worth a look at any floating junk or grass — a couple of small green/yellow feathers pulled fast will draw a strike almost every time there's fish under the weeds.

The bigger picture here is that this stable high-pressure stretch we've had for going on two weeks now is doing exactly what it's supposed to do — keeping the eddy water pinned up against the canyon wall instead of sliding off, and that's holding bait and fish in range instead of scattering them. We called the new moon tide would tighten bait up along the shelf break, and that's held true — the concentration we found on the sounder Tuesday night was about as tight as I've seen it this season.

It wasn't a lights-out trip. The daytime troll bite was good but not overwhelming — six yellowfin in four hours of trolling a known edge is solid work, not a feeding frenzy. If you're going, I'd plan around the chunk at night for the bigeye and treat the morning troll as the bonus round rather than the main event right now. That could flip if the yellowfin push harder onto the temp break like they were starting to Wednesday morning.

Looking ahead, if this high pressure holds through the weekend — and right now there's no reason to think it won't — I'd expect the pattern to keep building rather than fade. Wilmington, Hudson, Washington, and the canyons to the south are all reading similar setups.
