Billingsgate has been the fluke spot this week, and it's been solid, not spectacular — a few keepers in the 18 to 22 inch range mixed with a lot of shorts on white Gulp Swimming Mullets fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow across the sand-to-mud transition on the last of the incoming tide. That's typical Billingsgate — the fluke sit right where the bottom changes character, and if you're not paying attention to your chart you'll drift right past the good stretch without knowing it. Sandy Neck has had some bluefish action working the beach as bait pushes along the shoreline, mostly smaller blues in the 2 to 4 pound range, fun on light tackle but nothing to write home about size-wise.

We're coming up on the first-quarter neap later this week, and that's going to soften the current through the rips for a few days. That's usually a mixed blessing out here — it widens the window where you can fish productively because the tide isn't ripping through as hard, but it also spreads the bait out more, so you spend more time hunting and less time just anchoring up on a known spot. If I had one day to fish this weekend, I'd still start at Race Point on that last two hours of ebb, because that structure holds bait even when the current isn't screaming, and I'd have a backup plan to run out to Peaked Hill if the bass don't show inside the first hour.

Mackerel have been thick enough this week that livelining is the easy call over eels or bucktails, and I'd keep it that way as long as they're showing up on the fishfinder in that same tight window off the Race. If the mackerel schools move or thin out, that's when I'll switch back to swimming plugs and bucktails worked slow along the rip edges. For now, the pattern's holding — cooler water, daylight bass, dependable bottom fish deeper down. Not a blow-out week, but a solid one, and out here this time of year, solid is plenty.

reports.headline: Deer Island Drop Holds Daytime Bass on Live Mackerel — Rocks Fish the Same Trick
reports.subhead: Cooler harbor water is keeping stripers eating through the middle of the day while the rest of the coast goes nocturnal.
reports.body_markdown:
I made my call for this week Tuesday morning, standing on the dock at Winthrop watching a mackerel school push bait against the rocks off Grover's Cliff. Harbor islands, not the North Shore rocks, not a run down to Plymouth. When mackerel stack that thick this close to the ledges, you follow the bait, not the calendar. That decision paid off by ten AM.

Here's the thing that's different about our water right now compared to everywhere south of the Cape — the Gulf of Maine keeps this harbor cool enough that bass haven't shut down into a strict low-light pattern. South Shore guys, Cape Cod guys, they're grinding it out at 5 AM and 9 PM because the water's too warm for stripers to feed comfortably in the sun. We don't have that problem. Deer Island Light, Spectacle Island's northern ledge, the drop-off along President Roads — I've had bass hitting live mackerel at high noon this week, which tells you everything about why this stretch of coast is worth fishing right through midday in July.

The program at Deer Island is dead simple. Snag mackerel off the surface with a Sabiki rig, hook one through the nose on a 7/0 circle, and slow-troll or drift it right along that drop where the channel falls off from 15 feet to better than 40. Outgoing tide is the move — water pulls off the flats around Spectacle and funnels bait right past that ledge, and the bass know it. I had three fish over 30 inches Wednesday on the last two hours of the ebb, all within casting distance of the light itself. Nothing giant, but steady, and every one of them came up eating instead of sulking, which is the story of this whole zone right now.

Up on the North Shore, the rocks at Nahant and around Gloucester's breakwater are holding fish too, but it's a different bite — more technical, more about reading the wash. Dawn topwater with a Gibbs Polaris popper off the eastern side of Nahant has produced some quality bluefish mixed with schoolie bass, and once the sun gets up I've been switching to a white Savage Sand Eel jig, six inches, worked slow along the boulder fields where the pollock have been holding. Cape Ann out toward Halibut Point is fishing similarly — bass tucked tight to structure, not chasing far, so short precise casts into the wash beat long bombs every time. The mackerel and pollock schools sitting inshore right now are doing exactly what they're supposed to — feeding the whole food chain and keeping predators shallow and aggressive instead of pushing them out deep.

Down south toward Duxbury Bay and Kingston, the flounder bite is doing what we said it would last week — it's building. Guys working the mud flats on the dropping tide with sandworms and squid strips on a simple two-hook flounder rig are filling coolers steadier than they were two weeks ago, and I expect that to keep improving as the flats warm through the rest of July. If you've got a light spinning outfit and don't mind anchoring up and waiting, Duxbury's inner flats on the last two hours of the ebb are worth the trip right now.

We're heading into a first-quarter neap around the 21st, which softens the current everywhere from Deer Island to the Cape Ann rips. That's not a bad thing for us — weaker current means wider bite windows on structure spots like Spectacle and Nahant, since the fish aren't getting blown off the rock by a hard rip. It does mean the harbor channel bite at Deer Island might slow slightly on the tide change itself, so I'd plan around the two hours before and after the ebb rather than fighting slack water.

Cod and haddock reports have been thin close to shore, which is normal for late July — that fishery's mostly pushed out to the deeper structure off Stellwagen and the outer Cape Ann ledges now, and I wouldn't burn a day targeting bottom fish inside the harbor this week. If you want groundfish, it's a boat run, not a rock-hop.

Bluefish have been a bonus rather than a target — mixed in with the bass blitzes at Nahant and occasionally slashing through the mackerel schools off Winthrop, but I haven't seen the kind of dedicated blue run yet that they're getting further south along the bunker schools. If that bait moves north the way it has in past Julys, expect that to change fast, and I'll be watching Broad Sound and the outer harbor closely for it.

Looking ahead, if the mackerel stay stacked around the harbor islands the way they are now, I'd keep working Deer Island and Spectacle through the neap tide — the wider bite window should actually make this an easier week to time than a big-moon push would. If the bait scatters or pushes offshore, I'll shift the program north to the Nahant-to-Gloucester rocks, where the structure holds fish regardless of what the tide's doing. Either way, daylight fishing is still very much alive in this harbor — that's the edge we've got over the rest of the coast right now, and I'd use it while the water stays cool enough to let us.

reports.headline: 5:52 Ebb at the Railroad Bridge: Bass Deep, Blues on Top
reports.subhead: The neap is softening the current, but the low-light windows on both ends are still putting fish on the deck — you just have to be there for the turn.
reports.body_markdown:
5:52 AM. That's when the ebb hits full stride at the Railroad Bridge this week, and if you're not rigged and casting by 5:40, you're already behind the current. I've been watching this canal for thirty years and the clock still tells you more than any app ever will. Right now we're sliding into the July 21 first-quarter neap, which means peak velocity is backing off from the 5-knot spring tides we saw two weeks ago down into the high 3s, low 4s. That sounds like bad news, but it's actually opened the window up — instead of a tight 45-minute sweet spot at max ebb, guys are finding fish holding an hour on either side of peak current on both ends this week.

East end first. The rip line off the Bell Buoy has been the most consistent piece of water in the whole system. Bass are sitting deep in the trough where the ebb dumps out past the jetty, and they want something that gets down and stays down through the seam — a 2-ounce Kettle Herring bucktail tipped with a strip of mackerel belly, or if you're a plug guy, a slow-sinking Redfin worked with the current instead of against it. I had a report of a 34-inch fish taken right at 5:15 AM Tuesday, just as the current was building toward that 5:52 peak, and another keeper came off the rocks near Scusset Beach twenty minutes later on the same tide. That's the pattern right now — the fish are there for the buildup and the first half hour of max current, then they slide off the structure once it eases.

West end has been the bluefish show. Mashnee Island and the current seam off Hog Island are holding bait — pods of peanut bunker getting pushed and pulled with every tide change — and the blues have been all over them in the last hour of daylight. Poppers and 1-ounce metal like Kastmasters worked fast across the surface have been getting hit hard right at dusk, especially on the flood when that Buzzards Bay water pushes in past Wings Neck and stacks bait against the current seam. Nothing subtle about it — you see the bait get nervous, you see the surface break, and you've got maybe ten casts before the school moves off the seam. I had two guys texting me from Phinneys Harbor Thursday saying they lost count of blues in a 45-minute window right on the last of the flood before dark.

Bass on the west end have been more of a night bite than a daytime one, and that's exactly the pattern we flagged last week — night fishing carrying the load as the heat sets in. Daytime water temps on the Cape Cod Bay side are staying cooler than what the Sound and the South Shore beaches are dealing with right now, which is keeping our fish more willing to feed through the day than stripers south of here, but the biggest fish are still coming after dark. Guys working eels on the drop at the Bourne Bridge abutments after 9 PM have had the best luck — slow presentation, let the current do the work, and don't be afraid to fish it right through a full tide change since the neap current isn't ripping as hard as it will again in a couple weeks.

Fluke have been a bright spot for anyone willing to work the deeper water off the canal mouths. Both ends have channel edges dropping to 25-30 feet where fluke are holding on the last two hours of the ebb, and a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail, dragged slow along bottom, has been putting keeper-class fish in the cooler consistently. It's not blitz fishing, but it's steady, and on a week when the bass bite has been more about timing than volume, that steadiness is worth knowing about.

No albies or bonito yet — too early for the canal itself — but I'd keep half an eye on Buzzards Bay proper as you head toward Wings Neck and the mouth. Water's been climbing into a range where those fish start scouting, and if that pattern follows the rest of the coast, we could see the first scattered reports in the next couple weeks working up from the outer bay.

Looking ahead, the neap is going to keep softening current speeds through the weekend, which means longer bite windows but less violent current to concentrate fish tight against structure. I'd fish the buildup on both ebb and flood rather than waiting for dead-peak current — that's where the fish have been sitting this week, not right at the max. If you can only get one session in, make it the evening flood at Mashnee for blues, or the pre-dawn ebb at the east end rip for bass. Both have been the most dependable windows on the calendar, and with the moon easing off, the fish seem to be giving you a little more time to work them than they will again once we build back toward full.

reports.headline: Monhegan Ledges Give Up Pollock and Cod While Bass Push Deep Into Penobscot Bay
reports.subhead: Cool Gulf of Maine water is keeping stripers feeding in daylight while groundfish hold tight to the ledges and channel edges.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty-some years ago my father told me something I still repeat to every greenhorn who steps on my boat: "The bay doesn't lie, but it doesn't hurry to tell you the truth either." I thought about that Tuesday morning hauling gear off White Head, watching a school of pollock roll bait right on the surface not thirty yards from the buoy — something I hadn't seen that thick in years. My sternman, twenty-two and new to this, wanted to drop everything and go get a rod. I told him to finish the string first. The pollock weren't going anywhere. That's the kind of week it's been — steady, unhurried, and if you pay attention, generous.

Striped bass have been the story up and down the bay, and the reason is simple: our water hasn't warmed the way it has south of Cape Cod. Down there the bass have gone nocturnal, sliding off the flats at first light and not showing again till dusk. Up here, with Gulf of Maine water still running cool, the fish are willing to feed right through the middle of the day. I've been finding schoolies to 28 inches working the pinch points at Eggemoggin Reach on the last two hours of the flood, and better fish — a few pushing 34, 35 inches — holding off the ledges at Eastern Egg Rock where the mackerel and pogies have been stacking up thick enough to color the water. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, or a 2-ounce white bucktail worked slow along the rip, has been the ticket. The puffins are still working that same bait up there, which tells you all you need to know about how much forage is sitting on that ledge right now.

Rockland breakwater has been a reliable mackerel spot again this week — small jigs, no bait needed, tight to the rocks on the last of the outgoing. Bring a few extra Sabikis because the mackerel are running with a scattering of pollock underneath them, and those pollock will happily take a jig meant for something smaller. Boothbay Harbor's had the same pattern just inside the islands, mackerel thick enough that the charter boats have been filling bait wells in twenty minutes flat before running offshore.

Groundfish have been the quieter but more consistent part of the week. Cod are holding deep in the Penobscot Bay channels — 90 to 120 feet off the eastern side between Vinalhaven and North Haven, and out toward the deeper water past Matinicus. Jigging diamond jigs or bouncing a whole clam bait on a high-low rig near bottom has produced fish in the 20-to-25-inch range, nothing enormous but steady enough to make a morning worthwhile. Haddock have been mixed in with that same crowd, though you have to work for them — smaller fish, and you'll cull through some shorts. Monhegan remains the most dependable groundfish stop in the zone. The ledges on the northeast side, particularly on the ebb when the current sets up clean against the rock, have been giving up both cod and pollock, with the pollock often willing to hit right up near the surface on a slow retrieve with a soft-plastic swimbait — the same fish my sternman wanted to chase off White Head.

Bluefish haven't shown in any real numbers up this way yet, which isn't unusual for us — that's still mostly a southern New England story right now, with the big blitzes running from the Jersey shore into Raritan Bay. We flagged last week that bluefish would keep following bunker up the coast as long as the weather held calm and stable, and that's exactly what's happened south of us — the bite has spread, just not quite into Maine water yet. If it keeps pushing north the way it has, don't be surprised if we start seeing a few stray blues mixed in around Casco Bay by early August. I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet, but it's worth watching.

Tide and moon matter more than usual right now. We're rolling toward a first-quarter phase, which means the current is easing off peak strength through the Reach and around Stonington's tighter passages. That's actually good news for bass fishing — a softer current means longer, more comfortable feeding windows instead of a narrow slack-tide scramble, and it should widen the productive stretch on both the Eggemoggin and Fox Islands Thorofare drifts through the next several days.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and light like it has been, I'd put my time into the Eastern Egg Rock bass and the Monhegan groundfish — both have been the most consistent producers of the summer so far. If a northeast blow comes through and stirs up the outer ledges, shift inside to the bay channels off Vinalhaven where the cod have been holding regardless of surface conditions. Best case, this cool-water pattern holds and the bass keep feeding through daylight for another few weeks before the summer heat finally catches up to us. Worst case, a hot stretch pushes them into the same low-light pattern they're running south of us — but up here, that's usually a late-August problem, not a late-July one.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock's Ledge Holds Cod and Haddock While Mackerel Draw the Bass Shallow
reports.subhead: A neap tide settling into Casco Bay this week is stretching out the bite windows on the outer ledges — and the mackerel are doing most of the talking.
reports.body_markdown:
I was out past Halfway Rock on Tuesday morning, drifting the eighty-foot contour on the northeast face, and watched something I always look for this time of year — a pod of mackerel come up nervous and tight, dimpling the surface for maybe ninety seconds before something pushed them back down. That's the tell. When the mackerel get jumpy like that at first light, there's almost always a bass or two working underneath, and sure enough, on the next drift my rod loaded up on a bucktail I'd tipped with a mackerel strip, fished slow along bottom in about eighteen feet as the ledge falls off toward the deep water south of the Rock.

That's been the story of the week in Casco Bay — mackerel schools setting the table, and the rest of the food chain responding accordingly. The bay's water has stayed on the cooler side compared to what's happening south of Cape Cod, and that matters. Where warm shallow water down south has pushed keeper bass into a strict low-light and after-dark pattern, the Gulf of Maine influence here keeps our fish willing to feed through the middle of the day, provided there's bait around to trigger it. I've had good bass activity at ten in the morning this week off Peaks Island's eastern side and again in early afternoon along the Bailey Island ledges — something you don't see much of once the water down in Massachusetts Bay really warms.

Halfway Rock itself has been steady rather than spectacular for groundfish. Cod are holding on the deeper structure to the south and east of the Rock, in the seventy-five to ninety-foot range, and they're coming on diamond jigs worked with a slow lift-drop right off bottom, or on standard cod rigs baited with clam. Haddock have mixed in on the same drifts, a little shallower, sixty-five to seventy-five feet, and they've wanted a teaser above the jig — a small white or chartreuse fly seems to be drawing more strikes than the jig alone. It's not a fast bite. I'd call it a working bite: two or three keepers of each per drift if you're patient and willing to make several passes, not a bucket-filler. The fish are there, but they're not stacked the way I've seen them in some Augusts past.

The mackerel run itself has been a little inconsistent, which I want to be honest about. Some mornings off the Portland breakwater and around Cushing Island the schools have been thick enough to load a Sabiki rig in seconds. Other mornings this week they've been scattered and hard to locate, moving with the tide rather than holding in one place. My read is that the bay's forage is still shaking itself into its mid-summer pattern, and the mackerel haven't fully settled into predictable holding water yet. When you find them, though, they're doing exactly what they're supposed to — pulling bass up out of the depths and into range of bucktails, umbrella rigs, and live-lined presentations off structure like the Bailey Island ledges and the rocky shoreline running down toward Cape Small.

Bluefish have started showing in modest numbers inside the bay, working the same bait schools as the bass. This tracks with what's been developing along the whole coast this month — bluefish following bunker and mackerel wherever the forage concentrates, and as long as the weather stays settled and doesn't scatter that bait, I'd expect the pattern to hold and maybe build. We don't get the blitzes here that they're seeing farther south, but a few three- and four-pound blues mixed in with the bass on a mackerel school is a welcome variety, and they'll hit the same bucktails and small metal you're throwing for stripers.

Tide-wise, we're sliding into a first-quarter neap on the 21st, and that's worth planning around. Neap tides mean softer current on the outer ledges — Halfway Rock, the Harpswell approaches, the water off Two Lights — which typically widens the productive drift window rather than concentrating it tightly around the peak of the tide. If you've been frustrated trying to time a short window of hard current at the Rock, this is your week to fish it more loosely; the bite should stay workable through a longer stretch of the tide cycle rather than shutting off outside of an hour either side of the top.

Looking ahead, I'd focus effort on the Cape Small ledges and the deeper water off Bailey Island for cod and haddock, working the softer neap current with jig-and-teaser rigs, and I'd keep an eye out at first light around Peaks Island and the breakwater for mackerel activity — when you see that nervous water, get a bucktail or a live mackerel down into it quickly. The bay isn't giving up easy limits right now, but the pattern is sound, and a patient morning on the right ledge is still paying off.

reports.headline: Biddeford Pool's Incoming Hands Up a 30-Pound Bass, Blues Rip Through Higgins
reports.subhead: Cooler Gulf of Maine water is keeping stripers feeding in daylight while the south chokes on heat — this is our window and it's open now.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday evening, half-tide and building, I was standing on the bar at Biddeford Pool with a Gibbs pencil in my hand and green water sliding past my knees. Third cast, the plug got walloped right at the edge of the channel where the current pinches down before it dumps into the Pool proper — a bass that pulled drag like it meant it and measured out at 30 pounds when I finally got a tape on her in the wash. That's the fish of the week for me, and it came exactly where it should have: the last two hours of the incoming, when bait gets pushed up off the flats and pinned against that gut running along the eastern shore. If you've fished the Pool long enough you know that window — it's the best hour of the Maine striper day, full stop, and it hasn't let me down yet this July.

Here's the thing that's making this stretch of coast worth fishing right now while the water south of the Cape turns into a bathtub: our water hasn't caught up to that heat yet. The Gulf of Maine is still running cool enough that these bass haven't gone nocturnal on us. Down in Jersey and the Sound they're feeding at dawn, dusk, and after dark because the shallows are too warm to hold fish through the middle of the day. Up here, I'm still getting bites at eleven in the morning off the rocks at Prouts Neck. That's a real edge for us, and I don't expect it to close up anytime soon — cooler water tends to hold that daytime pattern well into August around here, and I said as much last week. Nothing's changed my mind.

Pine Point has been the more consistent producer for schoolie-to-mid-slot bass, fished on the dropping tide out of the river mouth where the Scarborough River dumps into the marsh channel. Bucktails, half-ounce and three-quarter, white and chartreuse, bounced along the bottom in eight to twelve feet as the current picks up speed past the jetty rocks. Nothing huge — most of what's coming over the rail is 24 to 28 inches — but it's steady, and on a good outgoing you can pick away at a dozen fish in a couple hours without much competition on the water.

Bluefish are the story at Higgins Beach right now, and it's the kind of blitz you smell before you see — oily, fishy, and the gulls are already working before the first blue busts bait on the surface. Peanut bunker have pushed in tight to the beach on the higher stages of the tide, and the blues have been all over them mid-morning and again in the last light before dark. Nothing subtle needed — a bone or chrome Kastmaster, a Hopkins spoon, or a topwater popper thrown right into the melee will get bit almost every cast. Bluefish season is following the bunker exactly the way it's supposed to, and I've been telling folks for two weeks that as long as this bait stays put along the beach, the blues will keep coming with it. That's held up. I don't see any reason for it to break unless a hard blow scatters the peanut schools off the beach.

Prouts Neck fished well on the southwest wind we had over the weekend — that wind pushes warm surface water and bait up against the rocks on the ocean side, and the bass tuck in behind the boulders waiting for it to get shoved past them. I worked a black Danny plug along the edge there Saturday morning on a rising tide and connected with two fish in the high 20s before the wind swung and killed the bite around midday. If you get another southwest blow this week, don't sleep on that spot — just get there before the wind direction flips, because once it does the current along those rocks goes dead and so does the bite.

Mackerel are still thick off Wells Harbor and out toward the Cape Elizabeth ledges, and that's no small thing — that bait is what's keeping both the stripers and whatever cod are still lurking on the deeper structure happy. If you want fresh mackerel for bait or the table, small diamond jigs or a mackerel tree worked in 20 to 40 feet off the harbor mouth will fill a cooler fast, usually first thing in the morning before the boat traffic picks up. Flounder guys have been doing quiet, unglamorous work in the Kennebunk River and around Wells Harbor on sandworms and clam bellies, fished on the bottom on the last of the ebb — not exciting fishing, but if you want a mess of flounder for dinner, that's still a reliable play.

We're heading into a neap tide the next few days off Thursday's first quarter moon, which means less current push through the Pool and around Prouts Neck — the water will move slower, and that generally widens the bite window instead of compressing it into one hard hour. I'd use that to my advantage and fish the Pool an hour either side of what's normally the sweet spot, because with softer current the fish don't have to commit to the same tight window. My money this week is on the incoming at Biddeford Pool early, Higgins Beach for the blues midday if the bunker hold, and Prouts Neck again if we get one more southwest wind before the weekend. Bring the big plugs. This bite's earned them.

reports.headline: 180 feet on the mud: haddock steady, cod scratchy on the gravel edge
reports.subhead: Jeffrey's is holding fish in two very different places this week — and the bluefin are starting to show sand eels on the surface.
reports.body_markdown:
One-eighty on the sounder, soft mud, twelve degrees cooler than the surface — that's where the haddock have been sitting all week on the northeast corner of Jeffrey's, inside the Scantum Basin flats where the bottom flattens out and holds that cold layer. I've had charters limit on haddock there three days running, working diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, working the jig just off bottom in a slow lift-drop so it stays in that thin zone where the fish are stacked. That's the mud pattern, and right now it's the more reliable of the two.

The gravel bite for cod has been tougher. I ran the ledge proper — the hard bottom stretch running north-south in about 130 to 150 feet, where the gravel breaks up into little cobble humps — and found fish, but scattered. Not the kind of structure-hugging school you can anchor on and grind. We're picking up cod in the 6 to 12 pound range on cut bait, herring chunks fished on a high-low rig, but you're working for every one. My theory is the water's warmed enough on top that the cod have pushed down tighter to structure and aren't roaming the flat gravel like they do in cooler months. I'd rather find three good marks on the ledge and work them hard than blind-drift the whole stretch hoping to stumble into fish.

Platts Bank has been quieter than I'd like for both species this week, but Tillies Bank redeemed itself Thursday — a pollock bite that surprised me, fish in the 15 to 20 pound class hitting jigs worked fast through the water column, 80 to 100 feet down over structure that runs about 200 feet total depth. Pollock like that kind of aggressive vertical presentation, and when they're on, they'll hit a bucktail jig or a diamond jig just as readily as a haddock rig. If the cod stay stingy on the gravel, Tillies is worth the extra run for a mixed bag.

Now the tuna. We flagged the new moon pattern a week back — said it would push bait and concentrate fish on sand eels, mackerel as the backup forage — and that's exactly what's showing up on the ledge now. We're seeing scattered bluefin working the surface off the southern end of Jeffrey's, chopping through balls of sand eels in loose pods, not the tight, boiling schools you get come October, but definitely present and definitely feeding. A few boats have hooked up jigging vertically through the bait balls with metal jigs, and there's been some success trolling small spreader bars along the edges where the sand eel schools are getting pushed up against structure. It's early yet — this is the leading edge of the run, not the main event — but the pattern lines up with what I expected watching the moon phase build bait concentrations through the second week of July.

We're heading into a first-quarter neap around the 21st, which is going to soften the current on the ledge for a few days. That typically spreads groundfish out a little more and can make the haddock bite on the mud even more consistent since they're less pinned by strong tidal flow — but it can also slacken the current enough that the cod on the gravel get lazier about feeding, which might explain part of what we saw this week. I'd expect the haddock pattern to hold steady into early next week regardless, since that basin bite doesn't depend much on tide strength the way the ledge structure bite does.

Mackerel have been thin around the boat this trip, which is a little unusual for late July — usually by now we're marking bait schools thick enough to snag right off the transom for fresh cod bait. We found a few pockets working bait rigs off Thatcher Island on the way out, enough to fill a bait bucket, but nothing like the walls of mackerel you'd expect. That thinness might be tied into why the tuna are working sand eels instead — less mackerel around to hold them, so they're keying on the smaller forage.

For next week, my plan is straightforward. I'll keep working the Scantum mud for haddock since that's been the bankable bite, run a few passes on Tillies for pollock since that fishery showed real promise, and keep an eye on the sand eel schools on the south end of Jeffrey's for early tuna activity. If the neap tide holds the current down like I expect, I'd look for the cod bite on the gravel to stay slow through midweek and then pick back up once the tide builds toward the next moon phase. Anyone heading out should have a haddock plan and a backup — right now the mud is paying better than the gravel, and that's not the way it usually runs on this ledge in July.

reports.headline: Appledore Ledges on the Slack: Cod Steady, Stripers Stacking the Piscataqua Bridges
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty when you fish it like it's a hundred and thirty — the Shoals gave up cod on the drop, and the river's holding bass all week.
reports.body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and figure there's nothing to it. I've had guys at the launch ask why I bother trailering the Lund out past Rye Harbor every morning instead of running down to the Cape where everybody else fishes. Thing is, those thirteen miles include the Isles of Shoals, and the Isles of Shoals fish like they're a hundred and thirty miles offshore. Structure, current, cold water holding right through summer — I don't need more coastline, I need to know where the rockpiles are. I was on the water before 5 AM most days this week, and I was back at the dock with fish in the box before most folks had poured their second cup.

The cod bite at Appledore held up better than I expected for late July. I worked the ledges off the southwest corner in 65 to 80 feet, and the trick has been timing it to the slack — that window either side of the tide change when the rip between Appledore and Smuttynose lays down enough to actually hold bottom with a jig. Fight the current out there and you're not fishing, you're just paying out line. Diamond jigs, the heavier ones, tipped with a strip of clam, dropped straight down and worked in short lifts off the rock. Took cod to 8 pounds Tuesday morning, a mixed bag of keepers and shorts most other days. Haddock have been mixed in but thinner than I'd like — a few nice ones came up off White Island in 70 feet on the same drops, but it's not the kind of numbers game it can be come fall. If you're going out there, plan your trip around the tide table, not the clock. Miss the slack and you'll be jigging your arm off for nothing.

The river's been the more consistent producer, honestly. Stripers have parked themselves around the Memorial Bridge and down toward the Sarah Long Bridge pilings, working the current seams on the last of the ebb and first push of the flood. Cooler Gulf of Maine water is doing us a favor up here — while the water south of Boston has pushed bass into a strictly low-light, after-dark pattern, our stripers are still willing to eat in daylight because the Piscataqua and the water off the Shoals just haven't warmed up the way the Sound and the Bight have. I've been running live mackerel under a slip float through the bridge shadows on the tide change, and jigging soft plastics — 5-inch white Slug-Go's, weightless, worked with a slow twitch — right along the pier faces where the current breaks. Fish from 24 to 34 inches, with a few short ones mixed in that needed releasing quick.

Hampton Harbor's doing what it does on a good push tide — bass working into the inlet on the flood, holding along the Seabrook side channel edges and around the mouth of Meadow Pond as bait gets flushed through. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig after dark have been the most consistent producer down there, but during the day I've had success with a bucktail, half-ounce, white and chartreuse, bounced along the channel drop-off where it meets the flats. Tide's everything in that harbor — fish the last two hours of the flood into the top, and you're in business. Fish it on a dead low and you're walking the flats looking for herons.

Mackerel are still thick right off Rye Harbor and around Odiorne Point, which is keeping everything fed and keeping the bluefish interested. I've seen the first real blitzes of the summer this week — blues busting through mackerel schools right off the Rye breakwater and out toward White Island, visible from shore in the mornings before the wind picks up. Diamond jigs or small metal, cast right into the boil, and you'll connect. Nothing huge yet, mostly 2 to 4 pounders, but they hit hard and they're fun on light tackle, and where there's blues on mackerel there's usually stripers not far behind working the same bait.

We flagged a few days back that the summer striper pattern up here would hold into August, and that's exactly what's playing out — the Piscataqua's been the steadiest thing on my whole beat this week, more reliable than the ocean side has been for cod.

Looking ahead, we're heading into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which should soften the rip between the Shoals enough to widen that cod window beyond just the dead slack — worth getting out there and testing the edges of the tide change rather than just the exact turn. Flounder should start showing better in the harbor mud as the neap tide settles things down, so I'll be soaking clam bait off Rye Harbor's inner basin if the cod bite off the Shoals gets picky. If the mackerel schools hold tight to shore like they have, I'd expect the bluefish blitzes to keep showing up in the mornings, and I wouldn't be surprised to see the first false albacore scouts nosing around the deeper water off the Shoals before the month's out. Worth a look if you've got a rod rigged light and ready.

reports.headline: Squid Showing on the Ledges, Tog Tucked in the Cracks at Fort Wetherill
reports.subhead: Fluke slid out to the reefs right on schedule, bass have gone nocturnal in the warm water, and the first squid of the summer are working the rocks from Jamestown to Sakonnet.
reports.body_markdown:
First thing I noticed hopping down onto the ledges below Fort Wetherill this week wasn't a fish — it was squid. Small ones, an inch or two, working the wash right up against the rock in the last hour of daylight. That's early for us. Usually that shows mid-August when the water settles into that late-summer green. Squid pushing into the South Shore this soon tells me the whole food chain out here is running a few weeks ahead, and it's worth paying attention to because everything from scup to stripers keys on that bait once it commits to the rocks.

Tog fishing has been the most dependable thing going, and it's a slack-water game right now. I've been fishing the ledges off Fort Wetherill and the rock piles below Beavertail in 18 to 25 feet, green crabs on a standard knocker rig, and timing it so I'm dropping right through the last hour of the ebb into the dead slack. Current ripping through those cracks pulls your bait right out of the strike zone — tog want it sitting still against the structure, not swinging. Same story up at Sakonnet Point, working the boulder field off the point itself on the turn of the tide. Fish have been mixed sizes, plenty of teasers in the 12-14 inch range picking crabs apart, but enough keepers in the 16-20 inch class coming off the deeper cracks to make the trip worthwhile. With the neap tide coming in behind the July 21 first quarter, current's going to slack off across the board for the next several days — that's actually good news for tog guys, because it stretches that workable slack window out longer instead of cramming it into twenty minutes.

Striped bass have gone almost entirely nocturnal on this stretch, which tracks with how warm the water's been running everywhere south of the Cape. Daytime, the bite off the Newport Bridge rips and the east passage off Jamestown has been dead slow — a few short fish and that's it. But drop an eel or swim a Sebile Magic Swimmer through the rocks off Sakonnet Point or along the Second Beach reef line after dark, and you're in a different game. Best window has been the two hours around the bottom of the tide into the first push of the flood, fishing tight to structure, not out in open water. Nothing giant yet — mostly 26 to 32 inch fish — but they're eating, and eating consistently enough that a few guys have made it a regular after-dinner routine instead of a weekend event.

Fluke is where the real story is. We said a week back that back-bay fluke would push out toward the inlet mouths and ocean structure as the water warmed, and that's exactly what's happened. The bite inside Narragansett Bay proper has gone quiet, but out on the reef structure off Sakonnet Point and along the edges of Block Island Sound, it's been genuinely good — not blow-up numbers, but quality. Fish to 5 pounds coming on 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the incoming, right where the sand meets the rock edge. The pattern's been consistent enough that if fluke's your target this week, I'd skip the bay entirely and run straight to structure.

Bluefish have been showing in patches wherever bunker pods push along the beach — Second Beach in Middletown had a solid blitz for about forty minutes one morning last week, blues busting bait right in the wash, choppers to maybe 4 pounds hitting anything metal you threw at them. Matunuck's had similar flashes. It's not a sure thing — bunker schools move, and when they slide offshore or up into the bay the blues go with them — but if you see gulls working tight over bait close to the beach, that's your window, and it doesn't last long.

No albies yet on this stretch, and I want to be straight about that rather than sell you something that isn't here. There's early scouting activity building around Montauk and out toward Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard, which is usually the tell that our push is coming — Sakonnet Point and the mouth of the Sakonnet River are typically the first water in Rhode Island to see them once that happens, ahead of Newport and well ahead of Watch Hill and Napatree. I'd watch for the first false albacore showing at Sakonnet in the next two to three weeks, not this week.

Looking ahead, the softer currents from this neap tide should widen the tog window and make the breachway structure a little more approachable for slower presentations generally. Weather's stable, no fronts pushing through, which keeps the bunker pods predictable and the bluefish blitzes possible along the same beaches. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd spend the morning slack on the Fort Wetherill ledges for tog, then come back after dark and swim an eel through the Sakonnet rocks. That's the pattern that's actually producing right now — not the fastest week we've had, but an honest one.

reports.headline: SW Ledge slack at 5:52: bass still eating in the dark, bonito nowhere yet
reports.subhead: Neap tide is softening the rips around Block Island, and that's changing how — and when — you need to fish them.
reports.body_markdown:
Slack at SW Ledge fell at 5:52 this morning, and I had the boat sitting over 58 feet of water with the fishfinder marking bait stacked tight to bottom fifteen minutes before the tide even finished turning. That's the tell this time of year — the bass move onto the structure ahead of the last of the current, not after it, and if you're not positioned and ready when that happens you're watching it happen instead of fishing it. We worked eels on 3-ounce jig heads down through the water column as the tide started to build south, and by 6:10 we had two fish in the 20-pound class and a short one released clean. Not a blitz. A working bite, on structure, on the tide window that actually matters.

Here's the thing everybody needs to understand this week: we're sliding into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, and that changes the whole rhythm out at the Ledge and around Block generally. Weaker current means the rip doesn't stand up the way it does on a full or new moon push — less white water, less defined seam — but it also means your presentation has more time to work before the drift blows you through the zone. I've been fishing slower retrieves and heavier jig heads than I would on a strong tide, letting the eel sink and swim instead of just getting dragged. If you're used to bombing that rip on peak current, back off the pace this week. The fish are still there. The water's just behaving differently.

The striper pattern right now is squarely a low-light and after-dark program, and that's not going to change until nighttime water temps drop back down, which isn't happening in July. Daytime, the bigger fish are sitting deep on structure — SW Ledge, the rip off North Light, and the drop-off north of Sandy Point — and mostly not feeding hard until the sun's off the water. We've had solid results running bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs in 40 to 55 feet off Sandy Point right at last light, and the tube-and-worm crowd trolling the edges of the Ledge at dawn has been connecting on fish in the high-20s and low-30-pound range. There's still a genuinely big class of bass around Block Island this summer — I've heard of and personally seen fish well north of 35 pounds coming off these grounds in the last few weeks — but they're not stupid about it. Dark water, moving tide, quiet approach.

Fluke fishing has been the one thing I can point to and say with confidence: it's dependable. The reef grounds south of the Judith — the rock piles and mussel bottom in 25 to 40 feet — keep producing keeper fluke on white and chartreuse Gulp paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifted slow on the last two hours of the ebb. We flagged the reef bite as a season-long producer a couple days back, and it's holding up exactly like that — nothing flashy, just steady numbers of fish in the 3-to-5-pound range with the occasional 6 mixed in. Sea bass are riding shotgun on the same drifts, and the quality has been noticeably better than earlier in the summer — squid strips or clam on top-and-bottom rigs dropped right to the structure is still the simplest way to put a limit in the cooler.

Bluefish have been showing in pockets off the beaches west of the Point, chasing bait pods that are pushing this direction from the bunker runs further up the coast. Nothing sustained yet on our side, but if that bunker migration keeps moving south the way it's been, I'd expect daylight blitzes to start showing off Charlestown Breachway and working east toward Galilee within the next week or two. Worth keeping a topwater plug rigged and ready if you're running the beach.

Now, the question I'm getting at the dock every single day: where are the bonito. Short answer — not here yet, not confirmed. Water off Montauk's been sitting around 71-72 degrees, and that's in the range where we typically start seeing the first scouts show around Block, but I haven't personally marked one or heard a credible report off North Light or the rips at Clay Head. We called this a few days ago as a two-week window, and we're still inside that window — I'm watching the temperature breaks off Southeast Light and the rip off Sandy Point closely, because that's usually where the first fish show before anybody's talking about them. If you're itching to run out and blind-cast for albies right now, I'd hold off one more week and save the gas.

Looking ahead: the neap tide through the 21st and into the 22nd is going to keep softening the rip structure, which I actually think helps the bass bite at SW Ledge — longer windows, less current to fight, better presentation control on eels and swimbaits. I'd fish the two hours around slack rather than chasing peak current this week. Fluke and sea bass stay the safe bet on the reef south of the Judith regardless of moon phase. And if you want a longer shot, the offshore tuna grounds out toward Block Island canyon are still very much in play for boats running from Galilee — stable weather's holding, and that door isn't closing yet.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point after dark: stripers on bunker chunks, fluke holding steady off Prudence
reports.subhead: The herring are long gone from Buckeye Brook, the bay's pushing warm, and the bass have gone nocturnal while fluke and scup carry the daylight hours.
reports.body_markdown:
I was down at the Conimicut town dock Tuesday night listening to two guys argue about whether it was worth running lines out past ten o'clock, and one of them said something that stuck with me: "Buckeye's been dry since May, bud, this ain't that fish no more." He's right. That herring run that gets everybody's blood up every spring — the one that pulls bass up into the Warren and Barrington rivers chasing river herring stacked thick enough to walk on — that's done and gone for the season. What's left now is a different animal. Bigger, warier, and mostly a creature of the dark.

The bay's been running warm, pushing into the low-to-mid 70s on the surface, same story that's got bass locked into a low-light pattern from here down through the Sound and the Jersey beaches. During the day the fish just aren't interested in banging around in bright water — too much effort for too little payoff. So they're doing what smart striped bass do in July: sliding into deeper water and structure through the afternoon, then coming up to feed hard in that hour before dark and again well after the lights come on.

That's exactly what's happening under the Nyatt Point bridge and around the pilings at the old Rocky Point pier. Guys are soaking chunk bunker on fishfinder rigs in 15 to 20 feet, right on the edge of the light line where the current sweeps bait past the structure on the last two hours of the ebb. I had a 29-incher there myself Thursday night on a chunk, and heard of a couple fish pushing 34, 35 inches taken the same window on live eels swung off the current seam below the bridge. If you're going to fish it, fish it slow and quiet — no spotlights on the water, no slamming hatches. These bay bass have seen enough boat traffic to get cagey.

Daytime, it's fluke and scup carrying the weight, and that bite's been the more dependable one all week. Fluke are holding on the channel edges off Prudence Island and along the drop outside Greenwich Bay, working best on the last stretch of the outgoing into the first half hour of the flood when the current's still got some push to it. Four-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a squid strip, dragged slow along bottom in 20 to 28 feet — that combo's been putting keeper-class fluke in the box, nothing giant but steady, a fish or two on most drifts if you're patient about covering ground.

Scup are stacked on the rocky ledges the way they always are this time of year — Conimicut Point out to the can, the rock piles off Nyatt, and the ledge work up toward Rocky Point. Incoming tide is the move, small hooks, sandworms or clam bait, light enough tackle that you can feel every pluck. Nothing fancy about it, just steady meat-and-potatoes fishing that fills a cooler if you've got the patience to sit on the anchor.

Here's the one I want to flag: we said last week the weakfish bite would rebuild on calm, warm evenings, and that's exactly what's happening in Greenwich Bay and up around Bullocks Point. Squid have been running into the bay in decent numbers, which is a good sign for bait availability across the board, and the weakfish have been sliding up on those calm dusk tides to work the edges where the squid concentrate. Small swim shads and soft plastic shrimp imitations worked slow just off bottom at last light have been drawing strikes — nothing huge, mostly schoolies in the 16 to 20 inch range, but a legit bite where there wasn't much of one two weeks ago.

Sea bass are still there for anybody willing to make the run out toward Dutch Island and the humps off the west side of Prudence — squid strips and clam on bottom rigs in 25 to 35 feet, best on the last of the ebb when the current settles enough to hold bottom without dragging your sinker halfway to Newport. Sizes have been decent, a few fish pushing four and five pounds mixed in with the usual dinner-plate class.

Bluefish have been more of a rumor than a pattern in the bay proper this week — a few scattered blitzes on peanut bunker up around Conimicut and off Nayatt, but nothing sustained. If the bunker schools that have been working the beaches outside the bay decide to push in further, that could change fast, and it's worth keeping an eye on the surface for diving terns.

We're heading into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which is going to soften the current through the bridges and the ledge spots for a few days. That's not a bad thing — it widens the productive window on the fluke drifts and takes some of the urgency out of hitting peak tide exactly right on the scup grounds. What I'd do this week: fish the bridges and points after dark for bass on chunk and eel, hit Prudence and outside Greenwich Bay midday for fluke on the moving water, and keep a rod rigged light for weakfish if you're out at dusk with calm conditions. If the squid keep pushing into the bay the way they have been, that weakfish bite has room to build further before the month's out.

reports.headline: Wreck 6-8-2 in 130 feet: sea bass to 5 pounds, bluefin working the Mud Hole lumps
reports.subhead: A warm filament pushing toward the Hudson and Wilmington approaches has mahi and yellowfin within range, while the reef wrecks keep filling coolers with jumbo bass.
reports.body_markdown:
Sixty-two feet of water over the top of Wreck 6-8-2, dead calm Tuesday morning, and the sounder painted a solid red-orange smear that told me everything before the first bait hit bottom. That's the kind of return I've been chasing on this piece of structure since I first punched the numbers into a loran box twenty years ago, and it hasn't let me down yet in July. Sea bass to five pounds came off that wreck on Gulp Grubs in white and chartreuse, fished on a high-low rig with 4-ounce bank sinkers to hold bottom against the current. The jumbos are sitting tight to the wreckage itself, not scattered on the sand around it, so if your drift walks you off the numbers, reel up and reset. I lost count of the shorts we threw back before the keepers started stacking, but that's a good problem to have this time of year.

Axel Carlson Reef and Sea Girt Reef are both fishing the same way right now — deep down in the structure, not up on top. Clam and squid strips on bucktail teasers are outproducing straight bait rigs for me this week, especially in the mid-morning when the sun gets up and the fish tuck deeper into the shade of the wreckage. Shrewsbury Rocks has been more hit or miss — I had one drift there Thursday that produced eight keepers in twenty minutes and then went dead for the next hour. That's typical for the Rocks in midsummer; the bait pods move through in waves and the bass follow them, so if you find the pod, work it hard before it slides off.

Offshore, this is shaping up to be one of the better midrange tuna stretches I've seen in a few years. The Mud Hole lumps have been holding bluefin in that 27-to-46-inch slot class consistently since the trophy fishery closed on the 3rd, and the two-fish recreational limit means guys are still going home with fish without having to grind through a full spread all day. I've been running green machines and cedar plugs off the riggers with a naked ballyhoo down the shotgun, trolling the deeper edges of the lumps where the temp break holds — the water's been clean and blue out there, not the usual green chop you fight through in a normal July. Barnegat Ridge has produced sporadically for the smaller bluefin class as well, mostly early, before the wind fills in out of the southwest by midday.

We flagged this last week — said the warm-water filaments pushing toward the Hudson and Wilmington canyon approaches would put decent yellowfin and mahi within range of the Jersey fleet, and that's exactly what's playing out. Boats running out to those canyon edges are finding mahi stacked on anything floating — lobster pot buoys, loose weed lines, the odd pallet or trap marker. Dink lines with small hookless teasers followed by a naked ballyhoo or a green-and-yellow feather have been the play once you spot the color change or a bird working low over the surface. Yellowfin are mixing in on the same water, and the size class has been ticking up slightly from what we were seeing two weeks ago — nothing giant yet, but a step in the right direction if this stable high pressure holds through the week like it's supposed to.

No bonito yet in our zone. Water temps up around Montauk and Block Island are creeping into the range where they typically show, but I haven't had a confirmed fish crossed off in the Mud Hole or along the Ridge. Worth keeping an eye on temperature breaks over the next couple weeks, especially if this offshore warmth keeps pushing inshore, but I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet.

Tog season's closed through the summer, so that's a fall conversation — I'll start pulling my blackfish numbers back out once the water starts to turn in September. Cod's the same story; not worth chasing structure for them until the water cools off considerably.

Looking ahead, if this high-pressure pattern holds through the weekend like it's forecast to, I'd expect the canyon bite to keep building rather than fade — the Hooper-style warm filaments don't usually collapse overnight, and mahi numbers tend to climb through late July as more weed and debris gets pushed into range. On the inshore side, I'd keep working the reef wrecks early before the wind builds, and I wouldn't be surprised if the Mud Hole lumps keep producing slot bluefin right through the week as long as the bait stays put on those temperature edges. If I had one trip to make this weekend, I'd run out to check the Hudson approach for color and bait before committing to a full canyon day — but I'd have Wreck 6-8-2 as my fallback if the offshore water looks wrong.

reports.headline: Cape May Rips: Fluke Picky, Bass Gone Nocturnal, Drum Done for the Year
reports.subhead: The rips are fishable but you've got to work the tide right — and the black drum run is a memory until next May.
reports.body_markdown:
Grade for the Rips this week: C-plus. Fishable, not easy. If you'd asked me in April I'd have told you July fluke at the Rips is close to a sure thing on the right tide — and it still is, mostly — but the last few days it's taken more patience than a lot of guys want to give it. Warm water's the reason, and I'll walk you through why.

Water out at the mouth of Delaware Bay has been sitting in the mid-70s, which is warm enough that it's changed the clock on everything. Striped bass down here have gone almost entirely nocturnal — same pattern you're seeing coastwide right now. Daytime, the bass at the Rips are down deep and lockjawed, holding on the current edges but not committing. Dawn and dusk, and especially after dark with the tide moving, that's when they'll eat. My best window the last week has been the top of the outgoing at first light, working bunker-pattern swimming plugs and 2-ounce bucktails with white or chartreuse Bass Assassins along the edge where the ocean push meets the bay current spilling out past Cape May Point. Nothing gaudy — a few keepers in the mid-20s to low 30s, mixed with plenty of shorts. You have to fish it like a night bite even in daylight hours right now, which means working the structure hard and not expecting a blitz.

Fluke's been the more dependable player, but even that bite has gotten picky. Last two hours of the incoming into the first hour of the outgoing, right over the humps and the sandy patches inside the Rips and along the edge of the Hereford Inlet channel, is still putting fish in the box — mostly 16 to 19 inches with a scattered keeper over 20, on white Gulp Swimming Mullets teamed with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with just enough lift to feel bottom. The bite window's tightened up though. Miss that tide change by 45 minutes and you're marking fish on the machine and getting nothing but taps. Triggerfish are mixed in around the wreck and reef structure off the Cape May Inlet jetties in decent numbers for anyone soaking clam or squid strips on the bottom — not a headline fish but a fun one when the fluke go quiet.

Delaware Bay's the more interesting story right now, and it's one we flagged coming — said the weakfish bite would rebuild on calm, warm evenings, and that's exactly what's happening. The back-bay channels and marsh creeks up toward Fortescue and along the edges near Brandywine Shoal are holding weakfish again after a slow stretch, and the warm water pushing through those mud-bottom creeks on the dropping tide is concentrating them along the channel edges. Nothing like a blitz yet — call it a steady numbers game, three or four fish an outing for guys working it right — but it's trending up, not down. Bucktail-and-squid-strip combos or soft plastics on light jigheads, fished slow along the drop-offs where the creek water dumps into the main channel on the last two hours of the outgoing, that's where I'd put my time in the evening.

Now the part I know some of you are going to ask about anyway: the black drum run. It's done. May was the show — that's when the big bay drum push up onto the shoals off Fortescue and the mouth of the Maurice River, and by mid-June they're gone, scattered back out to deeper water. If someone tells you they're marking drum in Delaware Bay in July, they're either mistaken or talking about a stray fish, not a run. I'm not going to sugarcoat that one — if drum's what you're after, mark your calendar for next May and don't waste a trip on it now.

Bluefish haven't shown much locally yet. The blitz action everybody's talking about up around Belmar and Raritan Bay hasn't pushed down this far — those bunker schools are still working the central Jersey beaches. If that bait keeps moving south the way it usually does through late July, we could see some of that blue-fish energy show up off the Wildwood beaches and around Hereford Inlet inside two to three weeks. I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet, but it's worth watching the bait reports moving down the coast.

Looking ahead: we're sliding into a first-quarter neap tomorrow, and that's going to soften the current through the Rips for a few days. Less water movement usually means a wider window on both sides of the tide change instead of one hard 90-minute bite — good news for guys who can't time their trip to the exact minute. I'd expect the fluke bite to actually get a little easier to hit through the neap, since the tide won't be ripping through as violently and the fish won't bunch up quite as tight to structure. Striped bass will stay a low-light game until this water cools off, which isn't happening anytime soon in July. And keep an eye on that weakfish pattern in the bay — if the calm, warm evenings hold, I expect those numbers in the marsh creeks to keep building through the end of the month.

reports.headline: Class Question: Why Are the Stripers Only Biting After Dark? Ask the Bait
reports.subhead: Warm water has pushed the bass nocturnal, but fluke, bluefish, and weakfish are keeping the daylight shift honest from Absecon to Stone Harbor.
reports.body_markdown:
I get the same question every July, usually from a reader standing at the rail with a bucktail he hasn't gotten bit on since 2 p.m.: "Professor, where'd the bass go?" The answer's the same lesson I teach every summer — they didn't go anywhere. They just clocked out for the day shift.

Water's been sitting in the low-to-mid 70s off our beaches and warmer than that in the back bay flats behind Brigantine and up in the Absecon meadows, and striped bass don't like working that hard in daylight when the metabolism's already running hot. What you're left with is a bass that feeds at dawn, at dusk, and best of all after full dark, staged tight to current edges where the water's moving and slightly cooler than the flats around it. If you want a striper this week, fish the last hour of light through the first two hours of dark on the outgoing at Absecon Inlet, working the rock jetty seam with a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig, or swing an eel through the deeper cuts off the Brigantine side. That's not a guess — that's the pattern holding up and down this coast right now, and it's the same reason the party boat guys are telling their sea bass and fluke customers not to bother with striper rods until the sun starts dropping.

Now here's where the classroom gets interesting, because the daylight bite hasn't disappeared — it's just changed subjects. Fluke remain the most dependable fish in this zone, and they haven't blinked at the warm water the way the bass have. I've had good drifts in 18 to 25 feet on the Great Egg Harbor Inlet edges, working the channel that runs out past the old Ocean City bridge pilings, using 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, teased with a strip of squid. The keeper-to-short ratio has been better on the last two hours of the incoming, when the moving water pushes bait up against the drop-offs and the fluke stack on the up-current side waiting for it. Sod bank fluking in the Absecon back bay — the skinny water behind the meadows toward Brigantine — has also been producing, especially on the sod bank drop from 4 feet down into 8, fished on the tail of the outgoing when the bait gets flushed off the grass edges. Chartreuse bucktails with a Gulp trailer have out-produced straight bait rigs there this week, probably because the water's got a little color to it after the recent thunderstorm runoff.

Bluefish are the story I flagged for you last week, and it's playing out almost on schedule. We said the bunker-driven blitz pattern working the beaches to our north was going to spread south along the barrier islands as the bait schools kept moving with the tide, and sure enough, guys working the surf at Ocean City and down toward Sea Isle City have been into slashing blues in the first hundred yards off the beach during the last few mornings, right under diving gulls and terns. If you see birds working tight to the wash, don't waste time — get a metal lip swimmer or a Hopkins spoon out there fast, because those blitzes come and go in twenty-minute windows. Townsends Inlet has had some spillover activity too, blues chopping bunker right at the inlet mouth on the last of the outgoing, which tells me the bait's pushing down past Stone Harbor as well. Watch for that same pattern to keep sliding south through this week if the weather stays calm — the minute we get a blow that scatters the bunker pods, this bite goes quiet fast, so I wouldn't sit on it.

Weakfish are the other bright spot, and this is a fish that rewards patience over horsepower. Calm, warm evenings have been rebuilding that bite in the deeper holes of the back bay channels — Great Egg has been the more consistent producer, particularly the bend behind the meadows where the channel drops to 12 feet or better. Light jigheads with a chartreuse or pink Gulp shrimp, fished slow along bottom on the last of the incoming tide right at dusk, has been the most reliable combination. These aren't the 4-pound weakfish of years past — mostly 14 to 18 inches — but enough of them showing to make an evening worthwhile if you're willing to work slow and quiet.

Kingfish are around in the surf troughs at Ocean City and Stone Harbor, small but steady on bloodworm-tipped high-low rigs fished in the first sandbar trough on a moving tide, morning or evening both working fine since kingfish don't care much about light the way bass do.

We're heading toward a first-quarter neap on the 21st, which is going to soften the current in the inlets over the next several days. That's actually good news for the fluke program — slower water means longer, more controllable drifts through the Absecon and Great Egg channels instead of getting rushed through the sweet spot on a hard ebb. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take an evening tide at Absecon — fluke on the last of the incoming, then switch over to bunker chunks for bass as the light fades and the current starts to slacken with the neap. Two lessons in one trip, which is really how I like to teach it.

reports.headline: Holgate's New Slough Holds Fluke, Bunker Pods Pull Blues Through Barnegat Light
reports.subhead: A fresh cut behind the Rip is stacking fluke on the slack while bunker schools drag blues past both inlets on the tide change.
reports.body_markdown:
I flew the drone over the Holgate cuts Tuesday morning before the wind picked up, and there's a new slough that wasn't there three weeks ago — carved out behind the second bar, running parallel to the beach for maybe 150 yards before it dumps into a bowl at the north end. That kind of structure doesn't happen by accident. It's a sign the sandbars down there are still shuffling from whatever swell rolled through in June, and it's exactly the kind of skinny-water trough that holds fluke on the last two hours of the outgoing before it goes dead flat.

We flagged this last week — said the bunker-driven blitz activity would intensify as bait kept pushing south with the tide, and that's precisely what's happening at Barnegat Light. Pods of bunker have been stacking up tight against the north jetty rocks on the last of the flood, and the blues have found them. Nothing like the Belmar-style daylight blitzes yet, but Wednesday morning I watched three separate boils inside the inlet mouth on the changeover, blues in the 3-5 pound class slashing through, gulls working hard overhead. If you're throwing metal — a 2-ounce Deadly Dick or a Hopkins — get it past the boil and let it sink a beat before you rip it back through. Don't cast right into the froth, feather the edges. That's where the bigger fish sit, picking off the cripples that drop out of the pod.

Fluke fishing is the one thing on this whole stretch I can call genuinely steady right now. Little Egg Inlet channel, the deep bend off Graveling Point, and the back side of Holgate are all producing on moving water — doesn't seem to matter which stage as long as there's current pushing. I've had my best drifts working 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets, bounced slow along the channel edges in 12 to 18 feet. Keeper-class fish, some pushing 22-23 inches, mixed in with a lot of shorts that make you work for your five. The back bay behind Beach Haven has been kicking out similar numbers on the same rig — smaller boat, same presentation, just shallower, 8 to 10 feet over the grass edges on the outgoing.

Stripers are the tougher story, and I'm not going to sell you a bill of goods here. Daytime bass fishing on this stretch has gone quiet — the water's too warm on the surface for keeper-class fish to want to feed hard in the middle of the day, and that's holding true from here up through the whole Jersey coast. The play right now is after dark, working the same bunker schools that are pulling the blues. I've had better luck live-lining a bunker on a fish-finder rig off the Barnegat Light rocks starting an hour before sunset and working through the first few hours of dark, or chunking bunker on a fish-finder rig anchored up-current of the pods at Little Egg. It's a slower game than daytime jigging, but the fish that come are worth the wait — I heard of a mid-30s fish taken off a chunk bait near the inlet mouth Thursday night, which tells me there's still some real size mixed in with the schoolies.

Weakfish have been quietly rebuilding around the Mullica mouth and up into Graveling Point on the calm, warm evenings we've had. Nothing like the old days, but if you're throwing a small swimming plug or a light bucktail-teaser combo on the last of the incoming right at dusk, you've got a real shot at a couple of weakfish mixed in with your fluke. Keep the retrieve slow — these fish don't chase hard in July heat, they want it presented right in front of their nose.

Kingfish showed up on the ocean side sandbars off Ship Bottom and Beach Haven this week, working the trough behind the first bar on high tide. Bloodworm or Fishbites on a simple high-low rig with a sandflea teaser has been the ticket — nothing exciting, but it's a fun beach-chair bite for the kids while dad works a bucktail in the same wash for a stray fluke.

Looking ahead: we're rolling into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which is going to soften the current through both inlets over the next several days. That usually widens my bite windows rather than shrinking them — less water moving means the fluke and bass have more time to set up on structure instead of getting flushed through on a hard rip. I'd expect the bluefish pattern to keep pushing south along the beach as long as this bunker migration holds together and the weather stays calm — watch Barnegat Light and Little Egg both for daylight action if the pods keep funneling through on the tide changes. If I only had one window this week, I'd fish the last two hours of Saturday's outgoing at Holgate for fluke, then swing north to the Light for the evening bunker show before dark settles in for the bass.

reports.headline: Double Creek fluke on the drop, weakfish rebuild at the sedges, blues push into the Inlet mouth
reports.subhead: Warm mid-70s bay water has fluke hugging the cool edges while bunker pods pull bluefish right up into Barnegat Inlet on the last of the incoming.
reports.body_markdown:
I remember a July back in the late '80s, running a party of three out of Double Creek with the tide dead low and the air already sticky by seven in the morning, and my old captain — a Greek fisherman who'd taught me half of what I know, God rest him — told me something I've never forgotten. He said the bay doesn't hide from you in summer, it just makes you work for the cool water. Forty years later and that's exactly where we are right now. The shallow flats are running warm, mid-70s by midday, and every species worth chasing has tucked itself into the drop-offs and channel edges where there's a degree or two of relief and a little current to keep things moving.

Double Creek Channel has been my go-to the last ten days and it's holding up. The drift along the edge where it falls from six feet down into twelve to eighteen has been steady for fluke — nothing enormous, but a real dependable pick of keepers to about 22 inches, with the occasional better fish mixed in. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along that break, has been the ticket, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing when the bait gets pulled off the flat and stacks up right on that lip. I've had my best drifts starting an hour before low and running through the turn — the fluke seem to sit tight to the channel wall waiting for that current to deliver breakfast, and a slow bucktail bounced right along bottom, tipped with a strip of squid, is about as close to a sure thing as this bay offers in July.

Now the weakfish — I'll be honest, I was cautiously optimistic about these fish rebuilding through the warm, calm evenings we've had, and that's exactly what's happened. The same sedge banks off Tices Shoal that were holding weakfish back in May and June are still producing, mostly at dusk and into the first hour of dark, on the calmest nights we've had. Small soft plastics — 4-inch chartreuse or pink shad bodies on light jigheads — worked slow along the edges of the grass has been drawing strikes from fish in the 16 to 20 inch range, with a few better ones mixed in for guys willing to stay out past sundown. It's not a blitz, and I want to be straight with you about that — you might make eight or ten casts before you connect — but the fact that these fish are showing consistently in the same water, week after week, tells me this isn't a fluke pattern, it's a real rebuild.

The bigger story this week has been bunker. Pods have been pushing through Barnegat Inlet on the higher stages of the tide, and where bunker go, bluefish follow. I've been working the inlet mouth — right around the rock jetty at Barnegat Light and out toward the sea buoy — on the last two hours of the incoming, and the blues have been all over those pods in broad daylight, which isn't something you see every week. Diamond jigs worked with a fast, erratic retrieve, or a simple bunker spoon trolled just outside the surf line, has been putting cocktail blues in the 2 to 4 pound range in the boat steadily, with the occasional bigger chopper mixed in when the pods get dense. If you're fishing from the beach at Island Beach State Park, this is the week to have a metal lip or a Hopkins in the bag — those bunker schools have been running close enough to shore that surf casters have gotten in on it too.

Striped bass remain the toughest read of the bunch, and that's typical for this time of year with water running warm right up into the mid-70s across the flats. The keeper-class fish have gone almost entirely nocturnal — best action has come after dark around bridge structure and current seams near Oyster Creek and up toward the Route 37 bridge, where a little current and some depth keep things bearable for a striper in July. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, or a fresh eel drifted slow along the pilings, has drawn a handful of solid fish in the 28 to 34 inch range for guys willing to fish the two hours around midnight tide changes. Daytime bass fishing in the bay right now is mostly a lost cause — I wouldn't waste your morning on it.

We're heading into the first-quarter moon on the 21st, which means the current is about to go slack for a few days — neap tides, less push through Double Creek and around the Inlet. That's typically when the fluke bite widens out a bit because the fish aren't pinned as tight to the strongest current lines, so don't be afraid to work the softer edges of the channel, not just the main thread. My read for the coming week: this pattern holds through late July as long as the weather stays settled and the bunker keep pushing through the Inlet. If a blow comes through and scatters that bait, the bluefish show could shut off fast at the Inlet mouth, so I'd get out there sooner rather than later if that's your target. Otherwise, Double Creek on the drop and the sedges at dusk remain the most honest bets on the bay this week.

reports.headline: Sea Bright Rocks at Dawn: Bunker Pods Thick, Blues Wide Open, Bass Waiting on the Dark
reports.subhead: The bait's stacked from Sea Bright to Manasquan and the blues found it — stripers are still playing it cagey until the sun drops.
reports.body_markdown:
Quarter to six, low tide bottoming out at the Sea Bright rocks, and there's a kid down from Rumson throwing a white bucktail into water that looked like it was boiling from the inside. Bunker everywhere — not scattered pods, but that dense, oily, nervous-water mess that tells you something's under it before you even see the first blow-up. He hooked up on his third cast. Ten-pound bluefish, maybe better, and it wasn't a fluke catch. Two guys down the jetty were doing the same thing with tin — Ava 27s dressed with surgical tube, red and white, worked with a fast retrieve just under the surface where the blues were slashing.

This is the pattern right now and it's not subtle. Bunker have been running thick along the beachfront from Sea Bright down through Monmouth Beach and into Long Branch, and the blues have found them in broad daylight, which is unusual enough to be worth writing home about. We flagged this exact setup last week — said the bait would hold as long as the weather stayed stable, and that's precisely what's happened. High pressure's parked over the whole coast, no wind to speak of most mornings, and the bunker schools haven't had a reason to move off the beach. When they finally do get pushed by a blow, this bite will shut down fast. Until then, it's about as gift-wrapped as jetty fishing gets — you just need to be there before the sun gets too high and the blues drop back down.

Here's the catch, and there's always a catch: the stripers aren't playing along with the blues in daylight.
