Wells Harbor's been quieter — some school bass working the channel on the last of the ebb, nothing to write home about, but a decent bet for someone who wants an easy evening with light tackle and a bucktail.

Cod's still mostly a boat game this time of year — the guys running out to the deeper water off Cape Elizabeth and the ledges past Wood Island are picking at them in 60-90 feet on diamond jigs and clams, but it's slow, technical fishing, not a surf story. If you've got a boat and patience, it's there. If you're standing on rock throwing plugs, don't bother chasing it.

Moon's swinging toward first quarter on the 21st, which means the big spring push we had is easing off into more moderate tidal current. That's actually good news for surf guys — those wild, ripping tides make wading the Pool's ledges a white-knuckle game, and the softer stages coming should let you fish the incoming a little longer without getting run off the rocks. I'd plan around that second hour of the flood at Biddeford Pool as your best window through the weekend, and if the wind stays out of the southwest and doesn't kick up too much chop, Prouts Neck should keep producing that mixed bottom bite.

Look, it's not a blitz every night and I'm not going to sell it as one. Some sessions this week I threw for an hour before anything touched the plug. But the pattern's real — cooler water, bait pushed into the river mouths and against the rocks, bass feeding by day instead of hiding by night. That's a gift this time of year, and Southern Maine's cashing it in while the rest of the coast waits for dark.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point after dark: bass go nocturnal while bunker pulls blues into the Bay
reports.subhead: The daytime bass bite has gone quiet with the warm water, but the bluefish are running hot on bunker and the fluke are sliding out toward the reefs.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into Sal down at the Fields Point bait shack Tuesday morning, and he's shaking his head about the same thing everybody's been telling me all week — nobody's touching a bass in daylight anymore. Water's sitting warm enough up in the Providence River and around Conimicut that the stripers have wised up and gone to bed during the day. That's not them leaving the Bay, that's just thermal common sense. I've fished this water my whole life and I know what it means when the day bite dies but the guys running eels off the Mount Hope Bridge abutments at eleven o'clock are still coming home with fish.

Buckeye Brook's herring run wrapped up weeks ago — that's ancient history now, a spring memory. What's driving the Bay this week is bunker. Big pods of peanut and adult bunker have pushed up into Greenwich Bay and around Rocky Point, and the bluefish are camped underneath them exactly like you'd expect this time of year. We said last week the blues would follow the bunker schools up the coast and settle into a consistent pattern, and that's precisely what's happening — Rocky Point ledge, the mouth of Greenwich Cove, and the flats off Nyatt Point have all had bluefish blowing up on bunker in the last hour of the outgoing tide. Snag-and-drop with a treble on a wire leader is still the simplest way to connect, but if you want to have some fun with 'em, a chrome Kastmaster or a Hopkins fished fast through the melee will get bit just as quick. Fish are running three to six pounds, plenty of them, and they don't seem to be going anywhere as long as that bait stays thick.

Stripers themselves — I'm not going to sugarcoat it, the day bite off the bridges and points has been tough. You want bass right now, you fish the tide change after dark. Mount Hope Bridge, the Jamestown-Verrazzano pilings, and the rip off Conimicut Light have all given up fish on live eels and bunker chunks fished on the bottom during the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood. That current break where the East Passage funnels past Conimicut is money at night — bass are stacking on the edge waiting for baitfish to get swept off the flat. Nothing huge, mostly schoolies to low-20-inch fish, with the occasional slot fish mixed in for guys willing to put the hours in after dark. The moon's building toward first quarter on the 21st, so the tide swings are still moderate — once we get closer to full, expect the current to pick up and that night bite to sharpen up around the bridge structure.

Fluke are the one thing you can still count on in daylight, and true to what we expected, that bite is starting to slide out of the back coves and toward the reefs and channel edges. Guys working the drop-offs around Prudence Island and the deeper cuts off Nyatt Point are finding keepers in 20 to 35 feet on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and chartreuse bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the tail end of the incoming. The shallow warm coves that were holding fluke back in June have gotten too warm to be productive during the day — those fish have pushed to the cooler, deeper structure, which is exactly the shift you want to anticipate this time of summer. If you're marking bait on the meter around the Prudence flats, slow your drift down and work it — that's where the keepers are hiding.

Scup fishing has been the most reliable thing going on the rock piles. Rocky Point, the ledges off Nyatt Point, and the rip line running along Poppasquash Point have all been stacked with scup in the 10-14 inch range. Small pieces of squid or a chunk of green crab on a high-low rig, fished right on the bottom in 15 to 25 feet, is about as close to a sure thing as this Bay offers right now. Kids on the pier at Rocky Point have been filling five-gallon buckets on bloodworms too, if you can find them — but squid's cheaper and works just as well.

Weakfish have started trickling back into the mix on the calmer evenings, which lines up with what we figured would happen once the water settled and the wind laid down. Nothing consistent yet — a fish here, a fish there around the mouth of Greenwich Bay on soft plastics fished slow near bottom during the last light — but it's worth keeping an eye on if these stable, warm evenings keep holding through the week.

Looking ahead, I'd focus effort on the night tide around the bridges for bass, keep hammering the bunker schools for blues wherever they show, and shift your fluke game out toward Prudence and the deeper reef edges rather than the shallow coves. If the wind stays out of the south and the water keeps creeping up, expect the bass pattern to stay nocturnal and the fluke to keep pushing deeper. Nothing wrong with any of that — just means you fish smarter, not longer.

reports.headline: Rips Report Card: Bass Get a C-Minus, Weakfish Climbing, Drum Long Gone
reports.subhead: Warm water pushed the stripers into the dark and pulled the weakfish back into the bay channels right on schedule.
reports.body_markdown:
Grading the rips this week: C-minus on bass, B-plus on bluefish, incomplete on weakfish because they're just now walking back into the room. That's the honest read, and I'm not going to dress it up past that.

The ocean side has been running warm and a little sloppy — 73, 74 degrees out at the edge of the shipping lanes, with a low swell out of the south keeping a light chop on the rip line most mornings. That's not a wall, it's just enough push to make the drift a little sloppier than I'd like on the last two hours of the incoming. Striped bass haven't left the rips, but they've gone strictly nocturnal on us, which is a thermal thing, not a fish-count thing. We're seeing them stack up over the humps off the Point on the sounder after dark and go quiet as soon as the sun gets any angle on the water. If you want a bass out there right now, you're fishing the last two hours before first light or right at last light on the ebb, working bucktails or eels down deep — 30 to 50 feet — where that water's still holding some coolness off the bottom. Daytime, forget it. I had two charters out there this week on the morning flood and we managed shorts and one 29-incher on a white bucktail tipped with a Fin-S strip, worked slow along the bottom edge of the rip. That's a C-minus day and I'm not going to tell you different.

Hereford Inlet's been the better story. Bunker pods are stacked up along the beachfront from the inlet down toward Wildwood, and the bluefish have been under them daily — not blitz-every-hour stuff, but reliable, especially on the last of the outgoing when that bait gets funneled and squeezed through the inlet mouth. Diamond jigs, an ounce and a half, worked with a hard snap-and-drop, have been getting bit steady, and if you've got poppers, throw them right into the surface nervousness when the gulls start working — those blues are eating up top more than they're eating deep right now. Fluke inside the inlet have been a grind on the smaller stuff, but we flagged this a week ago — said the back-bay fluke would start sliding out to the inlet mouths and ocean structure as the water kept climbing, and that's exactly what's happening. The keeper-class fish are showing on the reef sites — Wildwood Reef and the stone piles off Cape May Point — in 25 to 35 feet, drifting Gulp Swimming Mullets in white and chartreuse on 3/4-ounce bucktails. Back bay's still holding shorts by the bucket, but if you want a keeper for the cooler, you're running out to the reefs now.

Delaware Bay's a different animal this time of year. The drum run wrapped up back in late May like it does every spring — that fishery's closed out for the season, and anybody still soaking bunker chunks off Fortescue hoping for a straggler drum is wasting bait. What's interesting is the weakfish. Bay water's pushed into the mid-70s, and that's the exact trigger — we called this last week, said the warm bay water would bring them back into the channel drop-offs on calm evenings, and sure enough they're staging where the warm surface water meets that cooler current coming through the channel edges. Ship John, the deeper cuts off Egg Island, and the drop-off in front of Fortescue have all given up weakfish in the 2 to 4-pound range on the early morning outgoing, mostly on bucktails tipped with a strip of squid or worked slow with a swimming plug over the channel lip. It's not a stacked bite yet — more like three or four fish on a good tide instead of none — but it's building, and if the pattern holds on these calm, settled evenings we've had, I'd expect that grade to climb into next week.

Water's been clean out at the rips, cleaner than I'd expect for mid-July, which tells me the wind's been cooperating more than the tide charts have. We're running toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which means the current's easing off the bigger push we had around the full moon — that usually favors a slower presentation in the rips, less about horsing a big bucktail through and more about working it methodically along bottom structure. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd take the last hour of the outgoing at Hereford before first light, throw bucktails at the bluefish under the bait, then run out to the reef structure once the sun's up for fluke. If I had one evening, I'd be on the bay at Ship John working that channel edge for weakfish before the light goes flat.

Look, it's mid-July — the ocean side isn't going to hand you an easy bass day right now, and anybody telling you different is selling something. But the bluefish are reliable, the fluke moved right where we said they would, and the weakfish are starting to show up on schedule. That's enough to build a trip around if you pick your tide and don't waste time waiting on a daytime striper that isn't coming.

reports.headline: Why Are the Fluke Leaving the Back Bays? Class Is in Session
reports.subhead: Warm mud water is pushing the fluke program toward the inlet mouths while blues, weakfish, and kingfish fill in behind them.
reports.body_markdown:
I get the same question every July, usually from a guy standing at the Brigantine ramp with a bucket of Gulp and a confused look on his face: "Darnell, why aren't they in the same spots as June?" Fair question. Let's take it apart the way I'd take apart a lesson plan.

Back in mid-July the sod banks off Absecon Inlet and up through the Reeds Bay complex were holding a nice fluke program — three-to-five-pound fish stacked on the current edges, feeding hard on the incoming as bait got funneled off the grass. That water has since climbed into the low-to-mid 70s on a sustained stretch of calm, sunny weather, and fluke don't love sitting in shallow mud once it gets that warm. We flagged this shift last week — said the back bay fluke would start transitioning toward the inlet mouths and ocean structure as the water pushed warmer, and that's exactly the pattern I'm seeing play out from Absecon down through Great Egg.

The better fluke this week are showing at the mouth of Absecon Inlet in 18 to 25 feet, tight to the rock piles on the Brigantine side, and along the deeper channel edge off Great Egg Inlet near the old range markers. Both spots are running cooler, cleaner water than the back bays because they're getting flushed twice a day by ocean exchange. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails are the go-to, worked slow on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current is still strong enough to hold bottom contact but not ripping you into the rocks. I had a student — well, a former student, now grown and still fishing with me — put three keepers in the cooler off Great Egg Thursday morning doing exactly that, biggest going five and a half pounds. It's not a wide-open bite. You're covering ground and working the drift carefully, but the fish are there for anglers willing to hunt the structure instead of anchoring on memory from three weeks ago.

Striped bass are the quiet story right now, and if you're only fishing daylight hours you're going to think they've left the building. They haven't — they've gone nocturnal. With inshore water sitting in that same low-to-mid-70s range, the bass are avoiding the heat and feeding mostly after dark and in the gray light around dawn, holding on current breaks near the Ocean City inlet jetties and the deeper bends of Townsends Inlet. If you want a shot, fish the two hours either side of high tide at night with bunker chunks or a swimming plug worked slow along the rocks. Daytime bass fishing in the surf is mostly a bust right now, and I'd rather tell you that straight than send you out there disappointed.

Bluefish are about to become everybody's story. The blitz pattern that's been running hard on bunker schools up in Belmar and points north has been building steadily, and bait pods have been drifting south along the beachfront with the tide. We called this one too — said the blues would follow the bunker down the coast, and I'd expect that wave to reach the Atlantic City and Ocean City beachfronts within the next several days if this calm, stable weather pattern holds and doesn't scatter the schools. Keep an eye on the surf from the Ocean City boardwalk down toward Corson's Inlet — when the birds start working tight over a bait ball, that's your signal, and metal lures like a Hopkins or a 2-ounce Kastmaster thrown into the melee will get bit fast.

Weakfish are rebuilding on the evening tide, and this is a pattern worth being patient for. We noted last week that the weakfish bite should firm up on calm, warm evenings, and that's held true — the mouth of Great Egg Harbor and the deeper holes behind Ocean City have produced a scattering of quality weakfish in the last hour of light on the outgoing, fish in the 18-to-22-inch range hitting Storm Shads in root beer and pink worked slow near bottom. It's not the weakfish run of decades past, but for anyone who remembers what this fishery used to be, seeing legal fish show consistently on a July evening tide is worth noting.

On the sod banks — Brigantine marsh, the flats behind Longport, the grass edges up in Absecon Bay — kingfish and small blowfish have moved in, which is textbook July behavior in stable, warm shallow water. Bloodworms or small strips of squid on a high-low rig, fished on a light spinning outfit in two to four feet of water on a slack high, will keep a family entertained for an afternoon even when the bigger species are being stubborn.

Triggerfish are showing on the inlet jetty rocks and the nearshore reef structure off Ocean City and Sea Isle City, which happens every summer once the water settles into this warmer pattern. They're not a targeted fishery for most guys, but if you're bottom fishing sea bass structure with squid strips, don't be surprised when one of these odd, toothy customers shows up on the hook.

Looking ahead, I'd keep my daytime effort on fluke at the inlet mouths — Absecon and Great Egg both — while the back bay program keeps thinning out. If the calm weather holds through the week, I'd expect the bluefish blitz to arrive on our beaches by the weekend, and that's worth rearranging a Saturday morning around. Bass fishing stays a night game until we get a real cool-down. Class dismissed — go put in the work.

reports.headline: The Cut at Holgate Deepened Overnight — Fluke Moved In Behind It
reports.subhead: Bass have gone dark with the heat, bluefish are chewing through bunker on the beach, and the inlet structure is doing all the work now.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the north end of Holgate at gray light Tuesday, low tide, and the bar that's held shape since Memorial Day had opened a new cut about 150 yards south of the old washout — a foot deeper than it was two weeks back, with a hard rip line still visible where the outgoing water was funneling through. That's the kind of change you only catch if you're out there at the right stage of tide, and it explains why the fluke bite has been so lopsided this week. The fish followed the deeper water in, and they've been stacked on the seam of that new cut ever since.

Fluke's been the honest bite on LBI right now, and it's a daytime program almost exclusively — the last two hours of the outgoing, working the jetty rocks at Barnegat Light and the channel edge off Beach Haven Inlet in 8 to 14 feet. Four-inch white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow with the current rather than against it, is putting keepers in the cooler — nothing huge, mostly 18 to 20 inches, but steady counts if you work the drift right and don't rush the retrieve. We flagged this transition last week, that the back bay fluke would push out toward inlet mouths and ocean structure as the water warmed further, and that's exactly what's happened. The mud flats inside Manahawkin Bay have gone quiet for fluke — all the activity's moved to hard bottom now, Graveling Point's channel edge and the rock piles at the BL inlet jetty holding the better fish.

Striped bass are a different story, and I'll be straight with you — daytime bass fishing on LBI right now is mostly a waste of gas. Bay temps are sitting mid-to-upper 70s, and that's pushed the resident fish into a strict nocturnal pattern. This isn't a disappearance, it's thermal avoidance — the bass are still here, they're just feeding after dark when the water cools a few degrees and the current breaks near the Causeway bridge pilings and the deeper holes off Ship Bottom come alive. If you want a shot at a keeper, fish the two hours around the bottom of the tide, midnight to 3 a.m., swimming a Bomber Long A or a soft-bodied swimbait slow through the current seam. It's not comfortable fishing, but it's the only fishing that's working for bass right now.

Bluefish are the one species making noise in daylight, and it's the bunker that's driving it. Schools have been pushing south along the beachfront all week, the same pattern that's had the beaches north of us — Belmar on down — blitzing daily, and it's finally spreading into our stretch. I had reports of blues busting through bunker off Surf City and again off north Beach Haven on back-to-back mornings, blitz conditions right in the wash, fish in the 3-to-6-pound class hammering anything that moves. We called this one too — said the blues would follow the bunker down the coast, and here they are. If you see the bait balling up and the birds start working, don't overthink it — a chrome Kastmaster or a top water pencil popper thrown right into the whitewater will get bit almost every cast while it lasts. These blitzes are short-lived, twenty minutes and gone, so keep the plug bag light and be ready to move fast up the beach.

Weakfish have been the quiet surprise. Graveling Point and the mouth of the Mullica have both given up a handful of legal weakfish on calm evenings this week, taken on soft plastics — pearl white paddletails on light jigheads, fished slow along the channel drop where the river current meets the bay. We said this bite would rebuild on stable, warm evening conditions, and it's tracking that way, though I want to be honest — it's not a bite you can plan a trip around yet. A couple of guys got two or three fish in a session, nothing consistent, but the pattern's building and worth checking if you're already out there for stripers after dark.

Ocean conditions have kept most of the action pinned to structure. Swells have been running around 2 to 3 feet with a short period, sloppy enough that the open beachfront hasn't been fishing clean, so I've been steering people toward the inlet jetties and channel edges where the structure breaks up the energy. Water off the coast is holding in the low 70s, considerably warmer than what's typically pushing bass activity, which is another reason the daytime program has shifted so hard toward fluke and blues.

Looking ahead — the moon's building toward first quarter on the 21st, which should ease the tidal swing a touch by the weekend. Slacker current usually means the fluke bite gets a little tougher to time right, so I'd fish the last hour of the outgoing hard rather than spreading effort across the whole tide. If the bunker schools keep holding tight to the beach, I expect the bluefish blitz pattern to keep creeping south and get more consistent right through Ship Bottom and Beach Haven by the weekend. For bass, stick with the night program until we get a real cool-down — nothing on the horizon suggests that's coming soon, so plan your trips around the dark hours and the deeper current breaks, not the calendar.

reports.headline: Bay Water Pushes Past 78, and the Fluke Follow It Straight to the Inlet
reports.subhead: Weakfish wake up at the sedges on calm evenings, snapper blues crowd the creeks, and the stripers have gone strictly nocturnal.
reports.body_markdown:
Back in the late eighties I mated for a captain out of Point Pleasant named Whitey Corson, and every July when the bay water got thick and warm he'd cut the engine off Tices Shoal, hand me the thermometer on a string, and say, 'Gus, when she reads high seventies, the game changes — you don't fight it, you follow it.' I've dropped that same thermometer a thousand times since, and this week it's telling the same old story it always does in the third week of July: the bay's running warm, the fish know it before we do, and if you want to catch anything worth keeping you fish where the water still has some snap to it.

Right now Barnegat Bay proper is sitting in the high 70s from Toms River down through Double Creek Channel, and that's pushed the fluke bite exactly where I told you it would a week back — out of the mid-bay flats and toward the inlet mouth and the ocean-side structure where the water still moves and stays a few degrees cooler. Double Creek Channel is still holding fish, don't get me wrong, but they're bunched tight along the deeper bends near the channel markers, not spread out over the flats like they were in June. Drifting the outgoing tide with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, right down in that 8 to 12 foot cut, has been putting keepers in the boat — nothing giant, mostly 17 to 19 inches with the occasional 4 or 5 pounder mixed in, but steady if you work the drift slow and keep that bucktail ticking bottom. The better numbers, though, are showing up right at the mouth of Barnegat Inlet and out on the ocean structure past the rocks, where boats working white and chartreuse Gulp on the drift, or bouncing squid strips over the reef structure, are finding a heavier grade of fish. That's the pattern I flagged last week and it's holding — fluke shifting off the warm back bay flats and into the inlet mouths as the water keeps climbing. I don't expect that to reverse itself before September.

Weakfish are the pleasant surprise. I wasn't optimistic a couple weeks back with the bay running so warm, but on the calm, flat evenings — and we've had a few — the sedges along Tices Shoal and down toward Barnegat Light have been holding fish right at last light. Small chartreuse Bass Assassins on a light jighead, or a live spearing under a popping cork fished slow along the grass edges on the last of the incoming tide, has been the ticket. Nothing over three pounds that I've heard of, but a legal weakfish in this bay in mid-July is nothing to complain about, and it lines up with what we expected — the bite rebuilding on those quiet, warm nights when the water lays flat and the bait gets nervous along the marsh edges.

Striped bass have gone strictly nighttime on us, and that's just thermal common sense — nobody wants to burn energy chasing bait in 78-degree water during the day when they can slide into the current breaks after dark and feed when it's cooler. The rocks at Barnegat Light and the deeper rips right at the inlet are your best bet after sundown, working bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig or swimming a Bomber-style plug through the current seam on the last two hours of the outgoing. I had a report of a couple of schoolies and one fish pushing 30 inches taken that way earlier this week, fished right at the change of tide around midnight. If you want stripers right now, you're setting your alarm, not your watch.

Snapper blues are thick in the back creeks — Forked River, Cedar Creek, the mouth of Double Creek — and that's about as reliable a July signal as we get on this bay. Where you've got snappers stacked up chasing spearing along the docks, the adult bluefish and the bigger bait schools generally aren't far behind. We haven't seen the blitz conditions here yet that they're getting up around Belmar with those bunker schools working the surf, but given how consistent that pattern's been building along the coast, I wouldn't be shocked if it starts creeping south toward Island Beach and the Barnegat surf in the next week or two. Worth keeping an eye on the beach at IBSP in the early morning hours — bluefish under working bunker schools can show up fast and disappear just as quick.

Blowfish are doing what blowfish do this time of year — steady, unglamorous, and dependable on the bay bottom in 6 to 10 feet around Double Creek and the flats off Waretown, squid strips or a small piece of clam on a hi-lo rig. Kingfish are scattered but present on the ocean side and right in the surf at Island Beach on bloodworms and sandworm, best on the last of the incoming over clean sand.

Looking ahead, we're sliding toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which should ease the tidal push a touch and favor slower presentations in the rips and at the inlet mouth — good news for fluke guys working bucktails and good news for anyone soaking bunker chunks for stripers after dark. If this stable, calm weather holds, I expect this whole pattern — fluke pushing to the inlet, weakfish working the sedges at dusk, bass strictly nocturnal — to hold through the end of the month. That's about as safe a bet as you get on this bay in the height of summer.

reports.headline: Belmar Rocks at Dawn: Blues Under the Bunker, Bass Gone to Ghosts
reports.subhead: The bluefish blitz we predicted has arrived on the bunker schools, but the warm water pushed the stripers into a nighttime-only pattern up and down the jetty line.
reports.body_markdown:
Five-fifteen this morning, Sea Bright rocks, and I'm standing next to a kid I'd never met who just buried a Hopkins into a bunker pod so thick it looked like the water had a rash. He didn't know what to do next — I did. Told him to let it sink on a semi-slack line and rip it up through the pod, and thirty seconds later he's got an 18-inch bluefish trying to remove his fingers. Welcome to jetty country in mid-July.

This is the bunker week we've been waiting on. Peanut and adult bunker schools have packed tight against the beach from Sea Bright down through Monmouth Beach and into Belmar, and the blues are stacked underneath them instead of chasing them offshore — which is exactly the mechanism I flagged you on last week. Warm surface water concentrates the bait against structure, predators quit burning calories chasing open water, and you get this: violent, compressed feeding right off the rocks. I've watched three straight mornings of blitzes at the north end of the Sea Bright jetty field, another one working off the Sandy Hook side of the inlet on the last two hours of the incoming. Poppers, Hopkins, anything chrome and heavy that you can throw through a bird-and-bunker ball — doesn't matter much. The blues aren't picky right now, they're just there in numbers, cocktail-to-mid-teens mostly, with the occasional 6-pounder mixed in that'll make your drag sing.

Here's the part that's not as fun to write. Stripers have gone dark on us — literally. Inshore water's sitting in the low-to-mid 70s off the buoy readings I trust, and that's enough to push bass off the daytime bite entirely. This isn't fish disappearing, it's fish doing what warm-blooded thinking predators do when the water gets uncomfortable: they retreat to deeper structure and current breaks and they feed at night. I worked the Manasquan Inlet rocks two hours before first light on Tuesday — dead calm, incoming tide just starting to build — and put two schoolies in the 26–28 inch range on a black Bomber long-A worked slow along the north jetty face. That's the program right now. If you want bass on this beat, you're getting up when everyone else is going to bed, or you're fishing the last gray hour before sunrise like I did. Shark River Inlet's producing the same way on the last of the outgoing — bunker chunks fished tight to the rocks on a fish-finder rig, 2 ounces of egg sinker, enough to hold bottom without getting swept. Don't expect a pile. Expect one or two quality fish if you put the time in and fish the tide correctly.

Fluke is the one bite you can set your watch by right now, and it's exactly where I told you it'd be heading — off the back bay mud and into the inlet mouths and the nearshore reef structure as that water kept climbing. Manasquan Inlet itself has been steady on the last two hours of the ebb, boats and shore guys both picking through keepers in the 18-to-20 inch range in 15 to 25 feet of water right off the rock pile, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged dead slow along bottom. Belmar's inlet edge has done the same on the same stage of tide. If you're working the jetty from shore, cast up-current and let the bucktail settle before you start the retrieve — these fish are holding tight to the rock seams where the current breaks, and a bait that swims past two feet off the structure gets ignored while one that ticks the rocks gets bit.

Blackfish and porgies are a summer afterthought on this stretch until the water turns again in the fall, so I'm not wasting your time on them this week. Worth knowing the porgies are still around the deeper stone at Manasquan and Shark River if you need bait-shop consolation fishing on a slow morning, but nobody's writing home about it.

Moon's building toward the first quarter on the 21st, which means the tides are easing off the spring push we had around the new moon — that's actually good news for the fluke bite, since a softer current lets the bucktail stay in the strike zone longer instead of getting swept through in two seconds. For the bass, I'd keep working the same nighttime program through the week: high tide around dawn on the incoming stages is when I've had the best luck, working plugs slow along jetty faces at Sea Bright, Manasquan, and the Spring Lake rocks. If the bunker schools hold and the weather stays calm — no reason right now to think they won't — expect the bluefish blitz to keep spreading south along Belmar and Asbury Park through the weekend. The minute a stiff onshore blow scatters that bait, this whole pattern resets, so if you've got a window in the next few days, I wouldn't wait on it.

reports.headline: Night tide on the channel edge: bass go dark, bunker bring the blues topside
reports.subhead: With the bay pushing into the low 70s, I'm working two different clocks this week — stripers after sundown, fluke and blitzing blues in the heat of the day.
reports.body_markdown:
Here's the call I made this week, and it's the same one I'd make again: I'm splitting my trips by the clock instead of by the spot. Mornings and afternoons I'm running the channel edges off Keyport Flats and the drop into the Chapel Hill Channel for fluke. Nights, I'm parking the boat on the deep water off Flynn's Knoll and the edge of Romer Shoal and letting bunker chunks soak on the bottom. Two totally different programs, same week, same bay — and the reason is water temp.

Kings Point is reading 71.6 on the Sound side, and our water isn't far behind that — the bay's pushing solidly into the low-to-mid 70s now that we've had a stretch of calm, sticky weather. That's warm enough that the striped bass have made their move — not out of the system, just out of the daylight. They're sliding into deeper structure and current breaks and feeding almost entirely after dark now. This isn't a disappearing act, it's a thermal retreat, and if you're still fishing the Knoll at noon wondering where the bass went, that's your answer. Shift your trip to the last two hours of light through the middle of the night and fish the deeper cuts — 18 to 30 feet off Flynn's Knoll, the edge of the Chapel Hill Channel, and the deep bend by Romer Shoal. Bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, 3-ounce sinker to hold bottom against the current, fished on the front half of the incoming when that cooler water starts pushing back into the bay off Sandy Hook. That's when I've been marking the better fish on the graph — not big numbers, but real 28-to-34 inch bass willing to eat once the sun's off the water.

During the day, forget the bass and go to work on fluke, because that bite hasn't blinked with the heat. Channel edges are still the program — the drop-off along Keyport Flats where the flat spills into 12 to 18 feet, and the edges of the main channel running past the Highlands toward the Hook. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift, tipped with a strip of squid if the current's light. I'm also seeing decent counts on the deeper edge by the Rip at the Hook when the tide's really moving — that structure holds bait and the fluke sit right on the seam waiting for it to get swept past. Nothing giant this week, mostly 16 to 19 inches with a few keepers mixed in, but it's a dependable bite, and in July that counts for something. If you want a shot at a bigger one, work the deeper side of the channel on the last of the outgoing when the water's cleanest — that's usually when the better-grade fish show.

Now the wildcard: bunker. There are big schools stacking up around the Hook right now, the same pods that have had blues blitzing the surf from Belmar on north all month. That pattern is starting to push into the bay, and if it fully arrives — and I think it will, because the bunker aren't showing signs of scattering with this stable weather — we're going to have blitz-style bluefish activity right off the beach at Sandy Hook and up into the lower bay. Keep a topwater rod rigged and ready. If you see birds working or bunker getting nervous on the surface off the Hook or Romer Shoal, run to it and throw a pencil popper or a bunker spoon — blues under bait like that don't make you work for it.

Weakfish are the other piece worth watching. We flagged last week that the bite would rebuild on calm, warm evenings, and that's exactly the window opening up right now in the Navesink and Shrewsbury. Both rivers have been quiet through the heat of the day, but the last hour of light into dusk, on the tail of the outgoing, has been producing weakfish in the 16-to-20 inch range on light jigs — quarter-ounce bucktails tipped with a Gulp shrimp, worked slow along the deeper bends near the Rumson bridges. It's not a numbers game yet, one or two fish an evening if you put the time in, but it's building, not fading, and that's the direction you want to see it going in mid-July.

Sea state offshore has been a little rough — 44025 out in the Bight has been kicking up 2 to 3 foot chop on a short period, which is nothing to us inside the bay but it does mean bait and predators alike are staying tucked into the protected water rather than pushing out toward open ocean. That works in our favor. It keeps the bunker schools tight to the Hook and keeps the fluke locked onto the channel structure instead of scattering.

Looking ahead: we're running toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, current easing off a bit heading into that. I'd expect the night bass bite to stay steady through the week as long as the heat holds, the fluke to keep producing through the middle of the day on the channel edges, and if that bunker pod holds position off the Hook, I wouldn't be surprised to see the first real inside-the-bay blitz of the summer by the weekend. Have a topwater rod rigged just in case — you don't want to be digging through the rocket launcher when the blues show up under the birds.

reports.headline: Race Ebb at 3.8 Knots: Bass Go Nocturnal, Sea Bass Rule Plum Gut by Day
reports.subhead: The Sound's thermal split is rewriting the clock on the bass bite while Plum Gut's hard bottom keeps quietly loading the cooler.
reports.body_markdown:
3.8 knots on the tail end of Tuesday's ebb through The Race — that's down from the 5-plus we were riding around the new moon two weeks back, and it tells you almost everything you need to know about this week. We're sliding toward the first quarter on the 21st, current's easing off the peak, and that softer push is exactly why the bite windows have stretched out instead of snapping shut in twenty minutes like they do on the big tides.

Here's the other number that matters: Kings Point is reading 71.6, New London's sitting at 67.6. That's a four-degree spread across maybe fifteen miles of open Sound, and it's steep enough to change how these fish behave, not just where they hold. Striped bass hate that upper-60s-to-low-70s window during daylight — it's not that they've left, it's thermal avoidance, pure and simple. They're dropping into the deeper structure around Race Rock and Valiant Rock during the day and doing their real feeding after dark when the surface layer cools a notch and the bait comes up off bottom.

So that's where I've been putting my trips. Valiant Rock's slack window this week is running about 20 to 25 minutes after New London's posted high — close enough to the book that you can plan around it, but I'm still checking it against the actual boil before I commit gear. Wire line with a big tube-and-worm or a bunker spoon, worked through 25 to 40 feet on the drop from max current into that slack, has been the move for the bigger fish. If you're bucktail guys, go heavy — 3 to 4 ounces with a white or chartreuse curly tail — and fish it on the last hour of the ebb before the rock stops boiling, then again as the flood builds back. Night trips through Race Rock and down into the Sluiceway have put mid-30s and a few upper-30s in the box on eels drifted naturally with the current, no weight, just letting the tide do the work.

During daylight, forget the bass and go to Plum Gut, because that's where the sure thing is right now. Black sea bass have been outstanding on the hard bottom there — 35 to 55 feet, bucktail-and-Gulp combos or just a plain jig-and-bait rig with squid strips, dropped tight to the rocks on the up-current side. We had a 28-inch fish come out of there this past week, which tells you the resident population on that structure is mature and it's holding. Fluke are riding shotgun on the same drifts — keeper-class fish, nothing huge, but steady, on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and bucktails in the 3/4 to 1-ounce range depending on how hard the Gut is running that particular stage. The Gut doesn't care what the surface temp is doing up top; that current keeps it well-oxygenated and the bait pinned, so it's been the most dependable piece of water in the whole zone this month.

Little Gull and Great Gull have been quieter than I'd like for daytime bass, which tracks with the thermal read — that shallower structure warms fast and the fish are ghosting off it until the sun goes down. If you want a shot at bass in daylight, work the deeper current seams off the northeast side of Great Gull on the last of the ebb, right where the rip line goes glassy for a few boat-lengths. That seam has produced a handful of upper-slot fish on wire and umbrella rigs, but it's not a sure thing — I'd call it two good trips out of five this past stretch, and you need the tide stage dialed in tight.

No bluefish push into the eastern Sound yet, though the blitz pattern working the bunker schools from the Jersey shore up through western Long Island is the kind of thing that spreads if the calm weather holds — worth watching the Race and Fishers Island Sound over the next week or two for blues to show up chasing the same bunker north. And no albies or bonito in the Gut yet either — that's a straight watch item. Squid are building around Rhode Island and into Nantucket Sound as that water pushes into the high 50s and low 60s inshore, which is the setup piece that usually precedes the first scout fish showing at Montauk or the Vineyard. If that squid keeps building, I'd expect the first false albacore sniffs in our waters sometime in the first half of August, not before.

Looking ahead: as we ease into that first quarter moon, currents through The Race and Plum Gut will keep softening through the weekend, which favors slower presentations — slow-trolled tube-and-worm over fast-stripped bucktails, patient drifts over Plum Gut instead of covering water. If the stable weather holds, I'd fish the night tide at Race Rock for bass and hit Plum Gut in daylight for a mixed bag of sea bass and fluke — that's the two-part game plan that's actually been producing, not the exciting story, but the honest one.

reports.headline: Wamphassuc Boulders Holding Fluke and Sea Bass — Stripers Have Gone to the Dark
reports.subhead: The rocks off Ram Island and Wamphassuc Point are stacked with bait and bottomfish, but the bass have slipped into a nighttime pattern while the Sound warms from the west.
reports.body_markdown:
The boulders off Wamphassuc Point are wearing a coat of green crab shells this week — small ones, freshly cracked, scattered across the tops of the rocks where the tide drops out at dead low. That's blackfish work, even with the season closed here through the summer. I poled the skiff over that field Tuesday morning on the last of the outgoing and watched three good-sized tog nose up off a boulder the size of a Volkswagen, unbothered, in maybe six feet of water. Nothing to do about it but look — and be glad they're still there for October.

What I can put in the boat right now is fluke and sea bass, and both have been dependable on the current-swept structure through Fishers Island Sound. The water here reads cooler than the rest of the Sound — New London's been sitting around 67.6°F while the western Sound pushes into the low 70s — and that gradient matters. It's kept our rips fishing like rips instead of soup. I've been working the drift between Ram Island and the Fishers Island shore, 18 to 25 feet, dragging a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a strip of squid or a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet. Fluke to 4 pounds have come off that stretch on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current pulls hard enough to hold the boat on a controlled drift but not so hard you're bouncing bottom every other cast. Keeper counts have been honest — not a banner week, but two or three fish to the boat most trips, mixed with plenty of shorts that keep you paying attention.

Sea bass have been the better story. Hard bottom off Watch Hill Reef and the eastern end of Fishers Island Sound is holding a strong resident population — I heard of a 28-inch fish taken out that way recently, which tells you the population's got some age and size to it this year. I've been anchoring up on the structure with a high-low rig, squid strips and a chunk of clam, dropping straight down in 25 to 35 feet on the slower stages of the tide. Slack water and the first hour of a new tide have been the windows — once the current gets running hard, the sea bass tuck in tight to the rocks and won't leave.

Stripers are the tricky part of this report, and I want to be straight about it. The warm push from the western Sound has shoved bass into a nocturnal pattern almost everywhere south and west of us — daytime bites have gone quiet as the fish avoid the heat and feed after dark. Our water's a few degrees cooler thanks to that thermal gradient off New London, so we're getting a little more daytime activity than the boats working closer to the city, but it's still best at the edges of light — first hour after sunrise, last hour before dark, and through the night on the boulder fields off Esker Point and the mouth of the Mystic River. I've been running unweighted eels and 2-ounce bucktails over structure on the last two hours of the incoming, letting the current sweep the offering across the rock piles rather than working it hard. Fish have been there but not stacked — a few good bass in the 28- to 34-inch range each trip I've put in after dark, nothing you'd call consistent, but enough to make the late nights worth it if you're patient with the presentation.

One thing worth watching closely over the next week or two: we flagged the bonito setup last week, and the water's lining up the way we thought it would. Block Island's holding water in the high 60s now, well within the range bonito want, and that kind of temperature typically means a push into eastern Long Island Sound within a week or ten days. Nothing's shown yet off Watch Hill Reef or Napatree Point, but I'd keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small metal — a Deadly Dick or a 1-ounce Kastmaster — on the console starting now. When that first scout shows on the surface working bait against the current, you want to be ready, because the window before everybody else notices is short.

Tide's easing toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which should soften the current through the rips over the next several days. That's actually good news for the fluke and sea bass game — slower water lets you work a bucktail more deliberately instead of fighting the drift, and both species have been responding better to a controlled presentation than a fast one. For the stripers, I'd lean into the dark hours through this stretch and target the boulder fields where current breaks hard against structure — Ram Island's north side, the rocks off Esker Point, and the drop just outside the Stonington Breakwater. If the bonito scouts do show early, my money's on Napatree first, given the exposure to open water and the bait that's been stacking there. Until then, it's a rocks-and-patience week — nothing spectacular, but honest fishing if you put in the time on the right stage of tide.

reports.headline: Fort Trumbull Holds the Line: Thames Bass Still Eating in Daylight
reports.subhead: A steep temperature gradient at the river mouth is keeping stripers feeding through the day while the rest of the Sound goes nocturnal.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a seam off Fort Trumbull right now that you can practically see with the naked eye on the back half of the ebb — darker, cooler water sliding out of the Thames and shouldering into the warmer green stuff pushing up from the Sound. I've watched that line form for twenty years and it never gets old. This week it's doing more work than usual. New London's reading 67.6 degrees at the mouth, and Kings Point over in the western Sound is sitting at 71.6. That four-degree gap might not sound like much on paper, but on the water it's the difference between fish that eat all day and fish that only eat after dark.

Western Sound bass have gone nocturnal — that's a heat-avoidance thing, not a disappearing act, and I've seen guys down that way frustrated because they're fishing the wrong hours. Up here, the Thames is still flushing cool enough water on every ebb that stripers are holding right through the current seams at Fort Trumbull and staying willing to eat in full daylight. I had a message from a buddy who fishes out of the state pier who boated three keepers between 26 and 31 inches Tuesday morning, ten o'clock, sun straight up, working a chartreuse-and-white bucktail, 1 to 1.5 ounce depending on the push, right along that temperature line where the current stacks bait. That's not a fluke — that's the gradient doing what it does.

Gold Star Bridge is fishing the way it always fishes this time of year — inconsistent if you don't respect the pilings, very consistent if you do. The eddies on the downstream side of the center piers, especially the second and third from the New London side, are holding bass and some decent bluefish on the last two hours of the outgoing. Live eels drifted right into the slack pocket behind the pilings have been the ticket for the bigger fish, but if you don't want to mess with eels, a swimming plug like a Doc-style stickbait worked slow through the same seam has been drawing strikes too. Depth there runs 18 to 24 feet depending on where you are relative to the channel, and the fish are holding tight to the structure, not out in open water.

Bluefish have shown up with some teeth behind them the last week and a half, and we flagged this coming — bunker schools moving up the coast were going to pull blues with them, and that's exactly what's happening in the harbor now. Pods of peanut and small adult bunker have been working their way up past Pleasure Beach and into the lower Thames, and the blues are riding right underneath them. Metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters — has been the fastest way to connect when you see them busting on top, which has been happening in the early morning off Ocean Beach and again right at last light. Nothing blitz-scale, but enough consistent surface activity that if you see the gulls working, it's worth a dozen casts before you move on.

Fluke fishing has held up nicely on the structure adjacent to the sub base, which doesn't surprise me — that stretch of bottom stays cooler and better oxygenated than open Sound water thanks to the current running through there all day. Drifting 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet in the 15 to 22 foot range along that edge has produced a mixed bag, most fish in the 16 to 19 inch range with the occasional keeper mixed in. Slow drift, bounce it right off bottom, and don't rush the retrieve — these fish haven't needed to chase anything hard in this water.

Porgies are still going at Ocean Beach and around the rockier stretches off Pleasure Beach, and that new moon tide cycle from last weekend is still carrying some extra push through here, which the porgies like. Small hooks, squid strips or clam, right on bottom in 10 to 20 feet — simple, reliable, good for anyone who wants steady action without overthinking the presentation.

Tide-wise, we're easing off that July 13 new moon push and heading toward the first quarter on the 21st, so the current through the Fort Trumbull rip and under the Gold Star pilings should soften up over the next several days. That's actually good news for presentation — slower water lets you work a bucktail or an eel more deliberately instead of just holding on for the drift. If the thermal gradient at the river mouth holds — and there's no reason right now to think it won't, with the Thames running cool and steady — I'd expect the daylight bass bite here to keep outperforming the rest of the Sound through the week. My plan is the last two hours of the outgoing at Fort Trumbull early, then sliding over to the bridge pilings as the tide bottoms out. If the bluefish keep riding those bunker pods into the harbor, keep a rod rigged with metal ready — you won't get much warning before they show on top.

reports.headline: Niantic Boats Filling Boxes With Fluke and Jumbo Sea Bass — Bass Slide Into the Dark
reports.subhead: Dock talk from Waterford to Niantic says keeper fluke and 28-inch sea bass are stacking the reef structure while the stripers punch the clock after sundown.
reports.body_markdown:
I was standing at the bait shop counter Tuesday morning when one of the Niantic drift boat mates came in for squid and mackerel and just started grinning before I even asked. Said Monday's half-day trip put together a stacked box off Black Point — better than a dozen keeper fluke to 6 pounds and sea bass thick enough that they had a 15-fish limit wrapped up before the second drift was even over. That's the kind of morning that gets the whole fleet buzzing, and it's been the theme all week from Twotree Island Channel out to Hole-in-the-Wall.

The fluke bite has been the most dependable thing going in this zone, and it's holding to the pattern we called last week — the back bay stuff is drying up as the shallow water heats, and the fish are pushing out to the rips, the channel edges, and the reef structure where there's current keeping things cool and stirred up. Black Point and the mouth of Twotree Channel are the spots the party boats keep circling back to, drifting 4-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails, or the old standby — a strip of squid over a 4/0 fluke hook on a fish-finder rig, bounced right along bottom in 25 to 40 feet. Best drifts have been on the stronger stage of the tide, either side of the last hour of the incoming pushing into the top of the high, when there's enough current to keep the bait moving but not so much you're skipping bottom.

Sea bass are honestly stealing some of the fluke's thunder right now. Word out of the Waterford fleet is a 28-inch sea bass came off hard bottom over toward Fishers Island Sound — that's a genuine bull, the kind of fish that makes everybody on the rail start re-tying their rigs mid-trip. Closer to home, McCook Point and the rockpiles off Hole-in-the-Wall have been giving up steady limits of 15-to-18-inch fish on jigs tipped with squid strips, or the classic double-hook porgy rig baited with clam. These fish are locked onto structure and current, not chasing anything around — you want to be dropping straight down on the drift as soon as your fish finder shows relief, and you want weight enough to hold bottom in that current, usually 6 to 10 ounces depending on the stage of tide.

Porgies are mixed right in with the sea bass on that same hard bottom, and if you're fishing bait — clam, squid, sandworms — you're going to catch both in the same drift most days. It's been a nice bonus fishery for anybody targeting sea bass and not minding a mixed bag.

Striped bass are the trickier read right now, and I want to be straight about it. New London's water is sitting around 67.6 degrees, noticeably cooler than what they're dealing with out west in the Sound, but it's still warm enough that the bass in our zone have mostly slid into that nocturnal pattern — feeding hard after dark and holding deep on structure through the heat of the day. The guys working the Niantic River mouth and the deeper edges around Black Point after sundown have been finding fish, working bucktails and soft plastics slow along bottom, or live-lining bunker where you can find pods holding along the current seams. Daytime striper fishing has been a grind — a few fish here and there on the strongest part of the tide around Hole-in-the-Wall, but nothing you'd plan a whole trip around until the sun goes down.

Bluefish have been showing up wherever the bait shows up, which tracks with what's been happening up and down the coast all month — bunker schools pushing into the Sound and the blues stacking right underneath them instead of chasing offshore. If you find a bunker pod pushed up against the current off McCook Point or working the edges of Niantic Bay, there's a good chance there's blues under it, and metal — a Kastmaster or a Deadly Dick worked fast through the school — will get bit in a hurry.

Blackfish are basically off the table right now, which isn't a surprise for mid-July — they've spawned out and scattered off the structure, and nobody's targeting them seriously until the water starts cooling in September.

On the bonito front — we flagged last week that the eastward push of false albacore and bonito would reach this end of the Sound last, and that's exactly how it's playing out. Nothing showing yet from Niantic to Black Point; if there's early scouting fish anywhere, it's going to be out around Montauk or the Vineyard corridor first, and it could be another couple weeks before that shows up on our end.

Looking ahead, the moon's easing toward first quarter on the 21st, which should soften the current stages through the rips over the next few days. That usually means slower presentations produce better on the sea bass and fluke grounds — don't be afraid to downsize your bucktail or slow your drift speed if the tide's not ripping the way it has been. If the stable weather holds, I'd keep hammering the same program: fluke and sea bass during the day on the reef structure, and if you want a shot at stripers, save it for the last two hours of light into full dark around the river mouth and Black Point.

reports.headline: River Warms Past 70, Stripers Slide to the Night Tide at Saybrook Point
reports.subhead: Shad are a memory, snapper blues are thick in the coves, and summer flounder are finally showing where we said they would.
reports.body_markdown:
The silver maples along the Essex shoreline have that dusty, heavy-leafed look they get by mid-July, and the ospreys over Great Island are feeding fledglings now instead of sitting eggs. That's how I know where we are on this river without looking at a thermometer. The shad run wrapped up back in early June — those fish are long done spawning and gone back to sea, and if you're still swinging a shad dart above the Baldwin Bridge you're fishing a calendar that's already turned the page. This time of year the river tells a different story, and it's mostly a story about heat.

The water at the mouth has pushed into the low-to-mid 70s, tracking with what we're seeing out in the Sound — Kings Point up around 71.6, water off the Race and into Fishers Island Sound running similarly warm. That's plenty comfortable for a striped bass to tolerate, but not comfortable enough for one to want to feed hard in broad daylight anymore. I've watched this happen for fifty summers now: once the river mouth and the flats off Great Island cross that 70-degree mark and hold there, the bass go nocturnal. They don't leave — they just get smart about when they show themselves. We flagged this pattern last week, that the stripers would stay in the river right through summer, and that's exactly what's playing out, just not on the schedule a lot of guys expect.

My best fish this week came at 9:40 p.m. off the Saybrook Point breakwater, working the last of the outgoing into dead low, an eel drifted on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in eight feet of water. Two bass in the 26 to 30-inch range came off that same rock pile in under an hour, then it went dead quiet for the rest of the tide. That's the pattern right now — short, sharp windows right around the tide change, particularly the last two hours of the ebb when the river's cooler water is still pushing out past the warmer Sound water and creating that current seam off the mouth. If you're fishing bucktails instead of eels, go dark colors — black or purple, half-ounce to three-quarter, and work them slow along the drop where the channel falls off toward Cornfield Point. Daytime, don't waste your good tide on the open flats. Push up into the shade lines along Old Lyme's marsh creeks or work the deeper water off the DEP Marina where there's at least a degree or two of relief.

Bluefish are the noisier story this week, and they're consistent with what we expected — bunker have been holding thick from the river mouth on down the beachfront, and where there's bunker there are blues. Snapper blues, some no bigger than your hand, are chopping through the coves at Essex and up around the Great Island flats on any incoming tide with sun on the water. Kids with a bobber and a sliver of cut bait can load up an afternoon on those. But there are bigger blues mixed in too — three- and four-pounders working the outer edges of the bunker schools right at the river mouth, and those will hit a Hopkins or a small metal-lipped swimmer worked fast through the froth when you see the surface nervous water. Best window there has been early morning, right at first light, before the boat traffic pushes everything down.

And here's the one I'll take some credit for — summer flounder have started showing in the lower river exactly like we said they would. Not a banner bite yet, but real fish: a few keepers to 18 inches coming off the sandy stretches near the mouth on the last of the incoming, drifting Gulp in white or chartreuse on a light jig head, three-quarter ounce, bounced slow along bottom in ten to fifteen feet. If you're marking bait on the graph near Cornfield Point or along the edge of the main channel off Saybrook, that's worth a few drifts. It's early yet for this pattern to be dependable — I'd call it two encouraging trips out of five so far — but the trend is right, and it should build through late July as more fluke work up out of the Sound looking for cooler bottom.

White perch, meanwhile, are doing what white perch always do in high summer — holding tight to the deeper bends above Essex, biting best on the last hour of daylight into dusk on small pieces of bloodworm or a tiny beetle-spin worked slow along the mud. Not glamorous fishing, but it's steady, and it's a good one to fall back on if the tide's wrong for the mouth.

We're heading toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which means the tidal swings are easing rather than building — that generally favors the slower presentations I mentioned over anything you'd want to burn through fast current. If I had one night to fish this week, I'd be back at Saybrook Point on the evening ebb with an eel in hand, and I'd have a bucktail rigged as backup in case the current doesn't set up the way I expect. That's been the honest read on this river for fifty years running — the bass are here, you just have to fish the hours they're willing to give you.

reports.headline: New Haven Breakwall Porgies Run Deep, Charles Island Bass Go Nocturnal
reports.subhead: Structure fishing is carrying the week while the stripers slide into the dark — here's where the rockpiles are paying off.
reports.body_markdown:
Six-thirty Tuesday morning, outside the New Haven breakwall, and my rod tip is doing that little tap-tap-tap that means porgies are stacked under the boat and hungry. Two guys anchored off my stern were snapping their fingers trying to figure out why I had four fish in the bucket before they'd gotten bit once. Simple answer: I dropped a size 4 hook with a sliver of squid right on the up-current edge of the rockpile, not the flat sand ten feet off it. That's the whole game out here right now — inches matter, and the fish are exactly where the structure breaks the current, not where it's convenient to anchor.

The porgy bite on the New Haven Harbor breakwalls has been steady and honest all week, not spectacular, but you can count on it. High-hook boats are running double bottom rigs with size 4 to 6 hooks, squid strips or sandworm, working the outside face of the wall in 12 to 18 feet on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing. That current-edge window is when the bait gets stirred up and the porgies commit. Once the tide goes fully slack, they scatter and sulk, so if you're only getting one shot this week, fish the change, not the middle of the tide.

Sea bass are riding shotgun with the porgies on the same structure, and some of them are quality — I had a 17-incher come off the Charles Island rockpile Thursday that made my Ugly Stik bend like a bow. The black sea bass are holding tight to the rougher stuff, the boulder fields and the mussel-crusted rubble on the northeast corner of Charles Island and out around Falkner Island, where the bottom drops from 10 feet down to 25 in a hurry. Green crab or squid on a knocker rig, dropped right into the crevices, has been the ticket. Don't be afraid to lose a few rigs — if you're not getting hung up occasionally you're probably not close enough to the rock.

Blackfish are a slower story right now. Tautog like it a little cooler than what we're running, and with Kings Point reading better than 71 and the whole western Sound carrying that same warmth, the tog have gone quiet during daylight compared to spring. I've had a couple decent fish, 4 and 6 pounds, off Stratford Shoal on green crab fished tight to the rockpile base on a moving tide, but it's been one or two fish for an hour of work rather than a fill-the-cooler morning. I'd call blackfish a bonus right now, not a plan.

Stripers are the one that's testing patience. The water's pushed into the low-to-mid 70s through the western and central Sound, and the bass have done what warm-water bass do — they've gone deep and gone nocturnal. I fished the Charles Island sandbar on the last of the outgoing at first light Sunday and got exactly nothing, then talked to a guy at the ramp who'd worked that same bar at 5 a.m. with a big walk-the-dog plug and put two schoolies and a 28-incher in the boat before the sun cleared the trees. That's the pattern now — dawn patrol and after-dark, working the drop where the sandbar falls into deeper water on the outgoing tide, live eels or bunker chunks if you can get them, swimming plugs if you're working the surface in that gray light. Midday, forget it — those fish are sitting deep off Stratford Shoal and the drop-offs around Falkner, not up shallow where you can reach them easy.

Fluke have been the pleasant surprise. We flagged this shift coming — that back-bay fluke would push out toward inlet mouths and the harder structure as the shallow water warmed past comfortable — and that's exactly what's showing now around the Milford Gulf and the deeper flats off Charles Island. Keeper-sized fish, several in the 18 to 20-inch class, are coming on white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel edges in 20 to 28 feet on the outgoing tide. If you're marking bait on the finder anywhere near the Gulf's deeper cuts, slow your drift down and work it twice.

Bluefish have been mostly a harbor-mouth story — schoolies chopping bait pods near the New Haven breakwalls on bright afternoons, nothing like the blitz conditions farther down the coast, but if you throw a small metal like a half-ounce Kastmaster into a nervous patch of bait you'll get bit.

Looking ahead: the moon's sliding toward first quarter on the 21st, which should ease the current push a touch and make the rip zones fish a little slower and more deliberate — good news for porgy and sea bass guys working bottom rigs, since a hard-ripping tide makes it tough to stay pinned to the rock. If the calm weather holds, I'd spend my week mornings on the breakwalls and Falkner for porgy and sea bass, and save one dawn or dusk session for the Charles Island bar with a plug rod, because that's still where the bigger bass are going to show if they show at all. Blackfish and daytime striper guys, I'd wait for a real cool-down before betting the whole trip on it.

reports.headline: Cockenoe on the Last Ebb: Fluke Stack, Sea Bass Show, Bass Go Dark
reports.subhead: The reefs are producing daylight fluke and porgies while the stripers have punched out until sundown — here's how I'm working around it.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday morning to skip the Norwalk Islands entirely until the tide turned, and it was the right one. Cockenoe Reef at first light still had two overnight boats anchored on the good rubble, and with Kings Point reading 71.6 degrees, I knew the fluke bite there would hold into the morning regardless — those fish aren't going anywhere in this heat, they're just going to feed a little slower. So I ran the back channel behind Sheffield Island, worked some porgy structure on the Cows off Stamford while I waited out the crowd, and came back to Cockenoe at 10:30 when the anchor boats finally cleared for lunch. That's the chess piece you have to move on a July weekday morning on this stretch — traffic dictates timing as much as tide does.

Once I had Cockenoe to myself, the last two hours of the ebb into dead low did exactly what I expected. Fluke to 22 inches came off the drift in 18 to 24 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the edge where the reef rubble drops into sand. Keeper-class fish, not a banner day, but three in the boat with a handful of shorts thrown back is a solid morning for mid-July. We flagged last week that fluke would start sliding out of the back bays and onto the inlet mouths and ocean-facing reefs as the water warmed further — that's exactly what's happening now. The back-bay fish are thinning out and the reef bite is picking up the slack.

The Cows told a better story than I expected. Porgies are thick out there right now — 20 to 35 feet of water over that mixed rock-and-mussel bottom, bloodworms and green crab on high-low rigs, and you don't need to move much once you find the school. I sat on one drift for forty minutes and never stopped feeding fish into the box. Mixed in with the porgies were a few black sea bass pushing 15 inches, which lines up with what we called a few days back — that this fishery would keep improving into August. The hard bottom out there is holding a real resident population now, not just stragglers. If you're marking bait balls on structure anywhere from the Cows out toward Penfield Reef, drop a jig tipped with squid strip through them before you commit to anchoring — the sea bass are sitting right on the bottom edge of that structure.

Stripers are the harder conversation this week, and I'm not going to sugarcoat it. With the western Sound running warm through the mid-70s in the shallows, the bass have gone nocturnal — that's not a disappearing act, it's a thermal retreat, and it means daylight striper trips on this stretch are mostly a low-percentage play right now. I made two evening runs to Greenwich Point and worked the rock piles off the point on live bunker under a fishfinder rig, starting an hour before sunset and fishing into full dark on the last of the incoming. Both nights produced — nothing giant, schoolies to a couple of 28-inch fish, but consistent enough that I'd call it the pattern to lean on through the rest of July. Penfield Reef is holding the same story after dark: eels drifted along the reef edge on the flood, fished slow, have been the better producer than anything cast-and-retrieve.

Bluefish are the one species giving you daylight action without apology. Bunker schools have been holding tight off Greenwich Point and drifting east past the Norwalk Islands, and the blues are sitting right underneath them, same pattern we've been watching build up and down the coast. Snag a bunker on a treble, drop it back into the school, and you'll get bit — fish in the 3 to 6 pound range, plenty of blowups on top when the bait gets nervous around midday. If you want top-water action without babysitting a bass tide window, this is your play right now.

Tide-wise, we're easing toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which means softer current stages through the weekend — good news for anyone working slower presentations on the reefs, tougher news if you like a hard-running rip to concentrate bait. I'd expect the fluke and porgy bite to hold steady on Cockenoe and the Cows through this stretch since that pattern doesn't depend on a screaming tide, just clean structure and patience. For bass, I'm sticking with the last two hours of dark on the flood, working Greenwich Point and Penfield Reef with bunker and eels, and I wouldn't bother burning gas chasing daylight fish in the shallow coves right now — the water's too warm and they know it.

If the weekend boat traffic gets ugly around the islands, which it will, push east toward Penfield or stay tucked in behind Sheffield until the recreational fleet thins out midafternoon. That's the move I'd make, and it's the one I'm making again this weekend.

reports.headline: Plum Gut ran hard like we called it — bass went nocturnal, porgies never blinked
reports.subhead: The big tide stacked fish on the seams from Horton Point to Orient, but you'll need to fish the dark hours for the bass.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a kid — can't be more than sixteen — who's been putting a twelve-foot skiff in at Mattituck Inlet every morning this week, and every morning he comes back with fewer bucktails than he left with. Tuesday I watched him lose three in a row to blues he never even saw hit, just felt the line go slack and then heard him swear at the sky. I didn't say anything. Everybody learns the hard way that you don't run bare mono around bunker schools with teeth in them. By Thursday he'd wised up, tied on a piece of wire, and came in with a five-gallon bucket half full of chopper blues off Rocky Point. That's how it goes out here — the Sound teaches you, slow and a little expensive.

We said last week that the big spring tide would push hard current through Plum Gut and stack bass, blues, and fluke on the seams and drop-offs, and that's exactly what showed up. The current through there was running like a river for three, four days straight, and anybody who fished the edge of it — right where the fast water meets the slack behind the rocks off Orient Point — found company. Fluke to five pounds came off that seam on white Gulp on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last two hours of the ebb. Nothing spectacular in numbers, but quality fish, and consistent enough that a few of the charter boats made it their whole morning.

The water's been warm on this end of the Sound — Kings Point's reading better than 71, and even out toward New London it's holding in the upper 60s — and that's pushed the striped bass into the pattern we see most Julys: they don't want to feed hard in daylight when the water's carrying that kind of heat, so they've gone almost entirely nocturnal. I'm not going to tell you the bass disappeared, because they didn't. I'm going to tell you that if you're fishing Horton Point or the rip off Rocky Point at two in the afternoon expecting a bass blitz, you're going to be disappointed, and that disappointment isn't the fish's fault. Fish the last hour of light into full dark, working the current breaks with eels or a big swimming plug worked slow, and you'll find them holding tight to structure, using the deeper water and the current itself as cover from the heat. A few guys drifting live eels off Plum Gut after sundown this week put slot fish in the box — nothing giant, mostly high twenties to low thirties, but real fish, not shorts.

Bluefish are the daylight story right now, and they've been the most dependable thing on this whole stretch. Bait schools have been thick from Mattituck clear out to Orient, and the blues are sitting right underneath them the way they do — not chasing bait down, just holding under it and cutting loose whenever something swims through. Diamond jigs with a tube teaser, worked with a jigging motion off the reef structure near Horton Point, have been about as close to a sure thing as this Sound offers. Poppers work too if you catch them up shallow on the bait, which has been happening most mornings before the wind builds.

Porgies never asked anybody's permission to be good, and they're still the bread-and-butter bite on the reef structure from Rocky Point out to the rocks around Plum Gut approach. Sandworm and clam on a simple hi-lo rig, right on the bottom, drifting the reef edges — that's been filling coolers for the guys who don't need a story to tell, just dinner. Blackfish are closed this time of year in these waters, so leave the crabs at home till fall — but the porgy bite more than covers for it if you're after something to eat.

Weakfish have been showing in ones and twos on the calmer evenings — nothing I'd call a real bite yet, more a hint that they're around than a pattern you can plan a trip on. If the calm holds and the water stays warm through the week, I'd expect a few more to show up in the same spots as the bluefish, working the same bait. I wouldn't drive far for them yet.

Looking ahead, the tide's easing off toward that first quarter moon on the 21st, which means the current through the Gut and around Orient Point is going to soften up some. That usually means slower presentations start outproducing the aggressive stuff — smaller bucktails, lighter jigs, working the seams instead of bombing across them. If I had one evening this week, I'd fish the last of the ebb at Plum Gut into the first hour of dark, eel or plug for the bass, and not be surprised if a few blues crash the party too. The porgies will still be there in the morning regardless of what the tide does — they always are.

reports.headline: Four hours, forty minutes to Veatch — and the bluefin were exactly where the tide said they'd be
reports.subhead: A long run east put us on slot bluefin working sand eels at the edge, with yellowfin mixing in and the season's first marlin flag showing color.
reports.body_markdown:
We left the dock at 3:40 in the morning, which is about the only way you make Veatch and get home before the fuel gauge starts arguing with you. I run a 105-mile leg out of Montauk to get to the good water on the northeast corner of that canyon, and at a 22-knot cruise that's just under five hours each way — call it nine and a half hours of running to fish maybe six. You do that math before you leave the dock, not after. Every captain out here does. It's not complaining, it's just what the canyons cost you to get here from this end of the island.

Worth it this time. We picked up the first bluefin around 8 AM on the troll — a spreader bar and a naked ballyhoo working the color change where green water butted up against the blue, right along the 50-fathom break on the northeast lobe. Fish went 39 inches, right in the middle of that 27-to-under-47-inch slot that's been governing everybody's day out here since the recreational fishery settled into its rhythm after the trophy closure. Two-fish limit, and we had our second by 10:30 — a 42-incher that came up under a bird-working bait ball, sand eels balled up tight and getting hammered from below.
