That's been the story all month at Block and out through Atlantis and Veatch both: the bluefin are keyed hard on sand eels and small bait, and they're not running big, but they're running steady. Nobody's telling stories about giants this week. They're telling stories about limits.

Yellowfin mixed in on the same water, which made for a good multi-species day without much extra running around. We picked up three in the 40-to-60-pound class on the troll — same spread, same color change, just a little deeper on the shelf where the water held closer to that 72-to-74-degree window. One came unbuttoned right at the transom, a solid fish that just straightened the hook on a green stick bar, and that's the one I'll be thinking about for a few days. You lose one like that and it sticks with you longer than the ones you put in the box. Night chunking at Atlantis has been the other half of this pattern — butterfish chunks fished on a slow drift over 55 to 70 fathom, small bluefin coming through steady after dark, with the occasional bigeye showing on the sounder deeper in the column. Nobody's icing bigeye numbers yet, but the marks are there on the meter, which tells you the deeper water is starting to hold fish worth staying up for.

We flagged this last week — said the new moon spring tide would push hard current across these shelf breaks, and that's exactly what set up this bite. The current on the edge at Veatch was running noticeably harder than it had been two weeks ago, enough that we had to adjust trolling speed to keep the spread tracking clean, and that current is what's holding the sand eels tight against the break instead of letting them scatter. As we ease toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, that current should soften some — which usually means the bait spreads out a little and you have to work harder to find the concentrated balls, but it also tends to calm the surface enough to fish comfortably longer into the afternoon.

The other thing worth mentioning — we saw our first white marlin flag of the season Wednesday, up near the Atlantis edge working a dredge on light wind and a slick calm morning. Didn't get a bite, the fish came up, looked, and went back down, which is about typical for an early-season marlin — they're scouting before they're committing. But that's the first one anybody on our radio chatter mentioned this year, and it lines up with what we'd expected: the billfish migration building through July, right on schedule. If you want a shot at one, keep a naked ballyhoo rigged and ready behind the dredge, because these early fish are shy and a switch-bait presentation beats a straight troll hookup most days.

Not every trip out there this week was clean. A boat running out of Block Island got into a stretch Tuesday where the wind built out of the southwest into the high teens by early afternoon and the bite went cold for two hours before it turned back on at the evening chunk — that's the kind of afternoon that tests whether you brought enough fuel to wait it out or whether you have to make the call to head in. We had enough in the tanks to sit tight, and it paid off, but I wouldn't plan a trip assuming that's how it goes every time.

Looking ahead, if the current keeps easing through the weekend and the wind stays out of the south under 15 knots, I'd expect the bluefin slot fishery to hold steady at both Veatch and Atlantis, with yellowfin numbers building slightly as that warmer water continues to sit on the edge. Hydrographer and Oceanographer are still a longer reach from these ports — closer to six hours each way from Montauk — but the sand eel pattern that's working the closer grounds should be setting up the same way further east as the season moves through late July. If I had a weather window this weekend, I'd run Veatch again before first light and work that same break where the color changes, with the dredge out for marlin and the chunk bags ready for after dark.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Slow Monday, Money Thursday: Yellowfin and White Marlin Turn It Around at Spencer
reports.subhead: A rough start to the week gave way to a warm-water push that put chunk bites and marlin flags up across the southern grounds.
reports.body_markdown:
Give this week a C-plus. Monday and Tuesday were a wash — a weak frontal boundary kicked up a sloppy 3 to 4 foot sea out past the 60-fathom curve and killed two charters before they even got their spreads wet. But Wednesday the wind laid down, the swell went from lumpy to lazy, and by Thursday we were running four boats out of Cape May and Ocean City into some of the better mixed-bag fishing I've had all July. That's the canyon game — you eat the bad days so you're ready when the good ones show up.

Spencer was the story of the week. We ran out to the northeast edge, working the 100-fathom curve around 38°44'N/73°52'W, and found a hard temperature break where warm Gulf Stream filament water was shouldering up against the cooler shelf water — the kind of seam that stacks bait and holds fish tight to the edge instead of scattering them across open water. Trolled a standard ballyhoo-and-Islander spread through there Thursday morning and connected on yellowfin in the 35 to 55 pound class, six for nine on the day, plus a double-header of white marlin that came off a naked ballyhoo pulled long on the flat line. We flagged this pattern last week — said the moon-driven current push across the south canyon shelf breaks would concentrate bait right along that edge, and that's exactly what we found. The white marlin bite in particular has been building since the Fourth, and Thursday's action fits right into that seasonal climb — expect more flags through late July as more fish filter up from the south.

Lindenkohl was quieter but not dead. We worked the 90 to 120 fathom stretch off the northwest corner and had a decent night chunk bite on butterfish — three bigeye between 60 and 90 pounds, all in that two-to-four AM window when the current went slack and the fish came up off the bottom structure to feed. If you're going to fish Lindenkohl right now, don't waste daylight trolling the middle — anchor up or drift the edge after dark with a slow chunk line and a couple of baits soaked deep on 200 feet of leader. That's where the bigeye have been holding.

Poor Man's did what Poor Man's does this time of year — mahi. Lots of them, mostly schoolie-size in the 5 to 12 pound range, stacked up under any floating junk we found working the color change closer in, around the 40 to 50 fathom line. Small spreader bars and green machines with a naked ballyhoo teaser pulled fish up fast, and a few times we had triples going off the corner. Not a tuna show out there this week, but if you want a fast, fun day and a cooler full of dinner, that's your spot. We did mark one respectable wahoo on the troll near a weed line — high-speed lure, planer down about 30 feet, single strike, no hookup. Worth keeping a wahoo bait in the spread out there even when you're primarily running for mahi.

Norfolk was the longest run and the toughest call this week, but the guys who made the trip weren't disappointed. Working out past the 150-fathom break on the south wall, we had a solid yellowfin bite mid-morning Friday — fish in the 40 to 60 pound range eating cedar plugs and small green/yellow machines pulled fast, 7 to 8 knots, classic tuna trolling speed. There was also a single bigeye pulled off a deep drop bait fished on the down-current side of the temperature break, which tells me that warm water is still holding structure down there even though it's a longer haul than most weekend boats want to make.

The pattern behind all of this is straightforward: the stable high pressure we've had since midweek let the warm-core Gulf Stream water settle in and hold its shape instead of getting torn apart by wind-driven mixing. That's kept bait concentrated on the shelf breaks across all four canyons, and it's why the troll bite has been steady rather than explosive — fish are there, but they're locked onto specific edges rather than roaming open water. Night chunking has outproduced daytime trolling at Lindenkohl and Norfolk specifically because that's where the bigger, more cautious bigeye class fish are sitting deep during daylight and coming up after dark.

Looking ahead, if this high-pressure pattern holds through the weekend — and right now there's no reason to think it won't — I'd expect the yellowfin bite at Spencer to keep building along that same temperature seam, and I'd keep a rod rigged for white marlin any time you're trolling that edge, because the flag count has been climbing steadily since the holiday. Poor Man's should keep producing mahi as long as there's floating structure to hold them, so scan hard for weed lines and debris on the way out rather than running straight to a number. Norfolk is the wildcard — it's a long run, but the bigeye and yellowfin combo down there has been worth the fuel for anyone willing to make the trip and fish it properly after dark. If the wind stays out of the southwest under 15 knots, that's where I'd point the bow next.

reports.headline: Ran the East Wall on a Hunch — Six Yellowfin and Our First White Marlin of the Year
reports.subhead: A warm-water eddy tucked against the Wilmington's edge turned a coin-flip troll into the best day we've had since June.
reports.body_markdown:
Monday morning I had two options on the plotter and about ninety minutes to decide between them: run to the Baltimore and gamble on a temp break nobody had confirmed, or make the shorter run to the Wilmington's east wall where satellite showed a warm eddy pinched up tight against the canyon edge. I picked the Wilmington. Fuel math said it was the smarter play even if the fish weren't there — shorter run, more time on the trolley if we had to grind for bites. Turned out we didn't have to grind much.

We set up around 38°47'N, 72°38'W, working the spur where the bottom breaks from 600 fathoms up onto the 100-fathom curve, and the color change was obvious by 7 a.m. — that green-to-blue seam you can see without even looking at the water temp gauge. We had a nine-line spread out, naked ballyhoo in the shotgun and long riggers, Green Machines and a small Ilander in the pattern, and it didn't take twenty minutes before the left short corner buried. Yellowfin, maybe 55 pounds, clean fish, fat with squid. We picked at that same stretch of edge for four hours and boxed six yellowfin between 45 and 68 pounds, plus a mahi that came up on a teaser and wouldn't leave the spread alone until we stuck a naked ballyhoo in front of it.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the new moon tide would concentrate bait tight against the shelf break, and that's exactly what we found. The current was ripping harder than normal for mid-July, and everywhere that eddy pinched down against the canyon wall, we found bait balls stacked thick on the sounder, 180 to 240 feet down, with tuna working underneath them. That's not luck. That's the moon doing what the moon does this time of year — squeezing bait into a smaller window and making the fish easier to find, if you're willing to run to where the edge is actually working instead of where it worked last week.

Wednesday we switched gears entirely. Ran back out to the same general area but instead of trolling, we anchored up on the warm side of that break around dusk and started chunking butterfish over the transom. This is where the Wilmington earns its reputation — once that sun drops and you've got a slick of oily chunks drifting back into dark water, the yellowfin come up out of the depths and feed right under the boat. We used 50-pound fluoro leaders, small hooks buried in the chunk, no weight, just let it flutter down naturally. Landed four more yellowfin that night, one right at 70 pounds, and had a big fish — bigeye-sized run, heavy and slow — that pulled hook after ten minutes of stalemate. That's canyon chunking. You win some, you lose some, and the ones you lose stick with you longer than the ones you land.

The real story of the week, though, was the white marlin. We had one come up on the left long rigger Thursday, ate a ballyhoo clean, and we actually got the flag up — first white of the season for us. Talked to a few other crews working the Wilmington and Baltimore both, and they're seeing the same thing: scattered white marlin showing on the troll, not stacked yet, but building. That lines up with what we expected out of this month — the billfish migration typically starts trickling through the mid-Atlantic canyons in mid-to-late July, and this looks like the front edge of it. If you want a shot at marlin right now, keep naked ballyhoo or small skirted baits in the pattern along with your tuna spread. Don't rig the whole boat for tuna and be surprised when a white eats your teaser bait.

Wahoo have been quiet for us — we marked a couple of high-speed strikes on the wire but nothing stuck, and I haven't heard much wahoo talk out of Washington Canyon either. Bluefin are still mostly an inshore story right now, schoolies working bait balls closer to the 30-fathom line, which isn't really our program out here on the canyon edge.

Water's been running warm and stable, that eddy hasn't slid off the wall the way they sometimes do mid-week, and as long as it holds through the weekend I'd expect the same general pattern — troll mornings on the temp break, switch to the chunk after 6 p.m. if the current's right. The Canyon Challenge wraps up this weekend and from what I'm hearing at the dock, boats have found enough fish to make it a real tournament, not a coin-flip. If the eddy stays put, I'd run the same corner of the Wilmington Monday and Tuesday before the wind forecast for midweek potentially stirs things up. If it slides east like these things sometimes do, I'd shift effort toward the Baltimore's north edge and start the search over. Either way, this was a week where making the shorter, smarter run paid off — sometimes the math on fuel and time matters more than the rumor on the radio.

reports.headline: Southwest Ledge Still Holding Cold, Clean Water — Bass and a Strengthening Fluke Run
reports.subhead: The current stalls at the top of the ebb and you can feel the whole Ledge breathe — bass are still down there, and the fluke bite is building fast.
reports.body_markdown:
There's a stretch of water right at the top of the ebb on the Southwest Ledge where everything just stops moving for a minute — the boat sits dead still, the rod tips quit dancing, and you can practically feel the whole Ledge exhale before the tide turns and starts pulling the other way. That's the moment I wait for every trip out there this time of year. The water's still clean and cold enough to hold fish tight to the structure, and that stand of the tide is when the bigger bass show themselves before the current picks back up and pushes everything into the rips.

That's the story of Block Island right now — the water here is doing what it's always done for us in July, staying cooler and better oxygenated than the mainland beaches, and the bass know it. While stripers from the Jersey shore up through the western Sound have gone nocturnal, hunkering down in the low-to-mid 70s water and only really feeding after dark, our fish don't need to run that program. The current ripping over the Ledge and through the North Rip keeps things stirred and cool enough that we're still getting a legitimate daytime bite, especially on the stronger stages of the tide. I had a 38-pounder come off the bottom in about 55 feet on the west side of the Ledge on a bucktail-and-eel combo last Thursday morning, broad daylight, nothing subtle about the take. Southwest Ledge and the rips off Southeast Light continue to be the go-to structure — tube and worm trolled slow through 40 to 60 feet on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most consistent producer, with live eels taking over once the sun starts dropping and the bigger class of fish moves up onto the shallower boulder fields to feed.

Bluefish are mixed in wherever the bass are working, and some of them are legitimately heavy — I've seen a few in the 12 to 14 pound range busting bait right on the surface off the North Rip on calm mornings. If you want a change of pace from bass fishing, throwing poppers or Hopkins jigs into a blitz like that will wear your arm out fast, and it's about as much fun as this fishery offers.

The fluke run has been building steadily and it's worth making the trip for on its own right now. Drifting the sand-and-gravel edges off the west side of the island, along the approaches to the Great Salt Pond and down toward Charlestown, has been putting keeper fish in the box consistently on the incoming tide. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom with just enough lift to feel the structure, has been the ticket — and we're seeing enough size mixed in with the shorts that it's turning into a real target species rather than an afterthought while you wait for the bass bite to turn on. This is shaping up to be one of the better fluke seasons we've had out here in a few years, and the pattern's still building, not fading.

Porgies are doing what porgies do — thick on the reefs off the southwest corner, biting sea worms and clam on light tackle in 20 to 35 feet whenever the tide's moving. It's not glamorous fishing but it's about as sure a thing as this island offers right now, and it's a good way to fill a cooler on a day when the bigger stuff isn't cooperating.

Further offshore, the canyon boats running out of here have been finding a legitimate recreational bluefin window — fish in that 27 to 47 inch slot working over sand eels and small bait, with yellowfin starting to mix in for crews pushing to the deeper canyon edges. That's a longer run and a different game than the inshore stuff, but it's worth knowing it's out there if you've got the boat and the fuel for it.

No bonito yet, and I want to be straight about that rather than tease something that isn't here. The water's been climbing into the range where they'll eventually show, and squid are building in the protected coves around the island the way they do right before the false albacore and bonito scouts arrive — but the honest read is early-to-mid August before we see the first fish crash bait on the surface here. I'll be watching the coves off the southwest corner and keeping bait rigs rigged just in case, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them yet.

Looking ahead, the tide is easing toward the July 21st first quarter, which means softer current stages through the rest of this week. That usually means slower presentations produce better — less speed on the troll, more patience letting the eel or tube sink into the strike zone before working it. If the current stays manageable and the wind holds out of the south or southwest without kicking up a mess, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb on the Ledge for bass, then shift over to the fluke grounds on the building incoming. That's the play I'm making this week, and it's given up good fish two out of the last three trips — solid odds for late July, but you still need to be on the right stage of the tide when it happens.

reports.headline: Bay pushes into the high 70s — porgies mob Shelter Island, bass slide into the night shift
reports.subhead: Fluke stay steady in the channels, weakfish are trickling back on calm evenings, and the stripers have gone strictly after-dark.
reports.body_markdown:
By the third week of July the Peconic has fully caught up to itself. This bay warms faster than the Sound every spring, and by now it's paid the bill for that head start — surface temps are sitting in the mid-to-high 70s from Noyack clear out to Orient, and that's pushed the whole system into its classic summer rhythm. The porgies don't care one bit. The fluke are holding to their lanes like they always do. But the striped bass have punched the clock and gone to night shift, and if you're still fishing them at noon you're fishing the wrong hours.

Start with the good news, because there's plenty of it. Porgy fishing around Shelter Island right now is about as good as this fishery gets anywhere on the East Coast. Cedar Island, Ram Island, and the mussel beds off Coecles Harbor are stacked with scup running 12 to 15 inches, some pushing 16, and they're eating anything you drop — but if you want quality over quantity, small pieces of clam or squid on a hi-lo rig with size 6 or 4 hooks, fished right on the bottom in 15 to 25 feet, is still the way to go. Fish the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide — that's when they really turn on around the harbor mouths and the current isn't ripping your rig sideways. I had a half day out there Tuesday morning and we could have filled a five-gallon bucket in an hour if we'd wanted to keep grinding. Bring light tackle. These fish deserve it.

Fluke are doing exactly what we said they'd do — steady, dependable, unglamorous, and that's fine by me. The channels between Robins Island and the Southold shore, the deeper cuts off Nassau Point, and the drop-offs into Noyack Bay are all holding keeper-class fish in the 18 to 22 inch range mixed with a lot of shorts you'll have to sort through. White or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the drift, are still outproducing bait rigs for me. Best window is the last two hours of the outgoing when the current is still moving enough to keep your bait working but not so hard you're bouncing bottom like a jackhammer. We flagged last week that this bite would carry through summer, and it has — no signs of it slowing, just the usual grind of sorting through short fish to find your dinner.

Weakfish are the interesting story right now. They'd gone quiet for a stretch, but on these calm, warm evenings they're starting to show again in small numbers off the deeper edges — Threemile Harbor's outer flats, the mouth of Sag Harbor Cove, and the drop just outside Greenport Harbor. Nothing to build a trip around yet, but a few fish in the 20 to 24 inch class have come off soft plastics and small swimming plugs fished at dusk into full dark, which lines up with exactly what we thought would happen once the evenings settled down and stayed warm. If you're patient and you like fishing that last hour of light into darkness, it's worth a rod.

Now the bass. They haven't left — they've just adjusted, same as they do every July when the water climbs into the mid-70s. Daytime, they're tucked deep against current breaks and structure where it's a few degrees cooler, and they're barely feeding until the sun drops. Plum Gut is still the best bet in the whole system for this pattern because the current there never really stops moving and it keeps water churned and slightly cooler than the flat bay around it. Fish it on the last two hours of the ebb into the turn, right along the western edge where the rip folds back on itself. As we head toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, that current is going to ease up some, and that's actually good news — it means slower presentations will start working better than the frantic stuff you needed during full push. A 1.5-ounce bucktail cast across the seam and allowed to sink clean before a slow bottom retrieve has been the most consistent producer, especially after dark. Orient Point and the North Race are holding similar action for anyone willing to make the run and fish the same tide stages at night.

Bluefish are mixed in wherever the bass are working the rips, and they'll save a slow bass night — small to mid-size blues chasing bait through the Gut and off Orient, happy to jump on diamond jigs or poppers if you're covering water in the dark.

Looking ahead, expect this pattern to hold as long as the bay stays warm and calm. The porgy and fluke bites should keep rolling with minimal change — they're both tied more to structure and tide than temperature swings at this point. The bass will keep favoring darkness until we get a real cool-down or a stretch of wind that mixes the bay, which doesn't look imminent. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd be at Plum Gut on the last of the ebb into the turn, working that western seam slow and deep, with a light spinning rod rigged for porgies as a backup plan on the way home.

reports.headline: North Bar Bass Go Underground as the Blues Take the Day Shift
reports.subhead: Warm water at the Point has stripers feeding after dark while jumbo bluefish own the daylight rips — and the canyon fleet is finally cashing in south of Montauk.
reports.body_markdown:
Mid-July is a hinge point out here, and if you've fished the Lighthouse long enough, you learn to read it without needing a thermometer. The spring run bass — those chrome fish that came through on the herring and the worm hatch back in May — have settled into their summer pattern, and at the Point that means one thing above all: they've gone to the dark side. Surface water off North Bar and Shagwong Reef is sitting in the low 70s right now, matching what the open ocean buoys are showing out toward the Bight, and once that happens, stripers stop wanting to work hard in the sun. They don't leave the grounds. They just go underground until the light drops.

I've fished this rock pile since before I could see over the console, and this is the oldest lesson the Point teaches: when the day bite goes quiet, the night bite doesn't. I've been sliding out to the boulder field off the Lighthouse an hour before dark and working the incoming through the last two hours of daylight into full night, and that's where the better fish are coming from — 20 to 34 pounds, a few pushing into the 40s, on live eels drifted naturally through the white water where the rip stacks up against the rocks. Guys throwing bucktails are doing better working the wash at first light, before the sun gets on the water, than they are at midday. If you want a Point bass right now, you're either fishing the two hours around sunset and sunrise, or you're fishing under the stars. That's not a slump — that's just July.

What's filling the daylight hours is bluefish, and they're not shy about it. Skinner and the crew working the eastern beaches have been finding slot-and-overslot-heavy stripers mixed with genuinely big blues — 10, 12, 14 pounds — stacked tight on current edges and boiling visibly off Shagwong and out past Turtle Cove. These aren't scattered snappers. These are teeth-first cows that will straighten a hook if you're not paying attention. The pattern Skinner's using is the right one for these current seams: cast a 1.5-ounce bucktail across the far side of the rip, let it sink clean off the edge before it starts dragging, then work it back with a slow, rhythmic lift-and-drop along bottom. In the visible boils, don't bomb long casts into open water — feather it right into the seam where the bait's getting pinned. That's where the take happens.

Fluke fishing has been the dependable half of the week, and it should stay that way regardless of what the bass and blues are doing. The drifts off Frisbie's Bank and along the edges toward Southside have been giving up a mixed bag with enough keepers mixed in to make it worth the gas — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, worked slow along bottom in 25 to 40 feet, outgoing water. Nothing spectacular, but steady, which after a week of chasing nocturnal bass is exactly the kind of fishing you want to fall back on with a full boat.

Now for the part of the report I've been waiting to write. We flagged last week that the Canyon Challenge wrapping up this weekend would bring fresh yellowfin and white marlin reports out of the Montauk canyon fleet — and that's exactly what's happened. Boats working the edges east of the tuna grounds are connecting on yellowfin in the 40 to 70-pound class, with a scattering of bigeye mixed in on the troll. We also called that the bait piles building south of Block Island would keep bluefin accessible to the smaller boats, and that's held up too — schoolie bluefin have been showing within range of center consoles running south out of the harbor, not just the big canyon runners. If you've got a half-decent weather window this week, that's where I'd put my effort if tuna's the target.

There's another piece of this building quietly that I want everybody watching. Squid concentrations are stacking up hard around Rhode Island and into Nantucket Sound as that inshore water pushes into the high 50s and low 60s in the protected coves. That's the bait that historically supercharges the Montauk rips once it works its way down here — it's the fuel behind some of the best fall-run bass fishing we get, and it's also usually the first sign that bonito and false albacore scouts aren't far behind. Nothing definitive yet on albies at the Point, but if there's anywhere on the whole coast where the first scout shows, it's here or the Vineyard corridor. I'll be watching Shagwong and the rips off the Elbow closely over the next two weeks.

Looking ahead: the moon's building toward first quarter on the 21st, which means tidal current will ease through the week — good news for the rip fishing, because slower current lets a slow-worked bucktail or a drifted eel stay in the strike zone longer instead of getting ripped through in seconds. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it has been, I'd fish the last two hours of daylight and the first hour of dark off the Lighthouse for bass, switch to daylight bucktailing on the current seams for blues, and keep the fluke rods rigged as your insurance policy. Tuna guys — get your window in before the pattern shifts.

reports.headline: Midnight Outgoing: The Deep Hole Behind the Rocks, and Weakfish Waking Up at Ponquogue
reports.subhead: With the bay running warm and stripers going nocturnal, the smart money is on the tide after dark — and the bridge bite is finally worth the mosquito bites.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday night to skip the sunset bite entirely and wait for the tide to really start pulling — 11:40 outgoing, dead of night, nobody on the jetty but me and one guy from Riverhead who talks too much on the phone. That's the decision I keep making this time of year. When the bay's sitting in the high 70s like it is right now, the bass don't want anything to do with daylight. They slide into the deep water and wait for the sun to go down and the current to start moving bait past their nose. So that's where I put my hours.

The hole behind the north jetty rocks, the one that drops to eighteen, twenty feet on the last of the outgoing — that's been the address. I've been soaking bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, 3 ounces of lead to hold bottom against that current, and I've also had good luck swimming a live eel along the rock face on a light egg sinker, just enough weight to keep it down without killing the action. Fish have been coming in the 26 to 34-inch range, mixed in with a few shorts, and every single one of them showed up in that window from an hour before low water through the first hour of the new incoming. Bite the tide change wrong and you're just chumming for sea robins. I watched three guys leave at 1 a.m. with nothing because they fished the wrong two hours — showed up at high water instead of low. Timing is everything out here right now, more than usual.

We flagged this last week — said the back bay was sitting warm, mid-to-upper 70s, and that the tide swing around the new moon would flush hard through the inlet. That's exactly what set this bite up. All that warm water pouring out on the ebb concentrates bait right at the inlet mouth and the current seams off the rocks, and the bass that have gone deep and lazy during the day get aggressive again once that flow really starts ripping after dark.

Ponquogue Bridge has been the other piece of good news, and honestly it surprised me a little. Weakfish have been showing up on calm, warm evenings — not every night, but when the wind lays down and the water goes glassy under the lights, guys are picking off weakfish in the 3 to 5 pound class drifting bucktails tipped with squid strips right along the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing. Bloodworms on a simple hi-lo rig have worked too if you don't want to jig. It's not a blitz — you might get two or three fish in a session — but it's real, and it's the best that stretch has fished in a couple years. The bridge lights pull the bait, the bait pulls the weakfish, and the tide does the rest. I'd rather take three quality weakfish under those lights than grind out shorts anywhere else.

Daytime, the fluke have been the honest bite. Nothing spectacular, but dependable, which counts for something in mid-July heat. Drifting the inlet bar and the channel edge off the Coast Guard station, white and chartreuse Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, has been putting keepers in the 18 to 21-inch range in the boat on the last of the incoming. Tiana Beach flats have given up a few doormats to guys drifting squid strips over the sandy patches, but you have to cover water — there's no one spot holding fish all day. The canal end, where the bay squeezes into that current toward the Peconic, has had some sneaky good fluke action too on the push tide, plus the occasional weakfish getting flushed through with the bait. Worth a drift if the main bay's slow.

Bluefish have been more rumor than reality here so far — plenty of snappers in the bay, and a few cocktail blues mixed in with the bass on the rocks at night, but nothing like the bunker blitzes tearing up the beaches to the west. If that bait moves east, and there's a decent chance it does if this calm weather holds, Shinnecock could see its own version of that show. I wouldn't count on it yet, but I'd keep a bag of metal in the truck just in case.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward first quarter on the 21st, so the current should start softening up through the weekend. That usually means slower presentations pay off better — smaller bucktails, lighter drifts, less horsing the tide. If I had one night to fish this week, I'd still take the midnight outgoing at the inlet rocks over anything in daylight. The bass are there, they're just waiting for the lights to go out and the water to start moving. Bring bug spray, bring patience, and don't show up at the wrong end of the tide.

reports.headline: The New Moon Flush Cut a Fresh Channel Off Cupsogue — Fluke Moved Right Into It
reports.subhead: Moriches Inlet scoured deeper on the west side after the spring tide, and the bait — and the bass and fluke that eat it — followed the new bottom.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the jetty at Cupsogue Tuesday morning at half-tide and the bottom told me everything I needed to know. The west lobe of the inlet, the one that always builds after a hard spring flush, had pushed out another ten or fifteen yards since I was out here two weeks ago. That new moon on the 13th did exactly what I said it would — it ran a powerful flush through the throat of the inlet, and it scoured a fresh channel edge right off the tip of the jetty where the old one had started filling with sand. Bait got funneled through that cut on the ebb, and everything that eats bait followed it in.

That's not a coincidence, and it's not luck — it's just how this inlet works. Moriches doesn't sit still. Every big tide event moves sand, and every time the bottom changes, the fish reposition to the new edges. Right now the best structure isn't where it was in June. It's that new drop-off on the ocean side of the west jetty, roughly 4 to 7 feet of water butting up against a scoured trough that's running closer to 12, and it's holding fluke stacked tight on the seam.

We flagged the Moriches-Shinnecock corridor heating up for fluke through the back half of July, and that's exactly what's showing up. I had three solid drifts off the inlet mouth Wednesday on the last two hours of the outgoing, working a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged slow across that new channel edge. Picked off four keepers in the 19 to 22-inch range, plus more shorts than I wanted to unhook. The pattern holds through the corridor east toward Shinnecock too — same story, channel edges and current-swept structure, not open sand. If you're marking bait on the meter but not getting bit, you're probably ten feet off the edge. Move onto the lip of the drop and stay there.

Bluefish are the beach story right now, and it's a good one if you don't mind covering water. Incoming tide at Cupsogue and out toward Pikes Beach has bait pods getting worked over hard — snapper-sized blues mixed with cocktail fish in the 2 to 4 pound range, blitzing right in the wash some mornings. Metal — a 1-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins — thrown into the boil and cranked steady is all you need. The ocean's been sloppy, running 2 to 3 feet with a short period out of the south, so don't expect glassy conditions. The blues don't care. They're stacked under the bait, not chasing it around, and that pattern should hold as long as this bunker stays along the beachfront.

Striped bass are the tougher conversation. Bay water's pushed well up into the 70s, and that's shoved the bass into a nocturnal pattern — this isn't a fish that disappeared, it's a fish avoiding warm water during daylight and feeding on the temperature break after dark. I've been fishing the rocks at the west jetty and the drop-off on the bay side of the inlet from an hour before dark through the top of the tide, swimming eels slow along the bottom edge where that cooler water pools after sundown. Results have been real but not easy — a handful of fish in the 28 to 34-inch range over three trips, with a couple better ones lost in the rocks. If you want bass right now, you're fishing at night, you're fishing structure, and you're not complaining about the hours.

Weakfish are starting to show some life again, and this tracks with what I expected — calm, warm evenings are exactly when this bite rebuilds. I had a report of a few keeper weakfish taken on the bay side near Tuthill Point working a Gravity Tackle sand eel on light spinning gear, right at last light on a soft outgoing tide. It's not a numbers game yet, but the fish are there and the pattern makes sense — weakfish like exactly the still, warm-evening conditions we've had this week. Worth a couple hours at dusk if you're already out.

Porgies are steady and reliable on the inlet structure itself — clam on a standard high-low rig around the rocks at Cupsogue and the deeper holes inside the inlet mouth will keep a rod bent without much drama. Blackfish are out of the conversation until the fall opener, so don't waste bait there.

Looking ahead, the moon's easing toward first quarter on the 21st, which means the current through the inlet is going to soften over the next several days. That's going to change the fluke game slightly — slower drifts, lighter jig heads, maybe dropping to a half-ounce bucktail to keep contact with bottom without dragging too fast across that new channel edge. If the ocean lays down at all, I'd also take a look at the outside edge of that west lobe on a calm morning — that kind of structure right after it forms often holds fish nobody's found yet. For bass, stick with the after-dark program at the jetty rocks until the bay cools even a degree or two. And keep an eye on the bunker along the beach — as long as it's there, the blues will be too.

reports.headline: Forget the bunker blitz — the real bass bite at Jones is happening after the sun goes down
reports.subhead: Everybody's chasing bluefish under the diving gulls off the beach; I'm working the rocks at Short Beach at 10 p.m. because that's where the stripers actually are.
reports.body_markdown:
You want to know where every rod in a five-mile stretch of Jones Beach is pointed right now? At the bunker schools getting hammered by blues in broad daylight. And look, I get it — it's a hell of a show. But if you're only fishing that window, you're leaving the better fish in the water. I've been working the jetty rocks at Short Beach and the inlet edge after dark all week, and that's where the real striper bite is living right now.

Here's the why, and it's not complicated. The ocean off the beach is sitting around 73-74 degrees, and that's simply too warm for bass to want to feed hard in the sun. They're not gone — they didn't leave the zone — they just flipped the switch to nighttime feeding, same as they do every summer once the surface water gets into the low 70s. So while everybody's casting metal into the bluefish blitz at noon, I'm soaking eels off the rocks at Short Beach two hours either side of the tide change, after 9 p.m., and putting bass in the 20 to 30 pound class on the sand at my feet. Live eel, no weight if I can get away with it, just enough current to swing it into the current seam off the jetty tip. If the tide's really moving I'll add a small egg sinker ahead of a swivel. Bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig work too if eels are hard to come by at the shop — fresh cut, not the frozen stuff, makes a real difference right now.

Daytime, the blues are legitimately good and I won't tell you to skip them. Bunker pods are pushing tight to the beach from Short Beach on down toward the inlet, and when the birds pile up you'll see blues busting bait right in the wash. Bucktails, Kastmasters, anything silver and fast — cast into the froth and hang on. Just don't expect bass mixed in during those hours. They're down deep or tucked into the shadow line under the jetties, waiting for dark.

Inside the inlet, fluke have been the one honest, dependable bite all week regardless of what the surface temp is doing. Sloop Channel and the deeper cuts along the Jones Inlet structure are holding keeper fish in that 18 to 22 inch range, with a few pushing 4 pounds. I've been drifting the last two hours of the ebb, working white bucktails tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets right on bottom in 15 to 22 feet, slow drags with a pause — that pause is when they eat. The current edges where the channel spills out toward the ocean are holding the better grade of fish. Don't waste time on the flats mid-day when the sun's beating down; the fluke tuck into that deeper, cooler water and that's where you need to put your bait.

Now the weakfish — I said last week the calm, warm evenings would bring that bite back to life, and that's exactly what's happening in South Oyster Bay. Guys working the deeper holes off Freeport and around the Wantagh Bridge channel edge on quiet nights are picking up weakfish in the 18 to 24 inch class on small soft plastics — pink or chartreuse 3-inch shads on light jigheads, worked slow just off bottom. It's not a fast bite, and I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet, but it's real, and if this stretch of calm weather holds, it should keep building through the end of the month.

We also flagged the new moon tide pushing hard current through the inlet, and that's exactly what set the table for this week's bunker blitzes — that ebb flow flushed bait right out into the surf zone where the blues were waiting on it. That current is easing off now as we come into the first quarter moon on the 21st, which is actually good news for the fluke guys. Softer current means better bucktail presentation and less scope on your line, so I'd expect the inlet fluke bite to sharpen up over the next few days rather than fade.

Looking ahead, if the ocean stays flat and warm like this — and the buoy off the Bight is still reading rough with that leftover 2 to 3 foot swell — I'd keep my daytime energy on the bunker blitz for blues and save my best efforts for the dark hours at the jetties for bass. If we get a stretch of onshore wind that stirs things up and drops the surface temp even a couple degrees, watch for the bass to push back into feeding during last light and first light instead of full dark — that's usually the first sign the pattern's about to shift toward fall timing. Until then, I'm not chasing the crowd on the beach at noon. I'm home sleeping so I've got the energy to fish the rocks when the real fish come out to eat.

reports.headline: Canarsie Pier at First Light: Fluke in the Channel, Blues in the Shallows
reports.subhead: The bay's split into two shifts right now — daytime fish in the deep water, bass waiting for dark, and the weakfish starting to show like we thought they would.
reports.body_markdown:
I launched the kayak off Canarsie Pier before six this morning, and I picked that spot on purpose. With the bay running warm through the afternoons, the early paddle out to the edge of the flats is the only window where you're not fighting the sun and the heat both. Canarsie gives me quick access to the channel edge without a long haul, and it lets me check three different things in one trip — the deep water for fluke, the shallows for snapper blues, and the general mood of the bay before it gets crowded.

Fluke are the most dependable thing going right now, and they're doing exactly what they do in the heat — sitting deep, off the mud and sand transitions in Grassy Bay and along the channel edges by the Cross Bay Bridge, and feeding hardest on the moving water. I've been dragging four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on quarter- and half-ounce bucktails, slow enough that I can feel the bottom the whole drift, and the fish have been there on both the incoming and outgoing — just tucked a little deeper than they were in June. Fifteen to twenty feet has been the sweet spot. Nothing enormous, but a steady pick of keepers mixed with plenty of shorts, which is honestly what July fluking in the bay looks like most years. If you want a shot at a bigger fish, work the deeper holes off Motts Basin on the last two hours of the ebb, when the bait gets funneled out with the current.

Snapper blues are thick in every shallow corner of the bay right now — off the pier, along the bulkheads, up in the coves by Bergen Basin. This is the easiest, most reliable action going, and it's exactly the stuff that gets a kid hooked on fishing for life. Small hooks, a strip of spearing or a sliver of bunker under a bobber, and you'll have a bucket of them in twenty minutes. Nothing fancy needed.

The striped bass have gone nocturnal, and that's not them disappearing — it's a heat response. Daytime bay temps have been sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, and that pushes the bass off the flats and into deeper structure until the sun goes down. Marine Parkway Bridge is still the number-one spot, but you need to fish it after dark now to get consistent results. I've had my best luck working the outgoing tide, casting bucktails and swimming plugs tight to the pilings and current breaks under the bridge lights, letting the sweep carry the lure through the seam. The bite window tends to open an hour or two after sunset and hold through the strongest push of the outgoing water. Daytime trips around the bridge have been mostly quiet — don't waste your morning there right now.

We flagged this last week — said the weakfish bite would start rebuilding on calm, warm evenings as the bay settled into summer — and that's exactly what's starting to happen. I had two solid weakfish in the four-pound class off Ruffle Bar on a still evening, working a chartreuse soft plastic on a light jighead just as the light was fading and the water went glassy. It's not a full-blown bite yet, more like the first real signs of one, but if you can get out on a calm evening around the marsh edges — Ruffle Bar, the flats off Grassy Bay, the deeper holes near the Raunt — that's where I'd put my money over the next couple weeks.

Bluefish have been the story everywhere south and west of us — bunker schools stacking up along the Jersey beaches and pushing north, and it's worth keeping an eye on Rockaway Beach because that pattern has a habit of sliding up the coast as the bait moves with it. Nothing's blown up on the Rockaway sand yet, but if the bunker show, the blues won't be far behind, and that's a fast, violent bite when it turns on — bucktails, poppers, whatever you've got, just be ready to move fast.

Porgies are still worth a stop if you're fishing the rocks around Rockaway Inlet — small hooks, bloodworms or clam, and you can put together a nice mess of them on the bottom stages of the tide.

With the moon heading toward first quarter on the 21st, the current's easing up a bit, which usually means slower, more deliberate presentations pay off better than a fast retrieve — that's especially true for the fluke and the weakfish. Looking ahead, if the calm, stable weather holds, I'd expect the weakfish pattern to keep building on quiet evenings, the bass to stay locked into their after-dark rhythm around the bridge until the nights cool off some, and fluke to remain the most consistent daytime bet in the deeper channels. If the bunker push north and Rockaway Beach lights up with bluefish, I'll be out there — but for now, my time's split between a dawn paddle for fluke and a dusk cast for weakfish, and that's not a bad way to spend a July week on this bay.

reports.headline: Deep in the Gut: bass buried in the rip, eels doing the damage
reports.subhead: Cooler water and a hard three-way rig are putting quality bass, a 28-inch sea bass, and keeper fluke on the same stretch of bottom at Plum Gut.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday night, max ebb, Plum Gut. I dropped a 12-inch eel off a three-way rig into the seam where the current stacks against the eastern edge of the rip, let it swing down and back like it's supposed to, and felt the rod load up like someone hooked a mooring ball. Forty seconds of pure deadlift and a 38-inch bass came up thrashing right at the transom. That's the fish that tells you everything about how this zone is fishing right now — deep, hard, and on gear built to survive current that doesn't care about your drag setting.

The pattern at the Gut and out at The Race hasn't changed much in two weeks, it's just gotten more precise. Bass are holding low, tight to the rock piles and current breaks, feeding almost exclusively when the water's ripping hardest — peak ebb and peak flood, the windows where the eddies behind Plum Island and the western edge of the Gut stack bait against structure. Shad-body swimbaits in the 6- to 9-inch range, white or bunker pattern, fished on jig heads heavy enough to hold bottom in five knots of current, have been money during those windows. When the current's screaming, I go to the three-way with a bucktail dropper and a big eel trailing behind — that combo has out-produced everything else I've thrown this month, and it's the same read that's been paying off for the shore guys working the rocks at 3 a.m.

New London's reading 67.6 degrees, which is a full four degrees cooler than what Kings Point's showing out west. That gradient matters more than people give it credit for. Western Sound bass have gone nocturnal — the water's warm enough that they're avoiding daylight stress and feeding almost exclusively after dark. Out here, with the water still in the mid-60s, we're not locked into that pattern yet. I've had fish hit at last light and again right at first light, not just in the dead of night. If you're planning a trip, that gives you two windows instead of one — work it.

The surprise this week was a 28-inch black sea bass that came off the same rip structure at Plum Gut, on a bucktail meant for bass. That's not a fluke — sea bass have moved onto that hard bottom in real numbers, stacking on the same rock piles and current breaks that hold the stripers. If you're fishing bucktails or diamond jigs down deep in the Gut right now, don't be shocked when something with a spiny dorsal fin nearly pulls your arm off. Keep a few Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged light for exactly that scenario.

Fluke fishing has been the most dependable thing out here, full stop. The Race, the flats off Orient Point, the drift lanes along Fishers Island — keeper fluke are showing consistently in 20 to 40 feet on the last two hours of the outgoing, with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails doing the damage on the drift. It's not a blitz, it's a grind — cover water, stay on bottom, work the seams where the current speeds up over the humps. But it's producing fish in the box every trip, which is more than I can say for some of the flashier bites right now.

Weakfish are worth a mention because they're some life on the calm, warm evenings — small numbers, but legal fish coming out of the same rip zones at dusk on bucktails and soft plastics fished slow near bottom. We flagged that rebuild coming on quiet evenings, and it's tracking. Not a target species yet, more of a bonus if you're already working the structure for bass.

Bluefish are the wildcard. The blitz action everyone's talking about — bunker schools getting hammered daily — is still concentrated west, from the Jersey beaches up through the western Sound. It hasn't pushed into Orient or Fishers Island Sound yet, but bunker schools have a way of migrating east through July, and if that bait shows up here, the blues will be right behind it. Keep an eye on the surface around Orient Point and the eastern flats — first sign of nervous water or diving birds, that's your cue.

Current's easing as we run toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which means softer tide stages through the weekend. That's going to change the presentation game — less need to muscle a heavy jig through five knots, more room to work a slower swimbait retrieve and actually work an eddy instead of just surviving it. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the Gut on the last half of Thursday's ebb, right as the moon phase starts softening the push. Have eels rigged heavy for the hard stages and a lighter swimbait rod ready for when it lays down. Bring a jig for the sea bass too — that bite's real, and it's a lot of fun on light tackle when the bass go quiet between current stages.

reports.headline: Peanut Bunker Push Into the Middle Ground — Bass Slide Into the Dark
reports.subhead: Bait's stacked thick from Norwalk to Port Jeff, but the bass have gone nocturnal on you — here's how to find them anyway.
reports.body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning idling off Middle Ground Light with the sounder up and my eyes on the surface more than the screen, and here's what I found: peanut bunker balled up tight in maybe fifteen feet of water, nervous, flickering, with terns working them from above but no visible boils underneath. That's the tell. When the bait's getting pushed but nothing's exploding on it in daylight, the bass are down there working it after dark instead. Kings Point is reading 71.6 degrees this week — that's warm enough to push stripers into a thermal retreat, not gone, just smarter about when they eat.

This is the pattern across the whole Central Sound right now. Bunker schools — some peanut-sized, some already three to four inches and hardening up — are stacked from the Norwalk Islands down through Stratford Shoal and across to the Connecticut side off Charles Island. Where you find those schools tight to the bottom on the sounder during the day, you're looking at a night program. Anchor up on the drop-off edges around Stratford Shoal in eighteen to twenty-five feet as the sun goes down, soak a live bunker or a chunk on a fish-finder rig, and give it an hour either side of the tide change. I heard from two guys working the graveyard shift off Middle Ground last week who put overslot fish in the boat between eleven and one in the morning — nothing epic, two or three fish a trip, but real bass, upper 30s to low 40 inches, on fresh bunker chunks fished tight to bottom.

Daytime, the story shifts. If you want bass with the sun up, you need moving current and structure that breaks it — the last two hours of the ebb around the Norwalk Islands or the rips off Charles Island are still producing, but you're fishing the seam, not the flat. Bucktails in the three-quarter to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along the current break, have been the better call than anything trolled through open water. This lines up with what I've been seeing for weeks now — the fish that do feed in daylight are doing it where the tide concentrates bait against structure, not out in the middle of the Sound where the water's just soaking up sun.

Fluke fishing is the one thing I can point to and say is dependable right now, no asterisks. Stratford Shoal and the rip lines off Middle Ground continue to hold keeper-class fish in eighteen to thirty feet, and they're not picky — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails, tipped with a squid strip, dragged slow on the drift, are doing the damage. I had a report of a six-pound fluke off the Shoal on the last of an incoming tide, which tells you these fish are still using that current to set up ambushes on the same bait pods the bass are shadowing at night. Porgies are riding shotgun on the same structure — anchor up on any rocky patch inside the Norwalk Islands with sandworms or clam and you'll fill a bucket without much drama, though nothing trophy-sized to report.

Bluefish are the wildcard piece right now. They're not blitzing the surface like the beachfront stuff further south, but they're absolutely underneath these same bunker schools, and when you find a school getting nervous with no birds working it, drop a diamond jig or a bucktail through it and you'll usually connect. I had blues to six pounds come through off Port Jefferson harbor mouth chasing peanut bunker right at the mouth of the channel — fun fish on light tackle, and they'll keep showing wherever that bait holds.

Weakfish have been quieter than I'd like to report, but a few calm, warm evenings lately have started to rebuild some activity around the deeper holes off the Connecticut shore — nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around yet, but worth a few casts with a soft plastic on the dropoffs if you're already out there after dark for bass.

We flagged bonito working into the Western Sound last week, and while nothing's crossed my transom yet here in the Central stretch, the bait conditions are exactly what you'd want if that push is coming — tight bunker schools, warm surface water, clean edges around Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk Islands where bonito like to slash through. I'll be watching close over the next week, particularly on calm mornings when the water's glassy enough to spot fins.

The moon's building toward first quarter on the 21st, which means tides are easing, not surging — good news for the slower bucktail presentations working the rips, tougher for anybody hoping for a hard-current blitz. If I had one trip this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb off Charles Island for daylight bass on bucktails, then come back after dark and anchor a chunk off Stratford Shoal for the bigger nocturnal fish. Bring both game plans — this water's not making it easy on you right now, but the bait's here, and where the bait goes, eventually the fish follow.

reports.headline: Execution Rocks goes dark by day — bass feeding is a nighttime job now
reports.subhead: Warm water from the Throgs Neck to Matinecock has pushed the stripers nocturnal, but fluke and porgies are covering for them in daylight.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop this week asked me straight out — "Frank, what happened to Exec Rocks? I fished the ebb Tuesday morning, marked bait all over the sounder, and couldn't buy a bass." I told him what I've been telling everybody who'll listen the last ten days: the fish didn't leave, they just clocked out for the day shift.

Kings Point is reading 71.6 degrees right now, and that's warm enough to push stripers into a thermal-avoidance pattern — they're not gone, they're just smart. During daylight they're tucked deep on structure, breathing easier in whatever cooler water they can find, and they don't turn on the feed bag hard until the sun drops and the current gets moving again. I've seen this pattern plenty of Julys going back to the '90s. When the western basin runs a few degrees warmer than the middle Sound — and right now it is, with New London still down around 67.6 — the bass here get nocturnal and structure-locked. Execution Rocks, the rockpile off Matinecock Point, the drop at Stepping Stones — they're all still holding bass. You just need to be fishing them after dark or right at first light, not at 10 a.m. with the sun beating down.

I worked Execution Rocks last Thursday night on the last two hours of the outgoing, anchored up-current of the light and drifting live bunker back on a fish-finder rig, 3 ounces of lead, into the wash. Two fish over 30 inches in about ninety minutes, both came right as the tide bottomed out and the current eased to a crawl. That slower water at the bottom of the tide is when these fish commit — they're not fighting hard current, they're just sliding out of the rocks to grab what's drifting past. If you've got the stomach for a midnight run, that's still the highest-percentage bass play in the western Sound right now.

Daytime, though, is a different game — and a good one. Fluke have been steady on the reefs and humps off Matinecock and out toward Hart Island, holding in 25 to 40 feet on the last of the incoming and first two hours of the outgoing. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom with a slight bounce, have been outproducing bulkier rigs — the water's clear enough right now that these fish want a subtle presentation, not a big splashy teaser strip. Nothing gigantic, but a mixed bag of keepers to 22 inches with enough shorts mixed in to keep the rod bending.

Porgies are around the same structure — Hart Island rockpiles, the reef stretch off Matinecock — but I'll be honest with you, the grade is on the small side this year. Plenty of action, sandworms and clam on a high-low rig will keep you busy, but you're not filling a cooler with dinner-plate porgies like you would out east. We flagged that a week back and it's holding true — fun for a kid's rod, not a fish fry.

Bluefish have been the most reliable action of the week and honestly the most fun. They're not deep, they're not subtle, and they don't care what time it is — I've had them busting bait off the Throgs Neck at noon and again at dusk off Stepping Stones. Peanut bunker have been thick along the bridge riprap, and when the blues find them it's a five-minute free-for-all. Metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, anything silver you can chuck fast — will get bit the second it hits the water. Bring wire leader or you'll lose half your tackle box to the first pass.

Weakfish have shown up sporadically in Manhasset Bay and up into Little Neck Bay on the early morning outgoing, mostly smaller fish mixed in with the fluke crowd, nothing to build a trip around yet but worth a few casts of a bucktail-and-bait combo if you're already out there.

Looking ahead: we're running into the first quarter moon on the 21st, which means the tidal swings are easing up through the weekend. That's actually good news for the rip fishing — Stepping Stones and the Exec Rocks current line fish better on that softer water because these bass, still working around the thermal squeeze, don't want to burn energy fighting a hard rip. Slow it down, fish the last hour of any tide change, and give the fish time to commit. I'd also keep an ear out for the first bonito scouts pushing into the Sound over the next week or two — that's usually a late-July story out here, and with warm water already stacked up from the city end to Matinecock, conditions are lining up right for it. Nothing confirmed on my end yet, but it's exactly the kind of summer that produces an early one. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd take the night bite at Execution Rocks on the bottom of the outgoing, live bunker if you can net them, and I'd have a fluke rod rigged and ready for when the sun comes up.

reports.headline: SW Ledge slack at 6:50: keeper bass on the drop, fluke stacked on the flood
reports.subhead: No bonito yet off the Block, but the structure bite at SW Ledge is paying rent for anyone who fishes the tide right.
reports.body_markdown:
6:50 a.m. is the number I've been working off SW Ledge all week — that's when the morning slack sets up on the bigger tides, and it's a ten-minute window on either side where the current goes soft enough to hold bottom without ripping your jig sideways. Miss it by twenty minutes and you're fighting three knots of green water for nothing. Hit it right and you're marking fish stacked on the drop from 55 to 80 feet, right where the ledge falls off the hard sand into that rubble bottom south of the tower.

This isn't the October class of bass yet — I'm not going to sell anyone on giants this week. What's down there right now is a healthy population of 26 to 34-inch fish holding tight to structure, feeding hard on the last twenty minutes of the ebb and picking back up as the flood starts to build. I've had the best luck dropping 4-ounce diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid straight down on the upcurrent side of the ledge, letting it fall to the bottom, and working it up in long sweeps rather than the short jigging stroke you'd use in the fall. These fish are eating slow right now — the water's warm enough that they're not chasing hard, they're ambushing. A bucktail in white or chartreuse, 2 to 3 ounces depending on the drift speed, dragged just off bottom on the last of the ebb has worked just as well as the jig, and it's a lot less arm work for a morning charter.

Fluke have been the more consistent story the last ten days. The south side of Block, working the drift from the Coast Guard Channel out toward the deeper water off Old Harbor, has been giving up decent numbers of keepers in 30 to 45 feet on the incoming tide. Gulp swimming mullets in pink shad or white, threaded on a 3/4-ounce bucktail with a squid strip trailer, dragged slow along the sand-to-mud transitions — that's been the winning combination. Nothing giant, mostly 17 to 20 inches with the occasional 4 or 5-pounder mixed in, but enough action to keep rods bent through a tide change, which is more than I can say for some weeks out here.

Sea bass are doing what sea bass do in July — sitting tight on every piece of structure around the Ledge and out toward the humps southwest of the island, and they'll eat just about anything you drop if you're patient enough to find the right depth. Clam on a bucktail teaser rig, bounced right on bottom in 50 to 70 feet, has been steady. Not a bonanza, but a reliable fill-the-cooler bite if the bass and fluke go quiet on you.

Now, the question I'm getting at the dock every single day this week: where are the bonito? Short answer — not here yet, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Water off the Block has been running in that 68 to 71-degree range, which is right on the edge of what gets bonito interested, but I haven't had a confirmed sighting or a hookup to report. What I have seen is bait starting to show heavier around Sandy Point and North Light — peanut bunker pushing through on the last of the ebb, and some silversides working the beach at Clay Head in the evenings. That's the setup. Bonito follow that bait, and historically for this stretch of coast, late July into early August is when the first scouts show off the Block, usually right around Sandy Point where the current sweeps bait around the north end. I'd keep a bag of Deadly Dicks or small metal in the boat starting this week, because when they show, they show fast and they don't stick around long enough for you to run home and get gear.

Bluefish have been filling in the gaps nicely, and I mean that as a compliment this time of year — chopper blues in the 4 to 8-pound class are hammering bunker chunks fished on the bottom around the Ledge on the tide change, and they've saved more than one slow morning when the bass wanted nothing to do with anything moving. If you're marking bait on the sounder and getting refusals from stripers, there's a good chance blues are sitting under that same bait and will eat what the bass won't.

Looking at the week ahead, I'd keep working that 6:50 slack window at SW Ledge as long as the tide charts hold that timing, and I'd start checking Sandy Point in the evenings for surface activity — birds working, bait nervous, anything that looks like the first bonito showing. If the water pushes past 72 off the north end like it's been trending, I wouldn't be surprised to get a confirmed report by the first days of August. Until then, the honest move is fluke on the drift and bass on the structure — steady work, not spectacular, but the kind of fishing that fills a cooler if you respect the tide.

zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

reports.headline: Rough Monday, Green Gold by Thursday: Poor Man's Yellowfin Bail Out the Week
reports.subhead: A short-period blow shut us down early, but squid-soaked water off Poor Man's and steady bluefin at Norfolk turned a slow start into a real week.
reports.body_markdown:
Call it a split-decision week. Monday and Tuesday we sat at the dock watching 3 to 4 foot slop stack up on a nasty four-second period — that's wind swell, not groundswell, and it makes for a miserable ride out past the Baltimore Channel. By Wednesday afternoon it laid down enough to run, and from Thursday through the weekend Poor Man's Canyon flat-out bailed us out. If I'm grading the week, I'd call it a C-plus that finished like a B.

Here's the thing about running four canyons out of Cape May and Ocean City — you can't fall in love with one piece of water. I had three boats calling me Wednesday night asking where to point the bow, and I sent all three different directions based on what I was hearing from guys already out there. That's the whole game this time of year.

Poor Man's was the story. We worked the edge east of the tails, around 38°37'N/73°58'W, dropping down the 100-fathom curve where the water turned that milky jade-green that tells you the squid are thick underneath you. Illex and shortfin squid have been balled up out there for two weeks now, and the yellowfin are sitting right on top of them. Sizes ran the gamut — plenty of 40-to-70-pound class fish mixed with a few genuine bigeye pushing past 100 that came on the troll around daybreak. Standard spread of ballyhoo behind Green Machines and small Ilanders on the short riggers, but the real difference-maker was dropping a naked ballyhoo flat-lined off the shotgun in that green water — that's where the bigger fish were sitting. At night, guys anchored up and lit the water with underwater squid lights picked off a handful of bigeye on butterfly jigs worked slow through 200 to 300 feet. Not every boat that tried it connected, but the ones that did had a real shot at a fish over the century mark.

Norfolk, out of Ocean City, was the quiet steady producer all week — less flashy than Poor Man's but more consistent. Bluefin have been sitting on the humps in 20 to 25 fathoms working up toward the canyon edge itself, chewing on sand eels and rainbait pushed up by the same warm surface water we're seeing inshore — NY Bight buoy read 71.6°F this week, and that's roughly the flavor of water riding out over the shelf right now. We trolled small cedar plugs and green machines on the meat rig around the humps early, then shifted to jigging vertically once the sun got up and the fish went down — 200-gram speed jigs worked with a slow pump-and-wind put schoolie-class bluefin from 20 to 40 pounds in the box on three separate trips this week. Wahoo showed up as a bonus for one boat running a straight high-speed spread — 12 to 14 knots with cedar plugs and small Ilanders down the drop-off — but that was one fish, not a pattern yet. I wouldn't build a trip around wahoo at Norfolk this week, but I'd rig for the possibility.

Spencer Canyon gave us white marlin, but scattered — not the kind of week where you mark six or eight in a day. Two boats out of Cape May had multiple bites working the 50 to 60 fathom edge west of the canyon head, teasing fish up on a dredge and switching them over to naked ballyhoo on circle hooks. One boat went 3-for-5, another went 1-for-4, and a couple came home having seen fish but never converted. That's marlin fishing — you put your teasers in front of enough fish and some of them commit. Mahi showed as incidental catches around any floating structure or weed line we crossed on the way out — nothing giant, mostly schoolie-sized fish in the 5 to 12 pound range, though one boat did pull a 38-pound bull off a lobster pot buoy on a small green-and-yellow popper. Worth keeping a spinning rod rigged and ready on the run out, because you never know when you'll cross a good line.

Lindenkohl I'm giving a pass on this week. The water up there hasn't been holding the same bait concentration as Poor Man's — less squid sign, cleaner blue water instead of that jade-green tuna color — and the one report I got back was a long day for one modest yellowfin. I'd rather send a boat south to Poor Man's or Norfolk right now than gamble on Lindenkohl waking up.

Looking ahead, the forecast has southwest winds building into a heat dome pattern by midweek, which usually means calmer seas but also means watching afternoon thunderstorm cells pop off the beach — standard July stuff. If that squid stays balled up on Poor Man's, I'd keep pointing boats there first; that's historically been one of the better stretches of the season for yellowfin numbers, and the second week of July has a track record of turning it on in these canyons. Norfolk should stay steady for bluefin as long as the humps keep holding bait. My plan for next week is simple — Poor Man's at first light for yellowfin, with Norfolk as the backup if the green water moves or thins out. I'd have a naked ballyhoo rigged and ready either way.

reports.headline: Captree Dock Talk: Bridge Fluke Holding Steady While Bass Hug the Inlet Seam
reports.subhead: A sloppy ocean pushed the fleet inside this week, and the fish that matter most right now were waiting there anyway.
reports.body_markdown:
Ran into Vinny at the fuel dock Tuesday morning, just off a half-day charter, shaking his head about the ocean. "Three-footers on a four-second period," he said, like that explains everything — and honestly, it does. That's a mean, stacked-up chop, not a rolling swell you can fish through comfortably, and it's had the open-water guys running back through the inlet by ten a.m. all week. I told him what I've been telling everybody who'll listen: quit fighting the Atlantic and go find where the fish already are. They're inside. They've been inside.

The water temp out at the buoy off the Bight is sitting around 71.6, which sounds warm and it is, but that short, choppy 3-to-4 foot slop with a southwest-leaning swell direction has made the surf and near-shore ocean grounds miserable to fish with any precision. Meanwhile the bay and the inlet channels are calm, structured, and full of bait. That's the story this week — not one big bite everywhere, but a handful of very specific, very productive windows if you know where to put the boat.

Fluke first, because that's been the most consistent thing going. The Robert Moses bridges — both the Fire Island span and the Captree side — are still holding fish in that 25 to 35 foot band along the pilings and the current breaks off the pilons. I've been drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, working the last two hours of the outgoing when the current really combs bait past the structure. Doubles have come over the rail more than once when the drift lines up right — nothing giant, mostly 17 to 20 inches with a few pushing 4 pounds mixed in, but steady enough that a morning trip is worth your gas. If the current's slack or barely moving, don't bother — these fish want that pressure pushing bait to them, and dead water at the bridges is dead fishing.

Striped bass have settled into a real pattern at the inlet seam, right where the outgoing dumps out past Democrat Point and the current rips against the deeper channel edge. Bunker schools have been pushing through there on the last two hours of the ebb, and the bass are sitting underneath and behind them, picking off stragglers. I've had my best luck snagging a bunker and dropping it right into the seam, letting it sink on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that current — no need for anything fancy. Bucktail guys working the same water with 2-ounce white or bone bucktails, bounced slow along the bottom edge where the sand drops into the channel, have connected too, though the bunker-drop has been the more consistent producer. Sizes have been mixed — a lot of mid-20s to low-30s, with the occasional bigger fish mixed into the bunker pods right at first light or the last hour before dark. This isn't an all-day bite. It's tide-and-light dependent, and if you miss that window, you're just burning fuel.

Bluefish have been riding shotgun with those bunker schools at the inlet mouth, and they've actually been the more reliable action some mornings — chopper blues in the 3 to 6 pound range busting bait right on the surface off Democrat Point, visible from a hundred yards out by the birds working overhead. Simple diamond jigs or a topwater popper thrown right into the commotion has been all it takes. If you want fast, aggressive action without overthinking the tide, that's your play right now.

I'll be straight with you on weakfish — it's been quiet. A few guys working the deeper holes off Nicoll Bay after dark with soft-plastic grubs on light jig heads have picked at a fish or two, but it's nothing like the numbers we used to see this time of year in the bay, and I'm not going to sell you on a bite that isn't really there. If weakfish are your target, treat it as a bonus fish while you're doing something else, not a dedicated trip.

Porgies have been the honest, blue-collar bite this week, and I mean that as a compliment. Anchoring up on the rockpiles inside Fire Island Inlet and around Democrat Point with sandworms or clam on a simple hi-lo rig has produced steady, respectable numbers — not trophy fish, but a cooler full of dinner porgies for not much effort, which is worth something when the bigger stuff is being finicky about tide and light.

Looking ahead, the ocean forecast doesn't show that chop settling down dramatically through the weekend, so I'd keep planning around the inside game rather than fighting the surf. If the wind does back off and that swell period stretches out, Democrat Point and the ocean beaches west toward Cedar Beach could turn on for bass working bait pushed tight to the sand — that's the scenario I'd watch for. Until then, I'd fish the last two hours of the outgoing at the inlet seam for bass and bunker, hit the bridges on that same dropping water for fluke, and keep a rod rigged with a diamond jig for whatever blues show up chopping on the surface. It's not a blowout week, but it's an honest one, and there's enough happening inside that a well-timed trip should put fish in the box.

reports.headline: Canarsie Pier at Dawn: Fluke to Five Pounds While the Ocean Stays Angry
reports.subhead: With the surf blown out at Breezy and Rockaway, the smart money moved into the bay's channels — and got rewarded.
reports.body_markdown:
