I'd focus effort on Falkner Island and the Charles Island reef on the bigger tides, working the first two hours of the flood or the last two of the ebb. For stripers, I'd stick with early mornings on the sandbar and not expect volume — treat it as a quality-over-quantity game right now. If the wind stays out of the south and lays down like it has been, Falkner and the outer New Haven breakwall should keep producing steady porgy and sea bass action into next week. That's where I'll be.

reports.headline: July 13, and Washington's Already Fishing Like Mid-August
reports.subhead: The eastern wall lit up early again this year, and if you know why Washington runs ahead of the pack, you already know where to point the bow.
reports.body_markdown:
Thirteen days into July and Washington Canyon is fishing like it's the second week of August. That's not hype, that's just the calendar catching up to what the water already told us back in mid-June. I've run this canyon long enough to know the pattern: Washington sits far enough south and far enough west that the Gulf Stream's warm filaments find the eastern wall before they ever reach Wilmington or Baltimore to the north. Every year, without fail, we're pulling yellowfin out of this canyon two to three weeks before boats running out of Cape May or Manasquan start talking about it. This year's no different, maybe a hair earlier.

What's happening right now is a warm push riding up onto the eastern wall, roughly the 38°18' to 38°22' line, 73°00' to 73°08', where the shelf breaks from the 100-fathom curve down into the canyon proper. That's the color change we've been working — clean blue water butting up against the greener inshore stuff, and that seam has been holding bait and holding fish. Boats working the temp break with the spread down have been picking off yellowfin in the 40 to 65-pound class, mixed in with a scattering of smaller schoolies that come through in wolf packs on the troll. Small Green Machines, naked ballyhoo behind a chin-weighted Sea Witch, and a couple of Ilanders in dark colors have been the difference-makers. Nothing fancy — just get the spread tight to the seam and let the current do the rest.

The deep-drop bite at night has been the more consistent producer if I'm being honest with you. Bigeye have been sitting on the wall in 350 to 450 fathoms, and the guys willing to put in the dark hours with squid strips and glow sticks on the deep-drop rigs are getting rewarded. It's not a numbers game — one or two quality bites a night, fish in the 100 to 180-pound range — but for mid-July that's ahead of where we usually are. I had a report from a boat working the western edge of the canyon head last week that put two bigeye in the box before 3 a.m. and never had another sniff after sunrise. That's the nature of that fishery right now — short windows, quality fish, and you need to be exactly where the current is stacking bait against the wall.

White marlin have shown up on the pinnacle just inshore of the canyon proper, working that 40 to 50-fathom structure where the bottom breaks up sharp. Dink ballyhoo behind small skirts, a dredge down the middle, and light drags — that's the recipe. It's not a red-hot bite, I want to be straight with you, more of a two-to-four fish morning if you find the right piece of structure and the current is moving right. But for this early in the season, marlin showing on the pinnacle already tells me the biomass pushing up the shelf is ahead of a normal year.

Mahi have been scattered rather than stacked — a few here, a few there, mostly holding under floating debris and weed lines on the run out past the 60-fathom line. Nothing like the August pattern where you find a real mat of sargassum and load the box. Right now it's more a matter of running lines and eyes open, pitching small chuggers or a bit of ballyhoo when you spot color or debris. Decent fish, 8 to 15 pounds, but you're working for every one of them.

Wahoo have made an early appearance too, which fits the theme of this whole season. High-speed trolling along the eastern wall at first light, planers running Braid Marauders and small Ilanders at 12 to 14 knots, has produced a few scattered fish in the 40 to 60-pound range. It's not the August wahoo pattern where you can count on multiple fish a trip — this is more opportunistic, a bonus if you're already working the wall for tuna at dawn. But again, seeing wahoo this early tells me the water column out there is set up warm and stable, not just a surface skim of Gulf Stream water that'll blow out with the next cold front.

Honest read on the week: this isn't a slam-dunk bite. You need to find the seam, work the color change, and be willing to put in the overnight hours for the bigeye. The guys running blind troll patterns without checking the temp break have had quiet days. The guys who worked the eastern wall where the warm filament is pinching against the canyon edge have had good ones. That's Washington in July — it rewards the boats that read the water instead of just running numbers on a chartplotter.

Looking ahead, if this warm filament holds its position on the eastern wall through the weekend — and there's no strong reason yet to think it's sliding — I'd keep working that 38°18' to 73°05' box for the yellowfin and push the deep drop rigs out toward the 400-fathom curve after dark for bigeye. If the eddy slides east like it sometimes does after a blow, I'd shift attention to the pinnacle for marlin and work the shallower structure instead of chasing open water. Either way, Washington's running ahead of pace again this year, and I don't expect that gap to close anytime soon.

reports.headline: Squid Balling Up in the Rips — Woods Hole and Quick's Hole Are Loading the Table
reports.subhead: Bass and blues are eating well on the moving water while the bait build tells you what's coming behind it.
reports.body_markdown:
I stood on the seawall at Woods Hole Monday evening watching squid stack up thick enough to turn the water gray under the dock lights, and that's the tell I wait for every July. Not albies yet — don't let anybody tell you different, it's too early, and anybody claiming false albacore in mid-July on this water is either lying or fishing somewhere else. But squid balling up like that in the current seams off the Steamship dock, sand eels flickering through Quick's Hole on the last of the ebb, mackerel schools ghosting through Robinson's Hole at first light — that's the bait signature that eventually turns into the run. Right now it's feeding stripers and blues, and that's plenty to keep me busy.

The better bass action this week has been on the outgoing tide at Robinson's Hole and Quick's Hole, working the current seams where the Elizabeth Islands squeeze the tide down into a fire hose. I've been running 1 to 1.5-ounce bucktails, white and chartreuse, bounced along bottom in 15 to 25 feet where the rip lays down current-side of the ledges. Fish are holding tight to structure — not chasing bait out into open water, making you come to them. Keeper-class stripers, 28 to 34 inches, with a few slot fish mixed in, came on that pattern Tuesday morning on the tail end of the ebb into the first hour of slack. Night tide has been better than day tide for the bigger fish — eels drifted through Quick's Hole after dark have out-produced the bucktail bite for size, though not for numbers. If you're set up to soak eels on a moving tide at Cuttyhunk's east end or the Robinson's Hole channel edge, that's where I'd put my night trip this week.

Bluefish have been the more reliable bite, and reliable is the word — not spectacular, but you can set your watch by it. Buzzards Bay side, off Wilbur's Point and running down toward the Cuttyhunk approach, blues have been blitzing on top most mornings before the wind builds. Choppers to 8 and 10 pounds are hammering topwater poppers and Ava 27 jigs worked fast through the froth. This bite window closes early — by mid-morning when the sun gets high and the surface goes glassy calm, the blues drop down and go quiet. Get out at first light or don't bother waiting around midday; I've wasted enough afternoons proving that to myself already this season.

Fluke fishing in Buzzards Bay has been a mixed bag, and I'll be straight about it — some drifts have been outstanding, others have been a grind for two or three keepers over three hours. The Quick's Hole channel and the sandy stretch off Cuttyhunk's north side have been the most consistent, drifting white and pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 20 to 35 feet on the incoming tide, when the current is pushing bait up out of the deeper holes onto the flats. Doormats haven't shown in numbers yet this year on my end of the water, but fish in the 18 to 22-inch range have been steady enough to make a dinner. If you're grinding it out and only picking at shorts, move — don't sit on dead water hoping it turns on. I've learned that lesson the hard way more times than I want to admit.

Scup fishing around the Woods Hole draw bridge and the rocky structure off Nonamesset has been the easy money this week — squid strips or sandworms on a simple sinker rig, and you can fill a cooler in an hour if you're patient about finding the right piece of structure on the drift. Good option for a slow-tide afternoon when the bass and blues have shut down and you still want to bend a rod.

As for what's coming — I keep one eye on Nantucket Sound and the Rhode Island side because that's where the squid concentrations are building fastest, and historically when that bait pushes hard into Vineyard Sound and the water settles into that comfortable summer warmth we associate with peak season, bonito start showing at Robinson's Hole before the albies ever do. That's usually a late-July into early-August event on my water, not a mid-July one, so I'm not chasing ghosts yet. What I am doing is fishing the rips hard on the moving tides, watching the bait every single trip, and keeping gear rigged for a quick switch — smaller profile Deadly Dicks and epoxy jigs staged and ready — because when that first bonito flash shows up in the froth off Menemsha, I want to be the first phone call at the dock, not the last one to hear about it. Until then, work the tide stages at Robinson's and Quick's Hole, fish the bluefish blitz early, and don't sleep on the scup if the bigger stuff goes quiet on you.

reports.headline: Mackerel Push 40-Inch Bass Onto Duxbury Rips While Deer Island Pays Off on the Ebb
reports.subhead: Big bass are riding mackerel schools south of the harbor while Boston's own structure keeps grinding out slot fish and flounder on the tide change.
reports.body_markdown:
I had a choice to make this week — run the harbor structure I know like the back of my hand, or chase word of mackerel schools pushing big bass onto the rips south toward Duxbury and Kingston Bay. I split the week, and I'm glad I did, because both ends of my water are doing different things right now and a smart angler needs to know which one to play on a given morning.

Start with the harbor, because that's home base. Deer Island Light on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most consistent thing I've fished all month. The current rips hard off that ledge as the flow pulls out of President Roads, and bass are stacking on the downcurrent side waiting for whatever gets swept off the flat. I've been bouncing 1.5 to 2-ounce bucktails tipped with a strip of squid along the bottom edge of that drop, letting the current do the work and just walking the rod tip to keep contact. Slot fish, mostly 28 to 34 inches, with the occasional better one mixed in when the tide really starts ripping in the last hour before dead low. Spectacle Island's north ledge is fishing the same way — soft plastics, 6-inch RonZ in bone or pearl, worked slow along that drop on the same stage of tide.

Flounder are still around on the Deer Island flats and up into the Winthrop side, but you have to anchor up and fish it properly — spreader rigs with squid strips or bloodworm, fished dead slow on the last of the incoming when the water's pushing warm, cloudy bait-carrying current up over the sand. It's not a fast fishery this time of year, but it's a real one if you're patient and willing to sit still for an hour.

Now the part that had me running south. Word came out of the Duxbury and Kingston Bay area that mackerel schools have moved in thick, and where mackerel go in July, the bigger bass follow. I heard of a fish pushing 49 inches taken off the South Shore on a mackerel-matched presentation, and that's not a fluke-sized outlier — that's a signal that the bigger year classes are keying on that bait right now. I ran down to fish the Scituate ledges and the mouth of Duxbury Bay on a live-lined mackerel under a balloon, drifting the edge where the bay current meets the open water on the last of the ebb. That's when the bait gets pushed out and the bigger fish set up to ambush it. It's not a numbers game down there — you might get one good bite in three hours — but when it comes it's a fish worth the drive.

Nahant and up toward Gloucester and Cape Ann, the rocky shore is holding fish the way it always does this time of year, but the bite has been more of a dawn-and-dusk program than an all-day affair. Warm surface water midday is pushing the bass down and out, and the better window has been the last two hours of light with topwater plugs and soft-plastic swimbaits worked tight to the rocks off Nahant's east side. Bluefish have shown up mixed in with the bass along that stretch, which tells me the bait's thick enough to hold two different predators on the same structure — a good sign for August.

Cod and haddock guys working the Cape Ann bottom have had a mixed bag of it — some solid drifts over the traditional humps outside Gloucester on diamond jigs and clam-baited hooks, other days slow when the current's been light and the fish scatter off the structure. That fishery is always going to be feast-or-famine in midsummer; I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it right now without a backup plan for stripers inshore.

Be honest with yourself about this stretch of July — it's not the wide-open blitz fishing of May, and it's not going to be until the fall run gets going. What you've got right now is structure fishing and bait-matching. Find where the mackerel are holding, find the tide stage that concentrates current on a ledge or a rip, and be there when it happens rather than fishing all day and hoping.

Looking ahead, if the mackerel schools stay put around Duxbury and Kingston Bay, that's where I'd spend my better mornings this coming week — live-lined mackerel on the last of the ebb, working the edge where the bay drains into open water. Inside the harbor, Deer Island and Spectacle Island will keep producing slot fish on bucktails through the tide changes regardless of what's happening outside. And up on the North Shore, I'd fish Nahant hard in that first hour of light before the boat traffic and the sun push everything off the rocks. Watch the bait — where the mackerel schools sit is going to tell you more this week than any chart I can hand you.

reports.headline: Race Point at dead slack: bass to 38 pounds on live mackerel, cod stubborn on Billingsgate
reports.subhead: The rip gave up a good hour of big fish this week, but you had to be sitting on it when the tide stopped moving.
reports.body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, six of us on the boat, and I had my hand on the wheel watching the current line off Race Point go from a hard push to nothing in about fifteen minutes. That's the window. I've fished that rip long enough to know the bass don't care about the tide running — they care about the moment it quits. We had three rods out, live mackerel on 5/0 circle hooks, no weight, just letting them swim naturally off the stern as we drifted the seam where the green water meets the darker water pushing off the Peaked Hill Bars. Right at slack, rod number two just about got yanked out of the holder. Forty-five minutes later we had a 38-pounder in the box and two more over thirty that we let swim. That's the kind of morning that keeps you coming back to that piece of water for three decades.

The mackerel showed up thick again this week, which tells you a lot about why the bass are stacking where they are. I've seen bait balls off Race Point holding tight to the rip since late June, and the big fish know exactly where that structure funnels the bait when the tide turns. If you're jigging mackerel for yourself — small diamond jigs, no bait needed, they'll hit bare metal — do it early, before the boats pile up on the spot. Once you've got a well full of mackerel, that's your ticket for the afternoon slack.

Peaked Hill Bars has been more of a bluefish show the last ten days. Choppers in the six to nine pound range, blitzing on the surface some mornings when the light's still low and the water's calm enough to see them working. Poppers and metal — Hammered Kastmasters, or a bucktail with a swimming plastic if the blues are being finicky — worked fast across the top gets bit. It's not subtle fishing. When they're up, you can see the whole thing happen, gulls diving, water exploding, and it doesn't last more than twenty minutes before they push off to deeper water. I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it, but if you're out there anyway working the bass rip, keep a popper rigged and ready.

Billingsgate has been tougher than I'd like to admit. Cod fishing in July on that structure is never a sure thing — the water up top warms and the fish that are left slide down into the deeper holes off the shoal, 60 to 80 feet, where it stays cooler. We've been jigging diamond jigs and skirted bucktails tipped with clam, working them slow off the bottom on the drift, and getting maybe two or three keeper cod a trip where in the spring we'd have had a dozen. That's just where we are in the season. If cod is your main target right now, I'd rather send you to the deeper structure north of Billingsgate toward the edge of the Bay than the shoal itself — the fish that are still around this time of year want the depth and the cooler water, not the shallower rubble.

Fluke fishing off Sandy Neck and out toward the flats by Barnstable and Brewster has actually been the steadiest thing going. Sandy bottom, six to fourteen feet on the drift, working white Gulp swimming mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, and we've had a good run of keepers in the eighteen to twenty-two inch range, with a few pushing four pounds mixed in. That bite likes the last two hours of the outgoing, when the water's pulling bait off the flats and funneling it into the deeper guts. Slow drag, don't work it too fast — fluke on that bottom want it crawling, not swimming.

Overall I'd call it a mixed week. The bass bite at Race Point and Peaked Hill was legitimately good when you hit the slack right, but it's a tight window, maybe forty minutes on either side of the tide change, and if you show up mid-tide with the current still ripping, you're better off jigging mackerel for bait than expecting a bass to eat. The cod fishing has thinned out the way it always does by mid-July, and anybody telling you Billingsgate is stacked right now isn't being straight with you. The fluke bite has been the most dependable thing on the calendar, day in and day out, which is usually how it goes once the water settles into summer pattern.

Looking ahead, the moon's working toward the next quarter, which should tighten up the tide swings a little and might actually help the Race Point slack bite — shorter, sharper tide changes sometimes concentrate the bait better than the big moon tides do. If the wind stays out of the southwest like it has been, the water off Provincetown should stay clean enough to sight the mackerel schools from the surface, which makes locating the bass a lot easier than blind-drifting. I'd plan around the morning and evening slacks at Race Point this coming week, keep a jig rod rigged for mackerel to restock the well, and treat the cod fishing as a bonus rather than the plan. If you've only got one trip in you, that's where I'd put it.

reports.headline: 168 feet on the meter: cod holding tight to the gravel, bluefin finally pinning bait on top
reports.subhead: Haddock are stacked on the mud in the Basin, and the first real tuna push of the summer showed up chasing mackerel over the northern edge.
reports.body_markdown:
168 feet on the meter, marks stacked right on the break where the gravel gives way to hard bottom on the northwest corner of the Bank — that's where I found my cod Tuesday morning, and that's where I've been finding them most mornings this month. This time of year the fish crowd the edges where the current sweeps clean gravel, not the flat mud in the middle. Clam and herring combos on a standard cod rig, 6 to 10 ounces depending on the drift, and you want the boat moving just enough to keep the baits ticking bottom without dragging into the rocks. We've had keeper cod to 14 pounds, mixed with a lot of shorts that go back over the rail. Nothing to write home about in terms of numbers, but steady enough that if you fish three or four drifts on that edge you'll put fish in the box.

Haddock have been the better story. Stellwagen Basin, 190 to 210 feet of water, soft mud bottom — that's classic haddock structure and they've been sitting on it thick. Clam bait on a simple bottom rig outfishes jigs down there right now; the haddock are feeding tight to bottom and don't seem interested in chasing anything that moves fast. Limits haven't been automatic but a lot of boats are coming in with eight, ten, twelve fish in the 2-to-4-pound range, a few pushing 6. The mud holds its structure better than the gravel edges when the tide runs hard, so on the bigger tide swings this week that's where I've been sending people. Watch your drift speed — over the mud you want to be almost stationary, and if the current's ripping you're better off waiting for the tide change than fighting it.

Now the tuna. This is the part of the report I've been waiting to write. Mackerel have piled onto the Bank in real numbers over the last ten days, and where you get that much bait balled up on top, the bluefin show up to work it. We've had fish breaking on the surface over the northern part of Stellwagen and out toward Tillies Bank, mostly in that 100-to-160-foot range, chasing mackerel schools that are thick enough to turn the water black on the sounder. Trolling green machines and small spreader bars in the 6-to-8 knot range has raised fish, but the better bite has come from live-lining mackerel right into the melee once you spot birds working and fish showing on top. These aren't giants yet — mostly fish in the 60-to-150-pound class from what I've seen boated and what other captains are reporting at the dock — but that class of fish eats aggressively and gives you a real fight on standup gear. A couple boats have connected on bigger fish north of Tillies, closer to 200, but that's not the bulk of what's around.

The pattern makes sense if you think about what's happening with the bait. Mackerel schools have been moving up onto the Bank chasing the same current edges and thermoclines that push everything else around out here, and the stripers working the South Shore beaches this past week were feeding on the same push of mackerel closer to the beach. When bait stacks up like this in mid-July, it's rarely one species benefiting — you get bass working the inshore edge of the school and tuna working the offshore edge, sometimes within a few miles of each other. That's exactly what's been happening.

Conditions have been workable but not flat calm — a light chop most mornings, laying down by midday, which has made the surface bite easier to spot once the wind eases. I haven't seen anything that looks like a hard thermal break setting up on the Bank yet this week, which tells me the tuna showing now are opportunistic fish riding the bait rather than a school that's locked in and staying put. That can change fast. If the mackerel hold their position over the next few days, I'd expect the tuna numbers to build rather than fade — this early in the season, more fish tend to filter onto the Bank once word gets out among the school that there's food up there, so to speak.

For the week ahead: I'd keep working the gravel edge on the northwest corner for cod first thing, before the tide picks up too much, then slide into the Basin for haddock on the last of the ebb when the mud settles down. If you've got a tuna rod rigged, don't leave it in the rack — glass the surface on the ride out and ride in, because the bite has been coming in short, violent windows when the mackerel get pushed up and the tuna crash through them. Best case, this bait stays put through the weekend and the tuna action builds into something more consistent. If the mackerel push off the Bank the way they sometimes do with a wind shift, I'd expect the tuna to follow them east toward Tillies, and that's where I'd go looking next.

reports.headline: East End on the 5:52 Ebb: Bass Hold the Rip, Blues Crash the Bait Balls
reports.subhead: New moon current is running harder than it has all summer, and the fish know exactly where to sit and wait for it.
reports.body_markdown:
5:52 a.m., east end, and the ebb's already stacking up against the Sandwich side jetty like it's got somewhere to be. New moon Tuesday means we're building toward the biggest tide swings we'll see all month, and the Canal doesn't do subtle when the moon pulls hard. I stood on the rocks this morning watching four-plus knots of green water peel off the rip and I'll tell you straight — that's the kind of current that separates the guys who show up and the guys who show up at the right minute.

Here's the read for anybody who hasn't fished the ditch in a few weeks. We're past the mackerel run — that show wrapped up in June — and we're into the mid-summer pattern now: bass holding deep on the structure, waiting for the current to sweep bait past them, and bluefish willing to chase anything that moves in the top six feet. The east end rip, right off the herring run outflow toward the Sandwich basin, has been the most consistent stretch. Fish the last two hours of the ebb — that's when the rip really organizes itself into a defined seam instead of just churned-up water — and you want a darter or a Guppy swimming plug worked slow across the seam, right where the moving water meets the slower back-eddy. I had two fish over 30 inches Thursday night doing exactly that, both right at the color change where the sandy bottom drops into the deeper cut.

Daylight hours belong to the bluefish right now, and they're not shy about it. Anybody working topwater off the Scusset side in the last hour of daylight ebb has been into choppers busting bait on the surface — poppers, Hab's Hoo's, anything loud, thrown right into the boils. Just bring wire or heavy fluoro leader because these fish are running eight to twelve pounds and they don't care about your $20 plug.

West end's a different story and it's been trickier. The current there doesn't set up the same defined rip — it's more current seam than boil — and that seam has been shifting depending on how hard the flood is running into Buzzards Bay. Mashnee Island and the cut toward Hog Island have both produced, but only on the last two hours of the flood when the water's really stacking against the rocks. White bucktails, 1 to 1.5 ounce, tipped with a strip of squid or a chunk of mackerel, dragged slow along bottom right where the seam pushes against structure — that's been the presentation. Nothing spectacular, but honest fish, mostly 28 to 34 inches, with a few bigger ones mixed in on the darker tides.

Fluke have been a mixed bag, and I'll be straight with you — the strong current on these new moon tides has been dragging grass and weed through the water column on the flood, which makes drifting bucktails a pain. Best window has been the last hour of the ebb into dead slack, when the water clears up and you can actually keep bottom contact without hauling in a salad every other drift. Try the sandy stretches off Phinneys Harbor and along the edge toward Wings Neck — 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce jigheads, worked with short hops right on bottom. Nothing huge, but a few keepers in the mix, and enough action to make it worth the trip if you time the slack right.

What I haven't seen yet — and I get asked about this every single day at the bait shop — is albies or bonito. Too early. That show doesn't usually open up until the back half of August, sometimes not until Labor Day week depending on how the water in the bay warms. I know guys are itchy for it, especially with the ocean side running warm this year, but there's nothing in the Canal or the Bay side approaches yet that tells me that pattern's close. Save your epoxy jigs for now.

Looking ahead: this new moon is going to keep pushing bigger tide swings through the weekend, which means faster current and a tighter bite window on both ends. If I had one shot this week, I'd take the east end on the last two hours of Sunday morning's ebb — should be running around 5:15 to 6:15 based on the tide progression — because that's when the rip's been most organized and the bass have been most willing to commit. West end guys, watch for the flood to really load up against Mashnee in the late afternoon; that's been the better bite than the morning flood, probably because the water's had all day to warm up over the flats before it pushes through. Bring patience either way. This isn't a week where the fish are just sitting there waiting — you've got to be on the right rock at the right minute, same as it's always been out here.

reports.headline: Beavertail Tog Chew Green Crabs While Sakonnet's Rips Run Thick with Blues
reports.subhead: The ledges are holding fish on the slack, the rips are loaded with bluefish, and the breachways are still waiting on their September guests.
reports.body_markdown:
The crabs are moving on the ledges right now, and that's the tell. Green crabs skittering in the cracks at Beavertail, peelers working the rockweed at Brenton Point — that's what's had the tog interested all week, even though most guys still think of tautog as an October fish. Mid-July tog isn't a numbers game down here, it's a precision game. You find the right crack on the right stage of tide, drop a half a green crab on 20-pound fluoro straight to a jig head, and you wait for that thump you can't confuse with anything else.

I've been working Beavertail on the last hour of the ebb into the first hour of slack, 18 to 25 feet, right off the point where the current stacks up against the granite. Two keeper tog Tuesday, one that went better than seven pounds, both on green crab fished tight to the rock, almost no scope on the line. The bite shuts off hard once the tide starts pushing again — that current runs too fast through there for anything but a sinker the size of a doorknob, and even then you're just plowing bottom. Brenton Reef's fishing similar, though it's a longer commute if you're on foot; better as a boat spot where you can hold position on the slack instead of fighting for a rock to stand on.

Sakonnet Point is where the week got interesting. The rips off the point have been stacked with bluefish — 3 to 6 pounds, blitzing on peanut bunker that's in numbers along that stretch of shoreline. Dawn and dusk both, but dawn's been more reliable, right as the tide starts to move out of the harbor and pushes bait through the rip lines off the rocks. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce, worked fast through the white water — have been drawing crushing strikes. Mixed into that blitz have been schoolie stripers up to 28 inches, with the occasional better fish holding just off the edge of the feed, picking off cripples instead of joining the chaos. If you want the bigger bass, hang back from the bluefish melee and work a bucktail — 1.5 ounce, white — along the seam where the current edge meets the slower water. That's classic bottom-bounce structure fishing, and it's produced a few bass in the low-30s off that stretch this week.

Second Beach has had its own version of the same story — bunker schools moving along the beach front, blues underneath them showing up in the wash on the outgoing, stripers mixed in but outnumbered. If you're surfcasting there, don't waste time on the sandbar itself; work the deeper cut where the beach breaks toward Sachuest Point. That's held fish consistently on falling light.

Down toward the breachways — Charlestown, Weekapaug — it's been a fluke week more than anything else. Water's clean, not gin clear but working fine, and the sand flats just inside the breachway mouths have given up decent numbers of fluke to 4 pounds on the last two hours of the incoming, when bait gets pushed up out of the channel onto the flats. White Gulp Swimming Mullet on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow, has been the go-to. Scup fishing has been steady but unspectacular around the breachway rocks and the Jamestown bridge pilings — squid strips and clam on light tackle, good for the cooler box and good for kids, nothing to write home about beyond that.

Watch Hill and Napatree are quieter right now than they'll be in six weeks. The reef off Watch Hill has scup and the occasional keeper tog for guys willing to anchor up and soak crab, but I haven't seen or heard of peanut bunker pushing hard into that breachway yet — no sign of albies, and it's too early to expect them. That first wave doesn't usually show at Napatree or the Weekapaug cut until deep in September, sometimes not until the bunker schools get squeezed by cooling water further up the coast. Anybody telling you albies are around this week in RI waters is either mistaken or fishing a different ocean. What I'd watch for instead, over the next month, is how thick those peanut schools get in the coves — that's the real leading indicator, and right now they're just starting to organize.

Looking ahead, the pattern holds if the wind stays out of the south-southwest and doesn't kick up too much groundswell on the ledges — tog fishing depends on being able to hold bottom on slack, and a two-foot swell on the rocks turns Beavertail into a bad idea fast. If conditions stay clean, I'd keep working the ledges on the tide change for tog, hit Sakonnet at first light for the blitz, and use the breachways for a reliable fluke box while we wait on the real fall run to build. Nothing wrong with a mixed bag week — that's July on this shore.

reports.headline: Jeffrey's in 195 feet: haddock stacked on the mud, cod picking at the gravel edge
reports.subhead: Mackerel are thick over the humps and the first bluefin marks of the year showed up on Tillies this week.
reports.body_markdown:
One-ninety-five feet of water, soft grey mud, five knots of drift over the bottom — that's where I put the boat Tuesday morning on the north end of Jeffrey's, and that's where the haddock have been living for about two weeks now. Mud holds haddock this time of year, plain and simple. They stack up over that flat, featureless bottom in loose schools that move with the tide, and once you find the edge where the mud breaks into that slightly harder transitional bottom, you can anchor up or drift through it three, four times and keep connecting.

The gravel is a different story right now. I fished the classic cod ground on the southwest corner in about 140 to 160 feet — the rocky humps where the bottom goes from mud to broken gravel and shell hash — and the cod are there, but they're not stacked the way the haddock are. A few fish in the 24 to 30 inch class came over the rail, mixed with a lot of shorts we had to shake off quick. With the recreational cod season as tight as it's been in the Gulf of Maine the last several years, most of what we're doing on the gravel now is photo-and-release work, maybe keeping one if the regs and the size line up for the day. I tell my anglers up front: come out for haddock, treat any cod as a bonus, because that's the honest state of that fishery right now.

Haddock is where the real numbers are. We've been running hi-lo rigs baited with fresh clam bellies, two hooks, six to eight ounces of lead depending on the drift, right down into that mud in the 180 to 220 foot range between Jeffrey's and the approach to Platts Bank. On the better drifts — and you need drift, dead slack kills this bite — we've had guys with their two-fish limit of quality haddock, 18 to 22 inches, inside of ninety minutes. Diamond jigs tipped with a clam strip work too if you want to cover water faster, but the bait rig has been more consistent when the current is light, which it has been around the last few tide changes.

Pollock have been mixed in over the same mud, especially up off bottom ten to twenty feet, suspended over the haddock schools. A fast retrieve on a diamond jig or a Norwegian jig will pick them off — some nice fish in the eight to fifteen pound range, good eating and good sport, and they don't count against the same limits as the groundfish so they're a welcome addition to the box.

Bait's been the story on the surface. Mackerel are thick over the humps on Jeffrey's and out toward Tillies — Sabiki rigs loaded in a couple of drops, more than enough for chum and live bait both. That mackerel show is exactly why I've started seeing bluefin sign earlier than I'd expect for mid-July. We had a pod of school-to-medium fish, forty to eighty pounds by the look of the boils, working bait on the surface out toward the Tillies side Thursday afternoon. Nothing stacked, nothing you'd call a giant show yet — that's an October pattern on this ledge, when the bigger fish push in tight to feed ahead of their fall run south. But seeing tuna at all this early, with the amount of mackerel and pogy bait around, tells me the biomass is building faster than usual this season. I'd keep half an eye up while you're jigging haddock — a rigged spinning outfit with a stickbait or a topwater popper in the rocket launcher isn't a bad idea right now if you've got the crew to work it.

Water's been clean out there, no dirty water pushing off the coast, and the thermal layer feels normal for mid-July — comfortable on top, that hard drop-off into cold water once you get down near bottom on the mud, which is exactly what holds the haddock tight to that layer. Wind's been the bigger variable than temperature. We've had a couple of days where a stiff southwest breeze made the drift too fast to fish the mud properly, and on those days we shifted over to the gravel edges where the structure breaks the current a bit.

Looking ahead, I'd keep targeting the mud in that 180 to 220 foot band for haddock — that pattern has been the most dependable thing out there for three weeks running, and there's no sign it's slowing. If the wind lays down over the weekend, I want to run out past Tillies and check for tuna sign again; the mackerel schools aren't going anywhere and that's usually the tell. Cod fishing I'd treat as a bonus, not a plan — fish the gravel if you want variety in the box, but build your trip around the haddock and you won't go home disappointed.

reports.headline: Halfway Rock's Slack Water Still Paying Off in Cod and Haddock
reports.subhead: Mid-July has the bass scattered but committed to structure, while the groundfish bite off the Rock stays steady on the turn.
reports.body_markdown:
I was out past Jewell Island Tuesday morning, engine idling, watching the current build against the eastern ledge, when a school of pollock came up under a raft of gulls working bait that wasn't quite mackerel and wasn't quite pogy — young herring, most likely, pushed tight to the rocks by something bigger underneath. That's been the story of this bay for two weeks now: bait scattered, structure holding the answers, and the fish making you work a chart before you work a rod.

The mackerel run that the bay through late May and into June has thinned out considerably. I'm not seeing the tight, glass-ball schools we had off Peaks Island a month back. What's left has pushed deeper and farther out — I marked scattered pods on the sounder in 40 to 60 feet off the backside of Long Island, but you're jigging for them now rather than watching them boil the surface. If you want mackerel for bait or the pan, fish small, weighted jigs — the size 6 or 8 diamond jigs with no bait needed — worked slow through that depth range on the last hour of the incoming. Don't expect the manic action of June. It's a patient man's game now.

Striped bass have been the more honest story, and I'll be straight with you: it's not been easy fishing, but it's been productive fishing for those willing to move around. The ledges off Peaks and Diamond Island have held fish on the last two hours of the incoming tide, when current stacks bait against the rock faces and the bass set up in the eddies behind them. I've done well with 3/4-ounce bucktails in white or chartreuse, cast up-current and swum back with the tide rather than against it — that's the mistake I see visiting boats make, fighting the current instead of using it. Slot fish in the 26 to 32-inch range have been the norm, with the occasional better fish pulled off the north side of Bailey Island on live pogies fished on a fish-finder rig in 15 to 20 feet of water, dead-slack into the first push of the ebb.

Cape Small has been quieter than I'd like for mid-July. The bass are there — I know men who've taken them off the ledges near the Sisters — but they're not concentrated, and the bite windows have been short, tied tightly to the top of the tide and the first thirty minutes of the drop. If you're fishing that stretch, don't linger past the turn. Move rather than wait them out.

Halfway Rock remains the most dependable piece of water in the bay right now, and it's where I've spent most of my own time this week. The groundfish bite there has been steady rather than spectacular — cod running 3 to 8 pounds, with a scattering of haddock mixed in on the deeper drops to the southwest of the Rock, 90 to 110 feet of water. The pattern hasn't changed in thirty years and it hasn't changed this week: fish the slack, both top and bottom of the tide, when the current eases enough to hold bottom without a pound of lead dragging you sideways. Clam bait on a simple two-hook bottom rig still outfishes the jigging crowd out there, though I've seen guys do well jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid on the up-stroke, worked slow off bottom in 15-foot lifts.

Bluefish have started showing in the outer bay, which is about on schedule for mid-July as the surface water warms. I had a report of choppers in the 3 to 5-pound class working bait off Two Lights over the weekend, and I wouldn't be surprised to see that push into the bay proper over the next ten days as water temps climb another degree or two in the shallows. Poppers and metal — anything that throws a wake — will draw strikes once they set up on a bait concentration. They're not subtle fish and they won't require subtle presentation.

Wind's been the usual July pattern: calm mornings, building southwest in the afternoon, which means if you're planning ledge work around Peaks or Diamond, get out early. That afternoon breeze pushes a chop into the eastern approaches that makes precise bucktail work difficult by early afternoon.

Looking ahead, I expect the bass pattern to hold roughly as is — scattered, structure-oriented, tide-dependent — through the coming week. If the bait pods I saw off Jewell consolidate rather than scatter further, I'd expect the bass to follow them tighter to the islands, which would make for better fishing than we've had. The groundfish at Halfway Rock should stay consistent regardless; that's deep, cold structure that doesn't care much what the surface is doing. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd take the last of the incoming at Diamond Island for bass, then run out to the Rock and sit the slack for cod. That's given me the best mixed bag of the summer so far, and I don't see a reason it stops working just yet.

reports.headline: Monhegan's white water: mackerel thick, bass scattered, pollock still holding deep off the ledges
reports.subhead: A mid-July mixed bag from Boothbay to Isle au Haut — mackerel everywhere, stripers making you work, and the groundfish still down where they belong.
reports.body_markdown:
Forty-some years ago my father told me something I still repeat to sternmen who complain the fish aren't where they were last week: "The water don't lie, but it don't hurry either." I was hauling traps off Damariscove at the time, maybe nineteen years old, convinced the cod had vanished off the face of the earth because we hadn't seen one in a month. Three weeks later we ran into a pile of them stacked on a hard bottom patch we'd run over a hundred times and never marked. Same water. Same boat. We just hadn't been patient enough to let the season tell us where to look. I think about that every July, because this time of year Midcoast Maine never gives it up easy — it makes you go find it.

This week that lesson's holding true. The mackerel showed up thick — and I mean thick, the kind of showing where you can see the surface nervous half a mile off Ocean Point and again out past the Cuckolds — but the striped bass have been a different animal, scattered and moody, biting in windows instead of all day long. If you fished the last of the ebb at Damariscotta River mouth or down around the Thread of Life, you probably had a couple decent stripers, mid-20s to low-30s, on a white or chartreuse soft plastic swim shad worked slow along the current seam. But fish the wrong hour and you could soak bait for two hours and see nothing but mackerel stealing your sandworms.

The mackerel bite itself has been the most reliable thing going. Off Squirrel Island, Ocean Point, and out toward The Cuckolds, jigging small silver Swedish Pimples or mackerel trees in 20 to 40 feet is filling coolers fast on the last two hours of the incoming tide, when the bait pushes up against the ledges. Good news for anyone chasing bass too, because live or fresh-dead mackerel fished on a fish-finder rig has been out-producing plugs at spots like the Thread of Life and the mouth of the Sheepscot, where the current runs hard enough that a plug gets pushed around before it ever settles.

Out at Monhegan, the pattern I like this time of year is holding: fish the ebb along the ledges off White Head and down toward Manana, working the edge where the white water breaks off the rock into deeper green. Stripers have been mixed in with pollock right on the surface, chasing bait balls pushed up by the current, and if you've got a light spinning rod rigged with a 1-ounce diamond jig or a Kastmaster, you can work both species without changing tackle. The pollock have run smaller than I'd like — schoolies mostly, 16 to 20 inches — but there's enough of them to keep a rod bent while you wait for something with more shoulders to show.

Eastern Egg Rock has had bait balls stacked up tight most mornings, which means the puffins are working and so are the bass underneath them — but you've got to be there early, right around first light on the last of the flood, before the wind builds and pushes the bait down. By nine or ten the birds thin out and so does the bite. I had one morning out there last week where three casts with a Doc's Sand Eel got three fish, all in the 20-inch class, then nothing for the next ninety minutes. That's July for you — short windows, good if you time them, frustrating if you don't.

Further out into Penobscot Bay, the groundfish are exactly where they should be this time of year — deep, and staying that way with this warm surface water pushing them down. The channel between Vinalhaven and North Haven, and the deeper humps out toward Isle au Haut Bay, have been holding cod and a few haddock in 90 to 120 feet. Jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, or working a bottom rig with clam, has produced steady but not spectacular results — a few keeper cod in the 24 to 28-inch range mixed with a lot of shorts you've got to sort through. It's not the kind of bite that fills a fish box in an hour, but if you've got the patience to work the tide change slow, there's fish down there worth the trip.

Bluefish have been scarce so far, just the occasional slammer mixed in with mackerel schools off Boothbay, nothing consistent enough to plan a trip around yet. Deer Isle Thorofare and Merchant's Row have been quieter than I'd expect for mid-July — the current's there, the structure's there, but the bait hasn't concentrated the way it usually does by now. I'd keep an eye on that over the next couple weeks, because when it turns on out there it turns on fast.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and the water keeps warming the way it has, I expect the bass to tighten up their pattern by the weekend — probably pushing harder into the river mouths on the last two hours of the ebb, chasing that mackerel bait downstream. That's where I'd put my time if I only had one tide to fish. The groundfish out in the bay aren't going anywhere; that's a slow, steady bite you can count on right through August as long as you fish it deep and patient. Monhegan will keep rewarding early risers who fish the ebb off the western ledges. Nothing complicated about any of it — just old water doing what old water does, in its own time.

reports.headline: White Island Ledge Gives Up Haddock to 6, Bluefish Finally Crash Rye Harbor
reports.subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty when you know which six feet of it hold fish — this week it was the Shoals ledges and a sudden bluefish push at Rye Harbor.
reports.body_markdown:
People from away always ask me how I fish the same thirteen miles of coast every week without getting bored. I tell them the same thing every time: New Hampshire doesn't have thirteen miles of coastline, it has thirteen miles of front door and about a hundred and thirty miles of water once you count the Shoals, the ledges, the river mouth, and every piece of structure in between. You just have to fish it like you mean it. This week meant leaving Rye Harbor before 5 a.m. with the Lund loaded light, because the haddock have been up on the humps around White Island and Duck Island, and if you're not anchored up or drifting the top of that structure by first light, you're fishing leftovers.

The groundfish bite out at the Shoals has been honest, not spectacular. White Island Ledge in 60 to 80 feet gave up haddock to six pounds on the last two mornings I ran out, mixed with a few keeper cod pushing seven and eight, all on the bottom of the tide when the current eases enough to hold a jig vertical. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid have been outfishing bare metal — the fish are picky enough right now that they want a little scent riding down with the flash. Once the tide starts to run hard past half-flood or half-ebb, that bite shuts off fast. You get maybe a ninety-minute window on each side of the slack, and if you're not rigged and dropped when it opens, you watch it close. I've had mornings out there where three of us put a dozen fish in the box in that window and then sat on a stone-cold rip for two hours waiting for the next one. That's the Shoals in July — you fish the clock, not the location.

Mackerel have finally shown in numbers around Appledore and the backside of Star Island, which matters more than people think, because that's the bait that's been pulling bigger cod up off bottom to chase. If you see the birds working tight over showers of mackerel near the ledges, drop a sabiki first, then switch over to a bigger jig once you've got a few mackerel in the well — a live mack fished on a heavy jig head near bottom has out-produced anything artificial out there this week.

Inshore, the striper story is Hampton Harbor, and it's been better than the ocean side has any right to expect given how warm and quiet the surf's been. Fish are stacking up on the last two hours of the incoming, pushing bait up through the inlet channel and holding along the edges where the current breaks against the jetty rocks. I've seen slot bass to 32 inches taken on white paddletails fished slow along that seam, and live pogies under a slip float have been money for the guys willing to soak bait instead of cast all day. The key has been fishing that inlet on the push, not the drain — on the outgoing the current rips too hard and flattens out the structure the fish are using. Give it that two-hour incoming window around the new tide change and work the drop-off just inside the jetty tips.

Bluefish showed up harder than I expected this week, cutting through Rye Harbor and pushing bait right up against the rocks at Odiorne Point. These aren't the giant choppers yet, mostly two to four pounds, but they're aggressive and they've been busting bait on top in the mornings, which makes for the kind of visual bite that gets people using words like exciting instead of technical. Topwater poppers and single-hook Kastmasters have worked, but bring wire or heavy fluoro leader — I lost three good lures in two days before I remembered who I was dealing with.

Flounder in the Piscataqua and up into Portsmouth Harbor have been a mixed bag — some days you can put together a dozen keepers drifting the deeper holes off the Route 1 bridge on the last of the ebb, other days you soak clams and worms for two hours and get nothing but hermit crabs. The river's still cold enough on bottom to hold fish, but the bite's been tide-dependent to the point where I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it right now. Better to treat it as a bonus stop on the way back in from the Shoals.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and light like it has been, I'd keep working that White Island slack window early and expect the mackerel push to keep building, which should hold the bigger cod up shallower through the week. In the harbor, I'd fish that incoming tide hard at Hampton for another week or two before the bass start sliding out toward the open coast as the water warms further. And if you see bluefish showing at Odiorne again on a calm morning, don't wait — that bite's been unpredictable, on some days and gone the next, and I'd rather catch it than chase it.

reports.headline: Keyport's Bunker Blitzes Pull the Blues Tight While Fluke Keep Grinding the Channel Edges
reports.subhead: With a beat-up swell knocking the ocean side of the Hook around, I stayed inside all week and the bay paid me back — mostly.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call Monday to keep the boat inside the bay for the whole week, and I'd make it again. There's a southeast swell rolling into the Bight — 2 to 3 feet at a ten-second period — and while that's nothing that'll sink you, it turns the Rip at the Hook into a washing machine you don't need to fish through when the bay itself is loaded with bait. So I skipped the ocean side entirely and put my time into Keyport, Flynn's Knoll, and the Navesink, and that's where this report lives.

The story of the week is bunker. Big pods of adult menhaden have been stacked off Keyport Flats and rolling down past Union Beach and Port Monmouth since late June, and by mid-July they're thick enough that you can see them nervous-watering from a quarter mile off — that oily slick, the gulls sitting on top waiting. Where you've got that much bunker balled up in shallow water in the heat of summer, you've got bluefish underneath it, and this week they found it. I watched three separate blitzes off the Keyport side Tuesday and Thursday mornings, right at first light before the wind came up, blues busting bunker on the surface hard enough to throw spray. Poppers and metal — I've been throwing a 1-ounce Kastmaster and a bunker-colored Super Strike popper — will get eaten the second they hit the water when it's happening like that. The trick is timing. Once the sun gets up over the trees and the boat traffic starts, the blitzes pull down and scatter, so if you want the top-water show, you need to be on the water by 5:30, not 7.

Stripers are mixed into those bunker schools but they're playing it smarter than the blues right now. This is mid-July heat — the resident bass aren't chasing bait on the surface in broad daylight, they're sitting under the school working the edges and picking off cripples. If you want them, don't fish the blitz itself, fish the perimeter. I've had better luck free-lining a live bunker on a 5/0 circle hook with just enough weight to keep it down 8 to 10 feet, drifting the edge of the bait school on the last of the incoming tide off Keyport and down toward Ideal Beach. Snag-and-drop works too if you've got the stomach for it — snag one on a treble, let it flutter down wounded, and hang on. The bass we've boated this way have mostly been schoolies and a few solid mid-20-inchers, nothing enormous, but it's honest action and it beats standing on the bulkhead getting skunked.

Fluke are still the most consistent player in the bay right now, and Flynn's Knoll has been the address. The drop where the Knoll spills into the Ambrose and Sandy Hook Channel — 25 to 35 feet — has been holding fluke all week, and the pattern hasn't changed much from June: 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along bottom on the drift, working the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping your bucktail sideways. Romer Shoal has been productive too, especially on the western edge where it falls into deeper water — that's been giving up a better grade of fluke, a few pushing 4 and 5 pounds mixed in with the usual 16 to 18-inch keepers. I'll be honest, it's not a five-fish-per-drift kind of bite most days — you're working for two or three keepers over a few hours — but the fish are there and they're eating with confidence when you find the right depth change.

The Navesink has quietly turned into the best-kept secret of the week. Weakfish have been showing up around the Oceanic Bridge and down toward Red Bank on the night tide, and if you've fished this river as long as I have you know that's when they show their teeth — right at dusk into full dark, on the outgoing. Chartreuse bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, worked slow along the bottom near the bridge pilings, have been the ticket. Nothing giant — most weakfish going 16 to 20 inches — but it's a legit bite that a lot of guys overlook once the striper run ends in spring, and it's worth the late-night trip if you're patient with the mosquitoes.

Porgies have been steady filler fishing on Old Orchard Shoal and around Romer Shoal on high-low rigs baited with clam or sandworm, decent-sized fish in the 1 to 2-pound range, good for keeping kids occupied while you wait on the tide to turn for fluke.

Looking ahead, if that southeast swell backs off like it's supposed to by the weekend, I'd take one more crack at the Rip before the bunker schools push farther down the bay — they always do eventually, usually once the water starts creeping past 78 degrees, which we're not far from. Until then, I'm staying inside: dawn blitzes off Keyport for blues, the Knoll and Romer for fluke on the incoming, and the Navesink after dark for weakfish. That's the bay right now — not blowing anybody's mind, but honest, workable fishing if you put your time in the right places at the right tide.

reports.headline: Why the sod bank drains are outfishing the open bay right now
reports.subhead: A lesson in current, temperature, and why the fluke you want are hugging the mud lines this week, not sitting out in the open sand.
reports.body_markdown:
I get the same question every July, usually from a guy leaning on the rail at the ramp with a rod he hasn't wet yet: "Why am I marking bait all over the open bay and not getting bit?" It's a fair question, and it's a teaching moment every time. The answer, almost always, is temperature and current working together, and this week that lesson is on full display from Absecon Inlet down through Great Egg.

The back bays have warmed into the high 70s on the flats, and the ocean side, if the recent Bight buoy numbers are any indication, is sitting closer to 73 degrees with a lazy 2 to 3-foot swell running on a 10-second period. That's not rough water, but it's enough to keep the surf a little disorganized and push bait tight to structure rather than spreading it out. So the fish — fluke especially — aren't loafing on open sand in this heat. They're stacking where the water actually moves and cools a few degrees: the drains coming off the sod banks on the outgoing tide.

That's the pattern I've been fishing and teaching all week. Absecon Inlet's Rainbow Channel and Risley Channel edges, eight to fifteen feet, dropping tide, are the classroom. As that water pours off the marsh it's carrying grass shrimp and killies with it, and the fluke sit right on the edge of that current seam waiting for the buffet to come to them. A 3/4-ounce white or chartreuse bucktail tipped with a 4-inch Gulp swimming mullet, drifted slow and bounced just off bottom, has been the winning combination. Keep the boat moving with the current, not against it — that's the mistake I see most, guys trying to power-drift a falling tide and dragging the bait through the strike zone too fast. Slow it down. Let the current do the work. We've had keeper fluke to 22 inches coming out of that same seam three tides running, mixed in with a lot of shorts that need to go back — the size class isn't uniformly good, so expect to cull.

Graveling Point and the Great Egg back channels are fishing similarly, though I'd call that bite more moderate than hot — a few keepers scattered among a lot of teen-inch fish. If you're marking grass and mud bottom transitioning to harder sand on your graph, that's the spot to make repeat drifts.

Weakfish have been a first-light proposition only. Once the sun climbs and that back bay water heats up further, they slide off the flats and go quiet. Best window has been that gray hour right at dawn on the last of the incoming in the Rainbow Channel and up toward Longport, using a 1/4-ounce jighead with a pearl or chartreuse Gulp shrimp, worked with a slow lift-and-drop right along the channel edges where the mud gives way to shell. Nothing gaudy — a handful of legal fish mixed with a lot of short ones, but if you're up early it's worth the rods.

Bluefish are giving the inlet some life on the tail end of the incoming, chunked bunker fished on the bottom right along the Absecon Inlet rock jetty producing cocktail blues in the two-to-three-pound class, with the occasional heavier fish mixed in. If you'd rather cast than sit, diamond jigs worked through the same rip will connect just as well and keep you moving.

Kingfish are doing what they always do in mid-July — patrolling the surf troughs at Ocean City and Sea Isle City on incoming water, and they've been a reliable, if modest, producer. High-low rigs with small hooks, bloodworm or Fishbites, cast just past the first break. It's not a numbers game most mornings, but it's a teaching bite — good for kids and for anyone who wants steady action without needing a boat.

Striped bass are in their typical summer sulk. The resident fish haven't disappeared, but they've gone nocturnal and structure-bound. If you want a shot, fish bunker chunks on the bottom around the Absecon Inlet rocks after dark, on the last two hours of the incoming, and be patient. This isn't a volume bite in July — it's one or two quality fish for the guys willing to put in the hours after midnight.

Triggerfish have started showing on the near reef structure off Great Egg and around the outer rock piles at the inlet, which is right on schedule for this time of year. Small pieces of clam on a size 4 hook, light enough to still get bit but strong enough to handle their surprisingly stubborn pull. It's a finesse fishery — more about presentation and patience than volume — but a welcome change of pace when the fluke bite goes quiet on the tide change.

Looking ahead, the moon is building toward new phase this week, which means bigger tide swings and stronger current through the inlets — good news for the sod bank pattern, since more water moving means more bait getting flushed off those flats. If the swell backs off like it's been trending, I'd expect the surf kingfish bite to clean up and the triggerfish action on the reef structure to firm up too. My plan for the coming week is simple: fish the outgoing around Absecon and Great Egg for fluke, be on the water at first light for weakfish, and save the inlet rocks for after dark if stripers are the target. That's where the lesson plan says to be.

reports.headline: Double Creek Fluke Are There If You Work For Them — Blowfish and Kingfish Carry the Bay
reports.subhead: Weakfish have slid off the sedges for deeper water, but blowfish, kingfish, and a patient fluke drift are keeping rods bent through the July heat.
reports.body_markdown:
I remember mating on one of the Point Pleasant boats back when I was maybe sixteen, a July morning thick as this one, and an old captain named Sal telling me, "Gus, this time of year the bay gets lazy on you. You gotta go find the fish, they won't come find you." I've thought about that line every July since, usually right about now, when the sedges go quiet and the fluke stop cooperating on the first drift and you have to actually work the boat instead of just soaking a line and hoping. That's exactly where we are this week on Barnegat Bay — not a bad bite, but a bite that makes you earn it.

Start with the fluke, because that's what most of the calls to the shop are about. Double Creek Channel is still the play, but it's not the wide-open drift you had in June. The keepers are there, we're just seeing them stacked tighter around the bends near the range markers and the deeper cuts on the edges of the channel, 12 to 18 feet, and you need to hit the tide right — the first two hours of the outgoing has been the difference between a decent box and a long, quiet afternoon. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow right on the bottom, has been outproducing bare bucktails two to one. I had a father-son pair out of Forked River last Tuesday who ground out four keepers to 4 pounds on that combo after two hours of shorts — patience paid, but it wasn't handed to them.

Weakfish are the story of the season winding down, not winding up. May and early June had the sedge banks with tide-run weakies, but by mid-July most of that school has slid off into deeper water, probably staged somewhere off the inlet or holding in the channel humps where it's cooler. You can still scratch a few keeper weakfish working the last hour of the incoming at Tices Shoal, bucktail tipped with a shrimp or squid strip fished slow along the drop, but I wouldn't build a whole trip around it right now. If you connect, treat it as a bonus, not the plan.

Bluefish have been the more dependable fireworks. Barnegat Inlet, particularly the rocks on the north side, has had real morning blitzes on the incoming — chopper blues in the 3 to 6-pound class crashing bunker pods right at first light. Metal — Ava jigs, Kastmasters in silver or chartreuse — worked fast through the melee has been money, and if you want to have some fun with it, a topwater popper thrown right into the boil will get eaten just as quick. That bite tends to shut off hard once the sun gets up over the dunes, so if you're going for blues, go early.

Stripers in the bay proper have gone to their July pattern, which is to say they've gone nocturnal on us. Water in the shallow coves and up around Oyster Creek has been running warm enough that the bass just don't want to work during daylight — I'm seeing better results after dark around the bridge pilings and the deeper holes near the inlet rip, live bunker or eels fished on a fish-finder rig right on bottom. If you're a surf guy, Island Beach State Park at first light on the last of the falling tide has been quietly productive — the ocean side is still cooler than the bay, running in the low 70s off the coast, and that temperature break has been enough to hold some slot fish tight to the bar. It's not a numbers game out there right now, more a one-or-two-good-fish kind of morning, but those fish have had some shoulders on them.

The real bread and butter this week has been blowfish and kingfish, and I say that with real affection because this is the fishing that keeps kids and grandparents happy on a hot afternoon. Blowfish are thick around the Oyster Creek docks and the marina edges at Tices Shoal — small hooks, bloodworm or squid strips, doesn't take much skill, just patience and a bucket. Kingfish have been working the sod banks along Double Creek and out toward the Barnegat Light flats on the incoming tide, sandworm or bloodworm strips fished light on the bottom. Neither of these fisheries will make the cover of anything, but they've been steady when the marquee species have made you work.

Looking ahead, if the wind stays out of the southwest and lays down through the weekend, I'd expect the fluke bite in Double Creek to tighten up around that same outgoing window — moving water is doing the work right now, not the bait itself. The bluefish should keep showing at the inlet as long as bunker pods keep pushing through, and I'd bet the striper bite stays a dawn-and-dusk affair until we get a real cool-down. If you've only got one shot this week, I'd take the early flood at Barnegat Inlet for blues and finish the tide out with a fluke drift down through Double Creek — cover your bases, and don't be surprised if you have to move around to find them.

reports.headline: Holgate's Reshaped Third Bar Holds Fluke on the Drop, Bass Wait for Dark
reports.subhead: A groundswell chewed a new trough into the south end this week — fluke moved in fast, stripers are still playing it cautious until the sun's down.
reports.body_markdown:
I walked the Holgate stretch at low light Tuesday morning with the drone up before the wind picked up, and the third bar isn't where it was two weeks ago. That two-to-three-foot groundswell we picked up off a long-period east swell — ten seconds, out of the southeast — did some real work down there. It cut a new trough on the south end, maybe 40 yards off the dune line, deeper and tighter than the old one. Water's pushing through it hard on the outgoing, and that kind of current edge right up against structure is exactly what fluke want in mid-July.

So that's where I started the week, and it paid. Drifting that new cut and the flat behind it, 18 to 24 feet, on the last three hours of the outgoing — 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped light, just enough to feel bottom and no more. Picked up keeper fluke to 22 inches doing that, along with a pile of shorts that kept it interesting between fish. The Little Egg Inlet channel edge, right where it necks down before Graveling Point, has been doing the same thing — same depth range, same idea, current stacking bait against a hard edge. If you're marking bait balls on the meter there on the last of the ebb, don't leave. That's the window.

Barnegat Inlet's producing too, but it's pickier. North side near Oyster Creek Channel on the incoming has given up a few nicer fluke, 4 to 6 pounds, to guys working chartreuse bucktails with a Gulp swimming mullet trailer, dragged slow along the bottom edge where the sand meets the rock rubble. That's not a drift-and-hope spot — you need to know exactly where that rubble line sits, and it moves every season. I'd rather send you to Holgate or Little Egg if you're not familiar with that structure.

Bluefish have been showing up early, and I mean early — first light, Ship Bottom and Surf City beachfront, blitzing peanut bunker and small mullet that are starting to stage up for the run. Poppers and small metal, cast right into the wash where the birds are working. It doesn't last — usually blown out by 7:30 once the sun gets up and the bait scatters — but for that hour it's about as fun as this beach gets in July. Bring a spinning rod you don't mind getting slimed.

Kingfish are on the sod banks in Little Egg and up around Graveling Point, working the marsh edges on the high tide push and pulling back off the bank as it drains. Bloodworms and FishBites bloodworm strips on a high-low rig, small hooks, light sinker — these fish don't need much convincing right now, they're just not everywhere. Focus on the drainage guts where the marsh grass funnels bait out on the ebb.

Striped bass are the hard truth of this report. The resident fish are here, but July's ocean temp sitting in the low 70s and a back bay running even warmer has them doing what smart bass do this time of year — feeding at night and hiding in whatever cool water they can find during the day. I've had two decent sessions at Holgate after dark, working that new cut with a black needlefish on the slower stretches and switching to a small darter when I could hear bait getting nervous on the surface. Slot fish, nothing huge, but real bites on a real presentation instead of just soaking bunker and hoping. My plug bag right now is stripped down to three trays — swimmers for the last of dusk, poppers for when bait's showing, needlefish and darters for full dark. If you're bass fishing LBI in July and you're not out there between 9 PM and 2 AM, you're mostly fishing for the memory of spring.

Weakfish are thinning out fast. Great Bay and the deeper holes off Graveling Point still had a few respectable fish on soft plastics — Bass Assassins in pearl, worked slow along the bottom — but that bite's fading as the water climbs. The Mullica's gone properly warm and tannic, good for an hour at first light before it goes quiet and stays quiet through the heat of the day.

Looking ahead, that groundswell is backing off and the wind's supposed to swing more southwest by the weekend, which should let that new Holgate cut settle in rather than get reworked again. If it holds its shape, I'd keep drifting it on the outgoing for fluke through next week. For bass, until we get a real bait push or a cool-down at night, I'm treating it as a dark-hours program only — plan your trip around the tide stage after sunset, not the calendar.

reports.headline: Nyatt Point on the drop: scup thick on the ledges, bass working after dark
reports.subhead: The herring run's long gone, but the bay's settled into its mid-summer rhythm — bass gone nocturnal, fluke sliding onto the flats, scup piled on every rock pile from Rocky Point to Prudence.
reports.body_markdown:
I was down at the India Point pier Tuesday morning watching a kid with a Zebco reel haul scup over the rail two at a time, and his old man turns to me and says, "Where'd all the bass go?" That's the question I keep hearing up and down the river this week. Buckeye Brook's herring run wound down back in June, and once that bait ran dry, the bass that stacked up on it for weeks scattered. They didn't leave the bay — they just changed their address and their clock.

That's the story of mid-July here. The easy money bite off the herring is done. What's left is a bay that's warmed up top to bottom, tides running big off this new moon, and fish that have gone smart and nocturnal. If you want stripers now, you're fishing bridges after dark or you're chasing bunker schools that are holding off Prudence Island and down around the mouth of Greenwich Bay. I had a good hour Thursday night under the Mount Hope Bridge on the last of the outgoing, drifting a live eel down current past the third and fourth piling. Two fish in the 28-30 inch class, both right on the seam where the light meets the shadow line. That's been the pattern all week — small light, tight current, and patience. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig off the rocks at Rocky Point have also been picking off keeper bass on the last two hours of the ebb, right around midnight to 2 a.m.

Fluke are the better daytime bet right now, and they're pushing hard into the bay off the warm flow coming out of the upper river. Greenwich Bay has been holding fish in 10 to 18 feet on the drop of the tide — I'm dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, tipped with a strip of squid, nice and slow along the bottom off the Warwick side. Conimicut Point is doing the same thing on the outgoing — that current sweeping around the point concentrates bait, and the fluke sit right on the edge of it in 12 to 20 feet. Nothing giant this week, mostly 16 to 19 inches with a few keepers mixed in, but steady enough that a couple hours on the drift will put fish in the cooler if you keep moving and don't marry one spot.

Scup are the sure thing right now, and that's not a knock — that's just where we are in July. Nyatt Point and the rock piles down toward Rocky Point are loaded. High-low rigs with size 6 or 8 hooks, sandworm or squid strips, dropped into 15 to 25 feet right on the rocks. The bigger tides we're getting off this new moon are moving more water through those ledges, and the scup respond to it — best bite has been the first two hours of the ebb when that current really starts to rip past the structure. If you want a mess of fish for the pan without overthinking it, that's your spot this week.

Bluefish have shown up in patches, mostly chopping bait on top out toward the mouth of the bay and around Prudence Island in the early morning. I haven't seen the kind of blitz that stops traffic, but there's enough bluefish mixed in with those bunker schools that if you're throwing poppers or SP minnows at first light off Prudence, don't be shocked if something with teeth ends your leader. Black sea bass are still holding tight to the rock structure around Jamestown and the deeper edges off Prudence — small jigs tipped with squid, fished slow right on bottom, still producing a few keepers, though the season's ticking and the bigger ones have thinned out some.

Weakfish — I'll be honest, I haven't heard a real report on those this week. A few years back you could count on some around Greenwich Bay this time of year, but that fishery's a shadow of what it used to be around here, so I'm not sending anybody chasing ghosts.

Looking ahead, these new moon tides should keep building through the weekend, which is good news for the ledge bite — more water movement means more bait getting pushed around, which means scup and fluke both should stay active. If the wind stays out of the southwest and lays down at night like it has been, I'd put my money on the bridges again after dark for bass — that's been the more consistent program than daytime blind casting. Worth watching the bunker schools off Prudence too; if they hold position through the week, that's where the next real bass and blue action is going to break loose.

reports.headline: Wreck 3548 in 118 Feet: Sea Bass to 4 Pounds, Bluefin Working the Mud Hole Lumps
reports.subhead: A two-decade-old number still pays off, and the tuna bite on the inshore lumps is finally worth the run.
reports.body_markdown:
Wreck number 3548, sitting in 118 feet on the eastern lip of the Klondike, has been in my book since 2009. I marked it after a mate of mine snagged bottom there chasing bluefin and came up with a piece of steel plate on his jig.
