reports.subhead: With a lazy groundswell rolling into Rockaway, I kept the kayak in the bay this week — and found fluke, bridge bass, and a few surprises in the flats.
reports.body_markdown:
I put the kayak in at Motts Basin off Cross Bay Boulevard Tuesday morning instead of hauling it out to Fort Tilden, and that decision made the whole trip. There's a low groundswell running along the ocean side right now — nothing scary, 2 to 3 feet at a long 10-second period — but it's enough to turn a peaceful paddle into a workout if you're launching through the inlet surf. The bay side stays flat and glassy most mornings before the sea breeze fills in around ten, so if you're kayak fishing this week, that's your window. Get on the water by six, be back at the ramp before the wind starts pushing whitecaps across the open flats by Ruler's Bar.

The fluke bite inside the bay has been the most consistent thing going. I worked the drop-offs along the edge of the flats south of the JFK runways in 12 to 18 feet, drifting the first two hours of the incoming with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail teased with a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp strip. Nothing gigantic — most fish ran 15 to 18 inches, a handful of keepers mixed in — but it was a fish every other drift, which for mid-July in the bay is honest work. A few boats working the deeper hole off Big Egg Marsh reported better size, fish pushing 20 inches, on squid strips fished slow along bottom. If you're marking bait on the sounder — and there's plenty of rainfish and small mullet stacked in those channels right now — slow your drift down and let the bucktail hop instead of drag.

Marine Parkway Bridge is still doing what it does for bass, but you have to fish it on their schedule now, not yours. The daytime bite has gone quiet with the water this warm — I'm talking last two hours of outgoing right around dusk into full dark, working live eels or bunker chunks tight to the pilings on the Rockaway side. A guy I trust who fishes there three nights a week landed two fish over 30 inches last Thursday on eels drifted right through the current seam where the tide rips off the abutment. Daytime, forget it — the fish have slid into the deeper, cooler water under the span and won't commit to anything until the light drops and the current starts working bait past them.

Bluefish showed up stronger than I expected along Breezy Point and the surf just west of the inlet. With that ocean water sitting near 73 degrees and that long-period swell stirring bait up off the bar, we've had a few real toothy blitzes early — six to eight in the morning, gone by nine once the boat traffic picks up. Diamond jigs and Kastmasters worked fast through the wash have been getting hit, along with cut bunker chunked out past the breakers for the bigger ones. Nothing sustained, and I want to be straight about that — these are twenty-minute windows, not all-morning affairs. But if you're willing to be there right at first light with the tide dropping, it's been worth the trip more often than not this week.

Porgies are holding steady off Canarsie Pier and around the Cross Bay Bridge pilings, which is where I sent my nephew with a bucket of sandworms and a high-low rig — he came back with a dozen keepers in about two hours fishing the last of the outgoing. Nothing fancy needed there: small hooks, light sinkers, bottom in 15 to 20 feet, and patience. Weakfish, on the other hand, have been a ghost story this year in the bay — I've heard of exactly one legit fish caught off the Bay side near Motts Basin, and that was on a bucktail meant for fluke. If you're specifically hunting weakfish, I wouldn't build a trip around it right now.

Looking at the week ahead, I'd keep leaning on the bay for the daytime bite and save the bridge and surf for the low-light windows. The swell out front doesn't look like it's laying down much before the weekend, so kayak and small-boat guys should keep favoring the inside launches — Motts Basin, Canarsie Pier ramp, or the Cross Bay side — over fighting through the inlet surf. If that groundswell does back off and the ocean flattens out, I'd make a run out to Breezy at first light and see if those blues hold their pattern; that warm water pushing bait tight to the beach is exactly the kind of setup that turns into a real morning if the timing lines up. Bring both rods either way — this is a week where the bay and the ocean are both worth a look, just not at the same hour.

reports.headline: Outgoing After Midnight: Bass in the Inlet Hole, Weakfish Under the Bridge Lights
reports.subhead: With the ocean roughed up and warm, the smart money's inside — working the dark water on the back half of the ebb.
reports.body_markdown:
I made the call again this week to skip the dawn patrol and let the inlet come to me after dark. That's not stubbornness — it's math. The ocean side has been running better than 2 feet of leftover swell out of the southeast, water pushing 73 degrees off the Bight, and that kind of junk on the beach just isn't worth fighting when the real bite is fifty yards inside the jetty on the back half of an outgoing tide. So that's where I've been, rod tip low, eyes on the white water sliding off the north jetty rocks around midnight to 2 a.m.

The bass are there, but I want to be straight with you — it's not a blitz. It's a working bite. Two, maybe three keepers a trip in that deep hole on the ocean side of the inlet, mixed with a handful of shorts that keep you honest. The fish are stacking on the current seam where the outgoing water dumps out past the rocks and meets the flatter bay water — that seam is holding bait and holding fish. I've been soaking chunk bunker on a fish-finder rig, 3 ounces of lead to hold bottom against that push, and I've had my best luck in the last two hours of the ebb, right before the tide goes dead slack. If you're a plug guy, a black Danny swimming plug worked slow along that same seam has drawn a few solid strikes, but the bait guys are outfishing the lure guys right now — the fish are eating with their nose more than their eyes in this dirty, current-stirred water.

Bluefish are the other story at the inlet, and this part I don't have to sell you on. There's a real wave of big blues moving through the East End right now, and Shinnecock's getting its share. These aren't snappers — I've seen teens hooked off the rocks on the last of the outgoing, chopping bunker chunks to pieces before the bass even get a look. If you're throwing metal — a Kastmaster or a Hopkins — off the jetty at dusk into that boiling current edge, you'll know inside three casts whether the blues are stacked up or moved through. Lost a leader to one this week that I'd guess went better than 14 pounds. Bring heavier leader than you think you need.

Inside the bay, the fluke bite has actually turned a corner. It was a slow start to July, but the drift through the flats off Tiana Beach and down toward the Shinnecock Canal mouth has picked up nicely the last ten days. I'm not talking doormats — most fish are running 16 to 19 inches — but there's enough keeper-class fish mixed in that a few boats have had four-fish limits by early afternoon. Standard program: 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along the sand-to-mud transitions in 12 to 18 feet. Incoming tide has been the better half of the cycle for this — the clean ocean water pushing through the inlet seems to wake the fluke up, where the outgoing gets a little stained and slower.

Ponquogue Bridge is still doing what it does this time of year, which is to say it's producing weakfish for the guys willing to fish it right. That means after dark, that means working the shadow lines the bridge lights throw on the water, and that means fishing the current, not fighting it. I've had my best weakfish on 1/4-ounce bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, cast up-current and let swing back through the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing. Nothing huge — most fish in the 16 to 20-inch class — but there was a 7-plus-pounder weighed in at a Southampton tackle shop this week that tells you the bigger models are still around if you put your time in. Porgies are stacked around those same bridge pilings and the rock piles off Hampton Bays in 15 to 25 feet — clam and squid on a standard porgy rig will keep the rod bent between weakfish bites if you want to fill a cooler.

Nobody's running bass or weakfish through the canal in numbers yet this summer that I've heard of, but with water this warm on both sides, I wouldn't be shocked to hear reports of fish using it as a shortcut into the Peconic on a strong tide change. Worth a look if you're passing through around the lock timing.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working that inlet hole after midnight as long as the ocean stays sloppy — that thermal split between the rough Atlantic and the calmer bay water is exactly what's concentrating bait and bass where they are. If the swell lays down and the ocean cleans up, I'd expect some of that bass and blue activity to spread back out onto the open beach, and the inlet bite could thin out fast. Until then, I'm fishing the dark water and letting the daytime fleet have the sunburn.

reports.headline: One Cast, One Overslot: Plum Gut's Ebb Still Delivers
reports.subhead: Cooler eastern water is holding big bass tight to the current seams while the west side of the Sound cooks — here's where to find them.
reports.body_markdown:
3:40 a.m., chest-deep on the rocks below Plum Gut, current screaming through at what felt like five knots dead against the moon. First cast with a 2-ounce Danny plug, swing it across the seam where the white water folds into the slick — one thump, then the rod loads over and doesn't stop. Forty inches, high thirties on the scale I didn't have with me, and it came off the third rock out from the point where the rip pinches down hardest. That's the fish that tells you everything you need to know about this week: the big girls are still stacked on the structure, they're just not going to make it easy.

Here's the deal on temperature right now — it's the whole story for the Eastern Sound. New London's reading in the mid-60s, while Kings Point on the west side is pushing low 70s. That gradient is real and it's working in our favor. Cooler, oxygen-rich water moving hard through The Race and Plum Gut is exactly what big migratory bass want in July — they don't like warm, sluggish water, and they sure don't like getting pushed shallow when it's 70-plus. So while the western Sound bass are getting comfortable in the back bays, our fish are staying tight to current edges, rips, and the deep gut itself, feeding hard on the tide changes and laying up in the eddies in between.

The pattern that's producing: fish the last two hours of the ebb through Plum Gut and The Race, working bucktails — 1.5 to 2 ounces, bare or dressed with a white or chartreuse trailer — cast across the seam and let it sink clean off the edge before you start a slow, deliberate bottom retrieve. Don't rush it. These fish are ambushing bait that's getting swept off the ledge, not chasing anything down. At night I'm still going heavier and louder — Danny plugs, big pencils, and swimmers worked across the boil lines off Fishers Island and the Orient Point rip. Two solid slot fish and that overslot came off the rocks this week, all within the same two-hour window on the back half of the ebb. Daytime has been tougher and more technical — the fish are there, but you're working for one good bite instead of three.

Bluefish have been the reliable action when the bass go quiet. Jumbo class — eight to twelve pounds, some bigger — are chopping through bunker pods off Orient Point and along the north side of Fishers, especially on the last of the incoming when bait gets pushed up against the beach. Poppers and 3-ounce Hopkins spoons worked fast through the boils have been drawing vicious strikes. If you see the surface nervous and gulls working low, don't wait — that window can close in twenty minutes.

Fluke fishing has been a grind but productive if you put in the drift time. Fishers Island Sound, the sand and gravel patches south of the ferry channel, 20 to 35 feet, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with a strip of squid. Nothing huge — most fish going 16 to 19 inches — but enough keepers coming over the rail to make it worth the sea time, especially on the tail end of the outgoing when the current slows enough to keep bottom contact clean.

Porgies are thick around the rock piles off Plum Gut and the reef structure south of Fishers. High-low rigs with bloodworms or clam strips, fished on the bottom during slack water when the current backs off enough to hold position. This has been the most consistent bite of the week — not glamorous, but if you want fish in the cooler with minimal drama, this is it.

Weakfish are still around but thin — a few keeper-class fish mixed in with the porgy catches on bait, nothing worth targeting specifically. If the water stays on the cooler side through the rest of July, I wouldn't be surprised to see a better push of them show up, but I'm not betting the trip on it.

Looking ahead — if this gradient holds, with the west side running warm and the east staying cool off New London and through the Gut, I expect the pattern to keep producing right through the next lunar push. The rips are the whole game right now. If I've got one shot this week, I'm walking the rocks below Plum Gut on the last two hours of the ebb, throwing a bucktail deep into the seam before first light, and I'm not leaving until the current goes slack. That's where the big fish are living, and that first cast at 3:40 a.m. proved it's not a fluke pattern — it's the program.

reports.headline: Bunker Pods Push West Through the Shoal — Bass Riding Shotgun, Blues Right Behind
reports.subhead: The bait told the story before the boats did: peanut bunker piling into the Norwalk Islands and Stratford Shoal, and the predators followed the smell.
reports.body_markdown:
I spend more time watching bait than I do watching rods these days, and this week the bunker did all the talking. Monday morning off Charles Island I found a pod the size of a tennis court, balled tight and nervous, dimpling the surface like rain that wasn't falling. That kind of behavior means something's under them, and sure enough — a bass came up and cracked the edge of that pod hard enough to send bunker skipping across the calm. That's the tell I look for every July: not the birds yet, not the boats, just the bait acting scared before anybody else notices.

The reason it's happening here and not further east is written right in the water temps. Kings Point is sitting at 71.2 degrees, New London's still down at 66.4. That's a five-degree wall stretched across sixty miles of Sound, and bait doesn't like walls — it piles up against them. Central Sound, from Norwalk down through Stratford Shoal and across to Port Jeff, is sitting right in that warm pocket where bunker and peanut bunker are comfortable and slow-moving, which makes them targets. Every predator in the middle Sound knows it too.

Stratford Shoal has been the most consistent read all week. The rip on the west side, where the current stacks up over that 15 to 25 foot shelf, has been holding bass on the last two hours of the outgoing and first hour of the incoming — the current-edge window when the bunker get pushed off the shoal and funneled into the deeper cut. Guys live-lining whole bunker on a fish-finder rig with 3 ounces of lead have been connecting with slot fish and the occasional overslot pushing 34, 35 inches. If you don't want to mess with live bait, a bunker-colored umbrella rig trolled slow along that same edge, or a white 2-ounce bucktail with a chunk of pork rind bounced along bottom on the drift, has been drawing strikes too. Nothing about it has been easy money — you need to be sitting on that rip at the right stage of tide, and if you show up two hours late you're fishing empty water while the fleet twenty minutes away is hooked up.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player this week, and they've been downright violent on those same bunker schools. Middle Ground Light and the water just off the Norwalk Islands have both had blitzes — sometimes short, five-minute windows where the whole surface goes white, then it shuts as fast as it started. Metal is the move: half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks, cast into the froth and ripped back fast. No finesse required. If you see the gulls stack up and dive-bomb, you've got maybe ten minutes before the school pushes under or moves off, so don't waste time tying knots — have a rod rigged and ready.

Fluke have been more of a grind. The flats off Port Jeff Harbor and the mouth of the Housatonic have given up keepers, but it's been a pick, not a bite — three or four fish for a full afternoon of drifting 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 20 to 30 feet. The warm surface layer at Kings Point and points west seems to have pushed some of the better fluke activity deeper than usual for mid-July, so if you're marking bait on the sounder but not getting bit, don't be afraid to go down to a heavier head and slow the drift right down.

Weakfish have shown up here and there — nothing to build a trip around, but a few nice ones in the 18 to 20 inch class have come off the grass edges around the Norwalk Islands on chartreuse Gulp shrimp fished under a slow retrieve at dusk. That's a species I keep half an eye on every summer because when they show, they show in short windows, usually low light, usually over soft bottom near current. Worth a cast or two if you're passing through anyway.

Blackfish are off the table with the season closed through mid-August, and porgies have been steady but unspectacular on bloodworms and clam over the rockier stretches near Charles Island and the mouth of Oyster Bay — good action for a slow afternoon, not the headline.

Looking ahead, I'd keep my eye on that thermal gradient more than the calendar. If the warm water at Kings Point keeps holding and the bunker keep stacking against that cooler eastern wall, Stratford Shoal and the Norwalk corridor should keep producing through the coming week, especially on the tide changes when the current pushes bait off the structure. If a strong blow out of the southwest comes through and mixes that gradient down, I'd expect the bite to scatter and the bass to slide deeper — worth checking the rip before you commit to a whole day out there. Bonito haven't shown yet, but this is exactly the kind of bait concentration that usually tips them off early. I'll be watching the peanut bunker close for that first sign.

reports.headline: Forget the Ocean Front — I'm Working the Back Bay Seams This Week
reports.subhead: With the ocean stacking up sloppy off the beach, the real bass and weakfish bite is happening where the warm water dumps out of the marsh.
reports.body_markdown:
Every guy at the bait shop this week wants to talk about running the ocean front or making the run out past the bar for fluke. I let them talk. Buoy readings off the Bight are showing 2.3-foot swell at a nice tight ten-second period, which sounds fine on paper until you're standing on the beach watching it stack up and roll through like a bad washing machine. That's not fishable water for a guy with two feet planted on sand, and it's not worth the gas for a boat guy either when the real action is twenty minutes closer to the dock.

Here's the thing nobody wants to hear: the ocean's cooking at almost 73 degrees right now, and that's actually part of the problem, not the solution. When the open water and the bay start running close in temperature, the fish lose that hard edge they usually hold to. But inside the inlet and back in the bay, the afternoon sun is baking those shallow mud flats and marsh creeks, and on the back half of the ebb that warm water comes pouring out through the cuts and channels like a dinner bell. That's where I've been putting my time, and it's paying off better than fighting swell on the beach.

Jones Inlet itself has been the most reliable stretch. I've been working the rocks at Short Beach on the last two hours of the outgoing, right where that warm marsh water collides with the harder inlet current. Bass in the mid-20s to low-30s have been stacking on that seam, hitting bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig with 3 ounces of lead to hold bottom against the pull. If you want to work artificials, a white bucktail with a Gulp swimming mullet trailer, cast up-current and swung through the seam, has drawn some hard strikes right at dusk. Nothing gigantic, but a solid mixed bag of schoolies and a few keepers mixed in, plus enough bluefish in the 3 to 5 pound range crashing bunker on top to keep things interesting. If you see the gulls diving tight to the jetty rocks on that outgoing push, don't wait — those blues won't stick around long once the tide goes slack.

Fluke guys, don't sleep on Sloop Channel. I drifted it three times this week in 18 to 24 feet on the dropping tide, and while it wasn't a banner week, I put together a respectable box — nothing over 4 pounds but steady action on white and chartreuse bucktails tipped with Gulp, dragged slow along the channel edges where the sand meets the deeper cuts. The bite's better on the back half of the outgoing when that current really starts moving bait off the flats. Don't waste time drifting dead water on the top of the tide — I tried, and it was a lot of nothing.

Now here's what's got me more excited than anything else this summer — the weakfish. They're really coming back into South Oyster Bay, and I'm not exaggerating when I say it's the best I've seen this fishery in years. Freeport creeks and the deeper holes off the bay side have been holding weakfish in the 18 to 24 inch range, and a few pushing better than that. Sandworms fished on a simple bottom rig, or a bucktail tipped with a strip of squid worked slow along the bottom on the last of the incoming, has been the ticket. Evening tide, right around dusk into dark, has been the strongest window — those fish seem to feed harder once the light drops off the water. If this trend holds through the rest of July, it's going to be a real story for this bay.

Porgies are around too if you want an easy box to fill — Wantagh Bridge on the bottom with clam has been steady, nothing exciting but reliable if you've got kids along or just want dinner.

I won't sugarcoat it — the striper bite inshore is scattered right now, not blitz-quality. You've got to find the bait pods and work the current edges instead of blind-casting open water. But the pattern is consistent enough that I'm confident in it. We're sliding toward a new moon this week, which means bigger tidal swings and more water moving through the inlet — that usually sharpens up the bite on those current seams even more. If the wind stays out of the south and doesn't beat up the ocean any worse, I'd keep working the inlet rocks on the outgoing and hit the bay creeks for weakfish on the evening flood. That's where my time's going, and where I'd point yours too.

reports.headline: Captree dock talk: ocean's got some shoulder to it, so we're playing the inside game
reports.subhead: With the Bight rolling 2 to 3 feet and warm, the real action this week is happening inside the inlet and up in the bay, not out front.
reports.body_markdown:
Guy pulls up to the fuel dock Thursday morning, boat still dripping, and he says to me, "Mari, I ran out to the reef and it was lumpy as hell, didn't even bother dropping a line." I told him — good, don't. That's basically been my answer to everybody this week. The Bight's been carrying a 2 to 3 foot swell on a long period, water out there sitting around 73 degrees, and while that's not dangerous by any stretch, it's enough push that the bass and the bait have both tucked themselves inside where the water's calmer and, frankly, more comfortable. When the ocean gets a little shoulder to it like this in July, I stop fighting it and start fishing the inlet and the bay instead. That's where the week's been made.

Fire Island Inlet itself has been the standout. On the last two hours of the outgoing, with that warm marsh water dumping out of the back bay creeks around Oak Beach and into the main channel, you get this current seam that sets up right off the Democrat Point side, and the bass have been parking on it like they've got a lease. I've been working 1.5-ounce bucktails, white or that chartreuse-white combo, casting up-current and letting it sink clean before I start a slow bottom retrieve back through the seam. Most of what's coming through is schoolie to low-slot, 22 to 26 inches, but we've picked a few overslot fish in the 34 to 36 inch range right at the bottom of the tide when the current's really ripping through the throat of the inlet. If you're throwing eels, same idea — dead-drift them through that seam and let the current do the work, don't retrieve too fast.

Fluke have been the more honest story this week — good, not great, and you have to work for it. The Robert Moses bridges, both the buoy channel side and the flats off the Coast Guard station, have been giving up fluke in the 3 to 5 pound range on the outgoing, with the odd 6 or 7 pound fish mixed in if you're covering ground. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow along the bottom in 25 to 35 feet — that's been the winning combo. What I'm noticing is the bigger fish are sliding a little deeper than they were in June, which tells me they're feeling that warmer water up top and getting comfortable a bit lower in the column. If you're marking bait on the sounder around 28 to 32 feet, that's where I'd put the bait down first.

Bluefish have shown up with some teeth behind them the last ten days, mostly working the rips off Democrat Point on the first two hours of the incoming, chopping through peanut bunker that are starting to push into the bay in real numbers now. If you see the birds working and the water nervous, that's your cue — a wire leader with a diamond jig or a bunker spoon will get bit fast, and these aren't small blues, we've had several in the 8 to 10 pound class that will absolutely test your drag. Good problem to have, and it's a nice change of pace when the bass get finicky.

Bay-side, porgies have been steady over the reef structure off Nicoll Bay and around the Sayville flats, small hooks, sandworms or clam, standard high-low rigs, and they'll keep you bent while you wait out a tide change. Weakfish talk has been quieter than I'd like this year — I've heard of a few being taken incidentally on bucktails worked slow along the deeper edges of the bay near Patchogue, but it's not the kind of numbers that make me tell you to go target them specifically. If you stumble into one, count your blessings and don't tell anybody exactly where.

The bigger pattern here, and why I keep steering people inside instead of out front, comes down to that ocean-to-bay temperature gap. The open Atlantic's holding warm and rough, which is uncomfortable water for bait to sit in, so everything — bunker, peanut bunker, spearing — is sliding into the calmer, structured water of the inlet and the bay mouth to get out of it. Bass and blues are following that bait right to the door. It's a pretty simple equation once you see it: rough ocean pushes forage inside, predators follow forage, and suddenly your best water isn't the water everybody's staring at from the beach, it's twenty feet off the jetty rocks at Democrat Point on a dropping tide.

Looking ahead, if that ocean swell settles down even a little by the weekend, I'd expect some of that bass activity to spread back out toward the surf line at Fire Island and Robert Moses beach, especially at first light when the water's calmest. Until then, I'd keep my plans flexible — fish the inlet seam on the outgoing for bass, hit the bridges for fluke on the same tide, and keep an eye out for bird activity for the blues. The moon's working toward the new phase later this month, which should juice up the current a bit more and tighten these bite windows even further. I'll be out there most mornings out of Captree chasing it — come find me at the dock if you want to compare notes.

reports.headline: Skipped Poor Man's, Ran Straight to the Wilmington Elbow — Six Yellowfin, One White Released
reports.subhead: A warm eddy pinched against the canyon wall gave us a hard morning bite before the current went slack and the fish stopped feeding.
reports.body_markdown:
I had two options Wednesday morning and about forty-five minutes to decide between them. Poor Man's had been chattering for a week — small rats mixed with a few respectable yellowfin — but it's crowded water this time of year and the reports were already three days old by the time they hit my ears. Wilmington's eastern wall, up around 38°27'N, 74°09'W where the canyon breaks toward the Sausages, had a cleaner story: a Gulf Stream eddy had pinched in tight against the 100-fathom curve, and the satellite imagery I was working off showed a hard edge instead of a gradual smear. Hard edges concentrate bait. Bait concentrates fish. I ran the extra eight miles.

It paid off, but not the way I'd have scripted it. We started trolling the temp break at first light — naked ballyhoo doubled with a green machine on the shotgun, a small Ilander/ballyhoo combo down the middle, and a spreader bar out back to test the water before committing spread real estate. Inside twenty minutes we had a triple hookup on yellowfin in the 35 to 55-pound class, right where the color changed from that flat green inshore water to a cleaner blue-green push, water reading in the low 70s at the surface — consistent with what the offshore buoys were showing, 72-73°F out past the shelf. That's warm enough to hold yellowfin comfortably and it's exactly the kind of number that makes bigeye stack a little deeper on the same structure, though we didn't get into anything heavier than yellowfin this trip.

The morning bite ran about ninety minutes before the current went from ripping to lazy, and the fish shut off almost like someone flipped a switch. That's canyon fishing in July — the eddy edge is a moving target, and once the tide-driven current relaxes against it, the bait scatters and the tuna stop working the seam. We picked up two more yellowfin working the corner south of the break on a slow troll with cedar plugs before I made the call to switch tactics. Rather than keep burning fuel searching for a bite that had already shut down, we set up to chunk over a hard bottom notch in about 850 feet, butterfish chunks fished on 50-pound fluorocarbon leader, circle hooks, letting the current carry the chunks down without weight. That's where the sixth yellowfin came, and where we had a white marlin come up on a naked ballyhoo skipped just off the flat line — we hooked him, fought him about ten minutes, and released him healthy at the boat. No sail sightings, no wahoo, though the water temp and the bait presence out there suggest wahoo should start showing on the high-speed gear in the next couple weeks if this pattern holds.

Honest assessment: it was a good morning, not a great week. I ran two other trips to Wilmington this week that didn't produce like Wednesday's — one was a troll-only day where we marked plenty of squid on the sounder but couldn't buy a strike, and I suspect the fish had already fed heavy overnight on that bait ball and just weren't interested at 9 a.m. The other trip got blown out early by a building sea state, 2 to 3 foot swell at a short period that made working the spread sloppy, and we came home with one mahi caught incidentally on a rigged ballyhoo near a weed line in about 900 feet. Three trips, one that really produced, two that were work for modest reward. That's a realistic week out here right now — not a bad one, but not the kind where you fill the box without effort.

The bigger picture: squid presence out along the canyon edges this month is a real driver. Shortfin and Illex squid pushing up from the shelf edge are exactly the forage that keeps yellowfin and bigeye holding tight to structure instead of roaming open water, and it's why the bite has been more productive on the hard edges and canyon corners than out in open blue water. If that squid stays put — and there's no strong reason to think it's leaving with water temps sitting where they are — I'd expect the pattern to hold: troll the break at first light while the current's still moving, then be ready to switch to the chunk bag once the tide goes slack and the fish stop chasing.

Looking ahead, if the eddy holds its position against the Wilmington wall through the weekend, I'd run the same corner again — 38°27'N area, working the 100-fathom curve toward the Sausages. If it slides east the way these eddies sometimes do after a few days of current, I'd shift south toward the Baltimore side rather than chase it blind. Either way, I wouldn't leave the dock without both spreads rigged and a chunk bag ready, because right now the fish are telling you when the troll bite ends far more clearly than any weather app will.

reports.headline: Peconic's summer clock strikes porgy season — Shelter Island humps loaded, bass gone nocturnal
reports.subhead: The bay warmed early again this year, and now it's paying out porgies by the dozen while stripers wait for dark to feed.
reports.body_markdown:
By the second week of July the Peconic has usually settled into its summer groove, and this year is no exception — if anything it got there a touch early. The bay always heats faster than the Sound because it's shallower and more enclosed, and that head start shows up every summer in the same order: porgies first, fluke tucked into the channels once the flats get too warm for them, and stripers sliding onto the night shift as the surface temps climb into the mid-70s. That's exactly the pattern we're in right now.

Start with the porgies, because that's where the easy, honest fun is this week. The humps around Shelter Island — the drop east of Jennys Point, the rocky patches off Cedar Island, and the bar running out from Hay Beach — are holding thick porgy schools in 15 to 25 feet. High-low rigs with size 6 or 8 hooks, half a sandworm or a chunk of skimmer clam, fished on the bottom during the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing. That current-edge window is when the porgies really turn on and feed with confidence instead of picking. Anchor up rather than drift here — porgies want that bait sitting still on structure, not swimming past. Guys working these humps this week have had steady action, fish running 10 to 13 inches with enough 14s mixed in to make it worth culling for the pan. This is about as reliable as fishing gets on the East End right now, and it should hold through August as long as the water stays clean.

Fluke have done what fluke always do once the shallow bay water pushes past 70 — they've pulled off the open flats and settled into the channels where there's moving water and a little more oxygen. Noyack Bay channel, the Shelter Island Sound drop along the ferry route, and the deeper cut off Cedar Point have all been holding fish in 18 to 35 feet. The bite is honest but not a bonanza — you're covering ground to find the pockets. White or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift with the tide pushing you through the deeper water, has been the most consistent combination. Best window is the two hours around the tide change, when the current slows enough to keep the bait in the strike zone instead of racing past it. Fish are mostly in the 16 to 19 inch range with keepers mixed in — nothing to write home about size-wise, but enough action to make an afternoon worthwhile if you're willing to move around and not just sit on one drift.

Stripers are the honest disappointment of the week if you're fishing daylight hours, and I'll say it straight — the bay's warm enough now that the bass have mostly gone nocturnal. Regional water temps back that up; the Sound and ocean side are both sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, and the Peconic's shallower water is likely running a couple degrees warmer than that on a sunny afternoon. Bass don't like feeding hard in that kind of warmth during the day, so the smart money has shifted to the last hour of light and into full dark. Orient Point and the rip off Plum Gut are still throwing bass after sundown, working eels or bunker chunks on the outgoing tide when the current rips through that gut and disorients the bait. Gardiners Bay has some bunker schools moving through, and where you find those pods, there are bluefish underneath them tearing them apart — that's been a daytime bite worth chasing if you spot the surface commotion. Bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, or a diamond jig worked through the melee, will connect. Bluefish have been the more dependable daytime target the last couple weeks while the bass sulk in the heat.

Weakfish are showing in small numbers around Three Mile Harbor and the mouth of Northwest Harbor — nothing to build a trip around, but a nice bonus if you're working soft plastics in that zone for something else. A few 18 to 22 inch fish have turned up on light jigs fished near the bottom on the last of the ebb.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change dramatically this week unless we get a real cool-down or a strong blow to mix the water. The moon's past new and building toward the first quarter, which means tidal push is moderate rather than extreme — good for the porgy bite, which doesn't need a hard current to produce, but it also means the fluke channels won't get the strong flush that sometimes triggers a better bite. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd spend the morning on the Shelter Island porgy grounds while the tide's right, then switch over to Orient Point or the Gut for the evening bass and blues as the light fades. That combination — daytime porgies, evening bass — is about as solid a read on this bay as you'll get in mid-July. Keep an eye on the bait schools in Gardiners Bay too; if the bunker stick around, the blues and the occasional bass working them during daylight could turn into the best action of the week.

reports.headline: New moon springs load up the Canal rips as current runs hard both ends
reports.subhead: Bigger water this week means bigger bait pinned against the rock — here's where the current seams are stacking bass right now.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Canal was still shaking off that stretch of soft, lazy tides we get around the quarter moons — current running but nothing with teeth to it, and the bite matched it. Schoolies mostly, a few mid-20s mixed in at the turn, but nothing that made you want to skip breakfast. That's changing fast. We're sliding into new moon, and the springs that come with it are building toward peak alignment right around July 11-13. If you've fished this ditch as long as I have, you know what that means: current velocity ramps up at both ends, the rip lines sharpen from mush into something you can actually read, and bait that's been scattered in slack water gets pinned hard against structure. This is the week the Canal remembers it's the best current-fishing on the East Coast.

Here's the mechanics of it, because it matters. On spring tides the flow through the ditch can push 5 knots or better at max current off the Bourne and Sagamore Bridge pilings, and that extra push is exactly what turns the East End rip — the water spilling off Sandwich side toward Cape Cod Bay — from a gentle seam into a defined, foamy edge you can cast a plug into with confidence. Same story at the West End, where the Buzzards Bay outflow past Mashnee and Hog Island stacks up against the current seam running off the rock jetty. Bigger tide, bigger differential between the fast lane and the eddy behind it, and that differential is where stripers stack up and let the current do the work for them. I don't fish the middle of the flood or ebb on a big tide — I fish the last ninety minutes into the turn, when the rip is still cranking but starting to organize, and the fish move up onto the structure to feed instead of holding deep and coasting.

Right now the East End is producing best on the tail of the east-to-west flow, the stretch where the water dumps out of Cape Cod Bay past the Sandwich Marina and Herring Run. I've had reports of stripers to 30-plus inches taking white and chartreuse Ava jigs with a red surgical tube trailer worked through that rip at first light, bounced just off bottom and let it swing with the current instead of ripping it against the flow. At night, live eels fished on a fish-finder rig off the rocks near the Herring Run outflow have been drawing the better class of fish — not a lot of them, but the ones that show are the 20-30 pound Canal fish everybody's after. That's the honest read: it's not a numbers game right now, it's a quality-over-quantity bite, and you need to put your time in during that narrow window when the tide's still moving hard but hasn't gone full washing-machine on you.

West End has been the more consistent producer for volume. The current seam running off Mashnee Island and down toward Phinneys Harbor has held bluefish mixed with schoolie bass most mornings, and topwater guys throwing pencil poppers and Super Strike Zig-Zags off the rocks near the Weight Handling Facility have been connecting at first light before the sun gets up over the trees. Once that sun's up and the tide's still running, switch to bucktails — half-ounce to one-ounce white or olive, tipped with a strip of pork rind or a swim shad — and work the current seam where the fast water meets the eddy behind Hog Island. That's a textbook Canal ambush point and it's fishing exactly like it should on this bigger water.

Fluke guys shouldn't ignore what's happening at the west end either. The sandy stretches off Mashnee flats and the deeper water in the mouth of Phinneys Harbor have been holding keeper fluke on the drift, four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on a half-ounce bucktail, working the last two hours of the outgoing when the current sweeps bait off the flats into the deeper channel. Nothing spectacular in numbers, but a few fish in the 18-20 inch range have come out of there in the past week, which for Canal-adjacent fluke water is a solid showing.

What I'm watching for the coming week: the bonito corridor down south has widened out of Block Island into the Newport-Point Judith stretch, with the old cold wall between the islands and Rhode Island Sound collapsing. That water's a few days from us at best, but if that warm plume keeps pushing north through Buzzards Bay, Wings Neck and the west end approaches are where I'd expect the first scout fish to show — false albacore usually beat bonito into this zone by a couple weeks most years, so keep half an eye on the bait schools working the rip off Wings Neck in the next two to three weeks. Too early to fish for them specifically, but not too early to start checking.

For this week specifically: if the wind stays out of the southwest and lays down through the evenings like it's supposed to, I'd fish the East End rip on the last of the ebb Friday and Saturday night, right into the new moon peak. Big tide, hard current, bait pinned against the rocks — that's the recipe that's produced the better fish all summer here. Backup plan if the East End's blown out or too strong to fish comfortably: West End seam off Mashnee on the bucktail bite, which has been steadier even if the average fish runs smaller. Either way, fish the turn, not the middle, and let the current tell you when to be there.

reports.headline: New moon springs load the rivers — stripers stack the sunset flood as mackerel run thick off Monhegan
reports.subhead: Big water this weekend puts bass in the river mouths at dusk, while cod and haddock hold deep in the Bay against a cold upwelling push.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the wind sat out of the northeast more mornings than not, and that's the kind of wind that does something specific to this coast — it shoves the warm skin water offshore and lets colder bottom water well up underneath it. You could feel it stepping off the boat at Eastern Egg Rock and at the Monhegan mooring field — the air had that raw edge to it even with the sun out, and the surface felt a good clip cooler than it did two weeks back. That upwelling has kept the groundfish honest. Cod, haddock, and pollock in Penobscot Bay have stayed down in the cooler water instead of creeping up onto the shallower humps like they will in a warm stretch, and that's actually been good news for anybody willing to fish deep and patient.

We're coming into new moon now, peaking through the weekend, and that means spring tides — the biggest exchange we'll see until the next cycle. Fox Islands Thorofare and Eggemoggin Reach are going to be hauling water hard on both the flood and the drain, and out at Monhegan the current off White Head and the backside ledges is going to rip through midtide like a river. That kind of flow pushes bait — herring, mackerel, peanut bunker — and it pushes it hard, which is exactly why the sunset flood at the river mouths has turned into the thing to chase this week. Big springs concentrate feed in the funnel points, and predators know it. St. George River mouth, the Medomak, the run at Damariscotta — all of them are worth a look on that last two hours of incoming water right up through dusk.

Striper action has been real but not a gimme. I had three trips out toward the mouth of the St. George in the last ten days, connected on two of them, and the pattern was consistent — nothing doing on the early flood, then the fish showed up hard in that last hour and a half before and right at sunset, right as the current really got moving on this building spring tide. Schoolies mostly, 22 to 28 inches, with a few better fish mixed in that felt like keeper-class when they leaned into the drag. Swimming a white or bone Redfin along the current seams where the fresh water meets the salt has been the most consistent producer, and a chunk of mackerel on a fish-finder rig, drifted right through the funnel on the last of the incoming, has taken a couple of the bigger fish. If you fish it, get there before the tide peaks — once it goes to high stand and starts to slack, the bite shuts off almost like someone flipped a switch.

Mackerel have been thick around Eastern Egg Rock and off the east side of Monhegan, schools stacked from the surface down to about 35 feet over structure. Standard mackerel trees with a bit of bright jig on the bottom hook have been filling coolers fast on a slow bite window — you can tell when they're there because the birds are working the same water, terns diving and the puffins cutting through. That's also brought a few bluefish into the mix around Egg Rock, chopping bait on top in the early morning calm before the wind builds. Nothing giant — cocktail blues mostly — but they'll hit a small metal jig or a Deadly Dick worked fast on the surface, and it's a nice change of pace between mackerel drops.

Groundfish in the Bay have been the tougher story, and I'll be straight about it — this cold upwelled water has the cod and haddock down deep and a little sluggish, not aggressive the way they get when the thermocline sets up just right. Best luck has come from the channel between Vinalhaven and North Haven and out toward the deeper water off Matinicus, working diamond jigs and bar rigs tipped with clam belly down in 120 to 150 feet, right on bottom, slow lift-and-drop with long pauses. Pollock have actually been the more reliable eating fish this week — schooling up over the humps in 60 to 90 feet around the Fox Islands and hitting jigs worked with a bit more speed higher in the water column, 30 to 50 feet down. If you want fish for the table with less patience required, that's where I'd point the bow.

Looking ahead, this new moon spring tide peaks right through Monday, and that's the window I'd fish hardest for stripers at the river mouths — the flood-to-sunset overlap is about as good an alignment as you get up here, current, light, and bait all lining up together. If the wind backs off the northeast and lets the surface warm back up even a couple degrees, I'd expect the cod and haddock to come up a bit shallower and turn more aggressive, so that's worth checking again toward the end of the week. Mackerel should hold at Egg Rock and Monhegan for now, though once these big tides start really flushing bait out of the bay, they have a habit of pushing farther offshore fast — if you want a box of mackerel for bait or the table, I wouldn't wait too long. Plan A this week is the sunset flood at the river mouths; Plan B, if the bass don't show or the wind kicks up onshore and muddies the funnel, is running out to the mackerel schools and picking off a bluefish or two while you're at it. Either way, respect the current on these springs — it's moving a lot of water fast, and that cuts both ways for the fish and for you.

reports.headline: New moon springs push stripers deep into Biddeford Pool as bluefish crash Higgins Beach
reports.subhead: Big tides and a warming shoreline have the bass feeding on the push while blues chop bait right in the wash — but Prouts Neck cod fishing stays a grind.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the wind sat out of the southwest more days than not, which is exactly what you want along this stretch this time of year — it lays the surf down, keeps the green water tight to the beach, and lets the sand eels and pogies stack up instead of getting scattered by a northeast chop. We had a few gray, drizzly mornings mixed in, but nothing that rolled the water or dirtied it up bad. The shoreline temps have been climbing steady through the low-to-mid 60s, warm enough that the bait is thick and the fish are hunting instead of just passing through.

Now we're swinging into a new moon, and that means spring tides — bigger swings, stronger push, more water moving through the guts and creeks than we've seen since before the last full moon. That's the whole story this week. Biddeford Pool runs on tide more than almost any spot on this coast, and a new moon flood shoves a wall of water and bait through the mouth by the Yacht Club and up into the back channels. Friday through Monday, the high stand is lining up close to sunset, which is the exact scenario that gets stripers feeding hard right at last light instead of sulking off in deeper water. I haven't seen a window like this stack up since the June full moon, and if you can only fish one tide this week, make it the evening flood.

Stripers have been showing well but not everywhere — this isn't a blanket bite, you still have to find them. The Pool has been the most consistent read: fish stacking on the last two hours of the incoming, working the current seam off the rocks below the Bridge, and pushing bait up against the flats on the inside once the tide tops out. Live mackerel and eels fished on a fish-finder rig have been getting bit right at the color change where the clean ocean water meets the darker back-bay water, but the better move for most guys has been swimming a 3-ounce Savage Gear sand eel or a Game On soft-plastic paddletail right through that seam on the drift. Slow and steady beats a fast retrieve — these fish are eating sand eels, not chasing anything frantic.

Higgins Beach has had the more visible show. Bluefish, mostly cocktail-size in the 2-to-4-pound range with a few better ones mixed in, have been blitzing right in the wash on the last of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming, chopping bait practically at your feet some mornings. Pencil poppers — the old Gibbs wood ones or a Super Strike — worked with a walk-the-dog cadence right through the whitewash have been the ticket, and if the blues are up top busting you don't need to overthink the retrieve, just keep it moving and expect to get bit. Bring wire leader or you'll lose gear all morning. The bass have been mixed in at Higgins too, but they're holding a little deeper than the blues, so if you're getting cut off on wire but not connecting, downsize to a 40-pound fluorocarbon leader and work the outer sandbar where the stripers are sitting.

Prouts Neck has fished the way it usually fishes on a southwest wind — tough but not dead. The ledges off the point have given up a scattered bass or two on bucktails tipped with a strip of pork rind or a curly-tail trailer, worked slow along the boulder fields on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Cod fishing out deeper, on the rockier bottom off Cape Elizabeth, has been a grind — you're working for every fish, jigging diamond jigs or clam bellies on a high-low rig in 60 to 90 feet, and most trips are producing a few keepers rather than a pile. The water out there stays cooler longer than the beach water, which the cod like, but it also means the bite windows are shorter and tighter to the tide change. Mackerel have been reliable filler almost everywhere along the rocks — Wells Harbor breakwater, the Cape Elizabeth shoreline, even inside the Pool on the last of the flood — small Norwegian jigs or a mackerel tree worked with a quick snap have been good for fast action and a bait bucket full of fresh strip bait for the bigger stuff.

Flounder have been steady but slow-going in Wells Harbor and the calmer stretches behind Pine Point, working bloodworms or clam strips on a simple two-hook flounder rig, bounced along the mud on the bottom of the tide when the current slacks off. Nobody's filling a cooler with flounder right now, but if you want a change of pace and a fish that'll actually eat dinner, that's the play on a slow-tide morning.

Looking ahead, the spring tide push through the weekend is the thing to build around. If the wind stays out of the southwest like it's supposed to, I'd be at Biddeford Pool for the evening flood Friday into Monday, working that current seam below the bridge as the sun drops — that's where I'd put my money this week. Higgins Beach should keep producing blues on top through most tide stages as long as the bait stays pinned to the beach, so it's a good backup if the Pool's slow or crowded. If a northeast wind sneaks in behind this system, expect the outer ledges at Prouts Neck to cool off fast and the cod bite offshore to tighten up even further — that's when I'd shift effort back inshore and let the rocks do the work instead of chasing open water.

reports.headline: Springs tide builds on the new moon — stripers push Hampton Harbor, groundfish hold tight to the Shoals breaks
reports.subhead: NE wind upwelling sharpened the structure off White Island while the incoming build stacked bass against the Hampton inlet rocks.
reports.body_markdown:
We're heading into the new moon, and if you've fished this stretch of coast for more than a season you already know what that means before I say it: springs tides building all weekend, bigger swings on the Hampton and Piscataqua gauges, and current at the Shoals that'll flat-out move a boat if you're not paying attention to your scope. New moon lands midweek, and the buildup through Friday-into-Monday is when I want to be on the water, not after. Last week's wind sat out of the northeast more than I'd like for comfort but exactly where I want it for fishing — that upwelling pattern pushed cooler, cleaner water up onto the ledges around White Island and Halibut Rocks, and it sharpened the edge on those breaks the way it always does. Cold water stacking against warmer surface water off the Shoals concentrates bait, and bait on an edge means cod and haddock sitting tight to structure instead of scattered over mud. That's the setup I fish for.

Water temp in the harbors has been climbing on the flood — nothing shocking, just steady summer warm-up — while out at the Shoals the bottom stayed cooler under that NE push. That thermal split matters. It's why the mackerel showed up thick around Star Island and Appledore this week, working the surface in the morning calm before the boat traffic scatters them, and it's why the groundfish stayed deep and tight rather than spreading out. Going into this week, expect the wind to back around more southerly by the weekend as the new moon springs peak — that usually softens the upwelling signal, so if you're going to fish the Shoals structure hard, earlier in the week is your window before that cold edge relaxes.

Stripers are the story inshore right now, and Hampton Harbor is doing exactly what it does on a building spring tide — pushing bait and fish through the inlet on the last two hours of the incoming. I had a report of fish to 28 inches taken right off the jetty rocks at Hampton on the top of the flood, working white and chartreuse soft plastics — 4-inch Slug-Go style baits on a light jighead — swung tight against the rip where the harbor current meets the ocean push. Same pattern's working at Rye Harbor breakwater on the same stage of tide, though the fish there have been more scattered, more schoolie-sized, mixed with the occasional bluefish that'll cut your leader if you're not running at least 20-pound fluoro. Great Boars Head has been worth a look on the outgoing at first light — bait pods of pogies pushing off the beach have pulled some bass tight to the surf line, and a swimming plug worked parallel to the beach has produced better than anything thrown straight out.

The Piscataqua is fishing the way it always does in July — you need to time the tide precisely or you're wasting gas. Stripers are holding on the current seams below the Memorial Bridge and down toward Henderson Point, and they want the tide moving, not slack. Live mackerel under a slip float, drifted through the seam on the last hour of the ebb, has been the most consistent producer I've heard of, though it's not a numbers game — one or two quality fish a trip is realistic, not a bent rod every cast. Flounder are still around in Portsmouth Harbor and up in the back channels off Pierce Island — small hooks, sandworms or clams, fished right on bottom in that softer mud current away from the main channel. Nothing to write home about size-wise this week, mostly 12-14 inch fish, but steady if you're patient and anchored in the right spot on the bottom of the tide.

Offshore, the cod and haddock bite at the Shoals has been honest work, not easy work. Boats working Sunken Ledge and the rock piles south of White Island in 80 to 130 feet found haddock stacked tight on the NE-sharpened edge I mentioned, taking clam bait and diamond jigs tipped with a sandworm strip on the drift — but you had to hit the tide right. Slack water scattered them; moving water on either side of the tide change held them tight to structure. Cod have been mixed in but smaller than we'd like this time of year, mostly short fish thrown back, with the occasional keeper in the 24-26 inch range coming off bottom bounced jigs worked slow. If I had a boat this week I'd fish the two hours around the tide change, not the middle of the flood or ebb when everything's moving too fast to hold bottom without a pound of lead.

Looking ahead — the new moon Tuesday means the biggest tides we'll see this month, and that PM flood window at Hampton Harbor lining up with sunset over the next several days is worth building a trip around. Bass tend to commit harder on that last push of light with a strong tide behind them, and if the bait stays stacked at the inlet the way it has been, I'd expect that pattern to hold through the weekend. Offshore, watch the wind — if it backs southerly like it's forecast to, that cold upwelled edge at the Shoals will soften and the groundfish will spread back out over more bottom, which usually means slower, more marks-and-miss fishing instead of the tight, predictable bite we've had. Best case, one more good push of NE wind before it shifts gives us another day or two of that sharp edge. Either way, I'd rather fish the tide change with a plan than the middle of it hoping.

reports.headline: New moon springs push Little Egg fluke into the cuts as sunset stripers return to Barnegat Light
reports.subhead: Bay water cooked into the high 70s and shoved the fluke out — the ocean side and the inlets are holding the action while the weakfish stay a no-show.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what it does every July when we get a stretch of sun and slack air — it cooked. Great Bay's shallow flats and the back stretches up toward the Mullica pushed into the high 70s, and that shut the door on the grass-flat fluke bite fast. I had two guys tell me they marked bait and structure all over the meadows off Graveling Point and couldn't buy a bite past nine in the morning. That's not bad luck, that's biology — fluke don't like soup, and once the shallow water gets that warm they slide for the channels, the deeper cuts, and eventually the inlets where there's still some exchange with the ocean. We had a couple NE wind days midweek that helped push cooler water — I'm talking mid-70s pushing into the low 70s — through Barnegat and Little Egg inlets, and that's exactly where the better fluke have been sitting since.

This week the moon flips new on the 10th, which means spring tides are building right now and peak through Saturday into Monday. Bigger swings at Barnegat Light and Little Egg — more water moving means more current in the cuts, which means bait gets flushed and predators get organized around it. That also reopens a PM window we haven't had since the June full moon: the flood tide stacking up right around sunset. Low light, moving water, and warm surf temps — that's the recipe that's been missing on the striper side for weeks, and it's back starting tonight through Monday.

Fluke-wise, the shift to the inlet and ocean side is the story right now. Little Egg Inlet on the outgoing, working the drop-off just inside the throat in 14 to 18 feet, has been the most consistent stretch — 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom, picking up keepers in the 19 to 22 inch range with the occasional better fish mixed in. Same story off the Beach Haven side channels and the deeper bends up toward Ship Bottom — anywhere there's current scouring a defined edge. Bay flats are mostly done for now unless you're fishing early, first light, before the sun gets on the water. Don't waste a midday tide on the meadows this week — go to the moving water.

Stripers have been a grind through late June, mostly schoolie-sized fish scattered thin, but the pattern for this weekend into Monday is legitimate. With the spring tide flood lining up against sunset, I'd be at Barnegat Light working the rocks on the last hour of light into dark — white bucktails, needlefish, or a darter worked slow across the seam where the jetty current meets the open water. Holgate's north end rip has been holding fish too, mostly on the last two hours of the incoming, with some bigger fish mixed into the schoolies — nothing giant, but 28 to 34 inch fish have shown up enough that it's worth the walk. If the wind stays light through the weekend, that PM flood-into-dark window at both spots is where I'd put my time. If it kicks up out of the east and blows the surf out, I'd shift to Little Egg on the last of the outgoing instead — dirtier water there tends to concentrate fish tight to structure rather than scatter them.

Bluefish have been riding shotgun with the stripers, chopping mullet in the wash at Holgate and off the Ship Bottom beaches on calm mornings — nothing huge, mostly 2 to 4 pounders, but they'll hit the same bucktails and metal you're throwing for bass, so bring a wire leader or expect to lose gear.

Kingfish are doing their steady, unglamorous thing in the surf at Holgate and the south end beaches — bloodworm and Fishbites on a high-low rig, small sinkers, fished tight to the wash on the bottom stages of the tide. Not exciting, but it's been dependable, and it's a good one to hand a kid a rod for while you work a plug rod on the same beach.

Black drum are basically done for the season up in the Mullica and around Graveling Point — that bite peaked back in May and by now it's stragglers only, so I wouldn't plan a trip around them.

And I'll say this plainly because I think honesty matters more than hype: weakfish have been a ghost. Water temps in the Mullica and Great Bay have been in the range where weakfish are supposed to show, and they just haven't. I've heard it from enough people now that I don't think it's a fluke of reporting — the temperature threshold that used to be a reliable trigger isn't producing fish the way it used to. If you want to try, dusk on soft plastics — 4-inch pearl or chartreuse paddletails — around the deeper holes off Graveling Point is still the right idea. Just don't build your week around it.

Looking ahead: the spring tide peak Saturday through Monday is the best striper window we've had since the June full moon, and if the wind cooperates I'd fish the sunset flood at Barnegat Light first, Holgate second. Fluke will keep favoring the inlet and ocean-side channels as long as the bay stays warm, so work the moving water on the outgoing and don't bother with the flats past mid-morning. If the bass don't show at the jetty, my backup plan is always the same this time of year — Little Egg on the last of the outgoing with a bucktail, because something's usually willing to eat there even on an off night.

reports.headline: New moon springs flood the Hook at sunset as bay fluke push to the channels
reports.subhead: Big tides and warm bay water are moving fish out of Raritan Bay's flats and into the inlets — here's where to find them this week.
reports.body_markdown:
We're rolling into a new moon this week, which means spring tides — bigger swings, stronger current, more water moving in and out of the bay than we've seen since the June full moon. That matters more than people think. Last week the bay sat warm and mostly slack on the neaps, water pushing into the upper 70s over Keyport Flats and up into the Navesink, and the fish did what warm, sluggish water always makes them do — they left. Fluke that were happily working the flats in June are sliding out toward the channels and the ocean side where there's actual current and cooler water holding oxygen. The new moon change kicks that process into high gear. Bigger tides mean more exchange, more bait getting flushed out of the back bay, and — this is the part I'm watching closest — a PM flood tide that's now converging with sunset. That's the window. High stand meeting last light on a building spring tide is about as good a striper setup as this zone offers in July, and it hasn't lined up like this since before the last full moon.

So that's the why. Peak alignment on this new moon push is Friday through Monday, July 10-13, with the tide swings growing each day into the weekend. If you've got one evening to fish this week, that's the window — not because I'm promising fish, but because the mechanics are right: moving water, dropping light, bait getting squeezed through the Chapel Hill Channel and out past the Hook.

On the striper side, it's been a scratchy month but not a dead one. Guys working live bunker on fish-finder rigs off Romer Shoal and down along the edge of Flynn's Knoll have been picking at holdover bass in the 26-34 inch range, mostly on the last two hours of the incoming into dusk. Depths matter here — 18 to 25 feet along the Knoll's drop, tighter to bottom than you'd fish in spring. The Rip at the Hook has given up a few better fish to guys drifting live eels after dark, but it's been an every-other-trip proposition, not a sure thing. With this new moon flood-sunset window opening up, I'd be at Romer Shoal or working the edge of the Ambrose Channel with a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig right as that tide turns to flood and the sun starts dropping. That's where I'm putting my evening this weekend.

Fluke is where the real story is right now, and it's a mixed bag depending on where you fish it. Inside the bay, Keyport Flats and the Highlands flats have gone quiet — too warm, too slow-moving water, and the fluke know it. But push out to the channels and it's a different world. Sandy Hook Channel and the mouth of the bay near Ambrose have been holding good numbers of keeper fluke, 18 to 22 inches, with the occasional bigger fish mixed in — there was a doormat pushing 12 pounds weighed out of the lower harbor a couple weeks back, and that tells you there are still genuinely big fish working through this system on their way to deeper water. Drift 4-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, 25 to 35 feet of water, timed to the last two hours of the outgoing when the channel current really starts ripping bait out of the bay. That outgoing push is the whole game for fluke right now — the fish are stacking on the current edges waiting for it to deliver food, and if you're not fishing that tide stage you're fishing the wrong two hours.

Bluefish have been a bright spot and an honest one — no exaggeration needed. Bunker schools have been thick around Romer Shoal and pushing into the mouth of the Raritan, and the blues have been all over them, especially on that same outgoing tide when bait gets pinned against the channel edges. Poppers and metal — Ava jigs, diamond jigs in the 2-3 ounce range — worked fast through the peanut bunker schools have been producing non-stop action, 3 to 6 pound blues mostly, with some bigger choppers mixed in early morning. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod this week, this is it.

Weakfish, I have to be honest with you — they're just not here. Water's warm enough on paper, but that threshold alone hasn't meant anything the last few seasons, and this year's no different. I haven't heard of a single weakfish report out of the Navesink or the Shrewsbury in weeks. I wouldn't burn a tide targeting them right now.

Porgies are steady and unspectacular off Romer Shoal and along the edges of Flynn's Knoll — bloodworms or squid strips on a high-low rig in 15-20 feet will keep a rod bent for kids and beginners, which is worth remembering in July when everybody wants an easy win.

Looking ahead: the new moon spring tides build through the weekend and peak Sunday-Monday, so that PM flood-sunset striper window is going to be at its best then — I'd fish it two nights if I could swing it, because these alignments don't come around often. On the fluke side, keep working the channels and inlets on the outgoing as long as the bay stays warm, because that pattern isn't reversing anytime soon. And keep an eye on the ocean side of the Hook — with warm water pushing up the coast and the first bonito starting to show further east, it's not out of the question we see an early Spanish mackerel or bonito flash through the Hook's rip before the month is out. Nothing confirmed yet, but that's exactly the kind of signal worth watching for.

reports.headline: New moon springs load the inlets — fluke run to the rocks as bass play it coy
reports.subhead: Bigger tides and cooler upwelled water are pushing fluke out of the bays and into Manasquan and Shark River, while the bass bite stays a dawn-only proposition.
reports.body_markdown:
Twenty-five years of standing on these rocks and I still get excited when the tide chart tells me something's coming. This week it's telling me the moon's going dark — new moon lands right in this window — and that means spring tides building through the weekend, peaking around the 11th to 13th. Bigger swings, stronger current, more water moving through Manasquan and Shark River inlets on both ends of the cycle. That's the kind of setup that either turns a jetty on or blows it out entirely, depending on how much push you get and whether the wind fights the tide or rides with it.

Last week the story was heat. The back bays — Shark River especially, up past the Route 35 bridge — pushed into the high 70s, and that's too warm for fluke to sit comfortable. They did what they always do when the bay gets soupy: they ran for the inlets and the ocean front, where a little NE breeze has been upwelling cooler water along the beach, holding in the low 70s. That's a clean, predictable pattern, and it's the one I'd build a week around. The bass, on the other hand, have been more stubborn — some fish around at first light, but nothing you'd call consistent, and I'm not going to stand here and tell you otherwise.

Start with the fluke, because that's where the sure money is right now. Manasquan Inlet on the outgoing, from the Route 71 bridge down through the channel to the jetty mouth, has been holding fish in 15 to 25 feet. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom, tipped with a strip of squid if you want insurance — that combo has been taking keepers in the 19 to 22-inch range, with a few better fish mixed in on the last hour of the drop. Shark River Inlet is doing the same thing on a smaller scale — work the deeper hole off the Belmar side, tight to the rocks, same bucktail-and-Gulp approach, chartreuse if the water's got any color to it from the runoff. The key is timing: you want the last two hours of outgoing, when the bait gets pinned against the structure and the fluke stack up to ambush it. Don't waste your morning on the flood — that's when they scatter back toward the bay edges.

Stripers are the harder conversation. The jetty rocks from Sea Bright down through Belmar have given up bass at dawn, but it's a short window and you need to be standing there when it opens, not showing up after the sun's already up over the water tower. Sea Bright rocks, the stretch north of the Rumson-Sea Bright bridge, has thrown a few schoolies to guys throwing white Super Strike Zig-Zag needlefish and Gibbs Danny plugs on the first light of the outgoing, right as the current starts pulling bait past the tip of the jetty. Manasquan Inlet's north jetty has done the same on occasion — bunker have been thin but not absent, and when a pod pushes through the inlet mouth on that outgoing new-moon surge, the bass show up underneath them for ten, fifteen minutes and then it's over. I had one morning last week where three fish came in twenty minutes and then nothing for two hours. That's the read right now — short, sharp windows, not a sustained bite. If you're going to fish it, fish the tide change hard and don't linger past it.

Bluefish have been the wildcard filling in the gaps — cocktail blues, mostly, blitzing bunker pods off Asbury Park and Spring Lake on calm mornings, chewing through metal lips and poppers fast enough that you'll lose a few to the teeth if you're not running wire or heavy mono leader. Not glamorous, but it's action, and it keeps the rod bent while you wait to see if the stripers show.

On the albie front — I'm watching, not promising. The pelagic window that's had bonito and Spanish mackerel showing up on Long Island's south side is closing out over the next few days, and the water temperature signatures that usually precede our first false albacore push have been building. Nothing confirmed yet at Manasquan or Shark River, but the outer rocks at both inlets are worth a look with small Deadly Dick or Albie Snax on light tackle if you're already out there for the fluke. I wouldn't build a trip around it yet — it's a maybe, not a bet.

Looking at the week ahead: the new moon spring tide peak lines up Saturday into Monday, which means the strongest current push of the month at both inlets. If the wind stays out of the northeast and light, that's when I'd put my time in — dawn outgoing at Sea Bright and Manasquan for the bass, with the fluke bucktail as backup once the sun's up and the bite window closes. If the wind swings onshore and stiffens, the surf's going to get sloppy and the jetty game turns miserable fast — that's when I'd shift entirely to the inlet channels and fish the fluke on the last of the outgoing, working the deeper cuts where the current stays manageable. Either way, don't sleep past first light this weekend. The tide's doing the work for you — you just have to be standing on the rock when it does.

reports.headline: New moon springs squeeze The Race as bonito push west toward the Sluiceway
reports.subhead: Tighter slack windows at Valiant Rock, a mixed bass bite on wire, and the first real bonito sniff east of Plum Gut.
reports.body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does after a blow — it sorted itself out slow. We had a stretch of NE flow that sharpened the breaks out past Plum Gut and put some cooler, cleaner water back into the mix after that stretch of thick, warm surface water sat on us through the holiday run. That NE push is the same mechanism that's been sharpening the 20 to 30 fathom breaks offshore for the bluefin crowd, and closer to home it did us a favor — it knocked back some of the surface warmth that had been shoving bait deep and scattering the bass off Race Rock. The bigger story, though, is the cold wall between Block Island Sound and Rhode Island Sound falling apart. That wall has held bonito on the Block Island side for years. It just took a double-digit jump in RIS and it's not holding anymore, which means the corridor's opening up west — Newport and Point Judith are seeing early bonito, and I don't think it stops there. Little Gull and the Sluiceway are next in line if that trend holds.

This week the moon's the story that matters most for how you fish the rip. We're running into new moon springs, peak alignment landing Friday through Monday, and that means bigger exchange, faster water, and a slack window at Valiant Rock that's going to be shorter and meaner than it's been in weeks. When the tide's moving five knots through The Race on a spring cycle, the difference between fishing the turn right and fishing it forty minutes late is the difference between a rod-bending bite and a long boat ride home. High water at New London is running late afternoon into evening the next few days, and slack at Valiant Rock is stacking up right around sunset — call it 8:15 to 8:35 as the week rolls on. That's your window. Don't show up early and don't linger — spring tide current fills back in fast once it turns.

The bass bite has been honest, not easy. We've been working wire line with bucktails — the 2 to 3 ounce bucktail with a strip of pork rind or a white Fin-S trailer, dropped right on the edge where the rip meets the slick water off Valiant Rock, 25 to 40 feet down depending on the stage of tide. The pattern's been: stack up on the last twenty minutes of the ebb, hold through slack, and fish the first hour of the new flood before the current gets too strong to hold bottom without going to lead you don't want to lift. Fish have been mixed — plenty of schoolies in the 20 to 26 inch range mixed with a decent number of stripers in the high 20s to low 30-inch class, a few pushing 15 pounds. Nobody's filling a cooler with slot fish right now, but if you time the slack right you're not getting skunked either. Eels have worked too when you can find them — slow-trolled or drifted right through the seam at Race Rock on the last of the ebb has produced the better fish of the week.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player through Plum Gut and along the eastern face of the Sluiceway.
